Author’s preface

In the name of God, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate.

All praise belongs to God, who brings everything we can sense or understand into being and is the final end of every search and request. May blessings be upon the finest of His servants, the guide who showed creation its beginning and its return—above all, Muhammad, the chosen leader, sent to human beings and jinn. O God, bless him; bless the pure spirits among his family and children, and the radiant figures among his friends and descendants.1

The servant in need of his Lord's mercy, the One who is rich beyond all need, Muhammad, known as Ṣadr al-Dīn al-Shīrāzī, says:

Some people think happiness lies in bodily honors or positions of imagined power. But look closely at things and learn to understand them, and you will see that passing pleasures and bodily delights are not true happiness. They bring no joy to the intellect. Those who pursue them become consumed by them. Divine peace leaves them, knowledge of God finds no home in them, and they cannot form a pure intention from the heart of the rational soul. Worldly worries obstruct that intention, while immediate desires press against it. Yet it is pure intention that leads us toward true happiness. It lets us live in pursuit of that happiness and receive the higher outpouring of existence. This lifts the blindness2 from the soul's eye: the blindness of being confined to this unfamiliar world, dwelling in the house of the body, and losing sight of eternal beauty and everlasting majesty.

The highest goal any being can reach is the particular perfection suited to its nature. Anything below that is, in truth, a deficiency for it, even if it counts as a perfection beside the next lower level of existence. Every animal, and every being beneath it, is naturally disposed to reach the fullest state available to it unless something blocks the way.

Human beings, too, have a perfection unique to their essence and deepest reality. Nothing surpasses us in this, and nothing reaches it before us: it is to know the intelligible realities, draw near to the Creator, and rise beyond matter. At the same time, we share features with beings at lower levels. Like other bodies, we occupy space. Like plants, we take nourishment and grow. Like other animals, we live and breathe, move by choice, and sense. Our distinctive human perfection comes through knowledge and understanding, as the soul loosens its attachment to worldly adornments.

Knowledge has many branches, and the ways of understanding are numerous. It is difficult, perhaps impossible, to master them all. So people have divided their efforts, just as crafts have divided into specialties. Scholars have split into groups and schools: disciplines based on reasoning and those based on received reports, foundations and branches, grammar, syntax, astrology,3 legal rulings, jurisprudence, the study of religious narrators, and theology.

A thoughtful person should concentrate on what matters most. First, they should learn enough of the other sciences to meet the needs of this life and the next, and free themselves from what obstructs guidance and the Day of Return. Then they should devote their life to the knowledge that can bring their own being to its fullest state.

This knowledge perfects one of the soul's two powers. One belongs to what we are in ourselves and turns toward God; the other concerns our relation to creation and turns toward the created world. The first is our power to understand. It belongs to the soul in its own nature, apart from its connection to the body and the changes the body undergoes. Other fields of knowledge answer needs that come from the body: its powers, its activities, or its desires. Divine wisdom and knowledge of God are different. No other field can, by itself, bring the human soul to completion and free it from its faults when it leaves this world, returns to its deepest reality, and turns wholly toward its Creator, Originator, and Giver.

This pure knowledge of the intellect begins with God: His attributes, His angels, His books, and His messengers. It includes understanding how things flow from Him in the fullest order and how He knows, cares for, and governs them without flaw, weakness, harm, or weariness. It also includes knowledge of the soul: its path to the next life, its union with the highest company, its release from its bonds,4 and its freedom from matter in its most basic, formless state. Through this knowledge, the soul escapes the narrow limits of possibility and the blows of passing events.5 It immerses itself in the sea of the spiritual realm, joins the ranks of those who dwell in the world of divine power, and frees itself from captivity to desire, confusion, the effects of motion, and the rule of the turning heavens.

Any other field is useful if it serves this end. If it does not—if it is grammar, language, poetry, or another subject—then it is a craft or skill, like other crafts and skills.

Practical action and worship, both of the heart and of the body, are needed to cleanse and strengthen the soul through religious practice and bodily discipline. Without them, the soul may become attached to the body, its desires, and its demands.6 It can grow used to obeying the body and serving its appetites. Then, when the body dies, the soul may be kept from the pleasures that belong to it: the company of those brought near to God, the sight of beautiful realities, and the lights of the holy ones.

After death, the body can no longer distract the soul as it once did, keeping it from remembering what lies beyond it. Divine law therefore mercifully commands us to place the powers that rule the body under the rule of the tranquil soul. Religious laws and divine disciplines train the body and its desires, and help the human soul struggle against its own powers. The body can then join the soul in turning toward God, leaving behind the world's false show and source of delusion. It no longer blocks the soul's path; it supports the soul in what it seeks.

From the first years of my youth and early prime,7 I devoted my strength to divine philosophy as far as my ability and effort allowed. I followed the earlier philosophers and the learned thinkers who came after them. I drew on the results of their thought and insight, learned from the treasures of their minds and their hidden knowledge, and studied what I found in Greek books and the works of the leading teachers. I chose the heart of each subject and avoided needless length.

I avoided chasing distant hopes while doing little, or stretching out arguments as the hour of death drew near,8 merely to gain an imagined standing or become a leader in name, without gaining anything worthwhile from wisdom or reaching any result through inquiry. Yet many people in our time begin by studying scholars' books with great seriousness and effort.9 Before long, they grow tired of every subject and settle for only a sip from each jar.10 They do not find in those books what first drew them to study.11 Their desires are the desires of the impotent, and their motives those of an embryo.12 That is why they gain little knowledge, and even the most wretched among them does not become a clear-sighted, happy person.

You see students who hope to spend a long life searching and reviewing,13 deep into the night and at every turn of the day. In the end, they come back empty-handed,14 disgraced and ashamed. They are the people described in the Qur'an: “Shall we tell you who will lose most through their deeds? Those whose efforts are wasted in the life of this world, while they think they are doing good.” May God protect us from this bewildering trap and oppressive darkness.

I found shells of knowledge in the vast sea of wisdom. They were braced by dazzling proofs and filled with pearls of rare insight and hidden jewels of fine ideas. For a time, I turned the matter over in my mind, weighed my choices,15 and spoke inwardly with myself, out of care16 for those who need the truth.17

I wanted to crack open those thick shells and bring out their pearls. I would strain what I found through the filter of thought18 and sift the kernels from the husks with the sieve of sound judgment.19 Then I would write a book bringing together the best of earlier thinkers: the clearest arguments of Aristotle's followers, the finest insights of philosophers of illumination and Stoic sages, and new ideas absent from the books of philosophers in every age—ideas unlike anything seen in the turning heavens or the changing world.

But obstacles stood in the way, and the troubles of the times blocked my path.20 The age kept me from rising to the task, and fate kept me from reaching my goal. I saw ignorance and its lowest forms being raised up, while the fires of ignorance and error were fanned. People were left in a wretched state,21 and their leaders were weak and foolish.

We have been afflicted with people of dull understanding,22 whose eyes are blinded to the light and secrets of wisdom. Their insight fails before the light of knowledge, like the eyes of bats in bright sunlight. They call close study of divine matters and careful thought about God's signs an innovation. They regard any departure from the habits of the unthinking crowd as error and deception.

They are like those Hanbalites who read books of transmitted reports without distinguishing what must exist from what may exist, or what has always existed from what came into being. Their thought does not rise above bodies and what belongs to them, or beyond these dark structures and their shadows. Because they hate knowledge and wisdom, they have shut themselves off from sacred divine knowledge and the noble truths that prophets and saints have hinted at, and that philosophers and knowers of God have pointed toward.

So ignorance raises its banner and displays its signs. People turn away from wisdom and its worth, scorn those who know God, and oppose the path of insight. They frighten people away from philosophers and cast out learned, spiritually discerning, and pure people. Yet those who plunge deepest into ignorance and foolishness, and turn furthest from the light of both reason and transmitted knowledge, may rise highest in public favor and respect. As the saying goes: “Many a scholar never entered by knocking at the door of our house, while many an ignorant person walked in without knocking.”

Their leaders have neither virtue nor sound judgment. They wear no cloak of reason or guidance. Their hearts are bare of good manners, and their faces show no sign of goodness. I saw a land where no one valued its secrets or the knowledge of free thinkers. Learning and its secrets had faded; truth and its light had gone out; just ways had been lost; and false opinions had spread. The spring of life had dried up, its trade had failed, and faces once bright had grown dark with disappointment.23 Seeing all this, I turned away from the people of my time24 and cut myself off from them.25 A deadened mind and a rigid nature had made me weary of their hostility and the world's lack of support. I withdrew to a quiet corner, hidden in obscurity and defeat. My hopes were broken. I kept to the duties I owed and worked to repair the harm I had done before God. I was no longer teaching lessons or writing books.

To study the sciences and crafts, contribute to discussions, solve difficult problems, explain their aims, or clear up what is obscure, we need a clear mind. We need an imagination free from weariness and confusion, orderly circumstances, and peace of mind.

How can anyone find such calm amid the troubles they hear and see among the people of this age? People write of a lack of fairness and a rise in injustice, of the best and most capable being brought low while the lowest and worst are raised up, and of ignorant, harmful people pretending to be accomplished scholars and expert teachers. These are only some of the many wrongs and public harms that fill our times. In such conditions, even speaking with people and answering their questions becomes difficult—let alone solving the hardest problems and making obscure matters clear.

As one of my brothers put it in Persian:

Do not pour pearls of speech into every ear; let each ear keep its treasure sealed. Not every question calls for words in reply. A seeing eye will excuse lips that stay closed.

At first, I followed the example of my master, guide, and support: the first of the Imams and trustees, the father of the martyred Imams, the ally of the saints, the one who apportions Paradise and Fire. He practised caution and lived among the wicked, cut off from the position of leadership and with few supporters. He turned away from this world and chose the next. The Messenger of God called him his master, his brother, his cousin, and his companion through every great and small affair.26

I weighed the two choices he described: should I strike out with a powerless hand, or endure a blind darkness in which the old grow older, the young turn grey, and a believer toils until meeting their Lord? So I followed his example a second time.27 I judged that patience was wiser. I endured, with a speck in my eye and a lump in my throat. I stopped involving myself with people or keeping their company. I gave up on finding friendship and comfort among them. It became easy to bear the world's hostility and the opposition of those of my time. Their approval and disapproval no longer mattered to me; I became indifferent to their praise and their harm.

I turned wholeheartedly toward the One who brings about every cause and prayed with all my strength to the One who makes hard things easy. I remained hidden, withdrawn, and unknown for a long time. The long discipline kindled a light within me, and the many spiritual exercises set my heart ablaze. Lights from the unseen realm poured over me; hidden truths from the world of divine power came to rest within me. The light of God's oneness reached me, and His kindness came to my aid.

I came to know secrets that had never before opened to me. Meanings that had not been clear through proof now became clear through direct vision. Everything I had previously learned by argument became something I could see for myself, together with further glimpses of divine secrets, heavenly truths, and hidden realities. Morning and evening, the intellect drew breath from the light of truth. It drew near, became intimate with it, and found rest and relief.28

With my outward hands I dug into the earth, and water poured out in a stream. With the inner work of thought, I gathered what I had found for those seeking it, and it became a surging sea.29 Valleys of understanding flowed from this outpouring according to their capacity. Streams of reason ran from it as well. The valleys brought bright jewels and precious pearls to the shores of hearing; the streams grew fresh blossoms and fruit along their banks.

Divine mercy and care do not neglect anything people need according to their capacity. They do not withhold what can benefit their lives. So God's mercy required that the truths revealed to me should not remain hidden. The lights that flow from the Light of lights should not stay concealed. God inspired me to share a drink of what we had tasted with those who thirst for it, and to offer a glimpse of what we had found to hearts clouded by darkness.30 Whoever drinks from it may come alive; whoever sees it may have their heart lit up.

The appointed time for the book had come. God willed it to appear when He had chosen, through the person He had prepared. I resolved to bring it from possibility into actuality, from concealment into view. I turned my mind to the task and gathered my strength to bring its scattered ideas together. I asked God to strengthen me, lift my burden through His kindness, and open my heart so I could finish it.

My resolve rose after sitting idle; my energy stirred after lying still.31 My quiet strength woke up, and what had been still began to move. I told myself: “Now is the time to begin. I should set down principles from which further ideas can be drawn, fill people's ears with the finest jewels of meaning, and bring truth into a clear and beautiful form.”

So I wrote this book for those who seek perfection and occupied themselves with it. I set out divine wisdom for those seeking the secrets of the Presence of Beauty and Majesty. The truth almost appears in it as a light made visible, and its hidden meanings are close to being uncovered. God showed me ideas whose lights shine in knowledge of His essence and attributes, although the minds of the wise circle around Him and return exhausted.32 He inspired me, through the support He gives to whom He wills, with truths whose secrets lead to understanding their source and return, although the minds of the learned circle around them and return disappointed.

Thanks be to God, the writing came out without crookedness or doubt, without hesitation or confusion.33 It keeps a clear structure: it speaks in symbols when symbols are needed, and gives enough detail when detail is needed. Its ideas are easy to follow, despite their great depth; its subject is lofty, yet its language comes close to the reader.

Divine knowledge is woven into philosophical argument. Truths reached through direct insight are clothed in the language of instruction. Divine secrets are put into familiar words, and difficult ideas are expressed in language close to the ear. The proofs stride forward in brilliant clarity,34 while the objections of those who miss the truth shrink and are exposed.35

Look at the meaning with the eye of your mind. Do you find it lacking? Then look again at the words. Do they seem flawed? I have pointed in its symbols toward treasures of truth that only someone who has worked hard in intellectual discipline can understand.36 In its chapters I have also drawn attention to principles whose meaning37 only those who put their bodies through religious discipline will discover, so they can taste the drink for themselves. I wrote it for my brothers in faith and my companions on the path of direct insight and certainty. It will be most useful to those who have studied many earlier thinkers and read the books of the philosophers, without imagining that what they already know is all there is or rejecting everything beyond their present understanding.

Truth cannot be limited to what any one person understands, or measured by any one mind or imagination. If you find something here that goes against what you believe or what seems sound to you, do not reject it. Above everyone with knowledge is someone who knows more. Anyone who is trapped within their own knowledge and rejects everything beyond it has reached the limit of their own learning and remains shut off from the hidden secrets of their Lord.

I do not claim that I have reached the final limit in what I have written. Understanding has more paths than I have found or can count. The truths of God cannot be gathered within the limits I have drawn.38 If, through divine care, you solve a difficulty or open a difficult question, thank your Lord for the wisdom He has guided you to and praise Him for the gifts He has given you. Follow the teaching of the Lord of the two worlds and mirror of all worlds, may the fullest blessings and purest peace be upon him and his family: “Do not give wisdom to those unworthy of it, or you will lead it astray. Do not withhold it from those worthy of it, or you will wrong it.” Keep wisdom away from dead souls, and entrust it only to living ones.

You should know that I have sometimes gone beyond stating only what I myself hold to be true and believe. I have also presented the approaches of other thinkers, the objections made against them, and the replies to those objections. I have criticized39 and tested those views40, taken them apart, rebuilt their arguments,41 and defended them as far as I could. I did this to sharpen people's thinking42 and strengthen their minds. These discussions contain subtle, unfamiliar ways of understanding and elegant ways of reasoning. They train people seeking the truth to solve difficult problems and help students of debate understand questions that are hard to untangle.

The truth is that most of the discussions recorded in books and written on their pages serve mainly to alert us to the ideas of thoughtful people and give us a view of their arguments. They should stir the desire to reach the truth; it is not enough simply to fill the mind with statements, whether rational or transmitted. That alone brings no peace to the heart, no stillness to the soul, no ease to the mind, and no satisfying taste of knowledge. It should instead prepare the seeker to follow the path of the good and reach the hidden truths.

Knowledge of God, knowledge of the Return, and knowledge of the path to the next life do not mean the inherited belief that an ordinary person or a legal scholar may receive second-hand.43 Someone absorbed in imitation and fixed on outward forms has not opened the path to the truths that open to those close to God. Such a person does not see what is disclosed to those who look beyond the world of appearances and bodily pleasures: knowledge of the Maker of all things and the reality of realities.

Nor is this knowledge simply the skill of argument, as with the theologian, or a chain of abstract debates, as with the philosopher. All of these are layers of darkness, one above another. When a person holds out a hand, they can hardly see it. Whoever God gives no light has no light. True knowledge is a kind of certainty born from a light God casts into the believer's heart, through closeness to the world of holiness and purity, and through struggle against ignorance, bad character, love of power, attachment to the earth, and fascination with the body's ornaments.

I often ask God to forgive me for wasting part of my life following the views and fine distinctions of philosophers and theologians who relied on debate, learning their clever tricks of speech and their skill in debate. In the end, by the light of faith and God's generous support, I saw that their reasoning was fruitless and their path crooked. So we handed the reins of our affairs to God and to His Messenger, the one who warns and gives warning. Whatever came to us from him, we believed and affirmed. We did not force an imagined rational interpretation or argumentative theory upon it. We followed his guidance and stopped where he told us to stop, in keeping with God's words: “Take what the Messenger gives you, and refrain from what he forbids you.” Then God opened my heart to what He opened it to, and, by following the Messenger, I succeeded.

My dear friend, before you read this book, begin by purifying yourself of your desires. Those who cleanse the soul succeed; those who bury it fail. First build a firm foundation of knowledge and wisdom, then climb to its heights. Otherwise, you will be like someone whose building collapses from its foundations, bringing the roof down with it.

Do not busy yourself with the empty talk of ignorant people who call themselves Sufis, and do not accept every claim made by philosophers. Both are misleading trials that can pull you from the right path. They are like those who, when their messengers brought them clear signs, were pleased with the knowledge they already had; then the very things they mocked surrounded them. May God protect both you and me from the harm of these two groups, and keep us apart from them, even for a moment.

Know that the realized mystics and saints undertake four journeys.44 The first is from creation to God.

The second is through God, in God. The third mirrors the first: it is from God back to creation, through God. The fourth mirrors the second in one respect: it is through God in creation.

I arranged this book to follow their movement through the lights and effects, dividing it into four journeys, and named it Transcendent Wisdom in the Four Intellectual Journeys. I now turn to the subject, seeking help from God, the One worshipped, the Self-Sufficient and Self-Subsisting.

These are the four journeys. The first and third oppose one another because their starting and ending points are reversed. The third journey is carried out through God, unlike the first. The second and fourth are opposites in one respect: they begin and end at different points, but both take place through God.

The great philosophers and firmly grounded sages look at the horizons and within themselves. There they see God's signs shining forth. The effects of His power show them that His existence is necessary; the light of His wisdom reveals the holiness of His names and attributes. The heavens and earth exist, yet they could have been otherwise, and they move. These facts point to God. Their precise construction and ordered arrangement show His knowledge and care for creation.

The Qur'an says: “We shall show them Our signs on the horizons and within themselves, until it becomes clear to them that He is the Truth.” At this point, they see that every being and every perfection is absorbed in God's existence and perfection. Every being and every perfection is a glimmer of His light and a display of His presence. This is the first of the four intellectual journeys, corresponding to the spiritual traveler's journey from creation to God.

Next, they study existence itself. They recognize that it must exist through itself, and use this necessity to show that God is simple and one, and that He knows, has power, lives, wills, hears, sees, speaks, and possesses every other quality of perfection and beauty. They see that all these qualities are identical with His essence. His oneness reveals that He is absolutely one. Because He is one in this way, He depends on nothing; and in that complete self-sufficiency, He contains all things in the fullest and highest way. This is the second intellectual journey, corresponding to the spiritual traveler's journey from God to God, through God.

Then they study God's existence, care, and oneness. They discover that He acts as one, and consider how the many things come from Him and are ordered in sequence: the chain of intellects and souls, the higher and lower worlds of divine power and spirit, and, finally, the material world. “Is your Lord not witness over all things?” This is the third intellectual journey, corresponding to the spiritual traveler's journey from God to creation, through God.

Finally, they study how the heavens and earth were created and learn that everything returns to God. They examine the benefits and harms of created things and what brings happiness or misery in this life and the next. They learn how people live and what awaits them after death. With that knowledge, they warn against corruption and call people toward what is good. They study the next life and learn about Paradise and Fire, reward and punishment, the path, the reckoning, the balance, the scattering of records, and the way actions take visible form—in short, everything the prophets brought and the messengers reported, peace and blessings be upon them all. This is the fourth intellectual journey, corresponding to the spiritual traveler's journey from creation to creation, through God.

The book's discussion of general principles, substances, and qualities covers the first journey. Its proof of God's existence through Himself, and its account of His attributes, cover the second. Its proof of holy substances and souls that exist apart from matter covers the third. Its account of the soul and what awaits it on the Day of Resurrection covers the fourth.

So when the author says, “Know that the mystics and saints have four journeys,” he is referring to the spiritual journeys described first. When he says, “I arranged my book,” he is referring to the four intellectual journeys covered by the book and arranged to match the journeys of the spiritual travelers and saints. The powers of understanding and action mirror each other. Through understanding, a person reaches certainty by learning; through action, they reach the certainty of direct sight and the fuller certainty of lived experience. This is what I have understood by considering the words of these thinkers and following the discussions in the book. God knows best.

This account of the four journeys and their relation to the subjects of the book is by the divine philosopher Muḥammad Riḍā al-Iṣfahānī al-Qumshaʾī. May his memory be blessed.

As long as a person has not begun the intellectual journey of study and reflection, they see multiplicity everywhere and overlook unity. They see every thing as one among many, and that multiplicity keeps them from seeing unity. Unity remains hidden behind the many things they see.

When they begin their intellectual journey from effects to their cause, and from created things to their Maker, the many things slowly fade from view into the single, absolute, true unity. At last, they see no multiplicity at all. They become so absorbed in unity that they no longer look at individual things. At this stage, unity hides multiplicity, and the traveler sees nothing but unity. This is the stage of inward experience that corresponds to the first journey: from creation to God, or from multiplicity to unity.

Once the traveler reaches the world of unity and no longer sees multiplicity, they use intellectual reflection to move from God's essence and oneness to His attributes, names, and acts, one by one. They come to know the qualities of His necessary existence in a clear and ordered way. This is the second journey. It takes place in God because it concerns His attributes, names, and qualities. It takes place through God because the traveler is now grounded in God's reality and has turned away from the separate existence of the self and all other things. The traveler remains through God’s own abiding, not merely because God keeps the traveler in existence. Understand this, if you know these secrets.

At this stage, the traveler's heart may open. Their words may no longer be bound by feelings of helplessness. They may see multiplicity within unity and unity within multiplicity: seeing unity does not block their view of the many, and seeing the many does not distract them from unity. They can hold both worlds together. This comes from the breadth of their being and the openness of their heart. They can then teach those who are not yet complete and guide people whose minds and souls are still weak.

This stage of spiritual and intellectual travel corresponds to the journey from God back to creation, through God. It is the stage of prophecy and messengership. Above it is another stage, higher, more complete, more subtle, and more exact: proving the existence of God and of everything else through God, without placing anything between God and the proof. This is called the proof of the truthful. A person does not need to reach this stage in order to teach, guide, or be a prophet or messenger. It is a perfection of the person in relation to themselves. It is linked to the second journey, because becoming grounded in God's reality entails it, but teaching and guidance depend only on the first and second journeys. This highest stage corresponds to the fourth journey: through God in creation.

The correspondence between the four journeys described in the book and these four spiritual stages is as follows. The book's discussions of general principles, substances, qualities, and the states of existing things and their essences form the first journey: from creation to God. Its discussion of God—proving His existence, and considering His attributes, names, and actions—is the second journey, which takes place in God through God.

This second journey also contains the fourth journey, through God in creation. Anyone who follows the book's discussion of divine matters will see that it includes proof of the One who must exist, then uses His existence to show that everything else depends on Him.

The third journey is the journey of the soul. It studies the soul from the beginning of its development to its return to God, from its first weakness to its fullest perfection and strength. This is the third journey: from God to creation, through God. Keep all this in mind.

This account is by the learned Mīrzā Muḥammad Ḥasan al-Nūrī, son of the divine philosopher Mullā ʿAlī al-Nūrī. May God keep their secrets holy. The careful investigator Kamāl al-Dīn ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Kāshānī says:

A journey is the heart's turning toward God. There are four journeys. The first is the journey to God: moving through the stages of the self until reaching the clear horizon, the end of the heart's development and the beginning of the display of God's names.

The second is the journey in God: taking on His qualities and realizing His names until reaching the highest horizon and the end of the realm of divine oneness.

The third is the ascent to the point where all things come together and to the presence of absolute oneness. It is the station of “two bow-lengths,” as long as a distinction between the two remains. When that distinction falls away, it is the station of “or nearer.”

The fourth is the journey through God and away from God, to bring others to completion. It is the stage of remaining after the separate self has faded and of seeing difference after unity. End of quotation.

In this account, absolute oneness means considering God's essence without names, attributes, relationships, or distinctions. The other form of oneness means considering God's essence together with His names and attributes, which are linked to the fixed realities of things.

For this perfected knower, the heart is a luminous reality that is not material. It stands between the spirit and the animal soul, and it is what makes us human. Philosophers call it the rational soul. The spirit is the heart's inner reality; the animal soul is its vehicle, the outward side through which it connects to the body. The Qur'an compares this to a niche, a lamp, glass, and a shining star: “The likeness of His light is a niche containing a lamp; the lamp is in glass, and the glass is like a shining star, lit from a blessed olive tree, neither of the east nor of the west.” The tree is the soul, the niche is the body, and the lamp is the spirit.

For the mystics, the soul is a subtle vapour formed in the heart. It receives the powers of life, sensation, and movement. Doctors call this the spirit. The spirit, in the mystics' language, is the subtle, immaterial human reality between them, able to perceive general ideas and particular things.

Philosophers do not distinguish between the heart and this second meaning of spirit; they call both the rational soul. These are four of the seven subtle realities named in the mystics' writings: nature, soul, heart, spirit, secret, hidden, and most hidden. The careful knower mentioned above points to the last three through the stages of “two bow-lengths,” “or nearer,” and “remaining after the separate self has faded.” We could also call the third journey he describes the journey from God to God. The Qur’an also describes seven stages of the human being through the images of the niche, the blessed tree, the glass, the lamp, the shining star, the fire, and “light upon light.” Philosophers likewise speak of seven stages of the intellect: its first capacity, its trained capacity, active understanding, understanding gained through learning, and the two stages in which the separate self fades away.

What the author says here does not fully match what this knower says, since the author mentions no further journey after the journey from God to creation. Perhaps the author is using a different set of terms; there is no need to argue over names.

When the author says “the mystics and saints,” remember that they do not all pass through the same stages. The stages of the mystics who travel are like the self, the heart, the spirit, and the other subtle realities. The stages of the saints are the stages of traveling in God: taking on His qualities one by one, not just learning about them. This means having real knowledge of things, real power to act in the world, speaking truth from God, and perceiving sounds, sights, and smells that others do not perceive. The saints rise from the oneness that includes God's names to the complete disappearance of the separate self in absolute oneness, then travel from God back to creation. These are the stages suited to the saints.

The First Journey: From the World to God

The nature of existence and its basic features

The knowledge needed in every field of study — an introduction and six stages

Introduction: What philosophy is, how it is divided, and why it matters

Philosophy helps us develop our minds and our whole selves by learning what things really are. It asks us to establish what exists through sound arguments, rather than relying on guesswork or accepting claims without examining them. We can pursue this knowledge only as far as human ability allows.

Another way to put it is this: philosophy is the attempt to build an accurate understanding of the world's order in our own minds. By doing so, we become, in the ways open to human beings, more like our Creator.

A human being combines two very different aspects: an immaterial side, belonging to the realm of spirit,45 and a physical side, belonging to the world of matter. Our soul is likewise connected to the body but also has the capacity to rise beyond bodily concerns. This is why philosophy has two branches. One develops our understanding; the other guides how we live.

The purpose of the first, theoretical philosophy, is to understand reality as a complete and ordered whole. Through knowledge, the soul becomes like a world in miniature: not a physical copy of the universe, but an intellectual one, reflecting its structure, relationships, and patterns.46 This is what the Prophet sought when he prayed, “Lord, show us things as they really are.” Abraham sought it too when he asked, “My Lord, grant me sound judgment.” A judgment affirms that a thing exists, and this also requires us to have an idea of the thing.

The second branch, practical philosophy, concerns doing what is good.47 Its aim is to help the soul guide the body, rather than allowing bodily impulses to rule the soul. This is what is meant by the call to develop qualities worthy of God, and what Abraham sought when he prayed, “Join me with those who live rightly.” To the two branches of philosophy, the sacred text points when it says that humanity was created “in the finest form” and then brought down “to the lowest level.” The higher form points to our spiritual nature;48 the lower level, to the dense material world. “Except those who believe” points to the goal of understanding, while “and do good deeds” points to the goal of action. Practical wisdom is not just about private virtue: it should also help us live well in this world and prepare for what comes after death.

Theoretical wisdom, for its part, asks where we come from, where we are going, and what lies between. As ʿAlī is reported to have said: “May God have mercy on the person who prepares for the grave and knows where they came from, where they are, and where they are going.”49 These two branches are why the divine philosophers, following the prophets, have described philosophy as becoming more like God. They do not mean becoming divine. They mean broadening our knowledge and freeing our understanding from its dependence on the material world.

Wisdom's nobility is clear for many reasons. It helps bring things into being in the best possible form; in a sense, it is a cause of existence itself. Unless existence is known as it is, it cannot be brought into being. Existence is pure good, and all honor lies in goodness that exists. The Qur'an points to this when it says: “Whoever is given wisdom has been given abundant good.”

For this reason, God calls Himself Wise in many passages of His glorious Book, a revelation from the Wise, the Praiseworthy. He describes His prophets and saints as wise, and calls them people devoted to Him, wise in the true nature of things. He says: “When God made the covenant with the prophets: ‘Now that I have given you scripture and wisdom...’” And, speaking especially of Luqman, He says: “We gave Luqman wisdom.” All these verses speak of God's generosity and favor. A wise person is one who possesses the very wisdom we have described, a wisdom whose truth cannot be denied.

Nothing that exists is nobler than God and His messengers, who guide people along the clearest path. God calls both wise. That alone shows the dignity and glory of wisdom. We should follow its paths and seek its depths as well as its heights. Let us offer a few of its gifts and a taste of what it contains. Let us set out its foundations and rules, give its arguments and proofs as fully as we can, and gather the insights that reach us, scattered, from the Highest Source. The keys to clear understanding are in God's hand; He gives them to whomever He wills.

Stage One — Existence and its first divisions

First inquiry — The nature of existence

Why existence is the subject of the highest branch of philosophy, and why the mind grasps it first

Know that we describe a thing as one or many; as general, shared by many things, or particular to one; as already realized or only possible; as equal to, smaller than, or greater than something else; as moving or still; as hot or cold; and in other ways too.

A thing can have the kinds of properties in the middle of this list only because it has quantity. It can have the properties in the last group only because it has matter that can change.50 But a thing does not have to become a mathematical or natural object before we can call it one or many. It can be described this way simply because it exists: existence itself makes it fit to be called one or many, and to have the other features mentioned with them.

Mathematics studies the properties of mathematical things, such as shape, geometry, arithmetic, and music. The study of nature examines the features that belong to natural things, in its different branches.51 In the same way, the highest branch of philosophy studies the features that belong to things simply because they exist.52

This branch of philosophy studies existence in general. It asks about the highest causes of things that have causes, including the First Cause, which gives an effect existence because it is an effect.53 It also asks about the features that belong to existence simply as existence, and about the subjects studied in other, more specialized sciences.

The subjects of those sciences are like features that belong to the subject of this one. Our way of examining existence, the heart of divine mysteries, will show that the different natures of things are among the first features of existence itself, just as oneness, multiplicity, and other general ideas belong to the idea of what exists. This confirms that the subjects of the other sciences are also studied as features of existence in the most basic branch of philosophy.

In short, this branch of philosophy is so far-reaching that it studies existence simply as existence and its first divisions. So existence, considered as a whole, must be clear in itself and need no definition or proof. Otherwise, it could not be the subject of a general science. A definition is either an account of what a thing is or a description of it, and neither can define existence.

A strict definition explains something through its general kind and the feature that sets it apart. But existence is the broadest thing there is: it has no wider kind above it and no distinguishing feature that could define it. So it cannot be defined this way. A description, by contrast, explains something through what is clearer than it. Nothing is clearer than existence.54 Anyone who tries to explain existence through things supposedly clearer than it is badly mistaken. And since existence has no strict definition, it cannot be proved by demonstration.55 As explained in The Qistas, a definition and a proof have corresponding parts.56

Some statements cannot be known until we first know other statements. To establish that the intellect exists, for example, we need to establish other things first. We must eventually reach a statement that needs no earlier proof, because it is immediately clear to reason: a thing is what it is; a thing is not its opposite; and contradictories cannot both be true or both be false.57

The same holds for concepts. Some need other concepts before we can understand them, but not all do. Eventually we reach ideas that require nothing earlier, such as necessity, possibility, and existence. The mind already grasps these ideas through reason. When we put them into words, we are not teaching the mind something wholly new. We are drawing its attention to what it already understands, using more familiar words to help it recognize those ideas.

We do not need to prove that the subject of this science exists—that is, existence considered simply as existence. In truth, trying to do so would make no sense: to prove something is to affirm it of itself, and strict proof cannot do that. This is especially clear when the thing itself is existence, since “the existent,” “what is real,” and similar terms express the very idea of existence. Strictly speaking, a relation is the relation itself; anything else is called related only in a looser sense.58

Existence may be the existence of another thing, or the existence of its own reality. Considered just in itself—as existence in general—it is not limited to either. There is no need to prove that everything real is always the existence of something else, or always its own existence. Argument and observation show that both are true: some existence, with no cause, is its own reality; other existence belongs to something else, as in bodies. Existence that depends on nothing else is the reality of itself; existence that belongs to something else is that thing’s reality. Any gap we imagine between these two is a veil that reason can lift.

The highest branch of philosophy studies the features of existence simply as existence, including its basic divisions. These divisions apply without making existence a mathematical or natural object.59 Existence itself must therefore be capable of these divisions. It makes no difference whether a division covers every possible case. A division may cover every case yet still fail to be basic.60 If so, inquiry into it belongs to a narrower science, not to philosophy’s highest branch. For example, we can divide what exists into “black” and “not black” simply by negation. Think this through, and consider the confusion of those who have tried to explain the shared features studied in the two branches of philosophy that concern divine things.61 They have also been unsure what the subjects of the sciences are, as will become clear.

Some define these shared features as those that are not limited to any one of the three kinds of being: the One who must exist, substance, and attribute. But this definition fails because continuous quantity belongs both to substances and to attributes. A mathematical body belongs to matter; a surface belongs to a mathematical body; and a line belongs to a surface. Quality, too, occurs both in substances and in attributes.

Others define the shared features as those that apply to all or most things that exist. But this leaves out necessary existence, true unity, and absolute causation—features that belong only to the One who must exist. A third definition says that they are features that cover everything that exists, either by themselves or together with their opposites. To include features that belong only to particular kinds of being, this definition adds that scientific inquiry must concern both sides of each opposition. One respected later scholar objected that if “opposition” means only contradiction, contrariety, relation, affirmation and negation, or possession and its absence, then possibility and necessity do not fit. Their opposites in this sense—non-necessity, non-possibility, the necessity of both alternatives, or the denial of necessity on the relevant side—are not matters for scientific inquiry. But if “opposition” means any kind of incompatibility, then the features specific to each of the three kinds of being, together with the features specific to the other two, cover all things that exist. Every one of them would then count as a proper subject of scientific inquiry.

They then resorted to strained explanations to escape the problem. One suggestion was that these general features are derived words and similar expressions. Another was that a general feature must be considered together with one opposite, with both sides relevant to science. But such cases either involve several different features, or scientific inquiry is not concerned with both sides. For example, a body may be able or unable to be broken or joined; but “unable” can mean simple negation, not the absence of a capacity that belongs to the thing. A third suggestion takes opposition to include both direct and indirect opposition. On this view, what must exist and what may exist are indirectly opposed, as are unity and multiplicity. But this definition also applies to features specific to particular kinds of being. These are only a few of many strained and unconvincing explanations.

If you keep in mind that the highest branch of philosophy studies the essential features of existence simply as existence—features that apply to something simply because it exists, without requiring it to become a mathematical or natural object—you can avoid these complications. In defining a general feature, consider it from this standpoint and require that it be a universal description. This keeps inquiry into what things are in themselves from being mistaken for a shared feature. The point is not that a feature must belong only to one division of existence, as they assumed. This removes the objections and gives us a sound definition.

They were just as confused about the subjects of the other sciences. The subject of each science, as is well established, is that which the science investigates through its essential features.62

Some say that a feature belongs to a subject in itself when it follows from the subject's nature, or from something that applies to exactly the same things. But this creates a problem. Every science also studies properties found only in particular kinds of its subject. How can those count as features of the subject in itself?

To get around this, some say the earlier authorities used the term loosely.63 They claim it can refer to a feature of the whole subject, a feature of one of its kinds, or even a more general feature of that kind, provided it is not broader than the subject of the science. Some extend this to properties of a particular kind of feature, with the same restriction.64 Others distinguish what is said of a science's subject from what is said in one of its individual questions. They treat the former as what is obtained by gathering the various statements made in those questions. These solutions are forced. They have missed the fact that a feature belonging to just one particular kind can still belong to the general subject through what that subject itself is.

A feature can be narrower than a thing without ceasing to belong to that thing in itself. Think of a distinguishing feature that divides a general kind into more specific kinds.65 The feature applies to fewer things, yet it belongs to the general kind considered in itself. Some properties of particular kinds are basic properties of the wider kind; others are not. An initial division that covers all the possibilities may use properties that are not basic, while basic properties do not always give an exhaustive division.

There is an important limit. If a feature belongs to a thing only after the thing has become a special kind, ready to receive that feature, then it is not a basic feature of the wider kind. It belongs to the special kind instead. This is what Avicenna and others say. In the same way, when an existing thing has become a mathematical or physical subject, its special properties do not belong to the most general study of existence.

A line makes the point clear. Straightness and curvature do not belong to a line only after it has already become a special kind of line prepared to receive them. They are what make the line straight or curved in the first place. They apply to fewer things than the general idea of a line, but are still basic distinctions within that general nature.

Because some thinkers missed this, they believed Avicenna had contradicted himself.66 On one hand, he says that a feature requiring a subject to become a narrower kind is not a basic feature of the broader subject. On the other, he uses straightness and curvature to illustrate features that divide the nature of a line. There is no contradiction. His critics assumed that a narrower feature cannot belong to something basic about the wider kind. They therefore treated straightness and curvature as secondary, leaving only the general alternative between them as the line's basic feature.

Some things do not depend on matter in order to exist, either in the world or in the mind. Yet they can be treated as mathematical things, like quantity, or as natural things, like quality. A general science may leave them to a separate field, as arithmetic does with number, or they may be studied in a narrower science, as qualities are studied in the study of nature. This happens for one of two reasons.

First, we may consider them in relation to matter in some way, and study them from that viewpoint in a separate science. Number, for instance, can be considered in itself. In that respect, it is one of the things we can think of apart from matter, and it is studied among the general topics of unity and multiplicity. But number can also be considered as belonging to matter in the world itself, not merely in the mind. From that viewpoint, mathematics studies the operations that apply to number: addition, subtraction, multiplication, division, finding roots, raising to a power, and more. Number may exist only in people's minds, or in moving things that can be divided, separated, and joined.

Second, a science may study not these things in general but particular kinds that exist only when matter is ready for them and undergoes movement and change. Those kinds belong in a narrower science. If their features are mentioned in general here, they serve as starting points for inquiry, not as questions this science itself investigates.

How the idea of existence applies to many things, but not in exactly the same way

It is almost self-evident that different things share the idea of existence. Reason finds something in common between one existing thing and another, but not between what exists and what does not. If existing things shared no idea at all, but differed from one another in every respect, then any two of them would be as unrelated as existence and nonexistence.

This is not simply because they share the same word. Suppose we used one name for some things that exist and some that do not, while giving no single name to things that exist. Even then, the things that exist would not seem more alike to one another than to the things that do not exist but share that name—or even as much alike. This is clear to reason. For Mulla Sadra, this argument carries more weight than many other arguments offered on the subject, even if it may not convince someone committed to disputing the point.

In fact, people who deny that existence has a shared meaning still assume that it does. If the existence of each thing were wholly unlike the existence of every other thing, there would be no single idea that we could say was not shared. Instead, there would be endlessly many ideas, and we would have to examine each one to learn whether it was shared. Since we do not need to do that, existence must have a shared meaning.

Another sign is the linking element in statements and judgments. It is a kind of existence, and it keeps the same meaning even when the subjects and predicates change. We can see this if someone recites a poem and ends every line with the word “existence”: everyone recognizes that the same ending is repeated. But if every line ended with the word “spring”—which can mean an eye, a water source, and other things—people would not treat it as the same repeated ending. If we did not immediately understand “existence” as one idea throughout, we would not hear the repetition in the poem either.

Existence applies to things by degrees: some things have it more fully or more strongly, and some are prior to others. In some things, existence follows from what they are; in others, it does not. Existence without a cause belongs more fully to what exists than existence that depends on something else, and it is prior by nature to everything else. In the same way, each separate intellect is prior by nature to the one below it, and things that exist in their own right are prior to qualities that belong to them. Existence apart from matter is stronger than material existence. Bare matter, which receives different forms, is so weak in existence that it almost seems not to exist at all.

Priority and posteriority, strength and weakness, belong to existence itself, even if they do not belong to the essences of things in the same way. Existence at one level cannot occur at another level, whether earlier or later, and a different kind of existence cannot occupy the very same level. When Aristotelian thinkers say that intellect comes before matter by nature, or that matter and form come before a body by nature or cause, they do not mean that one essence comes before another. They mean that one thing's existence comes before another's.

There are two ways for one thing to come before another. In the first, it is earlier through the very feature that makes it earlier: what is prior and the basis of its priority are one and the same. The moments of time, for example, come before or after one another through their own changing realities, not through some additional feature. We will return to this later in the book.

In the second way, one thing is earlier in one respect because of another respect. What comes first and what makes it first are then different. A father is earlier than his son, not in their shared humanity, but in existence or time. Existence or time is the respect in which he comes first; fatherhood is what makes him prior. In the same way, one body may come before another, not in bodily nature but in existence. To say that a cause comes before its effect means that the cause exists before the effect does. The same is true when we say that two comes before four: without considering existence, there is no before or after.

So priority and posteriority, completeness and lack, strength and weakness belong to existences through what they are. In things and essences, they arise through their existence, not from the essence by itself. We will explain this further when we discuss the different degrees of existence.

The general idea of existence in the mind is not part of each thing's makeup

At this point, it should be clear67 that the idea of existence is general and applies to things with differences in degree, not with perfect sameness.

Any reality that can be pictured in the mind keeps its essence even when the way it exists changes. But existence, by its very nature, means being present in reality. Whatever by nature exists in reality cannot itself exist in the mind; otherwise, its nature would have changed. So the reality of existence itself cannot enter any mind. The idea of existence that does enter the mind and becomes general is not existence itself. It is one way of looking at existence, one of its aspects and names. The mind's general idea of existence does not apply to particular things as a broader kind applies to its members. It is an abstract idea we draw from particular essences that differ in their meanings, much as we draw the idea of “being a thing” from the different things around us.

If existence were a broader kind of all the things to which it applies, then the One who must exist would be separated from other things by a further feature. Its very nature would then be made up of a general kind and a distinguishing feature, which is impossible, as we will explain later. Some have also argued that anything which applies to things by degrees must be incidental to them. Since existence has been shown to apply to its instances in this way, they say, it must be incidental too. But this argument does not hold for a number of early Shia thinkers, as will become clear.

Existence has a reality outside the mind

Since what makes each thing truly what it is is its particular existence,68 existence has a stronger claim to reality than that thing—or anything else. Whiteness, for example, is more truly white than the thing that receives whiteness. Existence exists through itself; everything other than existence exists through the existence that belongs to it. Strictly speaking, existence itself is what exists, just as a relation is the relation itself, not the substance, quantity, or quality that has a relation to something else. A father, something equal, and something similar are examples of things described through relations.

As Bahmanyar says in Al-Taḥṣīl: “In short, the nature of existence is to be present in reality, and nothing else. How could something not be real when being real is its very nature?”

Discussion — Is existence real?

The philosopher of illumination Suhrawardi argued against the reality of existence as follows: If existence were present in the outside world, then existence itself would be an existent thing, because to be present is to exist. And if everything that exists needs an existence, then existence would need another existence, and that one another, without end.69

One reply is that existence itself is not an existent thing. We do not describe a thing by saying that it is itself, just as ordinary speech does not say “whiteness is white.” At most, existence is not something that has existence, just as whiteness is not something that has whiteness. Calling it “nonexistent” in this limited sense does not make it both real and its opposite. The opposite of existence is nonexistence, not “a nonexistent thing.”

Or we can say that existence is existent. Its being existence is exactly its being existent: it is the existence of things in reality, not a second existence added on top. Existence itself is existent simply by being existence. What another thing has through something else, existence has in itself; its being is its own reality. Consider time: priority and posteriority between events are measured by time, but the parts of time are prior or later in themselves, without needing another time to order them.

Someone may object: then every existence must be necessary, since the Necessary is simply what exists through itself. The answer is that the One who must exist has existence because of what it is, without needing a maker or something in which to exist. By contrast, when we say that existence exists through itself, we mean that once it occurs—whether by itself, as in the One who must exist, or through a cause—it does not need another existence to support it. Other things become real only after a cause brings them into being and they are described as existing.70

The point is that existence is real in itself, whether or not everyday language allows us to call it “existent.” When philosophers say that something is existent, they do not always mean that existence is an additional feature belonging to it. Sometimes it is; sometimes it is not, as with the One who must exist, whose existence is not separate from its essence. Whether something has an essence distinct from existence must be shown by a further argument. It does not follow just from saying that it exists. For philosophers, the idea of “existent” applies to both kinds of thing.

This also answers another objection. If calling existence “existent” means only that existence is existence, then “existent” cannot mean the same thing when applied to existence and to other things. For other things, it would mean “something that has existence,” while for existence itself it would mean simply existence. But we use “existent” in one sense in both cases. If so, we must treat existence like everything else—as something that has existence—and then we are back to an endless chain.

The difference between other things and existence itself is not in the meaning of “existent.” Philosophers use the word in the same sense in both cases, whether or not that usage matches the rules of ordinary language. Whether something that exists includes an essence beyond existence, or is existence alone, depends on the particular thing the word refers to, not on the meaning of the word itself.

Avicenna makes a similar point in the Metaphysics of The Healing. We can understand “the Necessary Existent” simply as the Necessary Existent, just as we can understand “one” simply as one. Or we can learn that its essence is, for example, a human being or another kind of substance, and that this human being is the Necessary Existent. In the same way, we may understand that what is one is water, air, or a human being.71 Avicenna therefore distinguishes between an essence to which existence or oneness belongs and existence or oneness considered in itself.

He also says in his Notes: If someone asks whether existence is existent, the answer is yes: the nature of existence is to be existent, because existence is existingness. A marginal note by al-Sharif supports this: the idea of “thing” is not part of the idea of “rational”; if it were, a general feature would be built into a distinguishing feature. And if “thing” were part of an adjective formed from a noun, a merely possible claim would become necessary: the thing that can laugh is a human being, and for a thing to be itself is necessary.72 The word “thing” in explanations of these derived adjectives simply identifies what their implied pronoun refers to.73

A respected later thinker also held that a thing's feature and the thing described by that feature are one and the same, though that later thinker did not hold to the view firmly.74 Similarly, Suhrawardi says at the end of The Book of Hints that the soul and the immaterial beings above it are pure realities and pure existence. I do not see how this can be reconciled with his denial that existence is a real thing in the outside world. Is that not a contradiction?75

Consider this further. If existence had no real instances beyond the different ways its concept applies to things, it could not have features tied to essences with different natures or levels.76 But it does: the One who must exist needs no cause by its own nature, while a possible thing needs a cause by its own nature. Dependence and independence belong either to what things are or to their different degrees of perfection and deficiency. So every existent must have something real beyond its share of the concept of existence.77 Otherwise, things that exist could not differ in their essences, as Aristotelian philosophers say, or in their degrees of existence, as another group says. A universal concept, considered in relation to its individual cases, does not vary by degree.

Someone may object: If existence had real instances in essences beyond mere conceptual shares, then the existence of an essence would depend on that essence already existing. Anything affirmed of another requires that other to exist first. So the essence would have to exist before it existed. But this objection does not depend on existence having real instances of its own. It applies whenever we say that an essence exists, even if existence were only a concept shared among things. The answer is that existence is the very reality of an essence, not something added to it after the essence already exists. Many thinkers missed this subtle point. Some make an exception to the rule that a feature depends on its subject; others replace that dependence with a relation of implication; still others deny that existence is attributed to an essence either in the mind or outside it. Instead, they say the essence simply coincides with the idea of “existent,” a simple idea like other derived words, called hast—“is” or “exists”—in Persian. On this account, the expression has no underlying source, either in the mind or in the outside world.78

What makes each existence distinct?

We should understand80 that each existence is made distinct either by its own reality,79 by its degree of priority or posteriority, strength or weakness, or by the subject to which it belongs.81

Printed commentator (س ره): Those who speak of an indeterminate existence have failed to see that what is wholly indeterminate has no individual existence or distinctness. They would have to treat features such as a person's particular temperament as signs of distinctness and use “indeterminate” to mean a broader reach of existence, as with a form that shares its cause with matter. If change in a thing's underlying nature is possible, there is no difficulty in treating the features that distinguish it as necessary consequences, since the subject itself is then changing. From this, a thoughtful reader can also see how change in a thing's underlying nature is possible. The difference between a feature and an adjective formed from it depends on how we consider it. Some features involve change in their very meaning, as with acting and “when”; others involve change in their existence, as with the four categories mentioned here. When a feature of the second kind changes, what it belongs to changes too, since they are united in existence.

When existence is made distinct by its own complete, necessary reality, or by degrees of priority and posteriority, strength and weakness, independence and dependence, it is distinguished through what belongs to its own simple reality, which has no general kind or distinguishing feature.82 When it is distinguished83 by its subject—that is, by the essences the mind considers as having existence—the distinction does not come from existence's own features but from the different essences that arise from it. Even so, in anything with an essence, existence and essence are one in the outside world. This is a strange point; its explanation will become clear later.

Avicenna says in The Discussions that existence in things with essences does not differ in kind. If it differs, it differs only in strength and weakness. The essences of things that exist differ in kind, but the existence in them does not. A human being differs in kind from a horse because of what each is, not because of its existence. In the first sense, then, existence is made distinct by its own reality. In the second, it is made distinct by the general features that accompany it at each level.

In The Notes, Avicenna says that existence received from something else is defined by its dependence on that other thing, just as independence from anything else defines the One who must exist. What makes a thing what it is cannot be separated from it, since it belongs to its very nature. Elsewhere he says that existence either depends on something else, in which case that dependence is part of what it is, or is independent, in which case its independence is part of what it is.

Dependent existence cannot be found without dependence, just as independent existence cannot be found in a dependent state. Otherwise, each would be made what it is by its opposite, and its nature would change. Read Avicenna carefully, and you will see the point we will prove later: every existence that depends on another is an aspect of the existence of the One who must exist. Such existences are rays and shadows of the light that sustains all things. They have no independent reality and cannot be treated as separate beings. Their dependence, connection, need, and poverty are what they are. They do not have separate natures to which dependence and need are later added. They are pure dependence: their only reality is that they follow one reality. There is one reality; everything else is its state, expression, aspect, mode, flash of light, or shadow of radiance. “Everything in the universe is illusion or imagination, a reflection in a mirror or a shadow.”

With God's help, we have built a clear, throne-like proof for this noble and subtle truth. We will give it later, as promised. We have also written a separate treatise on it, which we called Leaving the Two Worlds Behind.

Some say that dependent existence becomes particular through its relation to a subject, without acquiring that relation from outside. They reason as follows: existence in a subject is an accident, and every accident must exist in a subject. So, they conclude, the existence of each essence depends on a relation to that essence. They compare this to a thing's being in a place, where existing in itself differs from being in a place. But the comparison does not work. An accident's existing in itself may be the same as its existing in a subject, as the accepted account of accidents holds. Yet existence does not relate to its subject in the same way that accidents relate to their subjects. Existence is not something separate from the subject whose own existence becomes existence-for-the-subject. Existence is the subject's very being, not another thing that belongs to it. A light in a body, for example, is the body's appearing; it is not the appearance of something else to the body. There is a difference between something's being in a place and its being in a subject. That is what the view just mentioned implies.

There is another difference between something's being in a subject and its being the subject itself. Avicenna says in The Notes that accidents exist in themselves by existing in their subjects. But the accident that is existence differs from the others: they need existence in order to exist, while existence does not need another existence in order to exist. So we cannot say that existence exists in its subject in the same way that whiteness exists in a body—as though existence itself had a further existence. Rather, existence's being in its subject is the very existence of that subject. For other accidents, their being in a subject is the existence of something other than themselves.

This is how we should understand another passage in The Notes, not as some have taken it—as a claim that existence is merely a mental idea. Avicenna says: “The existence belonging to a body is the body's being existent.” This is unlike whiteness and a body being white, since being white requires both the whiteness and the body. Avicenna's student Bahmanyar says in Al-Taḥṣīl: “When we say that something exists, we do not mean the general idea of existence. Each existent must have its own particular existence. Existence is either made particular by distinguishing features, in which case existence as such is a general kind, or the general idea of existence is a necessary feature of the particular meanings by which things become existent.”

Bahmanyar also says that every existent with an essence has, within that essence, a feature by which it becomes existent, and that the nature of this feature is that it becomes necessary. Do not be misled by his later statement: “When we speak of the existence of something, we mean that it is existent. If existence were what made something present in reality, it would need another existence, and the chain would never end. So existence is the very becoming-real of a thing.”

By “being existent” he does not mean the general idea that the mind draws from particular existences. He means existence itself, which is existent through itself and through which an essence exists—not through anything beyond the reality of existence. This is how his statements fit together. Many later scholars misread these words, inherited from Avicenna and his circle, and took them to mean that existence is only an idea in the mind and has no real instances among essences. They have twisted the words away from their intended meaning.

I once firmly held that existence was only an idea and that essences alone were truly real. Then my Lord guided me, and I saw that the opposite is true. Existence is what is real outside the mind. Essences—what some people of spiritual insight call “fixed realities”—have never even smelled the scent of existence, as our later arguments will show. You will also see that the different levels of dependent existence—the realities of possible things—are only rays and lights of the true light and of the existence of the One who must exist. They are not independent things standing on their own. They are aspects of one reality, unfolding forms of a single truth. We will set all this out and establish it by decisive proof.

In short, it should now be clear that the general idea of existence is a mental abstraction, while its individual instances and the realities on which that idea rests exist outside the mind. The same is true of the idea of “thing” in relation to the particular things it describes. The idea of existence stands to particular existences as the idea of a “thing” stands to particular things. Yet these particular existences have no names of their own. That is true whether they differ in their underlying reality or only in how complete they are. We describe them as “the existence of this,” “the existence of that,” or “existence without a cause.” From them, the general, self-evident idea of existence follows in the mind.84 Essences, by contrast, have names and features that we can know.

Existences are simple realities; existence itself is not a general kind

A reality that is existence cannot be built from a general kind and a feature that sets it apart. Here is why. Logic tells us that a general kind needs no distinguishing feature simply to be what it is. It needs such a feature to become an actual, particular thing. In that sense, the distinguishing feature brings the general kind into actuality.

If the reality of existence had a general kind and a distinguishing feature, the general kind would either be existence itself or another essence to which existence belongs.85 In the first case, the distinguishing feature would have to make the very essence of the general kind real. The feature that divides the kind would then also make up its essence, which is impossible. In the second case, the reality of existence would be either the distinguishing feature or something else. Either way, the assumption breaks down, because a general kind, a distinguishing feature, and a species are one in existence but different in meaning. That is not what happens here.86

There is another problem: this would make existence, which has no cause at all, a composite thing, which is impossible. Some have argued against existence being a general kind in this way: if existence were a general kind, its distinguishing feature would either be existence or not existence. If it were existence, then the feature would have to be the species itself, since the general kind is predicated of it.87 If it were not existence, existence would have to be nonexistence.88 This argument is weak.
