The three cases that hold in themselves—necessity, impossibility, and possibility—form a genuine division that covers every kind of thing and concept as it exists in reality and at its different levels. The exception is a possible essence considered just as it is in itself. At that level, it is not described by possibility, even though possibility is its status in reality. Considered in itself, it is simply what it is.298

Still, every kind of denial can be made about an essence at that level, except denying what it is as a concept. This does not settle whether the essence itself exists or whether it is said of something else; those are separate questions. We can say that neither its existence nor its nonexistence is necessary. We can also deny those denials. But there is a great difference between denying something of an essence and saying that the essence has that denial as a feature. The first is a negative statement; the second makes a positive statement about a negation. Possibility, like necessity and impossibility, is said of an essence in the second way, not the first.299

If the three-way division is meant to cover a thing in every respect and at every level, including its own essence considered by itself, then it is not exhaustive. An essence may be none of the three at that level. Even if we granted that one of the three belonged to the essence at that level, the essence together with that feature would still belong to it. In that case the essence would no longer be simply itself; it would be itself and the further feature. The three classes would no longer be mutually exclusive and exhaustive.300

One of the three categories can belong to a subject at the level of its own essence, as necessity does with God. But that follows from the special nature of that case, not simply from placing it under the general concept. Merely classifying God as necessary does not show that the basis of His necessary existence is His essence itself. Otherwise, after defining each category, we would still need a separate proof that God’s necessity belongs to His essence and is not an added quality or some later consideration.301

A concept's being true of something is one matter; the thing's own reality being what makes it true is another. Keep that difference in mind. It will explain why I can later say that a possible essence is never without possibility, however we consider it, without contradicting what I have said here. And know that the concept “necessary in itself” includes several different kinds.302

The concept of necessity in itself includes several kinds. First is the Necessary Being: He cannot fail to exist303. Nor does His essence have to produce or require existence as though it were an added feature. This is God, who exists through Himself. His necessity is eternal, absolute, and belongs to Him in Himself.

In the second kind, a statement necessarily holds because of what its subject is, although the subject does not cause it to hold. For example, a human being is human, and a human being is an animal. These statements hold necessarily whenever their subject exists. Their necessity is not produced by that existence.

In the third kind, the subject’s own nature is what makes the statement necessary. A triangle, for example, has angles equal to two right angles because it is a triangle. Here the subject’s nature is the reason; its existence is a condition for stating the relationship, not the reason the relationship holds.

Impossibility in itself also has several kinds. One is what cannot exist by its own nature, not because its essence causes or requires its nonexistence. Examples are a second god, absolute nothingness, and pure evil.

Another kind is when a subject cannot have a certain predicate because of what it is, but not because the subject itself causes that predicate’s absence. For example, a human being cannot be an inanimate thing. A third kind is when the subject’s own nature rules out a predicate: four cannot be odd, because what makes four even is exactly what excludes oddness.

Possibility in itself also covers different cases. When something is possible in the strict sense, neither its existence nor its nonexistence is necessary. Both sides can be denied necessity, so we can express the judgment as an affirmation paired with a denial. Consider, too, an imagined whole made of two necessary things, two impossible things, or two opposites.304 Its existence or nonexistence may be necessary, but not merely because it is a whole. The reason lies in the particular things combined.

The two kinds that hold through something else—necessity and impossibility—apply to everything possible in itself. Neither applies to anything necessary in itself or impossible in itself. We have already seen that what is necessary in itself cannot be necessary through something else.

The three kinds that hold relative to something else do not conflict in reality with the three kinds that hold in themselves, though they differ in meaning. Necessity relative to something else applies to every existing thing, since each thing is either a cause of something else or brought about by something else. A cause and its effect are each necessary relative to the other. Here, “necessary relative to another” means that a thing’s existence is required when considered in relation to something else. This is broader than being caused: the other may demand the thing by its own nature, or the thing may depend on the other for its existence.305 One of the divine sayings puts it this way: “O Moses, I am what you cannot do without.”

Impossibility relative to something else applies to every existing thing, whether necessary in itself or possible in itself, when considered alongside the absence of its cause or effect, or of something whose absence would entail the absence of its cause or effect. Likewise, something nonexistent may be impossible or possible relative to another, depending on whether its cause or effect exists.

As for possibility relative to something else, it does not apply to the Necessary, Self-Subsisting Being in relation to any possible thing that exists. It would apply only if we supposed another Necessary Being, or things supposedly made by that other being.306 It also applies when we compare possible things that both exist, things that both do not exist, or one that exists with one that does not. But in each case, the two must be independent of one another: neither can be the cause or the effect of the other.307

This kind of possibility can also apply to things that are impossible in themselves, when they are considered alongside the nonexistence of things that are possible in themselves and what follows from them, provided no connection requires one side or the other.308

Clarification. A cause is necessary in relation to its effect because the effect requires that cause to exist. The cause may be necessary in itself, as the First Cause is, or necessary through something else. The effect, in turn, is necessary in relation to its complete cause: when that cause exists in full, the effect cannot fail to exist. For the moment, we are putting aside the fact that the effect receives this necessity from its cause. That is called being necessary through another. Being necessary in relation to another describes a different comparison.

The same distinction applies to two effects of one cause. Each is necessary in relation to the other, because their shared cause requires them both to exist. We are considering each effect in relation to its companion, not yet considering the necessity that belongs to the effect itself. This distinction works at the level of ordinary philosophical analysis. But in our approach309, if you follow it, you will discover what needs to be reconsidered. On the ordinary account, the effect is necessary both through its cause and in relation to it. The cause, however, is necessary in relation to its effect, not through its effect. And two effects of one cause are necessary in relation to each other, not through each other.

“Impossible through another” means that another thing makes a thing’s nonexistence necessary. “Impossible in relation to another” means that the other thing, when we compare the two, rules out its existence. Both descriptions apply when we consider the existence of an effect alongside the absence of its cause, or the effect’s absence alongside the presence of its cause. They come apart when those comparisons are reversed310—and when we compare the existence of one of two effects from the same cause with the other’s absence, or the absence of one with the other’s existence.

Strict possibility relative to another means that, given the other thing—whether it exists or not—neither the existence nor the nonexistence of the first thing is required. This occurs only between things with no natural causal connection, and no shared cause that produces them both.

Chapter — Why possibility cannot come from something else

Every thing must be either necessary, possible, or impossible. These three leave no fourth option. First ask whether its existence is necessary. If not, ask whether its nonexistence is necessary. If the answer to both questions is no, it is possible. So our three-part division is really two successive choices, each between a statement and its denial. Every division with more than two parts can be understood in this way. Whatever aspect of a thing we consider, one of the three must apply.

Suppose a thing is possible in itself, whether we consider its essence or one of its features while setting aside the influence of anything else. If it were also possible because of something else, then one and the same thing, in the same respect, would have two possibilities: one from itself and another from something else. This cannot be. Nor can a single possibility come from both the essence and something else at once. We have already seen the same with necessity: if a thing is necessary in itself, it is not necessary because of something else; if it is necessary because of something else, it is not necessary in itself. It is plainly impossible for one thing, in one and the same respect, to have two possibilities.

One thing cannot have two existences, or two nonexistences, in the very same respect. Nor can it have two necessities of existence, two necessities of nonexistence, or two instances of possibility concerning that same existence and nonexistence. These are meanings formed in the mind through their relation to something. They can be multiplied only when the things or aspects they concern are multiplied.

Suppose, then, that a thing’s possibility came from something else. If we set that other thing aside, is the first thing possible in itself? If so, it would have two possibilities in the same respect, which we have ruled out. Or is it necessary to exist or impossible to exist in itself? Then the other thing would have changed what the first thing’s own nature requires, making it the opposite of what it was. That is not what happens when something becomes necessary or impossible because of another while remaining possible in itself.311 Possibility in itself means that the thing’s nature does not require either existence or nonexistence. It does not mean that its nature requires both necessities to be denied. These are different claims. The first is a simple denial; it does not positively assign a feature of “not being necessary” to the thing. The second does assign a feature to it.312

A simple denial does not need the thing’s nature to bring it about. It is enough that the nature itself demands neither existence nor nonexistence. That is why possibility does not follow from an essence in the usual sense of a property produced by that essence. The essence is enough for the statement “it is possible” to be true, but it does not produce possibility.313

Some philosophers take possibility to mean that a thing’s nature is equally related to its existence and nonexistence, or that it is true to say that neither is necessary. They treat this as an essential property of the thing. But neither of these is possibility itself. As the argument shows, possibility is a still more basic lack of actuality: pure potential and dependence. The equal relation between existence and nonexistence, when the thing exists or is present in thought, and the truth of positively saying that neither is necessary may follow from the thing’s nature. But they are consequences of possibility, not its true meaning.314

Others define possibility as the equal standing of existence and nonexistence in relation to an essence, or as a statement affirming that neither is necessary.315 They treat it as a property that the essence itself must produce.316 But how, then, can one side become actual without overturning what the essence requires? Their answer is that the essence considered on its own is not the whole of reality. A feature may be absent at that level but present in reality. The essence, they argue, requires the two sides to be equal when considered by itself, while a cause may still make one side prevail in reality.

But what I have explained shows why this will not do. A possible essence, considered in itself, has no actuality at all. It is pure potential and complete dependence. It has no active power of its own, and it requires nothing until it receives existence from the Necessary, Self-Subsisting One. If it could bring something out of potential and into actuality by itself, then what is only potential, precisely as potential, would help make something actual. Our natural understanding of things rules this out. In itself, an essence that is possible does not require anything—not even the denial of something else.

Clarification and reminder

Some philosophers take possibility to be a property that necessarily follows from an essence. They then argue that, if possibility came from something else, either two independent causes would produce one effect, or a thing necessary or impossible in itself would become possible in itself. An opponent replies: perhaps each cause acts independently only when the other is absent. If both are present, neither is independent. Think of a whole with several parts. The absence of any one part can account for the whole’s absence; if several parts are missing, their absences do not each act as a separate, complete cause. But this reply cannot establish possibility in itself. On that account, something outside the essence would always matter, whether by being present or absent.

The truth is that the absence of each part causes the whole’s nonexistence only because it occurs alongside what is the real cause of that nonexistence. The real cause is the general fact that at least one necessary part, condition, or other cause is absent. This is one broad, undivided condition, even though the individual absences may be many. The individual absences are not causes in their own right; the shared condition is the cause. A cause of nonexistence may also be less definite than the thing whose nonexistence it explains.317

There is no need, then, for the elaborate proposal318 that the cause of a particular thing’s nonexistence is the nonexistence of that thing’s particular complete cause. Others argue that, if a thing’s possibility came from another319, then by itself it would still be allowed to be possible, necessary, or impossible. But if possibility came from another, how could the thing be any of these in itself? They also say that if we imagine the other thing having no effect, the first thing would have to be necessary or impossible in itself320, which cannot be.

These arguments lose their force once we understand what possibility in itself means. Consider a thing simply as it is, leaving aside everything else. Neither its existence nor its nonexistence is then necessary. This does not mean its nature produces the absence of necessity. It means we have left out every feature beyond the nature itself, even any denials or relations that might belong to it. Necessity in itself and impossibility in itself must be understood in the same way. These three classes describe the thing viewed on its own.

To clear up a doubt: we have already pointed out that a thing’s being described by a denial at its own level does not mean that its essence itself is the source of that denial. You might say: if we take an essence just as it is, we can deny of it everything that is not part of its essential nature. The denial that existence is necessary is a simple denial, so it can be said of the essence in this way. Then would not possibility in itself be part of the essence, even though we have said it is not?

The answer turns on where we put the denial. In saying that an essence “is not, considered in itself, anything but itself,” the denial must come before “considered in itself,” so that we deny the claim that the feature belongs to the essence precisely as such.321 If we instead make “considered in itself” part of the subject—“the essence considered in itself”—and then deny a feature of that subject, the statement may simply be false.322 Some features cannot in fact be separated from the essence. This distinction makes it possible to answer a puzzle that has troubled many sharp thinkers. If writing can be denied of a human being considered in itself, why can we not also deny that denial, since both writing and not writing are outside the human essence? In the same way, we might deny both necessities of a possible essence and then deny that denial, making it not possible in itself. But we have already shown that no thing is outside the three categories, and that a possible thing remains possible in itself.

The answer is that we must distinguish features that cannot be separated from an essence from those that belong to it only when it exists. An essence considered on its own need not have the second kind of feature—writing or movement, for example—so we may deny those features of it. But some features cannot be separated from an essence even though they are not part of its definition. We may truly describe the essence as having them, without making the essence itself the cause of their presence. Possibility is of this kind. It belongs to an essence before the question of its actual existence arises, so we cannot deny possibility of an essence simply by considering it on its own.323 This also shows why another reply fails. Some say that an essence can lack possibility when considered on its own, yet still have possibility in reality, just as it can lack writing when considered on its own and acquire writing when it exists.324 But the comparison is mistaken: possibility does not wait for the essence to exist. Nor is it enough to say that possibility is a simple denial, and that such a denial must therefore be true of the essence on its own. If that were enough, we could just as easily deny possibility itself.

The thing being divided among the three categories is its state in relation to existence and nonexistence. This is a positive state of being described325, even if one of its qualifications, such as possibility, is expressed negatively.326 That is why “this thing is possible” is an affirmative statement whose predicate is negative, not merely the statement “this thing is not necessary.” We affirm of the thing that neither its existence nor its nonexistence is necessary; we do not affirm either necessity. To call something possible is to say truly that this description belongs to it. A careful scholar has made this point.

You may now object: if a thing’s existence depends on another, then its nonexistence depends on that other’s nonexistence, since the absence of a cause brings about the absence of its effect. If a possible thing’s existence is made necessary by another, then the opposite—its existence not being necessary—must also come from another. Likewise, if something is made impossible by another, its nonexistence is necessary; so the opposite, that its nonexistence is not necessary, must also come from another. This would establish possibility through another.

We answer that possibility means being described by the denial of necessity, in the form of an affirmative statement with a negative predicate. It is not the same as a bare denial of necessity, which is a simple negative statement. The opposite of necessary existence is clearly the second kind of statement, not possibility in itself, which is the first.

Nor can we treat the necessity of existence and the necessity of nonexistence327328 as one feature with a single cause. They do not make up a whole whose absence could then be traced to the absence of one cause. They are two distinct and opposing features, each with its own cause, and their causes cannot be present together. Their two opposites therefore do not form one feature with a single cause for its absence—even if we imagine them as one combined whole, let alone as one reality.

Any division must have one clear basis; otherwise, we cannot say what belongs in each part. In The Clear Horizon, this objection is made in another way. If another thing makes existence necessary, the opposite is that existence is not made necessary by another. That, the argument says, is possibility when we consider the thing in itself. The same applies when another thing makes nonexistence necessary. Thus, the objector concludes, there must be possibility through another.

The reply is to look carefully at what the word “another” qualifies. The opposite of “necessity through another” is “not necessary through another”; it is not “a lack of necessity produced by another.” The same distinction applies to impossibility. Nothing prevents necessity produced by another from being absent. What cannot happen is for the absence of necessity itself—possibility—to be produced by another.329

Summary and clarification. Some early philosophers treated necessity, possibility, unity, and existence as things added to what exists in the world. Later philosophers said that these are added in the mind, but have no matching forms outside it.330 We have shown you a balanced way to understand how these concepts can be true and not true of things, and in what sense.331

You may hear people who are not engaging the argument seriously dismiss these concepts and say they add nothing to the things described by them, either in the mind or in reality. But our first natural judgment tells us otherwise. When we say that a human being is possibly existent, or that a heavenly sphere is possibly existent, “possibility” does not mean “human being” in the first case and “sphere” in the second. It is one meaning that applies to both. If “possibility” meant human nature when said of a human being, and the nature of a sphere when said of a sphere, the word would name two different things. It would add no shared meaning beyond “human being” and “sphere.” If it meant the same thing as “human being” and “sphere” in both cases, then those two things would have the same meaning, which is plainly false.

So when “possibility” is said of different essences, it is not identical with any one of them. It is another, shared feature that applies to them all. One philosopher was astonished that these thinkers agree with defenders of the truth when they argue that the world needs a Creator because it is possible and depends on a cause, yet, when discussing possibility, say that it is nothing more than the thing itself. It is as if they were saying: “The world needs a Creator because the world is the world.”

A principle of the Illuminationist school. Suhrawardī offers a rule for understanding why possibility and similar concepts exist in the mind without having separate forms in the world. Suppose a general concept had a separate form outside the mind. If that required the same concept to be applied again and again, a series would arise with no end. If existence were a thing added to an existing essence, that added existence would itself have to exist. Its existence would then need another existence, and so on without end. What is more, the whole chain would itself need to exist332, starting a second endless chain. The same reasoning would repeat. Yet the first existence could not be established unless all these chains were already established.

The same difficulty arises with unity. An essence and its added unity would each need unity; existence would need unity, and unity would need existence. Their combinations would generate further endless series. Possibility would have to exist, the existence of possibility would itself be possible, and new series would arise. If that existence were necessary, possibility would no longer be something added to a thing. And still more series would form between possibility and necessity through another, between existence and necessity, and between unity and necessity. So concepts that would produce these endlessly multiplying chains cannot have separate forms outside the mind. They are ideas drawn from things. They do not correspond to extra objects added to essences in the world, nor do they reach a final, fixed point at which the mind can stop repeating them.

Discussion and clarification

There are several reasons to doubt this rule. First, its defenders themselves say that the Necessary Being is nothing but existence and necessity: He exists through Himself and is necessary in Himself. They do not deny that He exists outside the mind. Yet their account of existence contradicts this. They say that existence is only an idea in the mind, with no form in the world, yet they also say that God’s essence is the source of all forms and the root of all realities.

Second, the person who introduced and defended this rule admits that one and the same meaning can exist in different ways. Sometimes it is a feature of something else; sometimes it is a reality in its own right. It can be stronger or weaker, more or less complete.333 Why not allow the same for existence and unity, as we argued earlier? Each can have different ways of being real, from the most complete to the least complete. At its highest level, each is one reality that depends on nothing else and is necessary in itself. At its lowest, it is only an idea in the mind or a relation, with nothing independently real corresponding to it.

The natures of things have no reality on their own; they are real only through existence. But existence does not need something else to make it real. It is what makes those natures real. How, then, could existence have no reality? Its reality is itself. Existence does not need a second existence to make it exist. Otherwise we would have to go on adding existences. The mind can imagine a further existence for it, just as it can imagine a further light for light. But light makes things visible, and is itself visible without the help of a second light. Otherwise we would need light after light without end. Yet the mind can imagine a light for light, then another light for that light, and so on, until it stops making these mental distinctions.

The same applies to unity. It is a feature of things in the world because it is existence itself in reality, though different from existence in meaning. Often something has a reality and essence beyond its meaning and beyond the form it takes in the mind, as existence and its perfect qualities do. Sometimes a thing has only a meaning and no reality in the world, as with possibility, impossibility, the joining of opposites, a partner to God, and similar ideas. The same is true of negations and relations. Sometimes several meanings exist through one existence and are one with a single reality. Knowledge, power, and life, for example, are one with the existence of God, may He be exalted.

This also answers an argument that a respected philosopher gives in Discussions. He calls it strong and convincing: “We can meet those who say that being existent is existence itself halfway. We say that existence and unity are alike: according to you, both must exist in the world; according to us, both are only ideas in the mind. Suppose you reject an endless chain in the case of existence by saying that existence is the state of being existent. Still, existence and unity have different meanings, and we can understand one without the other. Unity cannot simply mean existence, nor existence unity. So if existence exists, it has unity; and if unity exists, it has existence, which in turn has another unity, existing through another existence, and so on. An endless chain of existence and unity must follow. It is no answer to say that the unity of existence is existence itself, or that the existence of unity is unity itself. The meanings of existence and unity differ, and two distinct things cannot be one and the same thing in themselves.”

That is the heart of his argument. He assumes that two different meanings cannot come from one and the same reality. But he has not proved it. One reality, even considered in the same respect, can answer to several different descriptions. Zayd’s existence, for example,334 can be caused, known, provided for, and dependent. The difference among these meanings does not require each to have a separate existence. The same is true of the divine qualities, which all philosophers agree are one with God’s single existence. In short, different meanings alone do not prove that the reality or way of existing for each must differ. A further argument is needed to show that their underlying realities differ.

This is also supported by what Avicenna says in The Healing, in the section on divine things. The fact that something understands and is understood does not mean that its essence, or even our way of thinking about it, is two things. Nor does the fact that something in motion requires a mover mean that this requirement itself must be a separate thing, or the very thing it requires. A different line of inquiry is needed to show that what moves cannot be what moves it. For this reason, some people could imagine that there is something that moves itself until proof showed that this is impossible. The ideas “mover” and “moved” alone do not prove it. Likewise, two related things are known to be two because of something beyond the relation imagined by the mind. That is the end of Avicenna’s statement.

I say: Avicenna’s point is that two ideas can differ without proving that the things they describe are either one or two. We need a separate argument to decide whether the realities behind them are the same or different. “Moving” differs in meaning from “being moved,” just as “parent” differs from “child,” and “understanding” from “being understood.” But reason shows that, when no matter is involved, the one who understands and what is understood are one in reality, despite the difference between the two ideas. A mover and what it moves, by contrast, really are different. The same is true of the two sides of a relation. So understand this carefully: people have gone astray on this point.

The weakness of this rule is now clear in some cases, such as unity and existence. Showing that these have no reality in the world does not prove that other concepts lack it. Another argument is needed to show that those other concepts are only ideas in the mind. We have already pointed out how these meanings attach to realities and essences. Consider the matter carefully and reflect deeply.

You have learned that possibility describes an essence when we consider the essence just as it is, without considering its relation to a complete cause. What describes an essence considered in that way cannot be an actual feature in the world; it must be an idea in the mind. Also, possibility has a negative meaning. Negations, as negations, have no share in existence, whether in the world or in the mind.

Consider the First Effect. It shows why those who treat possibility as a real feature added to a thing’s nature are mistaken.335 They themselves say that the First Effect is possible in itself. They also regard it as beginning in its own being, so it must first be possible and only then exist. For something to gain existence through another, it must first be possible in itself. But if its possibility comes first, that possibility must itself be possible. It cannot be necessary in itself, since it depends on something else; nor can there be two beings necessary in themselves. So this possibility, too, would need a cause to bring it about.

If that cause were the Necessary Being, two impossible results would follow. First, one source would bring about both the First Effect and its possibility.336 But for one source to produce two things, it must act in two different ways. That cannot be true of the absolutely one divine reality.

Second, possibility would itself be produced by an agent outside the thing it describes. But we have already shown that a thing’s possibility cannot be produced by a cause—least of all by something other than the thing’s own nature.

They cannot escape this by saying that possibility does not come before the First Effect and the other eternal beings. That would mean possibility only comes about after the thing exists. Yet they admit that possible things begin in their own being. Their possibility must therefore come before the necessity they receive from another, since necessity through another depends on a thing first being possible in itself. What belongs to a thing through itself comes before what belongs to it through another, especially when what it receives through another depends on what belongs to it through itself.

Nor does it help to say that possibility has one meaning for eternal beings and another for other things. Real possibility—the opposite of necessity and impossibility—applies to every effect. If the beings that exist eternally through divine creation were not possible in themselves in this sense, they would be necessary in themselves or impossible in themselves. They are neither.

Nor does it help to appeal to a note found among Avicenna’s drafts, called Fairness and Redress, which says that the generosity of the First Truth does not allow possibility to come before the effects it creates. The question is not which came first in time. We are not claiming that possibility comes before things that begin in time but not before things created without a beginning in time. We are asking what comes first by its very nature. If possibility were an actual feature in the world, and existence through another required possibility in itself, then possibility would come first. What a thing has through itself comes before what it has through another. Those who say that possibility exists in the world have no way out of this difficulty unless they accept the account we have established: possibility and similar concepts exist through something else but have no existence in themselves.

If possibility had its own actual form in the world, even as an attribute attached to something else, it would not be a feature that belongs to an essence considered apart from existence and nonexistence. A feature that belongs to an essence in itself—whether the words are used in their strict sense337 or more broadly—must be an idea in the mind. If possibility had an actual form, existence through another could not attach to an essence. For if the lack of necessity for existence and nonexistence were an actual feature, it would attach to an essence that exists and conflict with the necessity that is also an actual feature. But if possibility describes an essence considered in itself, without regard to the source of its existence or nonexistence, then there is no conflict when existence or nonexistence comes to it from elsewhere. The two descriptions concern different subjects: the essence considered in itself, and the essence as it exists through another.338

It is also mistaken to define a possible thing by saying that its own nature makes neither its existence nor its nonexistence necessary. When we divide things into necessary, possible, and impossible, we consider how each stands in relation to existence itself. We do not restrict the meaning of existence or compare the thing with anything else.339

Objections and replies

Those who say that possibility and similar ideas—necessity, existence, thinghood, and unity—have real forms in the world, additional to the essence of the possible, necessary, existent, thing, or one, offer several arguments for their view.

Their first argument is this: we distinguish a thing that can exist in the world from one that can exist only in the mind. They say the difference must be that the first has possibility in the world, while the second has possibility only in the mind. They argue in the same way about the other descriptions.

Second, they say, a thing must be either necessary, possible, or impossible. So if its possibility were not real in the world, it would have to be necessary or impossible there. If its existence were not real, it would not exist; if its oneness were not real, it would be many. These conclusions would contradict our judgments that things in the world can be possible, existent, and one.

Third, if these were only mental ideas and descriptions, not realities in the things themselves, the mind could attach them to any essence it chose. Then every concept, even impossible ones such as a partner to God, the joining of opposites, and absolute nothingness, would be possible. The same reasoning would apply to the other ideas.

Fourth, an event must be preceded by possibility. An agent brings it about only because it is possible in the world, not merely possible in the mind. Otherwise it would exist only in the mind. So whatever exists in the world must have a possibility in the world before it exists.

These are the strongest arguments for saying that possibility and other mental ideas of this kind have actual forms in the world. But someone seeking the truth can answer them. What is agreed is that possibility and similar ideas are additional to the essences to which the mind relates them.340 When the mind considers, for example, the essence of a human being, it finds that possibility is neither that essence nor part of it. The same is true of other descriptions that are neither the essence nor one of its parts. But it does not follow that these additional ideas have forms in the world. The only exception is the description that is existence, and also individual unity, which, for those firmly grounded in knowledge, is existence itself. That claim rests on a special proof about existence.

None of these arguments proves that existence has a real form in the world. We came to that conclusion through a gift of unseen knowledge, support from the spiritual realm, aid from above, and heavenly grace. Nor does saying that something is “possible in the world” or “existent in the world” prove that its possibility or existence is itself in the world. We have already seen that a dependent existence—the existence a thing has through something else—can differ from existence in itself. The mind judges that a possible thing is possible in the world, as explained earlier; it also judges that it is possible in the mind. Possibility is therefore a mental feature: its own particular way of existing is in the mind. The mind may relate it to something in the world, or to something in the mind, or may judge without qualification that it applies equally to both.

No one can claim that, if impossibility has no form in the world, an impossible thing is not impossible there; or that, unless impossibility itself exists in the world, the thing must be either necessary or possible. The same answer applies to the second argument. Impossibility, necessity, and possibility are alike in this respect: they are ideas in the mind, with no separate forms in the world, even though things in the world and in the mind can be described by them.341

In The Paths of Discussion, Suhrawardi says that possibility, necessity, impossibility, and existence have no separate reality in things. He compares them with the ideas studied in logic: whether something is general or individual, whether a feature belongs to its nature or happens to accompany it, and whether an idea names a broader kind or what distinguishes one kind from another.342 These are ways the mind describes things; they are not separate objects inside those things. A particular person can be individual, and “human being” can be universal,343 even though universality and individuality themselves cannot exist as separate things in the world. In the same way, a thing can be described as possible or impossible even though these descriptions have no separate forms there.

But the comparison is not quite right.344 Possibility and impossibility do not work in exactly the same way as being general or individual. The descriptions used in logic depend on how a thing exists in the mind. The descriptions we are discussing here can sometimes depend on what a thing is like in the world. In both cases, the descriptions themselves exist only in thought.

As for the fourth argument, which concerns possibility in particular, it depends on what “possibility” means. If it means that something is ready to come into existence—that the conditions now allow it to receive existence from the cause that brings it about—then we can accept, for now, that every event beginning in time has this kind of possibility in the world before it occurs. We will explain later what it means to call this an actual thing in the world.

But if “possibility” means the state of an essence considered in itself, we agree only that this possibility comes before existence as an idea and a way of considering the essence. Even if a thing had no earlier period of nonexistence in time, the mind can consider it as not yet existing. We also say that not every event can have an actual possibility in the world before it exists.

There is no end to the events still to come. One event will follow another without limit, as religious teachings and philosophical arguments affirm. Examples include the movements of the people of Paradise and the punishments of the people of Hell. If each event, or each event still to come, had its own possibility in the world, matter would contain an unlimited number of possibilities. If some events had no possibility, then some would occur without a prior possibility, and by the argument just given they would have to be necessary or impossible.

Some may accept an unlimited series of possibilities and say that they are not ordered one after another: each event has its own possibility, and all these possibilities exist together. We will show that such a collection cannot exist, for two reasons.

First,345 possibility has one meaning. A thing, considered simply as possible, does not differ from another possible thing because of possibility itself. Nor can the differences come from prime matter, which holds these possibilities, because matter is pure potential and has no distinctions of its own, as we will explain. So possibilities in themselves could differ only because the things they are possibilities of differ. But these are events that do not yet exist, in an unlimited series. A thing cannot be distinguished from another by being related to something that does not exist: what has no reality cannot distinguish one thing from another.

You might reply that we can think about infinitely many future things and so distinguish the possibilities attached to them. But we cannot hold infinitely many separate things in the mind at once, each with its own details. We may have a general idea of an unlimited number, but that is different from holding an unlimited number of distinct things in the mind. If we think only of possibilities and future things in general, every possibility has the same relation to every future thing. One possibility is no more distinct from another than one future thing is from another.

Second, even if we grant this account, it in effect accepts our point. Where possibilities become distinct is also where they become real. If the mind alone distinguishes them, then they have this distinct existence only in the mind.346 If we suppose instead that their difference lies in the world, then our understanding of that difference must follow the difference already there. But the proposed account says that the mind’s own imagining makes them different. It would then make the thing depend on itself, which is impossible.

Here is the second reason. Suppose matter, which carries an unlimited number of possibilities, were divided into two halves. Then one of three things must be true: each half keeps the very same unlimited possibilities that the whole had; each half gains a new unlimited set of possibilities at the moment of division; or each half contains only a limited number.347 None of these outcomes is possible.

The first outcome would mean that one and the same thing existed at the same time in two different places, which is impossible.

The second outcome would mean that new possibilities appeared in each half. But because these possibilities are themselves new events, each would need an earlier possibility. If those earlier possibilities were new too, they would in turn need still earlier possibilities. At the moment of division, no agent could produce even the first layer unless endlessly many earlier layers had already come about. But nothing can happen at one moment if it requires an endless succession to have happened first. This would also mean that the events whose possibilities had just arisen were impossible before those possibilities appeared, even though the argument says that anything without an actual possibility must be impossible. Things would shift from being impossible in themselves to being possible in themselves.

The third outcome would leave each half with a limited number of possibilities. But two limited numbers add up to a limited number. The total number of possibilities in one body would then be limited, while the events they belong to are unlimited. Nor can we say that each half contains an unlimited set that is not new, each set being half of the unlimited set in the whole.348 A body can always be divided again. Each new cut brings back the same problem. Since we have supposed that the possibilities do not arise at the moment of division, they must have occupied distinct places before the division. They cannot move from one place to another. So, after the division, some would remain in one half and the rest in the other.

If infinitely many possibilities already occupied different places, then the body would contain infinitely many distinct parts, distinguished by the features—the possibilities—that belong to them.349 This would mean either that it is made of indivisible parts, which is impossible, or that it contains an unlimited number of parts of measurable size, making the whole body unlimited in size. That too is impossible, as we will prove later. How could a body with a fixed size contain endlessly many separate places, each with its own feature? And since each part can be divided again, the same problem returns inside every part.

Another objection to those who say that a possible event has an actual possibility in the world is this: possibility requires a relation to the thing that is possible. If possibility is only an idea in the mind, then it relates to something the mind has imagined. But if it is an actual feature in the world, it must relate to something that exists in the world. A real relation to something that does not exist in the world is not possible.

The mind can picture something that might exist and judge that it could either exist or not exist. It can judge this simply by considering what the thing is. That is possibility in itself. Or it may make the judgment by considering the thing’s causes, the readiness of what can receive it, the absence of things that oppose it, and the removal of what would prevent it from coming about. This is readiness for a thing to exist—a kind of possibility through preparation.350

Chapter: Features of what is possible in itself

We have delayed discussing the features of what is necessary in itself until the section on divine matters. They belong to a different kind of inquiry, and their subject is too exalted to place among the general rules about concepts and ideas drawn from things. We have mentioned only a few points needed to make the path of reasoning clear; we will return to them later by a sacred and higher path.

A gathering place:351 Just as what has always been necessary is simple, one, and indivisible, what is possible in itself involves being made of parts, mixing, joining, and pairing. Every possible thing is a composite. A possible essence cannot stand on its own without existence; and a possible existence has no definite character without some degree of limitation and weakness, from which the essence arises and from which the ideas that describe possibility are drawn. Its particular effects follow from that limited level. The broad, general effects that flow from the Necessary Being reach every recipient. The particular effects found in each possible existence also come from the First Source, though speaking of them as its effects is a comparison, as we will explain.

Every possible thing can therefore be understood through two aspects: what it is and the fact that it exists. Each involves the other, even when we consider the narrowest kinds and the broadest classes. Considered only in terms of what it is, a possible thing has the capacity to exist but does not exist by itself. Through its cause, it actually exists. Apart from existence, its nature is sheer “not-being”; existence comes to it through its cause. From these two sides, every possible thing has both potentiality and actuality. Nothing apart from the Necessary Being is entirely free of potentiality. Everything else combines these two meanings. Potentiality and possibility are like matter; actuality and necessity are like form. Every possible thing therefore has a composite structure, with one aspect like matter and another like form. True simplicity cannot exist in the world of possibility—not in the basic kinds of substance, nor in their properties and qualities.352

Oneness, too, belongs in its fullest sense only to the divine reality. The idea of any possible kind of thing can apply to more than one individual. Even a particular thing belongs to a broader description, whether that description comes from what it is or from a feature it happens to have. Other things could share that description. Something else may prevent those other individuals from existing, but nothing in the description itself rules them out. No possible thing, then, is absolutely one and unique. It is called one only in relation to something more divided and shared. The oneness of possible things is weak in its simplicity: their “oneness” is a union that includes some multiplicity. The single aspect in them is a shadow of God’s pure oneness, which gives all other kinds of unity, each at a lower level than the one before.

The closest is the individual oneness of the First Intellect, which is the same as its existence and the way it is made distinct. Next comes the oneness of the other active intellects, then the oneness of souls, then of forms. Below these is the connected oneness of a body, which contains multiplicity only as a potential. Then comes the oneness of prime matter, which gathers multiplicity and unfolds it into the realities of kinds and individuals. This is a vague, general oneness, like a broad class.353

There is another side to this. Just as possibility is involved in being made of parts, anything made of parts is possible in itself. Consider a whole simply as a whole, without looking at any particular part. It cannot be independent in its existence or in its nonexistence. That very dependence shows that it is possible.

As for imagined combinations of two necessary things, two impossible things, a necessary thing with an impossible one, or two opposites or contradictories taken together, these are only ideas. They do not name realities that stand on their own as substances. Such ideas cannot be true of themselves in the usual sense; they fall under their opposites. The idea of a partner to God, for example, is not itself a partner to God. Rather, it is a mental quality produced by the imagination and by confused thinking. The same applies to these imagined combinations. Their necessity or impossibility depends on whether their parts are necessary or impossible. They have only the status of dependence, need, possibility, and relation, whether considered in terms of existence or nonexistence. What is impossible in the case of contradictories or opposites is their being together in one thing—not the realities of the contradictories or opposites themselves, whatever their other status.354

There is another subtle point. Unity applies to the divisions of any meaning that can be the subject of a general rule. When we say that every thing made of parts is possible, we mean a whole that really forms one thing. When we say that everything necessary in itself is simple, we mean that such a being is one undivided reality. And when we make a rule about animals, we mean things that each have one animal nature.

A supposed whole made of two necessary beings has no reality beyond the two beings themselves. It has no third status of possibility, impossibility, or necessity beyond the necessity of each part. The same is true of a supposed whole made of two impossible things: there is no new impossibility beyond the impossibility of each part. A supposed whole made of one necessary thing and one impossible thing has only the necessity of the first and the impossibility of the second. There is nothing more.

The same is true if we imagine two animals as a single whole. Each animal has its own nature. Putting them together does not create a third animal with a third nature. If one animal can speak and the other brays, the two taken together do not speak or bray as a single whole. Nor do they exist as one thing. What exists is each of the two, with no third animal made from them. We will see, in the discussion of unity, that unity cannot be separated from existence: what has no unity has no existence.

Someone might object that if a whole made of two things that are impossible in themselves were possible in itself, then its nonexistence would be due to the lack of a cause that could bring it into existence. But the cause of the whole is the cause of its parts, and no such cause can bring these parts into existence, since they are impossible.

The answer is that the whole does not exist because its parts do not exist. The existence of the parts is what gives the whole existence; if the parts existed without a cause, the whole would exist as well. A cause is needed for the parts only when they are themselves possible things. When a part is impossible in itself, the whole’s nonexistence ultimately comes from that part’s necessary nonexistence. It does not lead to the absence of some other thing. The chain of existences, by contrast, ends at the Necessary Being, whose existence is necessary in itself.

Section: How a possible thing can entail something impossible in itself

Many people who discuss these questions without thinking deeply reject any necessary connection between something possible and something impossible.355 They assume that if something possible entails an impossibility in reality, then that possible thing must itself be impossible. Their reasoning is this: if a starting claim were possible but what follows from it were impossible, the starting claim could still hold while its necessary consequence did not. That would contradict the claim that one entails the other.

If this were right, it would also rule out a link between something necessary and something possible, and even between every complete cause and its effect. A cause may be necessary when its effect is not necessary, whether the cause is necessary in itself or necessary through something else. We will explain this further.

A stranger explanation appears in one set of notes: “The first claim is possible when considered in itself. What follows from it is possible in relation to that first claim, not necessarily possible when considered in itself.”356 When one claim entails another, what follows cannot have its opposite as something necessary in relation to the first claim. That tells us nothing about whether its opposite is necessary when considered by itself. The consequent may, in itself, be necessarily existent, necessarily nonexistent, or neither, when considered just as it is.357 So do not mistake this for “possibility through another,” which we have already shown to be impossible. This is possibility in relation to another, and the difference between them has been made clear.

This may sound like careful reasoning, but it fails. Possibility in relation to another applies only where neither thing makes the other necessary, gives it existence, or receives existence from it. In short, there must be no necessary cause-and-effect link between them, whether in existence or nonexistence. A similarly weak explanation comes from the distinguished philosopher al-Ṭūsī. He says that the First Effect’s nonexistence would entail the nonexistence of the Necessary Being only in the sense that the First Cause would not be acting as its cause. It would not entail that the First Cause itself did not exist. The First Cause is necessary in itself, whether it has an effect or not. So, he says, the possible thing entails an impossibility only incidentally: it would be impossible for the cause, considered as a cause, not to be necessary in itself. But this is impossible only because the cause is necessary in itself, not because it is considered as a cause. This differs from the opposite case, where we suppose the First Cause itself does not exist; that would entail that the First Effect does not exist, because it receives its existence from the First Cause alone.358

How did so great a thinker, with such strong judgment and careful insight into divine matters, overlook that what is necessary in itself is necessary in all its descriptions? The First Cause acts as a cause because of its own essence, without waiting for some new state or additional motive. It is the self-sustaining and wholly generous source. As its essence exists, its causal power exists too; there is no real or mental separation between them.

Suppose the First Cause’s being a cause were merely possible, rather than necessary to its very nature. We would then have to explain the link between the First Cause and its being a cause. That link would need a further explanation, and so on without end—or we would be back at the difficulty we started with.359

Here is the answer. What the First Effect is can be considered possible in itself; the fact that it exists comes from the Necessary Being. Its reality therefore has two aspects, comparable to matter and form. One is need, the capacity to exist, what is hidden, and what is possible. The other is self-sufficiency, actual existence, what is revealed, and what is necessary.360 Our way of understanding things shows that the relations of dependence and causation among existing things arise only from their kinds of existence. An essence has no essential tie to its cause except through the existence attributed to it. We have also seen that possibility as applied to a possible existence does not mean the same thing as possibility as applied to an essence. The first goes together with necessity; the second is opposed to it.361

Consider the First Effect in two ways. First, consider what it is. It has its own distinct identity, marked by a lack of the highest perfection and by a measure of darkness and nonexistence, although the First Reality’s light overwhelms and conceals these limits. From this point of view, its nonexistence is possible. From that side, its state of nonexistence is no different from its state of existence, from all eternity. Its essence, considered just as it is, has no share in either. Its nonexistence, considered in this way, does not entail the nonexistence of the Necessary Being, because there is no link between them on this side.362

Now consider it as something that exists through the First Truth. From this point of view, it cannot fail to exist, because the One who sustains its existence cannot fail to exist. Its existence entails the existence of its source, just as the existence of an effect entails the existence of the cause that brings it about.363 So a possible thing has not entailed something impossible. Its nonexistence in itself—that is, nonexistence considered simply as nonexistence—has no aspect of possibility, as existence has an aspect of existence.

This does not mean that every existence is necessary in itself. We have already distinguished timeless necessity from the kind called necessity “in itself.” For the same reason, it does not mean that every nonexistence is impossible in itself.

Someone might say: “If by the first way of considering the argument you mean that, when the mind looks only at the First Effect’s essence and considers nothing else, it finds no necessary link between it and its source, that does not prevent its nonexistence from entailing the source’s nonexistence in reality. The link remains there. But if you mean that, on this way of considering it, its nonexistence does not entail the source’s nonexistence in reality, that is plainly false. The First Effect is caused by the source in reality. How, then, could it fail to entail its cause?”

I choose the second meaning. The effect is not the essence of the possible thing. Its existence is caused by the existence of its cause, and its nonexistence by the cause’s absence.

The same person adds:364 “If by the second way you mean that nonexistence which is impossible through another is not possible in itself, that is clearly wrong. Being impossible through another does not conflict with being possible in itself; it does not cancel it. The thing described by impossibility through another or necessity through another must be possible in itself, meaning that existence and nonexistence are equally open to it when considered by its own nature.”

I mean that nonexistence, considered simply as nonexistence, has only the aspect of impossibility, just as existence, considered simply as existence, has only the aspect of necessity. Nonexistence cannot be described as possibility of existence, any more than existence can accept nonexistence; otherwise a thing’s nature would turn into its opposite. We do not accept that the thing described by necessity through another or impossibility through another must be possible in itself in the sense that existence and nonexistence are equally open to it by its own nature. We accept this only for things other than existence and nonexistence themselves. What is necessary through another is existence linked to another; what is impossible through another is the corresponding nonexistence.

Here is an objection. If something possible can lead to an impossibility, as we have said,365 how can a proof by contradiction show that the starting assumption is impossible? For example, we argue that distance cannot be unlimited because an unlimited distance cannot be enclosed within two boundaries. Perhaps an unlimited distance is possible in itself even if its existence would entail something impossible: being enclosed between boundaries.

We have already met this question and answered it.366 In that kind of proof, “possible”367 means possible in the world itself: things as they really are must allow it either to happen or not happen. Neither outcome is necessary.368 But the possible thing we are discussing here is an essence considered in itself, not a thing’s status in actual reality. The First Effect and other beings created directly by God are, in reality, fully actual—not merely possible. Their shadow of possibility is hidden beneath the brightness of God, the Sustainer.

A thing possible in itself entails something impossible, not because of its essence but because of its nonexistence. In the same way, it entails something necessary, not because of its essence but because of its existence. The possibility used in a proof by contradiction is possibility in actual reality, not possibility at the level of an essence considered by itself. The two meanings differ. The same is true of “impossible in itself”: it may mean that nonexistence is necessary when we consider only a supposed essence, as with a partner to God or the joining of contradictories. Or it may mean that nonexistence is necessary in reality because something else requires it, whether that requirement comes from the essence or from a cause that makes it impossible in the way things exist.369

This is why proofs by contradiction work. If assuming that something exists leads to an impossibility, then that thing cannot exist in reality. Many arguments of the form “if this, then that” rely on the same principle. The thing may be impossible in itself because of its supposed essence, as with a partner to God or the joining of contradictories. Or something else may require it to be impossible in actual reality, because a cause fully brings about its impossibility. The conclusion is the same.

For example, simple intellectual beings cannot have failed to exist in the past or cease to exist in the future. If they could cease to exist, their nonexistence would require the absence of the cause that gives them existence, and they would need matter able to receive either existence or nonexistence. Both results are impossible in themselves, as has been shown. Therefore the original assumption—that these beings could cease to exist—is impossible in actual reality too. The possibility meant in this argument is not possibility at the level of essence alone. If it were, these beings would have to be necessary in themselves, exalted far above that. You may have heard a weak argument dressed up as scholarship: anything possible must either exist or not exist, and in either state it cannot take on the opposite state. If the opposite cannot apply, then one side must be necessary, so there is no possible thing at all.370

Another argument says: a possible thing either exists with its complete cause present, in which case it is necessary, or exists without its complete cause, in which case it is impossible. Where, then, is there room for anything possible?371

People answer the first argument by saying that its division leaves out a possible case—if “exists” and “does not exist” mean that we consider the thing as either one or the other. There is a third option: we can consider its essence without either existence or nonexistence. The thing described as possible is an essence considered apart from both. Its inability to accept nonexistence in one respect, because existence has been attributed to it, does not mean that it cannot accept nonexistence in another respect; and the same applies in reverse. What makes it able to accept either side is the essence considered without those limits.

If the two alternatives simply refer to a particular time, either may be chosen. But it does not follow that a thing can never take on the opposite state. All we must deny is that it can have both opposite states at once. But this is not part of the meaning of “possible,” so no problem follows. The conclusion is harmless, and the problem does not follow.

The second argument’s division is also unclear if it means considering the essence and its different levels: it is either with its complete cause or without it. The second case must mean that the thing lacks the complete cause, rather than that it has the lack of the cause alongside it. If the division is about existence in reality, then it is valid. But the essence is not described as possible while it exists in reality, whether the cause is present or not. Possibility describes it in thought, when we consider it as it is in itself. So it is not true that a possible essence must either have its complete cause or lack it in reality.

It follows that every possible thing is surrounded either by two necessities, one earlier because its cause makes it necessary and one later because of its state in reality, or by two impossibilities on the opposite side. Neither set conflicts with what belongs to the essence when considered just as it is. That is their answer.

Those who give this answer have, in effect, admitted that what a thing is does not by itself connect it to the cause that makes it exist. Before and after are features of its existence, not of what it is when considered apart from existence. An essence, considered without existence and nonexistence, cannot be clothed in either state, whether through its own nature or through a cause. It has never left, and will never leave, its hidden state into the light of appearance. In itself it remains empty, concealed, and unseen.

Since an essence does not even have existence in itself, it is even less able to have the other real qualities that come after existence. None of the qualities of perfection or existence belongs to the essence except through existence. In all such qualities, the essence follows existence. Every kind of existence carries a particular essence with it. Some call this its determination; others call it its particular existence. Think of a reflection in a mirror. It follows what is in front of the mirror: its size, shape, color, movement, even its stillness. Yet all these features belong to the reflection only as an image. The reflection is not the original thing. The essence stands to existence and its qualities in the same way. Essence is an image of existence, reflected in the mind and the senses. This is why the most deeply knowing mystics and the perfected saints say that the whole world is an image within an image.

Muḥyī al-Dīn Ibn ʿArabī, a thinker devoted to knowledge of God, writes in chapter 63 of The Meccan Revelations:

“When a person sees their image in a mirror, they know for certain that they have seen their image in one sense, and have not seen it in another. The image may look very small because the mirror is small, or very large because it is large. A person cannot deny that they have seen their image, yet they know that their image is not inside the mirror, nor between the person and the mirror. They are neither truthful nor untruthful when they say, ‘I saw my image’ and ‘I did not see my image.’ What, then, is this image they see? Where is it? What is its nature? It is at once denied and affirmed, present and absent, known and unknown. God has shown His servant this truth by way of an example, so that the servant may know: if they are bewildered and unable to grasp the nature of this image, though they themselves belong to the world, then how much more unable, ignorant, and bewildered must they be before its Creator?”

Section: Refuting the idea that an essence naturally favors existence or nonexistence

If you have followed what we said about what things are, and why the mind calls them possible, you will need no further argument against the claim that something, by its very nature, favors existence over nonexistence—or the reverse.372 This claim can mean either that a possible thing’s own nature makes one side more likely than the other, without making it necessary; or that, when the thing is considered in itself, one side fits it better than the other, though not because an outside cause makes it so.373

Nor can the claim mean that a thing’s own nature causes this preference in the way that something necessary in itself causes its own necessity. We have already seen that an essence has no tie to the giver of existence except through existence. Existence is given to a thing, and existence itself gives rise to effects, in different ways according to its levels of completeness, weakness, and strength. The essence, considered just as it is, has no tie to anything else. Until existence is given to it, it is nothing—not even something we can truly say is itself. We can speak of it only by imagining what it would be. Possibility may be an idea the mind draws from an essence before it exists; but until the essence enters reality and receives existence from its giver, we cannot judge that it is anything in itself or that it is possible, even if those are features that, in thought, come before its existence.

You have learned that the mind considers an essence before considering its existence, as we consider a subject before one of its features. The same applies to what belongs to an essence in itself and what belongs to it once it exists. But outside the mind there is no subject and feature standing apart from one another. There is only existence and something that exists. The mind analyzes them and judges that some existent things involve a meaning beyond the idea of existence and being existent. It then treats one as a subject and the other as its feature—though in the world their order is the reverse. In thought, the essence comes before existence because we can grasp the essence fully, while existence cannot be grasped in its full reality. In the world, existence comes first, because existence is what is real there. The essence is joined to it only in a dependent way. This is a subtle point about why essence is an incidental feature of existence, one that most people have missed.

In short, the mind calls a thing possible only when it considers what the thing is apart from its existence, setting aside the light of existence that gives it reality. Outside this mental supposition, the thing is necessary because its complete cause gives it existence. It is necessary only in that dependent sense. Considered in itself, it has no feature at all—not necessity, possibility, or anything else.

The difference between a possible thing that does not exist and an impossible thing that does not exist is this: after examining it, the mind judges that the possible essence, if it were made into a real, self-standing essence, would have possibility as one of its features. The supposed impossible essence, even if we imagined it as a real, self-standing essence, would remain impossible by its own nature and could not be anything else. This does not mean that a nonexistent thing, simply as nonexistent, has possibility or impossibility. How could it, when what does not exist is no thing at all? Before something has been given existence, then, there is no independently real nature that could favor existence or anything else. To suggest that a thing makes itself and establishes its own reality, though it has no reality in itself, is not a thought a healthy mind could take seriously.374

Once these points are clear, we can see why a thing’s own nature cannot simply favor existence without making it necessary. The Second Teacher, Abū Naṣr al-Fārābī, points to this in a short work called The Gems of Wisdom: “If a chain of existences came about without necessity, then either a thing would bring itself into being—which is a grave mistake—or its own nonexistence would be possible, which is even worse.”

Here is why.375 If a thing exists because its own nature favors existence, it must be causing itself. If not, it has come into existence without anything making it exist, whether from within or from outside. It would therefore remain possible in itself: one side would be more likely, but not necessary. Its nonexistence would then also be possible, since it would not have been made necessary. In that case, the thing itself would be able to cease to exist, with no cause bringing about its nonexistence. This is worse than the first problem.376

There is a further explanation of why this is worse. A possible thing’s existence is not identical with its essence. Existence is a feature that needs an explanation. If the thing’s essence makes existence more likely, then that essence causes the thing to be described as existing, since a cause is whatever makes its effect more likely to occur. But because the essence has not made existence necessary, the thing could still fail to exist. Its nonexistence could then occur without any cause—even while the cause of its existence remains. That is sheer absurdity.377

This argument is needed before we have proved a Creator or established anything about reality in general. So no one can answer: “Perhaps some essences, in their existence as ideas in God’s knowledge or as forms in higher minds, incline toward existing in the outside world.” Mental existence faces the same problem as existence in the world: an essence does not exist as an essence until a giver of existence brings it into being.

Even if we set aside the impossibility of this supposed inborn preference, if it were enough to make an essence exist, one and the same thing would give existence to itself and receive existence from itself. It would therefore have to exist before it exists. Beware of relying, after God has let the light of truth reach your heart from the spiritual realm, on a flash of limited reasoning that may appear along the way. One such argument comes from al-Rāzī’s commentary on The Sources of Wisdom, and others have praised it.

Here is that argument. If one outcome is more likely, then its opposite must be less likely, because the two descriptions go together. The less likely side must then be impossible, since it cannot prevail over the more likely side. And if the less likely side is impossible, the more likely side must be necessary. Thus, what was assumed to fall short of necessity turns out to be necessary after all, which is a contradiction.

Here is the mistake. If one outcome is only more likely, the other is only less likely. Being less likely does not make it impossible. That would follow only if it were necessarily excluded, not merely less likely. In this case the less likely side is not ruled out. It is only less likely than the other side. In short, the less likely side has the same status as the side it is compared with; the more-likely side has no greater force than the side it makes less likely. If the existence side is more likely, then nonexistence is less likely, but only by way of a non-necessary preference. And if nonexistence is less likely, that too makes existence more likely, but still without making either side necessary. The two sides remain possible.

Even if we grant that the less-likely side is impossible when we consider the essence together with that description, the impossibility belongs to the essence only as qualified by the less-likely feature. It is therefore impossibility through another, not impossibility in itself. The preference of the other side would then be necessity through another, not necessity in itself.378379380 This does not overturn our argument. The impossibility that belongs to a description that can be removed can itself be removed; the same is true of the necessity that corresponds to it. This also undermines the other foundations people have offered on this question. Few of those arguments escape the same objection.

Some false assumptions

Some people say that certain possible things are naturally more inclined toward existence than nonexistence, while still needing an outside cause and remaining possible. They mean that a complete cause makes these things exist more often, more fully, or with fewer conditions. Others say the reverse: that some possible things are more inclined toward nonexistence than existence.381
