Some people thought that nonexistence was more likely for certain possible things. Others thought it was more likely for everything, because nonexistence is easier to bring about. Those who held these views belonged to philosophical schools from an earlier age, before philosophy had been corrected and brought to maturity.382 Some theologians, by contrast, say that whichever of the two sides actually occurs must have been more likely, because they deny that anything other than God can be necessary—not even something made necessary by another. A further objection follows from this.383

Take things that never stay the same, such as sounds, time, and motion. Someone may argue that nonexistence must be more natural to them; otherwise they could last unchanged. Yet existence must also be possible for them; otherwise they would never have existed at all. If one side can be more likely than the other, why should existence not sometimes be the more likely side?384

Another objection starts with a cause that is present but cannot yet produce its effect. Perhaps a condition is missing, a motive has yet to arise, or an obstacle remains. Even so, the objector says, the cause must tend toward producing that effect; otherwise, why call it its cause? So before it acts, the cause must be able either to bring about its effect or not to do so, even though producing the effect is more likely. Let the same be true of the existence of an essence: it could exist more often than not, without existing every time.385 A cause’s effects can occur more often than not, as when the nature of earth tends to make it fall, even though a force may throw it upward and prevent the fall. Both of these claims are made up.386

The first claim confuses the strength or weakness of existence with the idea that existence is more likely for an essence than nonexistence. As we have explained, every thing has its own level of existence. Some have a stronger share of it; others have a weaker share, as with movement and things like it. This does not mean that existence is more likely for them than nonexistence, or the reverse. A movement’s parts do not remain fixed and continue to exist in the way that the parts of a stable thing do. They cannot. Our discussion, however, concerns existence in general and nonexistence in general, as they relate to an essence. That is what matters when we ask whether a thing is possible in itself. One particular way of existing may be impossible for it. But the thing can still, by its own nature, either exist or not exist at all.

Movement and similar things that do not remain fixed are equally open to continued existence and to its absence when considered in themselves. Neither side is called for by their essence. A complete cause determines whether they exist or do not exist. If we consider them as made up of parts that all exist together, however, that kind of existence is absolutely impossible for them. We have already explained that the impossibility of one particular way of existing does not remove essential possibility in general.

The second claim mistakes something that is not yet a complete cause for a cause. Before all the conditions for its effect are met, a thing is not yet acting as a cause at all. Once those conditions are met, it brings about its effect without fail. An effect may be closer to happening when fewer conditions remain to be met. But this does not make the thing itself any more or less able to exist. What changes is its readiness for the effect, which can grow stronger or weaker and is a real feature of the world. Whether a thing, considered in itself, can exist or fail to exist is a different question—one the mind answers without measuring that readiness. A thoughtful reader can use the principles already given to dismiss the wild claims made by some disputants on this subject. There is no point in listing and answering them; doing so would waste time without purpose and spend the precious days of life for no return.

Section: What makes a thing need a cause: possibility in its essence and limitation in its existence

Some people make a show of reasoning and sound judgment without having learned enough to judge well. They have gone to extremes in denying the truth, and they disagree even among themselves. Some say that being brought into existence after not existing is, by itself, what makes a thing need a cause. Some say it is one part of what makes a thing need a cause. Others say it is a condition for needing a cause, while possibility itself is what makes a thing need one. Still others prepare for debate by questioning a judgment that comes naturally to the mind—a judgment present in children and even built into animals, as when an animal recoils at the sound of sticks or clubs. Their claims are not worth the time spent mocking them or the effort of wearing down one’s mind. Yet ordinary people and most students are drawn to them.

We say:387 if a feature must belong to a thing, or cannot belong to it, by the thing’s own nature, then the thing does not need something else in order to have that feature. Nor can that feature depend on something else. So if coming into existence after not existing is part of what makes a thing need a cause, whether as a condition or as one of its parts, that feature can only apply to something possible in itself—not to something necessary or impossible. In the end, then, the explanation comes back to possibility alone. That defeats the claim that origination is what makes a thing need a cause.

There is another way to see this. Origination is a feature of the relation in which existence comes after nonexistence. But that relation comes after existence;388 existence comes after the act of bringing something into being; that act comes after the thing’s need for a cause; and that need comes after its possibility.389 If beginning to exist were the reason a thing needed a cause, that beginning would have to come before itself, by several steps. That is impossible.

Someone might object that possibility, too, is a feature of a relation to existence, and so should come later. But possibility is a state the mind assigns to the relation between the idea of existence and an essence, when it considers the essence in itself. It is not a relation that takes place in the world. So possibility follows the ideas of essence and existence as the mind considers them; it does not follow an actual relation in the world.390 Origination, by contrast, is a feature of something as it actually exists in the world. An essence or existence is described as originated only when it exists. Origination plainly comes after the act that gives existence.

Those who deny the self-evidence of this claim say: “Put this judgment before the mind: existence and nonexistence are equally open to an essence in itself, so one side cannot be preferred without some cause outside it.391 Then put beside it the judgment that one is half of two. The second is clearer and stronger than the first. But this difference only makes sense if the first allows some doubt that the second does not.392 Once the opposite of a claim is possible, complete certainty is gone.”

Here is their mistake. Two truths can be equally certain even when one is easier to grasp than the other. How quickly someone sees a truth also varies. It depends on the ideas being considered, the person doing the thinking, and the experience they have gained. Some abilities are natural; others grow through practice. The mind learns to recognise how truths fit together much as the ear learns to hear the rhythm of words and the pattern of sounds. Both can recognise what belongs together and what does not. Anyone whose judgment is not weak or distorted, and whose mind has not been clouded by constant debate and argument, will see that one of two things alike in every respect cannot be preferred without some distinguishing cause.

Whoever accepts that one thing can be preferred over an equal thing without a reason is in danger of leaving human nature behind. This comes from an evil disposition, rooted in a flawed natural capacity and an inborn rebelliousness. In the unjust village of matter and the corrupt city of the lower world, that person’s corrupted nature has taken on the darkness of false imagination.

Those who accept preference without a reason have split into several groups. One group says that God created the world at one particular time rather than any other, without anything that made that time the one to choose. Another says that God assigned certain actions particular rulings—required or forbidden, good or bad—without anything in the nature of those actions calling for those rulings. Consider also393 someone fleeing a wild animal who reaches two roads identical in every respect, or a hungry person choosing between two identical loaves. The claim is that either person could choose one option for no reason at all.

Another group says that when one of two matching things has a feature or state that the other lacks, nothing explains the difference. For if the difference had a cause, they say, the cause itself would have to be explained, and the same question would arise again.394 Yet another group says that all essences are equal in being essences, even though some have one feature rather than another.395

These are the arguments they cling to. If they woke from their ignorance, they would see that God’s creation contains causes beyond our knowledge and sight. To be unaware of a cause is not to show that no cause exists. Each of the small examples they use to deny that one matching thing can be preferred over another—the two roads, the two cups of water, and the two loaves—may have hidden factors that people who trust in chance cannot see. At the very least, there may be the alignment of heavenly bodies, the arrangement of the skies, or conditions that prepare one outcome rather than another. Beyond these lie the highest causes through which God has determined and ordered events, including the forms of things that already exist in His highest knowledge, in the fullest and most fitting way.396

As for the claim that the philosopher Empedocles believed in luck and chance, it seems likely that he spoke in symbols, as he and other early thinkers often did when hiding divine secrets behind images and figurative language. Some scholars explain his words this way: he denied only that God, who is necessary in Himself, acts for a purpose beyond His own essence.397 He still accepted that what is not necessary does not come into existence. He and others called things “by chance” when they belong to an essence not because of its own nature but because of something else. In that sense, one can say that the world’s existence is by chance. This does not mean that the world brings itself into existence or that God acts at random. It means that the world does not exist by its own nature; it exists through another.

Another explanation occurs to me. As we have seen, what a possible thing is, considered apart from its existence, is only a shadow or reflection of its actual being. What is created is its existence, not its nature considered on its own. Likewise, a purpose belongs to the ways in which things exist, not to those natures taken by themselves. So the essence of the world comes about without being, in itself, the direct object of an end or an act of creation; its existence truly needs both an end and an agent. Empedocles may have called this “by chance” to mean “in a dependent or incidental way.” It resembles the aspects that, in their account, are joined to the First Effect to explain how many things can come from it even though it is simple. On that view, only one aspect—the existence of the First Effect—comes directly from the Necessary Being. Other aspects, such as its essence, its possibility, and the necessity it receives through another, come about only in a dependent way. Otherwise, many things would flow directly from what is absolutely one, or the First Being would have parts. Both are impossible.398399

The early philosophers often spoke in puzzles and symbols. Many who came after them either misunderstood their words because they did not know their place or purpose, or twisted them out of a desire to rule over people in this fleeting world. Others believed the words simply because they trusted the speaker, then openly adopted the claim that things happen by chance. They went far astray. What we should follow is certain proof or direct insight. Truth cannot be understood from words alone, since terms and languages differ, and ideas can be combined and separated in different ways. Those who say that things happen by chance have several arguments.

The first is this: if a thing exists because a cause acts on it, then the cause must act either while the effect exists or while it does not exist. The first seems to produce something that already exists. The second seems to join opposites: the effect exists and does not exist at the same time. The reply turns on a distinction. A cause may act when its effect comes into being. That does not mean the effect must already exist before the cause can act. In the first statement, we are saying when the action happens. In the second, we would be making the effect’s existence a condition of the action. There is no problem with the first case. It is simply how a cause acts together with its effect: a cause and its effect exist at the same time, or at times that count as one for this purpose, and neither exists without the other. Every cause acts when its effect comes into being. It brings about the effect as such—not on the assumption that the effect already exists, nor on the assumption that it does not exist. The cause produces the effect at the very moment it comes to exist. It brings about something that has come about through that very act, not through some other act. There is no contradiction in this.400

Here is another way to answer. If “while the effect comes into being” means that the cause and effect exist at the same time, then we choose the first option: the cause acts while the effect exists.401 If it means that cause and effect are together at the same level in the order of what they are,402 then we say the cause acts neither while the effect exists nor while it does not exist. Neither of the two problems follows. The cause acts on the essence of the effect considered just as it is, not on the essence as either existing or nonexistent. In that respect, the essence is not naturally tied to the cause. But the essence as it exists or does not exist comes after the cause’s existence or nonexistence and accompanies it in reality. Consider this carefully.403

Debaters have another difficult answer: the cause acts when the effect is coming into being,404 a state that is neither existence nor nonexistence. Some make the argument even worse by saying that the cause and effect do not have to occur together.405 They use sound as an example: it exists in one moment and comes from the person making it in the moment before.

The second argument is that a cause must act on one of three things: the essence, its existence, or its being described as existent. The first cannot be right, they say, because whatever depends on something else would cease to exist if that other thing did not exist. But an essence cannot be removed from itself. The second cannot be right either, because then existence would stop being existence whenever the cause stopped acting. Someone may object that this would not mean a human being remained human but became “not human”; rather, the human being would simply disappear. The reply is that even “the human being is not human” is a statement that needs a subject to be settled in the judgment. We cannot both take that subject as given and deny it in the same way. If the human being disappears, the subject of the statement is gone. So what disappeared is also what was there as the subject of the denial. The thing would have to be both there and not there, settled and unsettled. The same problem applies to existence.406

The third option also fails. Saying that something has a feature establishes a link in the mind. That link cannot be the first thing a cause brings into existence: we must first have the things it links. And the relation itself has an essence, so the question returns: is the cause’s effect the relation itself, the relation’s existence, or the relation of that relation to existence? The same question would apply to each new relation, and the chain would continue without end.407

A well-known reply is that the act of creation is directed to the human essence itself; existence and being described as existent then follow from it because they are ideas in the mind whose basis is the essence brought about by the creator. A human being is not human because an outside agent acts on it. Rather, the human essence itself comes from another. The simple essence is the effect of the cause; it is not the more complex state of the essence being joined to itself or to something else, as in the statements “a human being is human” or “a human being exists.” A human being is human by its own nature, but its essence comes from another. The difference between these two claims is clear.

If we first suppose the simple human essence itself, then its being human follows necessarily from that supposition. An outside cause cannot make it human, because what is already necessary in itself cannot depend on another for that very feature, and what has already been assumed cannot be made again. But before we suppose the human essence, the cause can bring the essence itself into being. We may say, “The human essence is necessary through the cause,” and mean the earlier kind of necessity—the necessity that comes before the thing exists.408

We have established the difference between necessity before a thing exists and necessity after it exists. People often confuse them because a word is used in two senses, or because they mistake something that is not a cause for a cause. A human being’s being necessary through a cause does not make the human being necessary in itself. Likewise, a human being’s dependence on a cause does not mean that its being human depends on that cause. The fact that the human essence comes from another does not show that it would cease to be human if the cause were absent. Only the fact that its being human comes from another would show that.

The same applies to existence itself, which, as we have said, is brought about by a cause. Some later philosophers instead say that it is the essence itself that is brought about. We will return to the insight we have gained in this field of direct knowledge and hidden truths.

The famous philosophers in Aristotle’s school choose the third option: the cause makes an essence be described as existent. They explain that what the creator brings about is a simple, undivided reality, which the mind can analyze into a subject, a feature, and the subject’s being described by that feature.409 In the case of a human being, the creator’s effect is what the statement “a human being exists” refers to. The effect is not just the human essence by itself, nor existence by itself, but the combined state called “the essence being described as existent.” Although this relation is an idea in the mind, it fits reality. So it must depend on a cause beyond the mind’s own thought of it: the same cause that brings about the essence.

What we have said shows that the three-part division was not carefully made.410 Consider the link we express when we say that a thing exists. We can use it simply to connect the thing with existence, without making the link itself another independent thing in our thoughts. In that role it is like a mirror: we see what it connects, not the mirror itself. But if the mind turns its attention to it separately, removing it from its role as a link, it becomes an object of thought in its own right, distinct from the two things it links. It then becomes like any other essence, and we can again ask: what aspect of it depends on the creator, and through what feature does the creator act on it? Those are among the questions people have raised.

Section — How a possible thing’s nonexistence needs a cause

Here is an objection.411 If something does not exist because a cause made nonexistence more likely, then the cause must somehow act on nonexistence. But nonexistence is nothing at all. How could anything act on it? Also, if a possible thing does not exist because the cause of its existence is absent, that seems to require different kinds of nonexistence—some acting as causes and others as effects. Yet absences have no distinctions or order, so there can be no cause and effect among them.

The answer is that nonexistence here is not simply nothing. The mind first considers what a thing would be. It then asks whether it exists or does not exist. Nothing about what it is, considered on its own, settles either question—in thought or in the world. Something beyond it is needed for one outcome rather than the other. A cause does not put something inside an essence for the essence to carry or possess in reality. Rather, it brings about something called existence.

The existence brought about by the cause has a nature of its own, without a second act producing that nature. What the thing is takes on the colour of existence and is lit by its light for as long as that existence lasts, as we have explained. Likewise, when a cause brings about an essence’s nonexistence, all that means is that it does not bring about something that joins with the essence in a certain way—as one of its features.

The mind can judge whether something exists in two ways. It can start from the cause, asking whether that cause exists and what must follow from it. Or it can start from the results: if they are present, they point to the thing’s existence; if they are absent, that can point to its absence. These are reasoning from causes and reasoning from effects.

So the factor that tips the balance toward nonexistence, like the factor that tips it toward existence, must have some share in existence. Sheer nonexistence, simply as nonexistence, cannot cause anything. A cause that tips the balance toward existence must itself be something real and actual, whether or not we think about it. By contrast, what tips the balance toward nonexistence is only an idea the mind considers; it has no reality outside that act of thought. That is enough for the mind to judge that it leads to the effect’s nonexistence, both in thought and in the outside world, though in different ways.

When the absence of a cause leads to the absence of an effect in the outside world, this means that neither exists at all—not even as something negative or as a relation. In the mind, by contrast, considering and affirming that the cause is absent leads us to consider and affirm that the effect is absent. The thought of the effect’s absence also leads us back to the thought that its cause is absent, but it does not make us judge that the cause is absent. In short, the mind can distinguish between ideas of absence and treat one as a reason for another. What cannot be distinguished is absence as sheer absence, and that is not what is happening here.

In summary, possible essences and other settled realities have states and relations that the mind considers before they exist in the outside world. The mind arranges some of these ideas in relation to others, though nothing outside the mind corresponds to them. Outside the mind, there is only existence.

The mind then pictures an essence as joined with existence, while recognizing that the idea of essence differs from the idea of existence. Considered in itself, the essence is bare of both existence and nonexistence: neither is necessary to it, and neither is ruled out. The mind therefore concludes that for either to be realized, something beyond the essence must tip the balance. Our reasoning therefore takes this order: the thing is possible; it needs a cause; the cause makes its existence necessary; the cause brings it into being; and the thing exists.412

This does not conflict with existence being first among all things that come from a cause. The discussion here looks at the essence in relation to its existence and to the cause that gives it existence. Something may also come later in its dependent existence than something that is prior to it in itself. For example, in natural philosophy, one establishes that motion exists before proving that it has a source and an unmoved mover whose power has no limit. The body’s changing nature is considered first; only later is it shown to have a mover that is necessary in itself, even though that Necessary Being is prior to all things in reality. So there is no contradiction in existence being prior to essence in itself, while the mind considers essence and its earlier conditions first as it traces their dependence on existence.

A point to keep in mind

We have hinted at this and will explain it further. A general idea in the mind, whether it describes what a thing is or a feature it has, is not what the One who exists through Himself brings into being.413 What is directly caused is existence itself, whether that existence is called originated or enduring. In fact, if both depend on another, enduring existence depends on its cause even more than originated existence does.

When you analyze originated existence into the fact that something was absent and then became present, you see that its prior nonexistence is not directly caused by an existing cause. The fact that existence follows nonexistence belongs to what that existence is. What depends on the cause is existence itself, considered apart from what follows from it.414 The cause produces nothing but existence. Some existence is therefore called originated by its own nature, not because another cause or the thing itself made it so. Likewise, a body depends on a cause for its existence, but its boundedness follows from the body itself.415

An essence needs a cause for its existence because, by itself, it is equally open to existence and nonexistence; the cause gives it existence. But its being equally open to both, or the fact that its existence follows a prior absence—whether that absence is prior in nature or in time—is necessary and does not need a cause. The same holds for existence itself: it needs and is sustained by its cause because it is, by its own nature, weak, dependent, and like a shadow. What it receives from its cause is this dependent existence itself, not its being described as originated or eternal.416

Some later scholars put the point this way: for a reality that comes from another, dependence on that other is part of what it is, just as independence from all others is part of the Necessary Being’s reality. A dependent thing cannot remain the same dependent thing while becoming independent, just as what is independent of all things cannot become dependent. Either change would mean its nature had changed.

Our view makes this especially clear. A thing that could exist or not exist depends on its maker because of its existence, not because of what the thing is. That very existence depends on its maker: the dependence is part of what makes it this existence.417 It cannot be thought of without that dependence; otherwise, it would no longer be this kind of existence. Likewise, existence that depends on nothing is what it is: if it became dependent, it would no longer be that. So dependent existence needs its cause at every moment, both when it begins and while it continues. Its need to continue is no different from its need to begin.

This does not mean that the cause makes existence come after nonexistence, or after some earlier state. Those are features that follow from existence itself without being caused. What the cause makes is existence itself, not its features, including its not being eternal.418 God’s act is to give existence to things, sustain and preserve them, and keep each one for as long as its nature allows. Their defects and limits come from themselves.

Here is an imperfect comparison. The sun shines freely on things that can receive its light. If something is kept in shadow, the obstacle is on its side, not the sun’s. Likewise, the One Being continually lights the forms of possible things and brings them from the darkness of nonexistence into the daylight of existence. If we imagine that He stopped giving them existence for even a moment, they would return to the darkness of their own nature.419 Glory to the Powerful, the Wise, who holds the heavens and earth so they do not fall; and if they were to fall, no one after Him could hold them.

How mistaken are those who think the world needs its Sustainer only when it first comes into being, and not while it continues! Some have even said, out of ignorance and stubbornness, that if God’s nonexistence were possible, the world’s existence afterward would be unaffected, since He had already brought it into being.420 This is a deeply mistaken view. Every genuine cause exists together with its effect, both when the effect begins and for as long as it continues, as we will explain in our discussion of cause and effect.421

Fire gives heat to the bodies around it because heat belongs to its very nature, or form. Water makes nearby things wet because moisture belongs to it, just as heat belongs to fire. The sun lights the stars and bodies below because light belongs to its nature. What a thing does by its own nature does not change.

Likewise, the soul gives life to the body. Life belongs to the soul’s nature and is a form that makes it what it is. The soul keeps giving life to the body, which is dead in itself but alive through the soul, as long as the body remains able to receive life from it.422 When the body loses this capacity, the soul leaves it. The same relation holds between every cause that produces its effect by its own nature.

A builder puts together a house; a tailor joins pieces of cloth to make a garment. But treating this kind of assembly423 as a model of creation mistakes an indirect cause for a direct one. God does not merely join existing parts together, as some have claimed. He creates: He brings into existence what did not exist before. That is something different from assembling parts.

Consider speech and writing. The speaker’s speech is like creation; the writer’s work is like putting parts together. When the speaker falls silent, the speech ends. When the writer stops, the writing remains. The world’s existence from God, exalted be His glory, is like speech from a speaker. All kinds of intellectual and soul existence, and all spiritual and bodily beings, are words of God that do not run out.424 If the sea of matter were ink for the words of existence spoken by its Lord, it would run dry before His words did, even if more seas were added from the matter of the heavens.425

This echoes the verse: “If every tree on earth were a pen, and the sea were supplied with seven more seas, God’s words would not run out. God is Mighty and Wise.”

Section — A possible thing exists only if its cause makes it necessary

We have established that a possible thing does not exist unless something else tips the balance in favor of its existence. It does not cease to exist unless something else tips the balance towards its nonexistence. So whichever side is realized, the thing must have a cause outside itself that tips the balance.

But how far must the cause tip the balance? Unless it makes one outcome necessary, it has not settled anything. Many theologians have thought that making existence preferable is enough, even if nonexistence remains possible. It is not. So long as either outcome can still occur, we must ask what makes one occur rather than the other. This supposed preference has left the choice between the two outcomes open.426427 We would need another factor to settle it. If that factor also leaves both outcomes possible, we must look for yet another—and repeat the search without end.

Even then, neither side has been settled. At every level, however many levels we suppose, the weak preference remains equally related to existence and nonexistence, even with all the assumed factors in place. So what we called the deciding cause has not decided anything. This shows that the assumption is impossible without appealing to the impossibility of an infinite chain of causes and effects; that question does not arise here. The contradiction is simpler: the factor assumed to decide the outcome does not do so. That would make the supposed deciding factor both a deciding factor and not one, which is impossible.

In short, necessity is where the chain of possibilities ends. Actual existence is the starting point from which the many branches of unrealized powers unfold. That is why people say: necessity comes before possibility, actuality before potentiality, form before matter. Good prevails over evil, existence overcomes nonexistence, and God’s mercy comes before His anger, as we will explain in our discussion of potentiality and actuality.

We have therefore shown that neither a thing that could exist or not exist, nor its dependent existence, becomes real unless its cause makes it necessary. A cause is not a cause of an effect unless it brings that effect about decisively. Once we speak of a cause and its effect, each necessarily stands in that relation to the other. The First Cause must not only exist; it must also be the source of other things. As we shall explain, God necessarily gives existence to what comes from Him. God willing, we shall return to this.

Section — The two kinds of necessity and impossibility

The last chapter showed that, before either outcome occurs, a complete cause makes one of two things necessary: the thing will exist, or it will not. At the same time, that cause rules out the opposite outcome. Once either existence or nonexistence has actually occurred, a second kind of necessity applies. While a thing has a feature, it must be described as having it. So while a thing exists, it must be described as existing; it cannot at the same time be described as absent. And while it is absent, it cannot at the same time be described as present.

Every possible thing—whether it exists or not, by itself or through another—is therefore subject to two kinds of necessity and two kinds of impossibility when we consider its cause and its actual state. In reality, it cannot be free of them, whether it exists or not. Yet what a thing is, considered by itself and apart from any cause or actual state, remains open to either existence or nonexistence.

The earlier necessity and impossibility of a possible thing both come from something else. The same is true of the later necessity and impossibility if by “possible thing” we mean its essence. But if we mean the existence it has actually received, the later necessity and impossibility follow from existence itself.

Here is why. When we say that an essence must exist at a certain time, we mean the essence under the condition that it exists. Existence is a condition for the statement, not a part of the essence. We do not mean that the essence and the idea of existence together form a new thing. The essence, considered under this condition, is already there; that is why the claim that it exists must be true. But the essence by itself remains possible, even though its actual existence is necessary in reality.

The word “existent” also applies to every actual existence in a way that must be true for as long as that reality exists.428 If we imagine a particular dependent existence cut off from its cause, it has no reality at all. The essence, by contrast, remains possible in itself even when its existence comes from a cause.

Every statement that describes something or connects it to a feature has this later necessity. It may also have another kind of necessity: the timeless necessity in “God exists and has power”; a necessity that depends on what the thing is; a necessity that depends on a description, whether the description is part of the thing or added to it; or simple possibility. In short, if existence or nonexistence applies to an essence at some time, the opposite remains possible when we consider the essence by itself. But if we consider the essence in the state it actually has, the opposite is impossible. This impossibility comes from that state or from the condition attached to it, not from the essence by itself. It is impossible through something else in one sense, and through the condition itself in another.

A possible misunderstanding

Someone may think that a possible thing, taken together with its existence, cannot fail to exist by its own nature. After all, existence and nonexistence cannot be true at the same time. This would make existence necessary in itself, and the whole possible thing necessary in itself too.429

But this misses a point we have made several times: the necessity here is not timeless or absolute. It holds only while the thing remains in the stated condition. Someone who is human must be human while they are human. Likewise, a person who exists must exist while they exist. This necessity is really through another, because possible things exist—and are described as existing—only after a cause brings them into being. The same goes for a whole made from two things that are each necessary: the whole is necessary through another, not by itself. Likewise, a whole made from two impossible things is impossible through another. Before all its parts are together, the whole is not yet there; it becomes necessary or impossible only while it is a whole.

Some have offered a poor escape from the argument. They say that an essence considered together with existence is only an idea in the mind, because they regard existence itself as an idea. How, then, could that imagined combination be necessary? But they have missed the point. No one is claiming that the idea alone must exist. We are speaking about what the idea refers to: the thing itself, considered while it exists. It necessarily exists in that condition, whether or not one accepts our view that existence is real outside the mind.430

Another respected scholar takes a different approach. He says that if nonexistence is impossible for a thing while it exists, then what must hold is only that the thing not be absent while it exists. This is a broader claim than saying that it exists at that time. It could still be true if the thing were absent at every time, because the condition “while it exists” would never arise. So, he concludes, the fact that a thing must exist while it exists comes from its cause and can be taken away from the essence itself.

This argument would help only if necessity of existence followed merely from nonexistence being impossible. But our claim is that the essence, under the condition that it exists, must have existence431—just as a part must belong to the whole and an effect must depend on its cause. A possible thing that exists must have existence, whether existence is its condition or part, or whether it depends on its cause or is produced by it. In the same way, a thing made by God cannot be separated from God while it is His creation: the cause is part of what sustains the effect’s existence. This is why the report has God say to Moses, “I am the one who stays close to you.” So we must return to the account we have established.

One critic who tried to answer the defenders of truth with argument alone, and to imitate people of spiritual experience with words alone—like someone trying to fight a battle by carrying heavy gear—wrote in a book called The Incoherence of the Philosophers that the opposite side can be compared to a possible thing in several ways.

First, we can compare it with the essence by itself, without considering what has actually happened to it. In that sense, the opposite side remains possible for it at that time and at every time.

Second, we can compare it with the essence under the condition that the other side has occurred, without making that condition part of the essence. If we ask whether the opposite applies to the essence by itself, it may remain possible at every time, even though the actual condition makes it impossible at that time. If instead we ask whether the opposite applies to the essence as it is under that condition, the opposite may be possible in itself, may actually occur, or may be impossible in itself.432 For example, if we consider a possible thing as existing, its nonexistence may still be possible for its essence, even though it now exists. This does not mean it both exists and does not exist, because each claim concerns the essence in a different respect.433 But if we consider a possible thing as nonexistent, its existence is impossible for it in that respect.

Third, we can compare the essence with its actual state as part of the thing we are describing. We can make the same two distinctions here. In this case there is even less reason to think that a contradiction follows.434 The critic concludes that the opposite is possible in itself in the first two ways of considering it, and impossible in itself in the last two.

The weakness of this argument is clear if we remember what we have already explained. The question is not whether one side can be imagined as impossible in relation to the other, while the mind ignores what is real. The question is what the opposite side would be like in reality. An essence that actually exists cannot, in reality, fail to exist at that same time, whether we consider its state as a condition or as part of what we are describing.

The subject of both claims is the same essence. We do not add the idea of “being under this condition” to the essence as if they formed a new thing in reality. We consider the real essence in a way that matches the mind’s description of it as existing. There is no real mixture in that essence—only a distinction the mind makes. So the opposite side is impossible for it in itself, and the side that actually holds is necessary in itself.

This critic’s argument also fails when applied to existence itself. Existence is what makes something actually real, and in every case it comes with this later necessity. It is itself a real thing. In a statement such as “existence is real,” it is both the subject and what is said of the subject; its opposite, “existence is not real,” is impossible in itself.435 The only way through this difficulty is to keep apart the two kinds of necessity: the necessity that holds while a thing remains in a condition, which causes no problem, and absolute, timeless necessity, which does not follow here.

Addendum

Any possible thing that has received existence and necessity through another at some time436 cannot fail to exist at that time. Nor can we say that it has no place anywhere in reality.437 That would mean it is absent from every level of reality, without restricting the claim to some other time.438 But we already know that it existed at one time.

Thus, when we say that a thing which exists at one time could have been nonexistent, we mean that nonexistence is possible for its nature considered by itself. We do not mean that what actually existed has no place in reality.

Section — Why some possible things have one kind of possibility and others have two

Some possible things439 can receive existence from the generosity of the highest source simply because of what they are. They need no outside condition and no further feature to make them ready. Their existence therefore flows from the generous source without delay, without a stretch of time when they did not exist, and without any bodily preparation. Each has only one way of existing; its kind is represented by a single instance. Different instances of the same kind arise only when causes outside the essence make them different. What follows from a thing’s nature, or from a feature that belongs to it, does not change. So there is no room here for many different instances of the same kind.

Other possible things cannot receive existence through their essence alone. Their nature gives them only the capacity to exist, not full readiness to receive existence. They need outside conditions and causes that do not belong to their essence. When the needed conditions come together in matter, the thing becomes ready to exist. What was once remote from its cause is now close enough to receive its action. Alongside the basic possibility of its nature, it has acquired a second kind of possibility: actual readiness. This readiness develops in changing matter over time, until the power to receive and the power to act meet. Through their coming together, something new is brought into existence.

Every possible thing depends on a cause that must exist and is fully able to act. Such a cause cannot give existence to one thing that is ready and withhold it from another equally ready thing without a reason. Differences in what things receive must therefore arise from differences in their readiness.

Anything that could exist has that possibility simply because of what it is. But suppose this alone were enough for God to bring it into existence. Since His giving is complete and holds nothing back, everything that could exist would exist immediately. Nothing would begin at one time rather than another. Yet we know that things do begin at different times.

If basic possibility is not enough, and a thing needs further conditions before it can receive existence, then that thing has two kinds of possibility. The first is basic possibility: one general idea shared by every possible thing and belonging to its essence. The second is readiness, which appears when a thing’s basic possibility is not enough to receive existence. This second kind belongs to matter that exists before the thing in time and prepares it to pass from potential to actual. We have discussed this readiness before.

With readiness, one essence can take on endlessly many forms. Matter can be prepared in endlessly many ways, and this receptive matter can meet a source whose power has no limit. So blessings continue to flow without end. If basic possibility were the only kind, the flow of existence would be blocked. Many possible things would remain forever in nonexistence, instead of becoming what they can be. We will prove later that this is impossible. Nothing in these claims conflicts with the sound teaching of religion or with sound philosophy.

The mistake lies in saying that things that begin in time have always existed, or that the power of possibility has no limit.440 Events that follow one another in time come about only through motion, change, matter, and time. But things brought into being by direct creation441 are not always preceded by time and place. This is true whether they exist beyond time and place or are joined to them without undergoing gradual change. They are sources of motion, whether as things that move or as things toward which movement is directed.442

God is above all: the First, with nothing before Him; the Last, with nothing after Him. He is wholly active, with no potential waiting to be realized; wholly necessary, with no possibility of not existing; wholly good, with no evil; complete, with no lack; perfect, with no shortcoming; the goal of all things, with nothing left for Him to await; pure existence, with no essence apart from it.443

When two contrasting features are in question, what God directly gives is the nobler one. The other is not separately created; it follows from the limits of possible beings.444 Their existence is weak and mixed with the darkness of the nonexistence that comes with their limitations. The farther things are from the First Reality, the more their possibilities differ, and the more they vary in completeness, weakness, brightness, and obscurity.

We have already said that necessity and possibility relate as completeness relates to lack. Anything that becomes necessary through another does so because of something that is not part of its essence. Burning, for example, is not necessary by itself. But when the active power of fire meets matter that can be burned, burning must occur. Think carefully: possibility and dependence come from distance from the source of necessity and independence. Actuality and existence come from nearness to that source. Possibility means separation and lack of connection, which lead to loss and disorder. Necessity means connection and union, which bring order. The more possibility there is, the more evil, loss, and disorder there are.445

When conditions remove some absences and block some obstacles to greater completeness, readiness appears. Readiness is a kind of perfection for something that is still only potential, considered as it exists in the outside world. Basic possibility, by contrast, belongs to an essence considered without existence at all. It is more hidden, darker, and more deficient than readiness, because readiness is actual in one respect even while the thing is still potential in another.

A sperm, for example, is only potential to become a human being, but it already exists as a sperm. It is not yet a complete human, but it is fully what it is as a sperm.446 Basic possibility, by contrast, is only a lack of necessity: it has no actual side of its own. Readiness concerns a particular outcome, such as becoming human. Basic possibility concerns existence or nonexistence in general. The agent, not the essence’s own possibility, gives it a particular form. Readiness also disappears when the thing it prepares for comes about. Basic possibility remains when we consider the essence in itself, apart from its actual existence. It is not a stage that comes before existence in time. So a thing’s becoming actual and necessary in the outside world does not remove the basic possibility of its essence. That possibility belongs to the essence as such and cannot be removed by an outside cause. Readiness, which belongs to the actual world, does disappear when the thing is fully realized. Basic possibility therefore involves a deeper kind of need, weakness, and lack.

Basic possibility is also the source of readiness. Matter, which makes room for loss and absence, comes from the active intellect through the possibility found in it. Since readiness has some existence, it can grow stronger or weaker according to how near the thing is to coming about. A sperm is less ready to become human than a clot of blood; the clot is less ready than a lump of flesh; and that is less ready than a complete body with the right organs, powers, and balance. Full readiness comes after basic possibility, when some causes have appeared and some obstacles have gone. It continues to grow until the thing comes about or opposing conditions arise.

In short, the word “possibility” is used in two different senses. In one sense, one side is favored over the other. This kind can grow stronger or weaker, is not part of the possible thing’s essence, and belongs to something that already exists. It is an actual quality that prepares its subject to receive existence from the generous source. The new existence may arise directly in that subject, as a form or feature, or indirectly, as with a soul that does not depend on a body.447 The other sense of possibility differs from all this.

When readiness is considered as belonging to the subject that has it, it is called that subject’s readiness. When considered in relation to the thing that will come about in it, it is called that thing’s possibility. This kind of possibility belongs to the thing that is ready, not to the future event as if it already existed. We describe the event as possible because its conditions are present in that thing.

Some scholars448 say that readiness is simply the bodily quality itself, considered in relation to the form that will arise from it. The mixture in a sperm, considered by itself, is a bodily quality; considered in relation to the animal form that will arise, it is readiness. A courtyard is a feature of the house; when we consider how many people it can hold, we call that its capacity. We will return to the correct account in the chapter on potentiality and actuality, God willing.

Section — Some rules about what is impossible in itself

Just as the mind cannot grasp the reality of the Necessary Being in Himself—because He is so great, bright, complete, and beyond all limits—it cannot directly picture what is impossible in itself, taken precisely as impossible. Its whole nature is failure and nothingness. Just as the Necessary Sustainer cannot be contained by the mind because He encompasses everything, what is impossible in itself lies outside being and thinghood. It has no reality to point to, no content for the mind to contain, and no object for awareness or imagination to reach. We reach the judgment that something is impossible in itself through an argument about what follows from it, rather than by picturing it directly. In a different way, the proof of the Creator also proceeds through an explanation resembling a proof from cause to effect.

A thing cannot be necessary both by itself and through another. Nor can it be impossible both by itself and through another. So anything that is necessary or impossible only through another is possible in itself. Anything that entails something impossible in itself is impossible in the respect in which it entails it, even if it may be possible in another respect. For example, giving a body infinite size entails the impossible claim that a bounded thing is unbounded. One side contradicts itself; the other is impossible because of that contradiction. So the body itself remains possible when we consider it apart from this impossible relation, just as an effect can be possible in itself but must exist because its cause exists.

In short, when one thing’s existence necessarily entails another’s, there must be a cause-and-effect relation between them. The same is true when one thing entails another’s absence or impossibility: there must be some relation between them. Just as two Necessary Beings, if we imagined them, might coexist by chance449 without necessarily implying one another, two things that are each impossible in themselves do not form a strict logical link. Such a link is between something impossible in itself and something impossible through another; the latter is possible in itself. This also distinguishes a strict “if … then” statement from one based on coincidence. In a strict statement, the truth or falsity of the second claim follows from the truth or falsity of the first because of a necessary link between them. In a coincidental statement, there is no such link.

In debate, people sometimes begin by assuming something impossible, hoping to show that another claim must be false. When challenged, they may reply: “Your assumption is impossible. Why could it not lead to the opposite conclusion? One impossibility can lead to another.” But that answer is wrong. An impossible claim does not imply just any other impossible claim. Even in a hypothetical case, the two must have a connection like that between cause and effect.

A strict “if … then” statement joining two false claims may therefore be true or false. If the claims have a necessary connection—for example, a human being’s being a donkey and braying—the statement is true. If the claims rule one another out, the statement is false. If neither follows from nor conflicts with the other, we can only suppose that they might go together. We cannot prove it. Certainty requires a necessary connection; possibility alone gives us grounds only for conjecture.

Section — How can we know what is impossible or nonexistent?

Whatever we know must be distinguishable from other things. And whatever can be distinguished must exist. It follows that anything we know exists, and that we cannot know what does not exist. Yet we do know that God has no partner and that contradicting claims cannot both be true. Neither of these supposed things can exist. How can we know them?

Something that does not exist may be simple or made up of parts. If it is simple—such as God’s having no opposite, partner, or equal—we understand it by comparing it with things that do exist.450 We can say, for example, that nothing stands to God as black stands to white. Nothing resembles Him, and nothing shares a kind or general class with Him. If we did not understand opposition, likeness, and shared kinds among existing things, we could not say that God has no opposite, likeness, or thing of the same kind, or anything else of this sort that cannot apply to Him.

If the thing that does not exist is made up of parts, we understand it by knowing those parts. To know that opposites, such as black and white, cannot be together, we first understand black and white, then consider them together, where that is possible.451 We then say that although we can understand the idea of their being together, it does not occur in reality. This is the answer others have given: we understand the absence of something simple by comparing it with what exists, and the absence of something made up of parts by understanding its parts.

My own answer is different. The mind can form an idea of anything, even what is impossible: absolute nonexistence, the absolutely unknown, two contradictions together, or a partner to God. The mind can make suitable claims about these concepts without saying that they exist outside the mind. As ideas, they have a kind of presence: we can call them things in a broad sense, say that they are possible to think about, or describe them as mental qualities, acts of knowledge, and the like. This gives us a basis for making claims about them.

But when those same ideas stand for things that cannot exist, they give us no basis for making claims about such things as realities. If we distinguish the idea in our minds from what it supposedly stands for, we can say that nothing can be reported or affirmed of the nonexistent thing itself. This resolves the famous puzzle in the claim “Nothing can be said about the absolutely unknown.”452453

The key is that some concepts apply to themselves as ideas, but not as real things.454 The idea of “a partner to God” or “the absolutely unknown” is itself a concept, but it does not name an actual thing. In one sense, the concept applies to itself; in another, it does not. This is why we can correctly say that such a thing cannot exist.

Section — How one impossible thing can entail another

Remember455 that debaters often say an impossible assumption may lead to any impossible conclusion. That is not generally true. Two claims, whether possible or impossible, can be linked by necessity only if they have a connection of their own. In that case, once we grant one claim, the mind cannot separate it from the other. The connection may be between a cause and its effect, or between two effects of the same cause.

A necessary link must be possible between the two things. So if two impossible claims could be linked, were they to occur, we may say that one entails the other. If there is no such link, we cannot. For example, if a whole made from two impossible things were to exist, then at least one of those things would have to exist. If Zayd were a donkey, he would bray. And a circular chain of causes would lead to an endless chain of causes.456 These are cases where one impossible claim entails another because of a necessary link.

But two impossible claims may have no necessary connection. They may even conflict. A whole consisting of two things impossible in themselves could not exist if only one of those things existed. Likewise, if a human being were a donkey, that person could not at the same time be a horse that neighs. Nor could a donkey, under that very assumption, understand general ideas as a human intellect does. We can see some of these conflicts immediately; others require an argument.

So the claim that one impossibility may imply another is true only in some cases. The claim that what actually occurs cannot imply an impossibility is true without exception.

A strict “if … then” statement joining two false claims is true only if there is a necessary link between them. If they conflict, the statement is simply false. If there is no necessary link and no conflict, they may happen to go together, but we can accept that only as a possibility, not as a proven fact. Coincidence applies to things that actually exist; when both claims are false, their coincidence can only be supposed.457 We can be certain only when there is a necessary link. Mere possibility leaves room for doubt.

Some people think that, for one impossible claim to possibly imply another, it is enough that the two do not conflict, even if there is no necessary link. Others require a necessary link. A third group thinks that two claims might necessarily imply one another even while they contradict each other. They try to allow both implication and conflict. But these cannot both be true in the same respect.

Someone may also argue that a contradiction implies that both sides are absent, since each side rules out the other.

The flaw is clear. If one side of a contradiction actually exists, then the other side is absent. But that is not the case we are considering. We are assuming the impossible situation in which both sides exist together. Under that assumption, the existence of one side implies the existence of the other, not that both are absent. So why would their being together imply that neither exists?

This also answers an objection about chains of strict “if … then” statements. Someone may say that the second link in such a chain can stop being true once the first claim is assumed. For example: “If this color were both black and white, it would be black. If it were black, it would not be white. So if this color were both black and white, it would not be white.”

The answer is that “black” does not mean the same thing in both statements. In the first, we are assuming that black and white can occur together. In the second, black means a colour that excludes white. Because the word changes its meaning, the two statements have no genuinely shared middle step. If “black” meant the same thing in both, the conclusion would follow. If it meant black as something that could occur alongside white in both, the second statement would be false.

Avicenna raises a similar puzzle in The Healing: “If two were odd, it would still be a number. Whenever it is a number, it is even. So if two were odd, it would be even.” The answer is that if the second statement is only a coincidence, the chain proves nothing; a valid chain of positive “if … then” statements needs a strict link. If the second statement is strict, it is not true in every possible case in which two is a number. One such assumed case is that two is odd, and under that assumption it is not even.458

Someone may object that two cannot be odd while still being two, so evenness must follow whenever two is a number. Another answer is that “two is odd” is false in reality, but can be granted for the sake of argument. Anyone who grants it must also accept the conclusion within that argument; otherwise, they are no longer talking about the number two.

Both answers make the same point. If being odd conflicts with being two in reality, that is no problem: a hypothetical case need not be possible in reality. But it is wrong to say the conflict holds under every assumption. We can suppose that two is odd, and under that supposition its being a number follows. So “two is even” does not follow from “two is a number” in every possible way the premise may be understood.

Section — In what sense existence is added to a possible thing’s essence

Saying that existence is “added” to a possible thing’s essence does not mean that the two are separate realities. The reality of a thing is its own particular existence. Nor does it mean that existence is a separate feature attached to the essence, like a color attached to a body.459 That would mean the essence needs another existence beyond its own.

What we call a possible thing’s existence is limited and dependent. Because of those limits, the mind can draw from it an idea distinct from existence itself: what the thing is. Think of the patterns cast by light as it grows weaker and gives way to shadow. The standard arguments for adding existence to what a thing is prove only that these are two different ideas. They do not prove that they are two separate realities.

The first proof is that saying “a thing exists” tells us something, while saying “a thing is what it is” or naming its essential features tells us nothing new. Second, we may need an argument to establish that something exists—for example, an intellect that is not bodily. But we do not need an argument to show that a thing is what it is or has the features that make it that kind of thing. The third is that we can deny existence of an essence: “The phoenix does not exist.” But we cannot deny an essence or its essential features of themselves.

The fourth proof is that existence has one shared meaning, while the essences of a human being, a horse, and a tree are different. The fifth is that we can think about what a thing is without deciding whether it exists in the outside world or in the mind. Someone might object: “But to think of something is for it to exist in the mind.” That has not been established. Even if an argument established it, thinking of something would not mean that we must also think about our thinking.460

Most people put the point this way: “We can understand an essence and still doubt whether it exists in reality or in the mind.” But this only shows that we can understand what something is without affirming that it exists. It does not prove that essence and existence are separate in reality. The reasoning shifts between what we understand and what we affirm, so it does not use the same middle term throughout.

These five arguments, once fully stated, show only that the ideas of existence and essence are different. Yet what their proponents want to establish is that they differ in reality.461 Consider the divine attributes: for those who hold the truth, they differ in meaning but are one in reality, because the reality of God’s essence is itself the reality of all His perfect attributes, as we will see, God willing.

Section — How a possible thing’s existence is one with its essence outside the mind, and joined to it in a certain way

As we have shown, existence in its true sense—not the general idea of existence formed by the mind—is something real.462 If the existence of a possible thing were not one with its essence in reality, as a real thing is joined to an idea, then existence would have to be either the essence itself in meaning or one of its parts. Both possibilities have already been shown, by agreement and by reason, to be false. We can understand an essence without being aware of whether it exists, among other arguments already mentioned.

Perhaps existence is something added to what a thing is, as whiteness is added to a body. But a quality can belong to something only if that thing already exists. Applied to existence itself, this would mean either that the thing exists before it exists, or that it has more than one existence in the same respect. Neither is possible. Something that has no existence of its own cannot carry a quality.

If the essence were made existent by an existence added to it, the essence would have to exist before that existence, since what bears a quality must exist before the quality. The essence would therefore come before itself. If it existed through another existence, we would face the second problem: one essence would have multiple existences. This would lead to an endless chain of existences all present at once. Such a chain is impossible by proof, and would leave an infinite number of things between two limits: existence and essence. This, in turn, proves the point we seek: in reality, existence is the essence itself. For if every existence added to the essence depends on it, with none left out, then the essence must have an existence that is not added to it.463 Otherwise, the set would not be complete.

Here is another argument. If existence were a quality present in an essence, then the essence bearing it would either be nonexistent, which is contradictory, or existent, which would lead to circularity or an endless regress. Someone might answer that existence belongs to the essence considered simply as it is—not to an essence that is nonexistent, which would be contradictory, nor to one that already exists, which would lead to circularity or an endless regress. But this reply does not solve the problem. Its defender compares existence with whiteness: whiteness, they say, does not belong to a body already white, for that would assume what we are trying to explain; nor does it belong to a body that is not white, for that would contradict the claim. It belongs to the body considered simply as a body.

A body considered simply as it is—that is, apart from being white or nonwhite—already exists outside the mind, before either quality is present. But an essence considered simply as it is, with existence and nonexistence set aside, has no reality outside the mind except through its existence. It does not exist before existence. So nothing can be established in it in reality just because we consider it simply as it is. Anything attributed to it in that respect is only an idea the mind draws from it, not something real that exists in it. This differs from a body, which already exists outside the mind before whiteness or nonwhiteness is attributed to it. Whiteness belongs to a body because the body exists, not because it is already white.

Likewise, any quality, whether whiteness or something else, belongs to any bearer, whether a body or something else, because the bearer exists in itself—not because the quality exists in it. So neither self-dependence nor an endless regress follows. Existence is different: if it were a quality added to an essence, the essence’s existence would depend on its own existence. To compare existence, if it were an added quality, with other qualities is a mistake.

The truth, as we said earlier, is that existence is added to essence in thought, not in reality. The mind can consider each without considering the other, and can treat existence as a quality of essence in thought. This is not like a body’s being white in the outside world, which would require the body to exist before the whiteness was added to it—whether before it in time or in its nature—and that would lead to impossible consequences. At most, the essence comes before existence in the mind, and we accept this. The mind can consider the essence by itself, without considering whether it exists outside the mind or within it. Although thinking of an essence without considering any existence is itself a kind of mental existence, the mind does not consider the essence from the standpoint of that existence. It does not attend to that existence, even though it is the very act of considering the essence. There is a difference between leaving something out of our thinking and thinking that it is absent. In this act of thought, the mind can describe the essence as existing in general, without describing it as existing in any particular way. If the mind then considers its existence in thought, no regress follows: the chain stops when the mind stops making that further consideration.

Some people deny that the bearer must exist before a quality can belong to it. They say this applies to qualities of existence, not to qualities of essence.464

A mistake and the answer

When we say that we can think about what something is without thinking about its existence, we mean without thinking about whether it exists outside the mind. If we also ignored its existence in the mind, there would be nothing there for us to think about. Even if we grant that we can overlook its mental existence while still thinking about the essence, this does not prove that the essence is not existence in every sense. What a thing is may itself be one particular way of existing. It can be said to exist in the mind when we think of it, and outside the mind when it is present there. We may be unaware of its existence in the mind while still thinking about the thing. In this way, we can speak of existence as existing without having to add another reality to it. The general idea of existence applies to particular ways of existing.

This is why some say that existence means being or being present. But the truth, as we and those who know God hold, is that the things we describe by their natures are each particular ways of existing.465 As the light of existence shows itself in its fullness, those things and their features appear—sometimes in our minds, sometimes outside them. Their brightness depends on their nearness to the First Reality or their distance from Him, on how much stands between them and Him, and on how ready they are to receive that light. Some display all the fullness that belongs to existence itself; others display less.

The ideas of these things in our minds are shadows466 of the real forms that God brings forth directly. They reach us as reflections467 from higher realities, or through the light of existence appearing within us to the degree we can receive it. This is why knowing things exactly as they are is so difficult. Only those whose hearts have been filled with God's light, and whose veil from pure existence has been lifted, can know them in that way. Through Him they perceive those realities as they are. Even then, their own separate identity still limits their knowledge. The furthest those who know God can reach is to acknowledge what they cannot grasp and to recognise that everything returns to Him, the All-Knowing, the All-Aware.

To explain this further, thinkers have disagreed about what makes things exist. Some eminent scholars say that each thing exists by being joined to the concept “existent,” a simple, self-evident idea expressed in Persian by the word hast, meaning “is.”468 Abu al-Hasan al-Ash‘ari said that each thing’s existence is its own essence. For example, what we mean by the existence of a human being is a living being with reason. The Arabic word for existence, like its equivalents in other languages, can have countless meanings. Most theologians say that existence is a quality present in essence, whether in the Necessary Being or in possible things.

According to the familiar view of Aristotle's followers, existence is added to what a possible thing is, but God's existence is His very essence. As we explained, with possible things the mind can distinguish the idea of their existence from the idea of what they are. Outside the mind, however, these are not two separate realities. The Necessary Being’s existence is identical with His essence because His reality is a particular existence that stands by itself. Nothing else is considered in Him besides existence—not even the relation of being brought into existence by an agent or of being supported by something else, even in thought. They hold that this differs in reality from the existence of possible things, although both share the general idea of existence.469

They call it pure existence, or existence “on the condition that it does not depend on anything else.” This means it does not depend on an essence as the existence of possible things does. They say that if the Necessary Being had an essence, He would either be the whole made up of essence and existence, and so be composite, even if only in thought; or He would be one of the two. In the latter case, He would depend on the other. An essence needs existence in order to be real, and existence, if it is present in something, needs an essence in which to be present, even in thought.

The philosophers in Aristotle’s school were asked: surely a particular existence still needs general existence, since no particular can be real without the general? Their answer is that this particular existence stands on its own. No agent brings it into being, and it does not need an essence to support it. Nor does it need a general existence, another feature, or any cause in order to be real. The general idea of existence applies to it as an external feature that follows from it, but does not make it what it is. Being a narrower case of a general idea does not mean a thing depends on that idea. How could it? For them, the general idea exists only in the mind, while particular existences are different realities in themselves. Their difference does not come just from being related to different essences, which would leave them the same in reality, nor from different defining features, which would make general existence a kind of category shared by them. Since each existence has no name of its own, as the different kinds of things do, some have wrongly thought that existences differ only in how they relate to the essences in which they are found. That is not their view.

Some distinguish kinds of existence by the degree of their reality, as when they compare God's existence with the existence of things that depend on Him. Others say that “existence” is a general idea the mind forms when it thinks about things. On their view, this idea is not itself the reality of anything that exists. The idea “existent” applies to the Necessary Being because of His own essence, and to everything else because it is made by another. So the idea we apply to anything as “existent” is added to it in the mind. For possible things, the basis of this idea is a feature they receive from their cause; for the Necessary Being, it is His essence. Suhrawardi, the Shaykh of Illumination, appears to have leaned toward this view. His main arguments against the philosophers in Aristotle’s school are these:

If existence itself existed, it would either exist through another existence, leading to an endless regress, or through itself. In the second case, “existent” would not mean the same thing when applied to existence and to other things: for existence it would mean “existence,” but for other things it would mean “having existence.”

If existence were a substance, it could not be a feature of things. If it were a quality, then what bears it would have to be established without existence, which is impossible. If existence belonged to an essence, it would have a relation to that essence. The relation would also have to exist, and it would need another relation to make it exist, leading to an endless regress. And if existence existed before the essence, it would stand on its own rather than belong to the essence as a feature. If it existed after the essence, the essence would already exist before existence. If both existed together, the essence would exist alongside existence, not through it.

Another group says that the Necessary Being is a particular, real existence, while possible things exist through their connection to that real existence, which is the Necessary Being Himself. On this view, existence is one individual reality. The many things that exist are many because of their different connections to it, not because each has a different existence. When real existence is related to a human being, that human being exists; when it is related to a horse, the horse exists, and so on. So to say “the Necessary Being exists” means that He is existence; to say “a human being exists” or “a horse exists” means that it is related to the Necessary Being.
