Saying “the existence of Zayd” or “the existence of Amr” is like saying “the God of Zayd” or “the God of Amr.”

On this view, the word “existent” applies both to existence that stands on its own and to things related to it in some way. A derived word does not have to mean that its source inheres in something else, or that the thing it describes bears that source as a feature. A blacksmith, for example, is connected to iron; a seller of dates is connected to dates. Ordinary language alone, however, cannot settle what things really are.

Nor does calling “existent” a derived word—a broad, self-evident idea in the mind—rule out its source being a real thing in its own right, even if we do not know its nature.470 Nor does calling an idea “secondary” in the mind conflict with its source being real in itself.471 A concept may be secondary when compared with some things, yet point to something real in a different way. This view is attributed to the direct insight of philosophers who know God, though we have already criticized it.

In the closing pages of The Intimations, Suhrawardi—the philosopher known as the Shaykh of Illumination—seems to hold that anything not made of matter, whether it must exist or depends on something else, is nothing apart from its own existence. This applies to both the higher intellects and souls. Such beings, on his account, exist in their own right, without a separate essence added to them. He first argued that the essence of the human soul is existence,472 then extended this claim to everything above the soul. His explanation is brief: “If my own being is this simple, then the intellects must be even simpler.” His point is that the intellects are causes of souls, as we shall explain. They stand closer to God in the order of causes. A cause must have a higher and more firmly established existence than what it produces. So what is nearer to God must be fuller and more complete than what is farther away. If souls are immaterial existences, not made from a general kind and a feature that sets them apart—since whatever has existence itself as its essence is completely simple—then the intellects above them, and the being above all, must be so even more.

Any perfection that belongs to a thing simply because it exists—and that does not require a body, parts, or any kind of lack—must also belong to its cause. If the effect has such a perfection, its cause must have it too, because the effect flows from its cause. But two objections arise if we say that the soul exists on its own. The first is that the Necessary Being is said to be necessary because His existence is not joined to a separate essence. If He were joined to one, He would be possible. If that is so, every existence not joined to an essence would be necessary. But if souls are essences that stand on their own and are identical with existence, then they too would be necessary, which is impossible. Second, if existence simply as existence required necessity, then every existence would be necessary in itself.473

Suhrawardi answers the first objection by saying that although the soul and the Necessary Being are both pure existence, they differ greatly in completeness. The Necessary Being’s existence is infinitely strong and complete; nothing greater is possible. The soul’s existence is incomplete because it is an effect, reached through many intermediaries. A cause is more complete than its effect, just as sunlight is stronger than a ray of light. This is only an example of the general rule that an effect is less complete than its cause. The difference between God’s perfection and the soul’s perfection cannot be measured by comparing them to sunlight and a ray. As we have already established, a difference in completeness does not require an extra feature to tell the two apart. So the Necessary Being is not made up of parts. The soul’s possibility is the incompleteness of its existence, as is the possibility of all other effects. There can be countless degrees of incompleteness. The Necessary Being’s necessity, by contrast, is the perfection of His existence, which nothing can surpass; nor can another existence equal it, since there cannot be two Necessary Beings.

Someone may object: 'Things that exist on their own cannot be more or less complete than one another.' We reply that this is only an assertion. Its sole support is that people do not usually speak of such things as stronger or weaker. But ordinary ways of speaking cannot settle what is true.474

He gives two answers to the second objection. To begin with, God is not necessary simply because His existence is free from a separate essence. He is necessary because His existence is so complete that nothing could be more complete. Not being joined to an essence follows from that. If self-subsisting things could not differ in completeness and incompleteness, the objection would stand. But the distinction between complete and incomplete answers it. The objection applies only if “existence” means exactly the same thing, to the same degree, everywhere. It does not apply if existence can differ by degrees.

The second answer turns the objection back on most of Aristotle’s followers. They say that God’s existence is not joined to an essence, whereas the existence of possible things is. So we may ask them: if existence as such requires separation from essence, then every existence must be separate from essence—which contradicts your view of possible things. If it requires being joined to essence, then the Necessary Being’s existence must also be joined to essence—which contradicts what you have accepted. If it requires neither, then the Necessary Being’s separation from essence must depend on a cause, and He would not be necessary. If this objection does not defeat the Shaykh’s view, their view is open to the same objection. And if they answer that the shared idea of existence applies by degrees, rather than in exactly the same way, the same answer works here too.

Discussion and clarification

The difference between the two positions is clear. For the philosophers in Aristotle’s school, shared existence is not a kind of essence or a general kind, because they do not think an essence, or any part of it, can apply to different things by degrees. They say that only an additional feature can apply in this way, while the things it describes differ in their own natures. The Shaykh, however, says that existence is one simple kind of reality.475

Aristotle’s followers have another possible reply. The general idea of existence, they might say, follows from particular existing things. It is not part of what those things are. The fact that one added feature applies to different things does not prove that the things themselves have the same nature. Light, for example, is one idea that applies by degrees to different lights. Sunlight can help a person with poor eyesight see, while other lights cannot. Heat is also one shared idea, yet some kinds of heat prepare the body for life while others do not. The differences come from the different things that have the light or heat, which vary in strength and weakness and, for these philosophers, in their natures. The deeper dispute is whether anything that applies to different things by degrees must be an added feature, as the Shaykh argues elsewhere.

The general idea of existence relates to real existences as the idea of humanity relates to human beings, or animal life to animals. In each case, the idea comes from the thing itself, without adding some other feature. So, even though existences differ by degree, their reality is one: a single idea cannot be drawn from completely different realities unless they share something. We discussed this point earlier while proving that there cannot be more than one Necessary Being. The reality of existence is not a general essence, even though it has one source and nature at every level. Its different degrees are not caused by an extra feature added to it. The difference and what they share come from existence itself.476

Some Sufis say that God, the Necessary Being, is existence without any restriction. They argue that it cannot be nonexistence or something nonexistent. Nor can it be an essence that exists through existence or alongside it, since either way it would depend on something and be made up of parts. So it must be existence itself. But it cannot be one particular existence: if it were taken together with general existence, it would be composite; if it were separate from what it describes, it would be dependent. A limited existence needs the unrestricted existence, and if it disappeared, every existence would disappear.477

Taken to its conclusion, this view would make the Necessary Being’s existence something other than existence, and would make everything that exists—even filth—necessary.478 God is far above what these unjust people say! General existence is a universal idea in the mind, with no reality outside it, while the things covered by that idea are many. The assumption that a limited existence needs general existence is false; the relation goes the other way. A general idea exists only within its particular instances. If it is part of what a particular thing is, that thing needs it in thought, but not as a separate reality outside the mind. If it is merely an added idea, the thing does not need it at all.

They also argue that if absolute existence disappeared, every existence, including God’s, would disappear. Since that is impossible, existence itself must be necessary. This confuses what cannot be absent in itself with what cannot be absent because its absence would mean the loss of something that cannot be absent in itself. Existence in general is not necessary merely because its absence would mean the absence of one of its instances, namely the Necessary Being.479 The same is true of other features attributed to the Necessary Being, such as being a thing, causing, and knowing. If someone says that existence cannot be absent in itself because a thing cannot be its own opposite, we reply: that is true when one thing is directly said to be its opposite—“existence is nonexistence”—not when we use a derived phrase such as “existence is nonexistent.”

How could it be otherwise? Philosophers agree that existence in general is an idea the mind forms about things, not something that exists separately outside it.480 Yet look at how much they disagree about existence,481 even though they agree that nothing is more obvious or familiar to the mind.

One disagreement is whether existence is universal or particular. Some say it is one particular reality, with no multiplicity in itself; the many things that exist are many only because of their different relations to it. The truth is that “existent, simply as existent” is a universal idea,482 and particular existences are its instances, or shares of its reality.483 Their individuality does not add anything to the reality they share. Existence takes different degrees through itself. The reality of existence is neither universal nor particular, neither general nor specific, even though it is shared by all existing things.484 This is a remarkable point, understood only by those firmly grounded in knowledge.

They also disagree over whether existence is necessary or possible. Many later thinkers have called the general idea of existence necessary in itself. That is a grave mistake. They also disagree about whether existence is a substance, a quality, or neither, since substance and quality are kinds of existing things, while existence itself is not another existing thing. Some say that it is neither. At first glance, Avicenna and his followers seem to treat it as a quality, but this is far from the truth. A feature of this kind cannot exist on its own. It needs something in which to exist, while that thing does not need the feature in order to exist. But nothing can exist without existence itself.

The truth, as I have said, is that the existence of a substance is a substance by virtue of that thing’s being a substance, and the existence of a quality is a quality in the same way, since each is one with the thing in reality. But if we consider existence itself, it does not belong to any class of things. It has no general kind or feature that sets it apart, because it is completely simple. Nor does it have a universal essence that would need further features to make it individual. So it is neither universal nor particular. Rather, particular existences are realities that are distinct in themselves, differ through their own reality, and share only the general idea “existent,” which is a mental concept.

People also disagree about whether existence itself exists. Some say that it exists through itself, so there is no endless regress. Others say that it is only a mental idea, with no reality outside the mind. Still others say it is neither existent nor nonexistent. The truth is that general existence is a mental idea, but it has real instances.

They disagree as well about whether particular existences are identical with possible essences or added to them. The truth is that they are the essences themselves in reality, though the mind considers them different in some respects. And they disagree about whether the word “existence” has different meanings for different things, applies to all in exactly the same way, or has one meaning that applies by degrees. The last view is the truth.485

Another disagreement concerns the meaning of “existent.” Must the idea of existence—whether it is real or drawn by the mind—be part of what “existent” means? Must existence belong to the thing in reality or only in the mind for us to call it existent? Or is “existent” a simple idea, with no source of existence and no relation to a bearer, and does each thing exist only by being joined to this idea? The first view is clearly true.486

From what you have heard, it should be clear that the reality of existence, considered in itself, is not limited by being general or specific, universal or particular, unrestricted or restricted. It is not one because of some added oneness, nor many; it is not made individual by an added mark, nor is it vague. We will make this clearer later. In itself, existence is simply real, actual, and manifest.487 Ideas such as possibility and necessity, universal concepts, and other mental descriptions apply to its different levels and positions, as the Qur'an says, “High in rank is He.” Thus existence may be described as unrestricted or restricted, universal or particular, one or many, without any change in its own reality.

Existence is not a substance like the essences of substances, which need an existence added to them. Nor is it a quality, since it does not exist through some further existence—let alone in a bearer, which would mean that it had to come before itself. It is not a mere idea, as some have wrongly claimed, since it is real even when no one is thinking about it. The fact that the universal idea of existence is mental, and that the general idea of being is only an idea, does not mean that the reality of existence is mental. Existence is the widest of all realities, embracing essences and even applying to ideas such as absolute or relative nonexistence, possibility, readiness, dependence, and other ideas of lack. Through the light of existence, the mind distinguishes different kinds of absence and judges some impossible and others possible. Whatever can exist can also be absent, along with many other judgments and ideas.

Nothing is clearer than the reality of existence; that is why some call it obvious in itself. Yet nothing is harder to grasp in its full reality; that is why others treat it as only an idea in the mind.488 Still, nothing can be real, in the mind or outside it, without existence. It encompasses and sustains everything through its own reality. Without existence, nothing would be real either in the mind or outside it. In this sense, existence is the things themselves.489 It appears at its different levels in the forms and realities found in thought and in the outside world, which we call essences and fixed realities. These, along with the other features of existence, are absorbed in existence itself.490 The only difference is one the mind makes. Even negative features, though they return to nonexistence, are connected to existence in another respect.

Existence cannot be divided into parts, either outside the mind or in thought, because it is simple. It has no general kind, no feature that sets it apart, and no definition. All perfections belong to it,491 and all qualities depend on it. In itself, it is living, knowing, willing, powerful, hearing, seeing, and speaking—not through something else that gives it these qualities. Rather, it reveals itself in different forms and appears as these perfections. In this way, it follows the things that bear those forms, since they too are particular existences.492 Each later existence is absorbed in an earlier existence that has greater power. All are absorbed in the oneness of the true divine existence, fading before the power, majesty, and greatness of the First, as we will prove later.

He is the Necessary Being, the Real, established through Himself and the source of all else. The prophets and saints call upon Him by His divine names, and He guides His creation to Himself.493 He has told us through them that He is with everything through His very reality, not by entering or mixing with it; and that He is different from everything in His reality, not by being separate from it.494 He brings things into being by being hidden within them even as He reveals them.495 At the Great Resurrection, He ends them by appearing in His oneness and overpowering them, removing their distinctions and marks until they fade away.496 As the Qur'an says: “Whose is the kingdom today? God’s, the One, the All-Dominating,” and “Everything perishes except His face.”

In the lesser resurrection, this is a passage from the visible world to the unseen. Just as created forms exist through God’s self-disclosure at the many levels, they pass away through the disclosure of His essence at the level of oneness. Essences are forms of His perfections and displays of His names and attributes. They appear first in knowledge, then in the outside world.497 The many names, the different attributes, and their detailed forms do not diminish His true oneness or His everlasting perfections, as we will explain, God willing.

Method Three — Another realm of existence beyond the one we witness, and related questions

Chapter — Proving mental existence and its shadow-like appearance

Most philosophers agree that things have another way of existing or appearing besides the way we see them in the world. Only a small group concerned with outward appearances disputes this. We call this other way existence in the mind: things appear to us through thinking and the senses.498

Preliminary remarks

Before presenting and discussing the proofs for this claim, we need to set out two points. First, as you know, possible things have both an essence and an existence. We will prove something we have already hinted at, and a careful reader will almost be ready to accept it: what a maker first brings about, and what is directly produced by an agent, is a way for the thing to exist, not its essence. A thing’s essence does not need to be made, produced, acted on, or completed. That is not because it must exist or is already fully real. It is because, considered in itself, it is incomplete, hidden, weak, and still only a possibility. As we have already noted, existence can be stronger or weaker, more or less complete. The stronger and more complete the existence, the more effects follow from it.

Since existence itself is the source of effects, one essence or idea can exist and appear in several ways, with different degrees of being and reality. Some are stronger than others, and some produce effects and features that others do not. A substance, for example, has one meaning and one essence, yet it can exist in different ways. It can exist independently, apart from matter, free from change, active and stable, as the separate intellects are at their different levels. Or it can depend on matter, be joined to it, be affected by something else, move or rest, come into being or pass away, as substantial forms do at different levels of weakness and dependence. A substance can also exist in a still weaker way, neither acting nor being acted on, neither stable nor changing, moving nor at rest. Examples are the images a person imagines when thinking of them as images.499500

The second point is that God created the human soul with the power to bring about forms of both immaterial and material things. The soul belongs to the spiritual realm, the world of power and command. Beings of that realm can bring about intellectual forms that exist on their own, and material forms that exist in matter. Every form produced by an agent is present to that agent; indeed, being present to its agent is the same as existing in itself. A thing’s presence to something else does not require that it be inside it as a quality or feature. All existing things, in their forms, are present to God more fully than they are present to themselves or to the things that receive them. Yet those forms are not qualities that exist within Him.501

Any form present to a being free from matter can be the basis of that being’s knowledge of the form, whether or not the form exists on its own. What makes a thing know another thing is that the other thing’s form is present to it. The form may be the same as the knower, as when the soul knows itself, or different from it. If it is different, it may be within the knower, when the knower receives it, or it may come from the knower, when the knower produces it. So a form’s presence to an immaterial being—that is, the being’s knowledge—is broader than the form’s own existence, its existence within the knower, or its existence for the knower.

The human soul therefore has a world of its own. It contains the forms of things without bodies and things with bodies, the moving and still heavenly spheres, the elements and their mixtures, and all the rest. The soul knows these things because they are present to it. It does not need yet another image of each one; otherwise, we would need an image of that image, and so on without end.

God brings into being both things created directly and things that come to be through change. He created the human soul as an example of His own essence, attributes, and actions. He is beyond comparison with anything, but can be shown through an example. Knowing the soul can therefore lead us toward knowing God. God made the soul’s essence free from bodies, place, and direction; He gave it power, knowledge, will, life, hearing, and sight; and He gave it a realm of its own, like the realm of its Creator, where it can create what it wills and choose what it wants.

Yet although the soul belongs to the spiritual realm and the world of power and greatness, it is weak in its existence and structure. It is at a lower level, with many stages between it and its Creator. The more stages between a thing and the source of existence, the weaker its power and existence. So the actions and effects that come from the soul are extremely weak.502 The intellectual and imagined forms the soul brings about are only shadows and outlines of the external forms created by God. Their essence is the same in both kinds of existence, but they do not produce the effects that belong to the forms’ external existence. There are exceptions: a few people who have risen beyond ordinary human limits can produce things outside themselves that have real effects. Their strong connection to the sacred realm and their great power allow them to do so.

This kind of existence, which has no external effects and is produced by the soul in this mode of appearing, is called mental or shadow-like existence. The other kind, which does produce effects, is called external or actual existence.

This is supported by what the great Shaykh Muhyi al-Din Ibn Arabi says in The Bezels of Wisdom: “By means of the estimating faculty, each person creates in his imagination things that exist only there. The knower creates through resolve things that exist outside the place of that resolve.503504505

“But resolve must keep what it creates in being, and it does not tire of keeping it. If the knower becomes inattentive to what he has created, that creation disappears—unless he has brought all the realms into his awareness.506 He is never completely inattentive,507 though he must always be present to at least one realm.

“When the knower creates through resolve and has this all-encompassing awareness, the creation appears in its form in every realm, and the forms preserve one another.508 If the knower becomes inattentive to one or more realms while remaining aware of another and sustaining the form created there, all the forms remain preserved through that one form in the realm he has not forgotten. Inattention never covers everything—not for everyone, nor even for a particular person.509

“Here I have revealed a secret that the people of God have always guarded, not wishing it to be made known. I have said that no one has written this in a book—not me or anyone else—except in this book. It is unique in its time, so do not neglect it. The realm in which you remain present, with its forms, is like the Book of which God says, ‘We have left nothing out of the Book.’ It gathers what exists and what does not. Only someone who is a Qur'an within himself can understand what we mean. ‘Whoever is mindful of God, He will grant him a way to tell right from wrong.’”

Ibn Arabi’s words strongly support what we are discussing. They also contain many further points, which we will explain in the discussions of the soul, God willing. Keep these two points firmly in mind; they will help you understand mental existence and answer the objections raised against it.510

Chapter — Presenting several proofs for mental existence

First method

We can think of things that do not exist outside the mind, even impossible things such as a partner to God, two opposites existing together, or an indivisible particle. We can distinguish each of these in thought from all the other nonexistent things. But pure nonexistence cannot be distinguished. So these things must exist in some way. Since, by assumption, they do not exist outside the mind, they must exist in the mind.

An objection follows: how can we know something that does not exist? We have said that knowledge takes the form of what is known. If the form of a nonexistent thing matches it, then even an impossible thing must have an external reality for the form to match. But a nonexistent thing has no reality of its own. If the form does not match it, then we do not know the thing, since knowledge requires a form that matches what is known.

The reply is that a mental form is not a copy or picture of an external thing, different from it in reality. The mental form is the reality of the thing known, appearing as a shadow without producing the effects that belong to it. To know something nonexistent is simply to have in the mind an idea that has no existence outside the mind. So we do not need to choose between saying that the idea matches the nonexistent thing or that it does not. Nor does either difficulty follow, since the form in the mind is the very thing that does not exist outside it.511

That is the answer according to those who hold this view. Those who say that the mind receives only a copy or likeness of the thing—not the thing’s own reality—answer differently. They say that knowing something means having its copy or likeness in the mind. If it has an actual external counterpart, this is knowledge of something that exists; if not, it is knowledge of something nonexistent. A mental image of something nonexistent does not actually match it, since it has no external reality; it matches only by supposition, in the sense that if the thing existed, the image would match it. So knowledge of a nonexistent thing is having a mental likeness with no actual counterpart.

This answer is not enough. It works only for things that are nonexistent but have a reality apart from their nonexistence. But if we think of absolute nonexistence itself, then saying that the mental form is the reality of the known thing through its mental existence and shadow-like appearance seems contradictory. Absolute nonexistence has no existence at all, and what is hidden cannot appear in any way. This is really the well-known problem of how we can know something that is completely unknown.512 We will find what we need to answer it, God willing.

Second method

We make true positive statements about things that have no existence outside the mind. We also make statements about existing things without limiting them to the examples that actually exist; we speak of all real and possible examples. For instance, “Every phoenix is a bird” and “The three angles of any triangle add up to two right angles.” A true positive statement requires its subject to exist, as ordinary human understanding confirms. Since the subject’s external existence is not enough to explain these statements, we know it must have another kind of existence: mental existence.

That is how the argument is usually presented. But it faces several objections. First, statements like these are not facts about things that actually exist outside the mind. “Every phoenix is a bird” does not mean that every actual or possible phoenix is flying right now. Those who deny mental existence do not accept that this statement is true. It is a conditional statement about a thing assumed to exist: anything that, if it existed and were a phoenix, would fly. A statement of this kind requires only that its subject exist by supposition.513 That could still be external existence, so the argument has not yet shown that there is another kind.

Second, if this argument were correct, then whenever we made a general statement about a kind of thing, we would have to hold every possible example in our minds, one by one. For instance, to say 'Every triangle has this feature,' we would have to think of every possible triangle separately and in full detail, even though there are endlessly many. Later logicians say that a universal statement applies to each individual example, not just to the general idea. So for the statement to be true, the individual examples themselves must exist, not just the general idea.

If, instead, we follow the more careful view that a universal statement is made about the general idea but applies to its individual examples, the difficulty goes away. But then we would have to limit the argument to terms with no external examples at all. Otherwise, someone could say that general natures exist through their external examples.514 If the subject has an external example, the general idea exists through it, and the statement applies to it on that basis.

Someone may say that in a universal statement we do not take the subject as one specific individual. In “Every human being is such-and-such,” we consider the subject as something that can apply to many people. In that respect, it does not exist outside the mind.

But a particular thing outside the mind cannot be one thing shared by many people. Neither can a particular idea, considered as this one event in the mind. Existence does not belong to something wholly undefined, just as it does not belong to an external thing without its particular identity. The mind can, however, consider the mental thing apart from that identity. It could do the same with an external thing, unless there is proof against it.

The truth is that what we consider as something shared by many exists only in the mind, though we do not consider it as existing in the mind.515 We will explain this further soon, God willing.

Third, we can think of a particular person who once existed and make an external claim about that person. For example, we can say that a body that has perished was once hard, heavy, and in motion. If so, the mental image of the person and the external person would have to be one and the same individual, since these claims belonged to the external person. But that is obviously impossible. Some try to answer that they are the same individual, saying the external person, with all its external features, is also present in the imagination. This is badly mistaken. One thing can have only one existence, and existence either goes with being an individual or is identical with it.

The answer is that the external feature, like the subject, has a mental form that matches the external reality and is joined to the mental subject. But in an external statement we are not looking at the subject and feature as they exist in the mind. We are talking about what they represent outside the mind. There is no problem with a thing in the mind representing something external: the point of representation is to show the thing represented, not the representation itself.

Third method

We can take different individuals, each marked by its own personal or defining features, and form from them one shared idea that applies to them all.516 We can say that each is that shared idea. For example, from different human beings we form the shared idea “human being,” which applies to both young and old. The general idea “animal” applies to mules and donkeys. It goes together with each individual’s particular features, yet in itself it leaves aside the material features and conditions that distinguish them.

This idea does not exist as one thing outside the mind. If it did, one thing would have opposite features at the same time: the individual distinctions and all that follows from them. The idea exists only where there are many examples. But we consider it as one idea; so in this respect it exists only in the mind.

Someone may object: philosophers agree that the natures of things, such as what makes something human or animal, exist outside the mind. Such natures are real; the labels 'universal,' 'kind,' and 'species' are ideas we form about them. These labels are not themselves things in the outside world. If so, there must be one human nature outside the mind, the very same nature present with the different features of Zayd, Amr, and all other people. It would be one thing, differing only in how it is related to each person’s features. When one person dies, that person’s features leave it, but the shared human nature remains. It is the same reality joined to many different features and distinctions, becoming the human nature of each individual through that person’s features.

The same would apply to animal nature in relation to different, conflicting features. So, they might say, there is no need to claim that general ideas exist in another way called mental existence.

The answer is that this confuses different points of view by ignoring the conditions we have to keep separate. When philosophers say that kinds and species exist, they do not mean that a kind as a kind, a species as a species, or a universal as a universal exists outside the mind. Nor do they mean that a nature exists outside the mind simply because it is universal. No one with even a little training in philosophy would say that, much less the great philosophers. They have explained that a universal idea, simply as a universal, does not exist outside the mind.517

Avicenna wrote a separate book on this question. He strongly criticized a distinguished, elderly man he met in Hamadan. The man mistakenly thought that, when philosophers say species and kinds exist in external things, they mean that one and the same thing exists in all the different individuals and is shared by them. Avicenna asked whether anyone could really think that this was a point of disagreement among philosophers.

The man had heard philosophers say that individuals share one reality and one meaning. He could not understand why they used “one” in this way, so he assumed they meant that one reality, as one universal idea, exists outside the mind. That is false. A shared idea, a universal, a general kind, or a species can exist in external things, but not in that universal or shared sense. Human nature, for example, exists outside the mind as human nature, stamped with existence—not as a species or as something shared by many. We think of it as something shared by many, but that shared character belongs to our thought, not to the thing outside the mind.

Avicenna says in his other books that the human nature found in different individuals is many, not one. Animal nature is the same. There is no single humanity that becomes many only because it is related to different individuals. The human nature joined to Zayd’s features is different from the human nature joined to Amr’s features. They are two human natures: one joined to Zayd’s features and one joined to Amr’s. They are not one nature made different only by being joined to different features, as though one animal nature could be joined to opposite defining features.

Someone might say: an external thing is particular and cannot be shared. A mental thing is also particular and cannot be shared or applied to many. Only the essence considered in itself can apply to many,518 and that essence exists outside the mind too. So the proof does not work.

The answer is that we are not claiming that the human being in the mind is not a particular mental experience, or that this experience can be shared. We mean that we can think of the idea “human being” as applying to many, and hold that idea in the mind in this way. It is clear that the idea of a human being considered as applying to many exists in the mind, not outside it, and is not marked by any one person’s external features.

Consider another point. We can think of relationships and features that do not exist outside the mind, and we can make true claims about them. They must therefore exist in some way.519 They cannot be outside the mind, since they are ideas we form; so they must exist in the mind. This is what we need to prove.

Another proof from the highest level: every agent acts for an end or purpose. If the goal of an action had no kind of reality at all, the agent would not act in order to reach it. But if the goal existed outside the mind, the goal would already have been achieved, and there would be no need for the action. So the goal must have a kind of reality that does not produce the effects it is meant to produce. That is what we mean by mental existence.

Another sign of what we mean is that imagined things, though they are not real outside the mind, can cause real movements and effects in the body, even if they do not produce their intended results. Picture something delicious, and your body responds. Imagine tasting something sour, and you may shiver. If the image of a house you hope to build had no reality of any kind, it could not prompt you to move your body and build it.

It is said that a skilled doctor once treated a king who was paralyzed, when bodily medicine had failed, by using mental exercises and imagined events that stirred the body’s natural heat, until it overcame the cause of the illness.

Some souls grow so strong and noble that their thoughts gain a force and vividness that can take effect outside the mind. They may heal the sick, harm wrongdoers, or even change one element into another, turning something other than fire into fire or moving bodies that ordinary human souls cannot move. All this happens through a higher power and spiritual support.520

Someone may object: philosophers clearly say that natural things have purposes in their actions. If these purposes exist in a way that is not external, then natural things must be aware of the results of their actions and the ends of their movements, even though they are material bodies.

Fakhr al-Din al-Razi raised this objection against the philosophers. They maintain that the powers of nature, at every level, work toward ends of their own. They also hold that an end gives an agent a reason to act and to reach completion through its action. The careful commentator on Avicenna’s Pointers answered by accepting that natural powers have some awareness of their ends, but that this awareness is very weak.521

Look at date palms: the female trees lean toward the male trees, even when the males grow in the opposite direction. Trees beside a river bend toward the water. Trees growing beside a wall lean away from it as they rise. They put out many leaves between their fruit and possible sources of harm, and their fruits protect their kernels with coverings. These sights point toward the view described above. There are flashes of insight here that would not fit this discussion; perhaps they will come up later, if God wills, through His grace and generosity.

Chapter — Objections to mental existence and replies to them

Aristotle and those who followed his school, including al-Farabi, Avicenna, their students, and most later philosophers, held that things appear to us through understanding, imagination, and the senses. These powers are where things have a mental, shadow-like presence. On this view, general ideas exist in the soul, which is not material; particular ideas exist in the power of imagination; and bodily forms exist in the senses and imagination. This view raises several questions, which we should set out and answer.

The first objection is this: If a thing is a substance—that is, if it exists in itself and not as a feature of something else—then that is part of its basic nature. The proofs for mental existence also imply that a thing keeps its essential features through its different ways of existing. So a substantial nature should remain something that exists in itself wherever it exists. How, then, can such a nature exist in the mind as a quality that depends on the mind? And since you treat every mental form as a quality, it seems that the basic natures of all the things we understand, though they differ from one another, must all fall under the category of quality.

The answer, as we can learn from Avicenna’s books, is that the meaning of substance that serves as a broad category and names these natures is not simply “something that exists and does not exist in something else.” That meaning could not serve as a broad category. If it did, the feature that separates one kind within the category from another would have to make up the category itself. But a broad category does not need the features that divide it in order to be what it is. It needs them only for the category to exist in one definite way or another. Each such feature brings about an actual kind of the category; it does not combine with the category to form its basic meaning. So if the meaning of a category were actual existence together with the condition “not in something else,” then the feature that divides it into kinds would both bring about its existence and make up its meaning and nature, as we explained earlier.

There is another reason. If 'substance' meant 'something that actually exists on its own,' then the nature of a kind would change whenever one of its individual members ceased to exist. The same view would also lead to more than one Necessary Being. A nature in itself is not brought into being or affected by a cause. If existence were identical with a nature, or part of it, then that nature would be eternally necessary. God, the one who sustains all, is far above having any partner or equal. Things that can either exist or not exist, by contrast, are nothing but their dependence on a cause; their very being is need for the one who brings them into being.

Likewise, our phrase “something that actually exists”522 cannot be the basic meaning that defines substance. Otherwise, anyone who understood something that was a substance by nature would also know that it actually exists. The meaning of substance that can serve as a broad category is this: a thing with a nature that, if it existed outside the mind, would not exist in something else. This remains true whether its nature exists in thought or outside it. Its presence in the mind does not stop it from being the kind of thing that, if it existed outside the mind, would exist in itself. In this sense, the mental idea of substance is still substance.

Another point confirms this. Calling something a substance in this sense does not depend on an outside cause. But saying that it actually exists—and that it exists in itself rather than in something else—does depend on an outside cause. That is not an essential feature, which belongs to a thing without needing another cause. If adding a negative condition, “not in something else,” made a highest category, then adding a positive condition, “in something else,” should make one too—and this case would be even stronger. But that is not the accepted view.523 This explains what they mean when they say that the mental idea of substance is substance.

There is a further point to keep in mind. We will explain it when we discuss what it means to say that one thing is another. A concept can mean “what exists in itself” and yet be applied to something that exists in something else. Think of ideas such as nothingness, nonbeing, impossibility, a partner to God, a letter, a position, movement, and infinity. As ideas in the mind, they exist; by their meaning, they may point to what is absent, impossible, or dependent. The same idea can be called both, depending on which sense we mean.

This explains why an idea of a substance can also be called a feature of the mind. What the idea represents is a substance; the idea itself depends on the mind in which it exists. There is no contradiction here. A contradiction would arise only if we placed one thing under two categories that are essential to different kinds of things.

Some philosophers count forms of knowledge as qualities. This seems to mean that a mental idea of a substance is both substance and quality, and so belongs to two categories. They explain the word “quality” in one of two ways. If it means a kind of thing whose existence outside the mind depends on something else, and which does not itself involve size or relation, then it is a separate basic category, opposed to substance. In that sense, one thing cannot belong to both categories. But if “quality” means more broadly a feature that, when it actually exists, does not of itself involve size or relation, then it is a general term that can apply to all the basic kinds when they exist in the mind. In that broader sense, it does not conflict with substance or with the other kinds normally called qualities. This is how their argument should be understood. We will give our own account later.

Be clear about this: when philosophers say that the universals of substances are substances, they do not mean that a mental idea of substance, though it is in the mind, is independent of the mind. Nor do they mean that this same mental form can leave the mind and return, existing at one time outside the mind without a subject and at another time in the mind as something that depends on it. That would be like a magnet in the hand: outside the hand it attracts iron, but when held in the hand it does not.524 That comparison fails if we forget the difference between a general idea and a particular thing, or between what a thing is and how it exists. The universal idea, as something in the mind, cannot move outside the mind or become independent of a subject. A particular magnet can move from one place to another and remain the same individual magnet, attracting iron in one place but not in another. Mental forms are not like that.

By “universal substance,” they mean the nature of a thing considered by itself, without adding that it is general, particular, or joined to any other condition from thought or the outside world. This is sometimes called the natural universal. It differs from a nature already considered as universal, which is called the intellectual universal.525 The intellectual universal cannot exist as a particular thing outside the mind, but the nature considered by itself can. Because it is so open-ended, that nature can be joined to many conditions that do not fit together, such as being one or many, existing in something else or in itself, and being an object of thought or of sense. So although the mental idea of substance is a quality because of its particular existence in the mind and its generality, it is substance by its nature: if that nature existed outside the mind, it would not exist in something else.

When philosophers compare an intelligible substance to a magnet, they mean only this: the magnet’s nature includes the ability to attract iron, whatever its current state. If it is held in a person’s hand and does not attract iron, or is placed beside iron and does attract it, we do not say that it has changed its nature. In both cases it is the same kind of stone, with the ability to attract iron. This much is enough to make the comparison useful.

Someone may object that Avicenna says in The Healing and elsewhere that the features which distinguish kinds of substances do not themselves have to be substances by nature. Although the word “substance” can be applied to them, it applies as an incidental feature, not as part of what they are. This avoids an endless chain in which every distinguishing feature would need another feature to distinguish it. But if these features are not part of the category of substance, they must belong to another category of qualities. Then one and the same thing would be both substance and quality in the same existence, since each kind and its distinguishing feature are one.

Even if the feature that distinguishes one kind of substance from another is not itself a substance, it does not follow that it belongs to some other basic class or must be a quality. Neither reason nor religious teaching rules out simple natures with no broader kind or distinguishing feature from any of the categories.526 Avicenna states this in the section on categories in The Healing.

A theologian offered an answer to this problem:527 how can the same thing be a substance and a quality, general and particular, knowledge and the thing known? When we think of something, he says, two things arise. First comes a general idea, which the mind knows. It is present in the mind as a thing can be present in time or space, but it is not a feature of the mind. Second comes the individual act of knowing, a quality that belongs to the mind. On this view, there is no problem. The problem arises only if the same thing is both substance and quality, or both knowledge and known, or both general and particular.

If these are two ways of considering one thing, as the philosophers and careful thinkers hold, his answer may explain how something can be both knowledge and what is known, or both general and particular. But it still does not explain how the same thing can be both a substance and a quality. If, instead, he means that they are two different things, then his view goes against experience and reason, and introduces a third position without proof.528 It also leads to this: every immaterial form that exists on its own is aware of itself and known to itself. Philosophers use this to explain how God knows Himself and how spiritual beings know themselves. So, by his account, whenever the human soul thinks of something, it creates or brings into being an immaterial intellect that knows and acts by itself. He has admitted that an intelligible thing arises when we think of something, and that this thing is not in the mind or in anything else.

But the soul cannot bring an independently existing intellect into being, not even by preparing for its arrival. The soul can receive things it understands, but that ability is only a potential one. Something already able to act must bring it into use. If the soul produces such an intellect, it must either be the source that gives it existence or merely prepare a place to receive it. The first is impossible: what exists only as a possibility cannot make something actual in itself. The second does not fit his view, because whatever is prepared to receive something must be its subject. If the soul is neither its source nor the subject that receives it—and is not its goal or form either—then there is no connection by which it could bring the intellect into being. Moreover, something that comes into being or changes cannot itself be an intellect fully actual in itself, as their own principles make clear.

His view also makes the known thing general and particular at the same time. It is general because it is understood apart from the features that distinguish particular things. But if it exists on its own rather than depending on the mind, it must itself be particular, since anything that exists outside the mind is particular. Here is the point.529 Individual things of the same kind differ in their outward features. If we grasp what they have in common without those features, that shared nature must be present to us in a different way. It cannot be called general or shared among many unless it exists for something that strips away the features that prevent it from applying to many. A thing’s being stripped of those features cannot be separated from its existence for the thing that strips them away. And this stripped existence must be the very existence the nature has for that mind.

If a nature’s existence in a stripped form is the same as its existence for the mind—the mind that draws ideas from particular material things and removes their material features—then the nature must exist for the mind as something that depends on it. That is the only way it can be present there.530 For something to exist in a subject means that its existence in itself is the very same as its existence for that subject. From this we can see531532 the position taken by those who accept mental existence. In brief, particular forms of sense and imagination depend on the soul as an action depends on its source. They are images that the soul brings about in the lesser imagination, the imagination joined to the soul, not in a greater imagination that exists apart from it.

General forms are different. On this account, they are intellectual beings that exist apart from the soul, but the soul can reach them. Because it sees them indistinctly, it takes a single form to be something that could apply to many things. This is like a person with weak eyesight who sees a dim shape and cannot tell whether it is Zayd, Amr, or someone else. Since these intellects exist more fully than the soul, they cannot be effects produced by the soul or forms that exist within it as its own products. The soul is a place where they appear. This is the position he takes. It rests on the view that mental forms are immaterial, that the soul has an imagination joined to it, and that there are universal intellectual forms. He accepts all three.

We can raise two objections to this view. The first is that being a cause or an effect, being material or immaterial, and similar features belong only to real existence outside the mind. Mental existence, which has none of the effects that belong to real things, cannot have these features. The author himself says in his discussion of creation that bringing something into being is a feature of external existence. He also lists mental existence at the beginning of this inquiry as distinct from both immaterial and material existence.

Here is the second objection. He says that an idea has a weaker existence than a thing outside the mind. Yet he also says that images and beings known through the intellect exist more fully than material things. This seems to make the mental images of particular and universal things both stronger and weaker than the things they represent. The image of Zayd represents the actual Zayd; the idea of a human being applies to actual human beings. Since these images belong to the imaginal and intellectual worlds, they should be stronger than their examples. Yet because they exist in the mind, they should be weaker. So they would be both stronger and weaker than what they represent. That is a contradiction.

Both objections confuse questions that need to be kept apart. Once we distinguish them and explain what it means for something to exist in the mind, the difficulty disappears.

The proofs for mental existence establish that the very things which exist outside also exist in another way: in that other mode, they do not produce the same effects they produce outside. By “effects” we mean everything true of a thing in the outside world, both what it is and the features it has. For example, Zayd as an object of thought is not a substance, a body, a living thing, an animal, or a human being. Nor does he have any of the further perfections of the actual Zayd. This is another mode of existence, different from external existence, where Zayd has both his basic features and his further perfections.

This answers all the objections that expect a thing’s features in the outside world to appear in its mental existence as well. The proofs show that those external features are absent from mental existence. But this does not stop mental existence from having other features shared by existence in general, such as causing and being caused, being particular and distinct, or being free from matter. A feature that comes from a thing’s relation to something else is different from a feature that belongs to the thing in itself.

We must therefore look at an idea in two ways. First, consider it as a picture of something outside the mind. The idea does not have the effects that the real thing has. This is what makes it a representation: it points beyond itself, and its role is to show what it represents. This is what we are discussing when we speak of mental existence. Second, consider the mental form in itself, apart from its relation to the external thing. It is something real, not nothing, and it can have features of its own. From this point of view, it may even have a fuller existence than the thing it represents. In this sense it is a real existence, not a mental one.

This second aspect raises two further questions. First: when the mental form exists for us as an object, is it a quality of the mind, as most of the philosophers in Aristotle’s school say? Or is it a form that completes us: an imaginal or intellectual form with which the soul becomes one in knowing it, as matter takes on the form that shapes it? It will become clear later that a form and the feature that distinguishes it do not belong to one of the basic categories in themselves, but only incidentally. This seems to be Alexander of Aphrodisias’s view. Or is it a substantial form for our soul when we know substances, and a quality or further perfection when we know things that are themselves qualities? This is the question discussed in the theory of knowledge.

The second question is this: what is the thing known by this act of knowing—the external thing that becomes clear to us? Is it a material example, with the soul removing some of its material features, as it does when we perceive particular things, or all of them, as it does when we grasp general ideas? That is the usual view. Or is the thing known a complete imaginal or intellectual being that exists in its own right and is free from matter?

If it is such a being, then the soul, through the senses, connects in some way with the material world and becomes ready to see that imaginal or intellectual being in its own world. The soul then becomes one with it as knower and known, and receives a form from it. In this direct kind of knowing, the soul encounters the very thing it knows, existing outside it. Its connection with a material object then leads it to apply the form to that object and identify the object as what the form represents. The form does not produce the effects of the material thing. This gives us a second kind of knowing: knowing something through an idea of it. These are the questions to keep in mind so that the arguments in each discussion remain clear.

Several points follow from this. First, the effects absent from mental existence include both a thing’s basic features and its further perfections. Second, mental existence is relative: it is what a thing is for a knower, and it ends when that relation ends. This is what it means for the mental form to represent something beyond itself.

Third, whenever we know something through an idea, that knowledge is also accompanied by direct awareness. If the form in its physical example had no connection to or presence in the soul, it would be particular and perceptible, not general and intelligible. It would not yet have been freed from the material coverings that keep it from being an object of thought. Yet we have assumed that it is intelligible to the soul and exists there in a way different from its material existence, which comes with those coverings. Think about this. Now suppose both the known thing and the soul exist in their own right, free from matter. In what sense could one be inside the other? And why should the soul contain the thing rather than the other way around?

One independently existing thing can literally contain another only when both have size, as bodies do. Still, someone whose heart has been lit by God and who has tasted some of the knowledge of spiritual beings may accept what we suggested at the start: in relation to what we sense and imagine, the soul is more like an active maker than a passive container. This answers many objections to mental existence that assume the soul is a place where perceptions sit, and that for something to exist in another thing means it is inside it. These objections include saying that the soul is the matter of substantial forms,533 that a substance becomes a quality,534 and that the soul takes on features it does not have, such as heat, cold, movement, rest, being even or odd, or the nature of a horse or a stone.

If perceptions arise through the soul without being lodged inside it, these problems fall away. Nor do we need to split what the soul perceives from what becomes present to it. This is clear for things perceived by the outer senses and by the inner senses.

The soul relates to universal intellectual forms through an illuminating connection to intellectual realities in the creative world. Their relation to bodily kinds is like the relation, in the familiar account, between ideas drawn from individual material things and those things themselves.535 Although these intellectual realities exist in their own right and are individuals, the soul’s perception of them is weak in this world because it is tied to dense bodily things. It can see them only partly, like something far away in dusty air, or like a person with weak eyesight who sees a shape from a distance and cannot tell whether it is Zayd, Amr, Bakr, or Khalid—or whether it is a person, a tree, or a stone. In the same way, an illuminated form or intellectual reality may seem unclear to the soul.

Generality, vagueness, and the ability of one idea to apply to many are signs of weak existence or weak understanding. This weakness may come from the knower: the power to understand may be weak, like a child’s, or something may prevent it from working fully, as happens to souls tied to the body in this dark world. But the weakness may also come from what is known. This can happen because it is faint or incomplete, like time, number, and basic matter.

Or the thing known may be too great and bright for the soul to grasp fully, as with the higher beings known through the intellect. Their beauty and brightness may overwhelm our understanding. This is why the mind cannot fully grasp the Necessary Being, God.

In short, when the soul understands general ideas, it sees immaterial intellectual beings. It does not do this by stripping an idea from something sensed, as most philosophers say. Rather, it travels from what it senses to what it imagines, then to what it understands; from this world to the next and beyond; from the world of bodies to the world of imaginal forms, then to the world of intellects. The Qur'anic verse “You know the first creation. Why, then, do you not reflect?” points to this. We truly understand the next life by knowing this one, because two things that are related can be understood through one another.

We have almost left the subject at hand, so let us return. Knowledge, then, is a kind of existence,536 a form of existence that belongs to the perceiving soul or is present to it, as we will explain later. Every substantial or accidental existence is accompanied by a general nature, which the people of spiritual insight call the “fixed essence.” We hold that in itself it is neither existent nor nonexistent.537

Nor does this fixed essence have any of the features of existence, such as being a cause or an effect, coming before or after something, and the like. As we have explained, what exists in itself, whether it is sensed or understood, has either material or immaterial existence. Its nature is joined to it and exists through it. In the same way, what is present to our powers of perception—the thing known, witnessed, or held before them—exists as a sensory or intellectual form.

Sensory forms begin to exist independently of the human soul and appear before it in another world through something that reveals them, such as the eye, a mirror, or the imagination, without being inside those things. Intellectual forms, by contrast, are reached when the soul rises toward them and connects with them; they do not enter the soul. These intellects are particular in themselves,538 but their natures can apply to many individuals of their kinds.

In each of these ways of existing, the thing’s nature appears along with it, but only as a dependent image. Think of a clear reflection in a polished mirror. The reflection is a likeness; it is not itself the kind of independent thing, or the quality, that it shows. The image of a person seen in a mirror is not an actual human being; it exists only because the person exists. In the same way, the ideas of animal, plant, movement, and heat that appear in the mind are the meanings of those things, not the things themselves. A concept does not have to be an example of the thing it means.

In short, when external things come before the human soul, the soul’s freedom from matter allows sensory, imaginal, and intellectual forms to appear in it, as reflections appear in a mirror. The difference is that the mirror receives its image, while the soul brings its forms about through its own activity.

Do not take this to be the same as the view that mental forms are only copies or likenesses. That view says that a person’s essence exists in the outside world, while only its shadow or copy—not its essence—is present in the mind. We hold instead that human nature, or its fixed essence, is preserved in both places, though it does not exist by itself in either. Rather, it is joined to different kinds of existence in different ways.

For example, outside the mind, the idea of a human being is joined to an existence that can be described as a substance with dimensions, growth, sensation, and the ability to understand intellectual realities.539 In another kind of existence, it is a separate intellectual substance, which Plato and earlier philosophers called the Holy Spirit. In the mind, it is joined to yet another kind of existence: a mental quality that cannot be divided or related, and that exists either as a passing state or as a settled ability.540

When we say that something is something else, we can mean two different things. In the first sense, we say that an actual thing has a particular description. The thing we are talking about is one example of what that description covers. The claim may be about the subject as a concept or about the particular things it applies to. What is said may describe what the thing is or add a feature to it. All these are ordinary predication, whether the claim is essential or incidental.541

The second kind means that the subject is precisely the meaning and nature of the predicate, though we still notice a difference between them.542 The predicate names the subject’s nature; it does more than say that the two share an existence.543 This is the first, or essential, way of saying something about a thing. It tells us what the thing is by its very nature, not merely a feature it happens to have. That is why it comes first when we affirm or deny something about the thing. A single claim can be both true and false of the same subject, depending on which kind of predication we mean.544 The same concept can even be said of itself in one sense and denied of itself in another. For example, something is particular by its definition, but the idea of “particular” is general in ordinary predication because it applies to many things. The concept of a grammatical particle is a particle by definition, but as a word it is a noun.

With this distinction in place, we can say that general natures known by the intellect do not belong to any basic category insofar as they are general ideas.545546 But insofar as they exist in the soul as a state or ability—and the soul either shows them or brings them about—they fall under the category of quality as features of the soul.547548

You may ask: if something is a substance, does that not form part of its very nature? And are size and relationships not part of the natures of things that have them? My friend, there is an important difference. Calling a human being a substance when we define what a human being is does not turn the definition itself into a substance. The concept of “particular,” for example, is itself not particular, even though its meaning is what cannot apply to many things. A thing’s definition may express its nature, but that does not make the definition an example of the thing.

Likewise, saying that the concept of substance is identical with itself does not make it one of the substances or kinds of substance. The same applies to the other categories. It would follow only if the effects of the category applied to the concept.549 For example, if the idea of substance, considered as a general idea, existed outside the mind, it would have to exist independently of a subject. But a general idea cannot exist outside the mind, because every actual thing outside the mind is particular. The same holds for most definitions. The definition of animal—“a living, sensing substance”—does not itself fit that definition by ordinary predication, though it does by primary predication.

Someone might object: if the natures of kinds do not themselves belong to the categories, in any mode of existence, then the categories are not essential to those natures or true of them in any sense. Nor would actual individuals belong to those categories, since a thing’s reality is its kind. We reply that belonging to a category requires two things.550 First, the concept of that category must be part of what the thing is. For example, a surface is a continuous quantity that is stable and divisible in two directions. These ideas form parts of its definition. Second, the effects of the category must apply to it: because it is a quantity, it can be divided and compared; because it is continuous, its parts can meet along shared boundaries; and because it is stable, its parts exist together.

Now consider what happens when things of a given kind exist outside the mind. Their defining features have real effects, because the things themselves exist. But when we think about that kind, the idea still contains the meaning of those features without producing their effects. Effects belong to things, not to the ideas we have of them.

For example, the idea of a surface contains the meaning of quantity. But the idea itself does not divide into parts. As something that exists in the mind and depends on it, it is a simple, immaterial meaning. If that meaning existed outside the mind, the effects of quantity would follow from it. The same is true of the idea of a human being: it contains the general meaning “a living, rational being,” but it is not itself an animal with actual size, location, growth, sensation, or voluntary movement. It contains the meaning of animal and the meaning of reason, but not their actions and effects. The same is true of the idea of reason.

Someone may object: you have separated a thing’s nature from effects that are actually part of its nature. To be a quantity is to be divisible. How, then, can the idea of a surface involve quantity but not itself be divisible? If it is divisible by its nature, it cannot be a quality.

We reply that the idea contains the meaning of quantity. The proofs for mental existence show only that the natures of things are present in the mind, not their individual examples or their particular modes of existence. We have already shown that modes of existence and individual features cannot move from one realm to another. The definition of knowledge as a form that comes from the thing known is enough to show this.551

Applying the meaning of quantity to these kinds is like including the meaning of quantity in its own definition: the meaning is part of what they are. Just as the idea of quantity does not become an example of itself or divide into parts simply because it means “divisible,” neither do the kinds that appear in the mind become divisible.

What we have explained shows that mental ideas, considered as natures, are not examples of the basic categories.552 The category meanings are either the ideas themselves or part of them. But insofar as the ideas exist as features of the mind, they belong to the category of quality only incidentally, not by their nature.553 The original problem depends on assuming that every category is essential to each of its examples in every respect. No proof establishes this, and experience does not support it. This assumption has confused people: some deny mental existence, some say a thing’s nature changes, and some say that knowledge is called a quality only by a figure of speech. Each has chosen a different view, but none has found a satisfactory answer.

The second objection is this: when we imagine high mountains, wide deserts with their trees and rivers, hills and valleys, or huge planets and stars, we imagine them as particular things. So, on their view, all of these must exist inside the power of imagination. Yet that power is not a body and has no size; it is a mental quality or power that depends on a small amount of vapor in the brain.554 When we imagine Zayd together with other people, does this tiny power contain people who perceive, move, understand, and carry on their trades and crafts? The mind is sure this is impossible. The same difficulty arises if the place of these images is said to be the spirit in the front of the brain: that too is small. A huge image cannot be imprinted in something tiny. It does not help to say that both can be divided without end. A hand cannot hold a mountain, even if both can be divided endlessly.

This objection applies only to those who say that bodily likenesses and images exist inside the powers of imagination or sense. They have not proved this with a clear and sufficient argument, as anyone who follows their claims can see. These powers may prepare the soul to see images in a greater world of images that exists apart from it. That was Suhrawardi’s view, following the ancient Persian philosophers and the Stoics. Or they may be the means by which the soul makes images in its own smaller world, as I hold.555 In short, the objection does not apply to someone who says that sensed things have another kind of existence besides their bodily existence in the material world.

The proofs for the existence of forms known by the soul show that there is another world, and that these images and likenesses exist in another way besides the way they appear to the outer senses. Through this other existence they appear to our inner powers. The soul, freed from both these kinds of existence and higher than both worlds, may even see them with the help of its inner powers, just as it sees images with the help of the outer senses.

From what the outer senses perceive, the soul knows of the material world. From what its inner powers perceive, it knows of another world of images. And from its knowledge of itself and of realities grasped by the intellect, it knows of a third world beyond both. We remember particular people we once saw, even after they have disappeared from this world, and picture them with the same size, shape, and position. The image stands before us in its particular form. It must exist somewhere, though not in this material world, so it exists in another world.

Plato, the ancient sages, and the mystics who saw these realities taught that the beings of the imaginal world exist without a place or direction. This world lies between the world of intellect and the world of sense. Intellectual beings are entirely free from matter and from place, shape, size, color, and light. Sensible beings are immersed in these features. Images in this middle world are different from both: they do not occupy a physical place, yet they still have size and shape.

Here is the substance of Suhrawardi’s argument in The Wisdom of Illumination. Vision does not happen because the image of the thing seen is stamped on the eye, as Aristotle held, or because a ray leaves the eye and reaches the thing, as mathematicians said. Vision happens when a luminous object faces a healthy eye. This gives the soul direct awareness of the object, and so it sees it. The image in a mirror is not in the eye, since something large cannot be stamped into something small. Nor is the mirror image exactly the same as the person or thing seen, as some have thought.556557

The image is not in the mirror or in any other body. The eye’s clear lens relates to visible things as a mirror relates to the images that appear in it. Since the mirror’s image is not in the mirror, the image perceived through the lens is not in the lens either. It appears when the soul’s direct awareness meets a luminous object and no obstacle blocks it. If the thing has an existence outside the mind, the soul sees it. If it is only an image, it needs something to show it, like a mirror.

When the eye’s lens faces a mirror in which images appear, the soul’s direct awareness reaches those images through the lens and the mirror, when the right conditions are present and obstacles are removed. Just as the large image cannot be stamped into the eye, it cannot be stamped into a place in the brain. So imagined images are not in the mind, where a large thing could not fit into a small place. They are not in the outside world either, or everyone with healthy senses would see them. Nor are they nothing, since we can imagine and distinguish them and make different true or false claims about them. They exist in another region: the imaginal world, also called the separate imagination because it is not material like the imagination joined to the soul.

This is the world whose existence was taught by ancient philosophers such as Plato, Socrates, Pythagoras, Empedocles, and other spiritual thinkers, as well as mystics from many peoples. They spoke of two worlds: the world of intellect, which includes the divine world and the worlds of intellects and souls; and the world of images, which includes sensory forms and imaginal images.558
