For example, being before Friday belongs to Thursday; being after Thursday belongs to Friday. The same applies to each part of time in relation to all the others. Thursday cannot simply be moved to Friday. If it could, Friday would have to be Thursday too, because Thursday’s place in time is part of what makes it Thursday. The restored time would still have its own identity and nature. If we suppose it restored, it would remain a beginning in its actual nature, even while we call it restored. If it were no longer a beginning, it would not be the same time. The objection therefore fails in both its premises and its replies.

The third argument is this: if a nonexistent thing could be restored as exactly the same thing, then a new thing could appear for the first time that matched it in its nature and every feature that marks it as an individual. Like cases should be treated alike, and the existence of an individual with these features is assumed to be possible. But then there would be no difference between the new thing and the restored one, since they would share the same nature and all the same identifying features.

Two objections are raised. First, the things need not be indistinguishable in reality. If they could not be distinguished, they would not be two things; but the mind’s inability to tell them apart does not show that they are indistinguishable in reality. Second, if this argument worked, it would also rule out two similar things appearing for the first time. This would not be an argument about restoring a nonexistent thing at all.

The first reply fails because two things cannot differ in reality unless they differ in some individual feature. If they have no such difference, they are not two things. To say “If they were not different, they would not be two things” simply assumes the very point being disputed. The question is whether, once restoration is allowed, a restored thing and a new thing can both exist without any real difference between them, even though one is restored and the other begins for the first time.

The second reply says that two things alike in every respect may lack any real distinction wherever they appear. But that is not our case. Here, the supposed difference between the two comes only from calling one restored. We are asked to accept a real distinction between them on that basis alone.

Someone might object that they are not wholly indistinguishable: one existed before, while the other did not. But that is precisely the distinction that the argument calls into question. We have already shown that nonexistence is the destruction of the thing itself. A thing that does not exist has no identity, and there is no distinction among things simply as nonexistent. There is only sheer absence. So the subjects of the two existences, and of the nonexistence between them, cannot be one and the same thing: its identity is not preserved through nonexistence.

If the restored thing is distinguished from the new one by an identity that links its two existences across the time when it was absent, then the nonexistent thing would have an identity after all. But it does not. If they are distinguished because one existed earlier, that is just the very relation whose possibility is in question. Both things would have an equal claim to it. Without continuity to make them two moments of one individual, how could one alone be linked to the thing that existed before?

No one should argue that, for philosophers, a thing’s existence in the mind is like the Muʿtazilite idea of things that remain fixed while nonexistent. Perhaps, they might say, an individual identity could be preserved in some higher form of knowledge, such as God’s knowledge or the Preserved Tablet, beyond the reach of change.637

We have already explained that an individual’s mode of existence and identity cannot be preserved while its realm of existence changes. This applies only to general natures, whose different modes of existence and individual features lie outside their meaning. Every mental image, considered in itself, is general: whatever its details, the mind can suppose that it applies to more than one thing. Only some further reason, such as the impossibility of two exact duplicates, may lead the mind to rule out this possibility. So if the same mental image first exists in the outside world and then appears there again, the second is a different individual from the first, because nothing has preserved its individual identity.638

An image formed by the senses becomes an image of this particular thing because the senses connect it with the world outside. Imagination, too, singles out its image through what the mind supposes and connects it with. If you picture Zayd, who has died, then set aside what you know about his past life and look closely at the image itself, you will see that it could apply to many people.

The fourth argument is this: an individual thing could be restored only if some part of its complete cause were restored, along with the particular readiness of its matter and the other conditions that complete its cause and make its effect possible. We can ask the same question about the final part of its cause, and about the readiness of the matter for that cause, and continue back through the chain to the highest principles and causes. As will become clear, the conclusion is impossible; so the claim that led to it is impossible too.

The connection is plain. If the cause and the matter’s readiness were not exactly the same as before, the supposed restoration would really be a new beginning, a likeness of the earlier thing. A being could return as the same individual only if all the conditions that made it ready to exist returned too: the cycles of the heavens, the positions of the stars, and everything that came earlier in the whole order of the world, with all its conditions and consequences—even its being a first beginning. A sound nature does not hesitate to reject this idea.

Most theologians who allow nonexistent things to be restored oppose all the philosophers. They think that allowing restoration is what makes bodily resurrection possible, as the religious laws and revealed books say it will be. They do not understand that divine truths cannot be learned through theological debate and argument. There are only two ways to know them. The way of the righteous is to establish the practices of worship, keep to justice, and free oneself from the habits that cloud the mind. Those brought near to God take another path. They develop their understanding and turn their powers of awareness toward what is holy. They polish the soul like a mirror, so that bad character will not stain it, the impressions brought by the senses will not cloud it, and false opinions will not distort it.639

Then the truths of faith appear to the soul, which can see what the senses cannot and understand it through its own clear nature. But a soul stained by bad actions, dulled by poor character, or bent by false opinions—as happens to many who make a career of disputation—remains shut off from the truths of faith. It cannot reach God, and it loses the happiness of the next life. As God says, “No indeed! On that Day they will be kept from their Lord.” Whoever hopes to learn through debate and argument about God, His attributes and acts, the sending of messengers and the revelation of books, the next world, life after death, or any of the other mysteries of creation and return has mistaken a swelling for sound flesh. When we come to discuss how souls return to their Maker in the two worlds and reach their Sustainer in both realms, it will become clear how bodily resurrection takes place: souls return to their bodies by permission of the One who brings all things into being, in both their beginning and their return, just as the revealed teachings state.

Although these theologians agree that substances can be restored, they disagree about attributes, or accidents. Some say no accident can ever be restored, since it would have to be restored through another accident, which would make one accident depend on another.640 Some Ashʿarites hold this view. Most of them say that accidents that do not endure, such as sounds and musical notes, cannot be restored, because they belong only to the times in which they occur.641 They divide enduring accidents into those within human power and those beyond it. They say that neither a person nor God can restore the first kind, but that God can restore the second.642 They offer separate proofs for these claims, filling their books with flimsy arguments and other fancies.

Many of their other mistaken views are just as disgraceful. They claim that there are several eternal beings. They say God acts by an arbitrary will with no purpose, and that His creation has no wisdom. They also say He has an inner speech and an imagined conversation, and that things which do not exist are somehow fixed. Finally, they claim that matter is made of indivisible atoms. But that would mean a moving thing is at rest, a millstone comes apart, or an object jumps from one place to another without crossing the space between. These and other tricks and embellishments all come from rejecting wisdom and opposing the philosophers. In truth, these people are innovators who lead others astray, guides for the ignorant and the low-minded. They are a danger to religious and devout people, and a threat to scholars. Among all groups, they are most hostile to the believing philosophers and those who know God.

These quarrelsome debaters plunge into questions of reason without understanding what the senses show us. They attempt proofs and logical arguments without knowing mathematics, and speak about divine things while ignorant of nature.

Most of what they argue over consists of dressed-up claims that have no truth or existence outside their own false imaginings. They can offer no proof when challenged, even about things whose reality most people accept. When pressed, they deny these things rather than admit, “We do not know; God and His Messenger know best.” Yet their language is polished and their expressions elegant. They present false fancies and mistaken beliefs in the clearest words, write them in the neatest hand, and read them aloud to the young and the uneducated. They plant these ideas so deeply in people’s minds that they are almost impossible to remove. Through all this harm and hardship for religious people, they still claim that their weak minds and limited understanding defend Islam and strengthen the faith. To this day, we have not heard of a Jew who turned back through one of them, a Christian who became Muslim, or a Zoroastrian who came to believe. Rather, when people of those faiths see the debaters’ views, they cling to their own religions even more. May God protect the faith and the believers from their harm and corruption.

It is also strange that some of them have used the philosophers’ saying as proof that restoration is possible: “When you hear of wonders in the natural world, leave them within the bounds of possibility unless a clear proof rules them out.” Because they have not trained themselves to reason carefully, they have failed to distinguish two meanings of possibility. One means that the mind has not clearly seen either side as necessary. The other means that a thing is possible in itself: by its own nature, neither its existence nor its nonexistence is necessary. They then assume that anything not proved necessary or impossible must be possible in itself. On this basis, they claim that restoring a nonexistent thing is possible in itself. Many who came later clung to this flimsy and harmful idea, woven by the spider’s web of their own imaginings.

We say to them and their followers: if by “the default” you mean what is common or more likely, it is not clear that most things whose necessity or impossibility has not been proved are possible. Even if they were, this would not help your case. Restoration might be one of the few exceptions. If you mean that a claim should stand unless there is proof against it, as people sometimes argue when interpreting religious law, that rule does not apply here. None of the three ways a thing can be—necessary, possible, or impossible—is a default of this kind. Each follows from the nature of the thing under discussion. If no proof has been given, we simply do not know which applies.

This is what Avicenna meant: when there is no proof that something is necessary, or that it is impossible, we should not deny it or claim that it is impossible. We should leave it within the bounds of possibility—that is, regard it as something reason may consider. He did not mean that we should believe it possible in itself. He also said that anyone who makes a habit of believing things without proof has turned away from human nature.

Chapter — Why nonexistence is not a relation

The early philosophers held that the connection expressed by a statement is always affirmative, whether the statement says that something is so or says it is not.643 A negative statement does not create a new connection of its own. It denies the connection asserted by the matching positive statement. It does not join the thing named to what is said about it; it denies that they are joined. We call it a statement that links a description to its subject only by comparing it with a positive statement.644 For this reason, a negative statement has no separate status based on negation. Its status is the status of the matching affirmative connection. Later philosophers disagreed. They said that a negative statement has its own negative connection, different from an affirmative one, and that it too has a status of its own.

Both affirmative and negative statements fall under three statuses: necessary, impossible, or possible. We usually explain them through affirmative statements because a negative one can be expressed through its positive counterpart.645 For example, if a thing must be absent, its existence is impossible; if its absence is impossible, its existence is necessary; and if it may be absent, it may also exist. A statement’s status tells us whether what it says about a thing must be true, cannot be true, or may be true.

In a simple statement, such as “A human exists,” the status concerns the thing itself: whether it must exist, cannot exist, or may exist or not. It does not concern a link between that thing and a separate description. In a more complex statement, such as “A human is a writer,” the status concerns whether that description applies to the thing, and how firmly or weakly it does so. A negative statement says either that the thing itself does not exist, or that the description does not apply to it. It does not introduce an entity called “absence,” or a thing that has absence as a feature. So there is no negative connection that could itself have one of the three statuses.646

What the early philosophers called a statement’s “element” or “status” is, in a simple statement, the thing’s own condition: whether it must always exist, must always be absent, or may go either way.

In a more complex statement, it is the description’s condition when applied positively to the thing. The difference between possibility and necessity or impossibility is like the difference between weakness and strength, or looseness and firmness. This will become clear in this book and in our way of doing philosophy. If we state a claim’s status in words, that wording can differ from the way things really are.647 We have now shown that a negative statement has the same status as its corresponding affirmative statement. If the claim were made positively, it would have one of the statuses already described, whether or not anyone actually makes it.648

Someone may think that a statement has one status when its predicate is “nonexistent” and another when its predicate is “existent”; or that the status changes when nonexistence, rather than existence, is treated as the link. The mistake is to treat “Zayd is nonexistent” as though it gave Zayd a feature called nonexistence. The intended meaning is simply “Zayd does not exist.” Once we treat the first sentence as a positive claim with a negative description, we have changed what it says. That is why the status of the two statements differs. Whatever idea we take as a predicate has a certain status in its positive relation to a particular subject. That status does not change when the relation is denied.

When we mean to say that Zayd does not exist at all, we should not treat “nonexistent” as a feature that belongs to him. We mean that he himself is absent. Then the statement is a simple negative one. It is not an affirmative statement that attributes the absence of existence to him, nor a compound negative statement that removes existence from a subject that is already there.

Anyone who fails to distinguish simple statements from more complex ones, and assumes that every statement must either attribute something to a subject or deny something of it, will not accept that “A human exists” or “A human came to be” means that the human being himself exists or came to be. They will think instead that it means some feature called existence belongs to him. Likewise, “A human’s nonexistence” means that the human being himself is absent, not that a feature called existence has been removed from him. But “A human is a writer” attributes writing to him, while keeping a person’s fingers still denies the act of writing. Failing to see this difference is a deep-rooted error in human thought, one that must be corrected. Otherwise, people will feel forced to make an exception to the general rule that what is affirmed of a subject depends on the subject’s existence—even in simple statements, as we explained earlier.649

Now that you understand that negation, as negation, has no definite content that can be affirmed or denied of something as necessary, impossible, or possible, you can see that there is no negative link that is itself necessary, lasting, actual, or possible. To say that a negative link is necessary means that the corresponding positive link is impossible.650 To say that a negative link lasts means that the positive link is absent at every time. We consider the status of the affirmative statement, then deny that link for each time under consideration. So, in this refined account, “It is necessarily not the case that this is so” means that the positive claim is impossible; and “This is never so” means that the positive claim fails at every time. This differs from the usual account in general philosophy. The same applies to the other kinds of qualified statements and to unqualified statements, which stand in contrast to them. An unqualified statement has no added mode; its contrast with a qualified one is like the contrast between lacking a feature and having it.651 An unqualified negative statement is simply a negative statement without any added mode. We cannot separate “an unqualified denial” from “denying that something is qualified.” A full explanation would take us beyond the scope of this book.

Our aim here is to show the way to truth and how to travel toward God. The detailed work belongs to the discipline of logic.

Chapter — Why a negative statement still needs its two terms

What we say about a thing may or may not exist outside the mind. But to make a judgment, we must have both the thing and what we say about it present in thought. We cannot judge what is not before the mind. The subject, too, must exist in thought in every statement, whether affirmative or negative. If a statement affirms something about the outside world, its subject must also exist there. You cannot affirm one thing of another unless that other thing exists in some way.

There is one exception: what is said may itself mean pure negation, as in “Zayd does not exist outside the mind” or “A partner to God is impossible.” Although these statements seem to speak about the outside world, they deny that anything exists there. In effect, they say: “The Zayd we picture in the mind is not outside it.”

When a statement denies something about the outside world, the act of denying does not require the thing named to exist there. We may deny something of what does not exist, or deny that an absent thing exists. This is true of negation as negation, not of a judgment made by the human mind, which requires something to be present in thought. So when people say that the subject of a negative statement is broader than the subject of an affirmative statement with a negative description, they do not mean that only the negative statement can be about something that does not exist outside the mind. Affirmative statements can do that too, as in “A partner to God is impossible” or “Contradictions cannot exist together.” Nor do they mean that a subject of an affirmative statement can be present in the mind while the subject of a negative one cannot. Both must be present in thought. They mean that a negative statement can apply to something precisely as absent—as something that has no existence at all. The mind can consider it in that way. An affirmative statement cannot describe it from that same standpoint; it can say something of it only where it has some kind of existence.652653

That is why one may say that what is wholly nonexistent is nothing and has nothing, so long as one means it in the respect in which it does not exist. We may also deny every positive feature of a subject precisely as absent.654 But we cannot affirm some other feature of it from that same standpoint. The exception is when the feature named is itself negative or impossible: then the statement can be true without requiring the subject to exist in that respect, even though an affirmative link normally requires some existence. This is why people have said that the subject of a negative statement is broader than the subject of an affirmative one. That wording is misleading unless understood in the way just explained. It does not mean that a negative statement may have a subject that is absent outside the mind while an affirmative statement may not.655

Some argue that if the subject of a negative statement is broader than the subject of an affirmative statement with a negative description, the two statements cannot contradict each other, because they would apply to different things. But if the subject is not broader, they say, then there is no difference between the statements.

The answer depends on what “broader” means. It may mean that a statement covers more things. Or it may mean that we can consider the same thing in more than one way. Here it means the second, not the first. The two statements need not apply to different individuals. Here it means only the second. So the difference does not break the contradiction between the statements. A negative statement can apply to a subject under a broader description even when it does not cover more actual cases. An affirmative statement is narrower in this respect, though the two may happen to cover the same cases. This is because every concept and every fixed reality is present in the higher levels of existence, and every judgment requires the subject to be present in thought. Something wholly unknown cannot be denied or affirmed. We can also answer the objection by remembering the difference between the two ways of making a statement: something may be denied of itself in one way and affirmed of itself in another.656

This difference applies only to statements about particular things or kinds. It does not apply to statements such as “Every G is B,” because that form already includes a positive assumption about its subject: anything described as G, in thought or in reality, with or without a qualifier, is B.657658

There are more puzzles here, and they can hold back someone on the path toward God. One is that a negative statement with a negative description seems broader than the matching affirmative statement, because it can be true when its subject does not exist. Sometimes the negation of a broad idea has no real example at all, as with “not a thing,” “not known,” or “not possible in general.” Then the rules of logic seem to fail. The negation of a narrower idea may be true of something where the negation of a broader idea is also true, simply because the subject is absent.

This would make a statement such as “It is not the case that some non-substance is non-animal” true just because no such subject exists.659 The same problem seems to arise with “Some non-body is not non-spatial.” That, too, could be true simply because the subject does not exist. These cases appear to upset the rule that the negation of a narrower idea applies more broadly than the negation of a broader idea. They also seem to undermine the rule that the negations of two ideas with the same scope have the same scope, along with other rules of logic.

These objections seem to undermine not only the rule for reversing an “all” statement through its opposite, but other rules of logic as well. The usual reply is to treat a negative statement as a positive statement that says the predicate does not apply.660661 Its defenders then set apart positive statements with a negative description. They say these do not require the subject to exist, and group them with negative statements.662 They also set aside rules that concern the negations of very broad ideas. All these replies are reckless guesses by later imitators of the philosophers, people without a firm grounding in knowledge or insight.

The right way to untie the knot is the distinction we made earlier. A negative statement has a broader subject than its matching affirmative statement only in how the mind considers it, not in the number of actual things it covers. This does not mean that one statement can be true of an individual when the other is false of that same individual in the same respect. It means that one can be true of something under one way of considering it, while the other is not true of it under that same way—even though in both cases the subject must exist in some sense.

Every affirmative statement, whether it uses a negative description or a plain one, requires the subject to be established in some way: in the outside world, in thought, or by supposition. Every statement requires some kind of existence. The truth of a negative statement rests on the opposite condition: its subject is taken as assumed or supposed. This resolves the difficulty. Such claims are truly valid, and their subject need exist only as assumed. What makes the statement true is that if something were to fit the description named as its subject, the description named as its predicate would fit it too.663

The relation between ideas—whether one applies more broadly, more narrowly, or to the same range as another—does not mean that they must apply together to some actual thing. This is clear in the general idea to which such rules apply: it need not have an example in the outside world or even in the mind.

For example, anything possible in the strict sense is also possible in the broad sense. But anything that is not possible in the strict sense is possible in the broad sense too: it must either exist or be impossible, and both count as possible in the broad sense. If the opposite of what is broadly possible were always narrower than the opposite of what is possible in the strict sense, the first rule would imply that anything not broadly possible is not strictly possible; the second would then imply that the same thing is broadly possible. That is a contradiction. The same contradiction follows if we reverse the two steps.

The philosopher al-Tusi replies that broad possibility divides into two cases that are mutually exclusive and cover every possibility: either one side is necessary—existence or nonexistence—or neither side is necessary.664 If we take broad possibility to include both cases, then denying broad possibility falls outside the two opposite sides of the contradiction.

Now consider the two arguments just given. The first argument uses the same phrase in two different senses. In one statement, “not strictly possible” lies outside both sides of the opposition; in the other, it falls within one of them. Because the meaning changes, the argument fails.

The second argument also fails. Its first statement is false. The correct reversal of “Everything that is not strictly possible is broadly possible” is not “Everything that is not broadly possible is strictly possible.” It is “Everything that is not broadly possible is not not strictly possible,” meaning again what lies outside both sides of the contradiction, not strict possibility itself.

Someone might object that what lies outside both sides—what we call “nothing”—is not a thing at all. Nothing can be said of it, so how could it be broader than anything? The answer is twofold: “not strictly possible” can apply both to this “nothing” and to what falls under one of the two sides of the contradiction, namely what must exist and what cannot exist. That is all we mean by calling it broader.665666

A leading philosopher has clarified the issue this way. Broad possibility means that it is not necessary for a thing to be absent. This denies that the opposite side must be true. The opposite side may be the absence of a link between subject and predicate, if possibility concerns their relation; or it may be the subject’s own nonexistence, if “possible” is what we say of the subject itself. Since a thing’s necessary absence would make it impossible, broad possibility means either that the subject itself is not impossible, or that the description applied to it is not impossible. In either case, something impossible in itself is not broadly possible.

Most logicians use “opposite side” to mean whichever of existence or nonexistence goes against the actual state of things.667 For something necessary, the opposite is nonexistence; for something impossible, it is existence. Broad possibility can then apply to either one. If “broad possibility” means what this philosopher first described, the claim that something impossible in itself is broadly possible is false.

If instead we mean broad possibility as most people do, there are two ways to understand the necessity involved. We may say that each of the necessary and the impossible requires one side only. Then what is not strictly possible falls into three groups: what must exist, what cannot exist, and what must both exist and not exist. In that case, we cannot say that something necessary on both sides lacks necessity on the side that does not occur.

Or we may say that each requires one side without asking whether the other side is also necessary or not. Then we still cannot say that every impossible thing lacks necessity on the side that does not occur, because something necessary on both sides would count as impossible, and yet it would not lack that necessity.668

The author of Durrat al-Taj tried to challenge the claim that anything not strictly possible is broadly possible. He argued that if we consider a nature entirely by itself, it is neither strictly possible nor broadly possible. This objection does not work. The claim concerns how things stand in reality, not how the mind views them at one particular level.

Chapter — Can God have a particular kind of nonexistence?

Philosophers commonly say that some particular ways of existing are impossible for God, whose existence depends on nothing. This does not conflict with His necessary existence. In the same way, a particular way of existing can be impossible for something that depends on another, without contradicting its basic possibility. It may even confirm it. Particular kinds of absence can also be impossible for something dependent, or for something impossible in itself—for example, an absence that comes after existence.

It is clear that God cannot exist in any of the dependent ways of existing: He cannot come into being, pass away, have a body, exist inside another thing, or be a feature of it. These ways involve limits and lack. Some ways of existing are impossible for certain dependent things, and others are impossible for all of them. Existence that depends on nothing is impossible for every dependent thing. Existence as a substance is impossible for a feature; existence apart from matter is impossible for a material thing; and lasting, fixed existence is impossible for something whose being flows from moment to moment.

So a thing that exists only through change cannot, by its very nature, have a time before its existence when it was absent, then appear after that absence, or later become absent after it existed. These “before” and “after” relations belong to time. This does not mean that existence or nonexistence in general is impossible for such a thing. Likewise, once a real existence has taken place, a particular kind of absence that would remove it from reality—given its time, place, or qualities—is impossible for anything that depends on another. This is impossible as a feature of the thing, not by its nature.669

Critique and clarification

There is no doubt that ways of existing that involve limits cannot belong to God. But it is open to question whether a particular way of existing is impossible for Him simply because it is existence. Existence, taken as existence, is one simple reality. Its levels differ only in fullness or lack, strength or weakness. Lack and weakness amount to absence. Each level below God therefore has two sides: it is existence, and it falls short of complete perfection. Insofar as such a level falls short of perfection, it cannot belong to God. But insofar as it is existence, it must belong to Him, for He is necessary in every respect.

If one way of existing were impossible for God simply because it is existence, then His own reality would include both necessity and impossibility. That would make His being a combination of different sides.670 Someone might object that the same applies to His necessary existence and the impossibility of His nonexistence. But those two descriptions do not point to different things. One reality is the source of both descriptions: its existence is the very reason its absence is impossible. There is no difference in reality or in thought. This is unlike the case we are discussing, where the same reality would stand in two conflicting relations to existence.

This principle supports what we have said: all existing things depend on God. They are flows of His existence, like rays and gifts from the divine reality.671

It is also open to question whether particular kinds of absence can be impossible for something that is dependent, or for something impossible in itself. Absence has no distinct kinds, as we have explained. These descriptions of absence may follow from features of existence. For something impossible in itself, an absence that comes after existence is impossible only because the earlier existence is impossible. If the earlier existence cannot happen, then no later absence can follow it. That later absence is impossible only because it depends on the impossible existence. So any kind of absence that belongs to something impossible is impossible because of something else, not in itself.

Here is a well-known puzzle that people have found difficult. If time cannot have an earlier or later absence by its very nature, then time must exist necessarily, just as God does. The common reply is that only God cannot have any kind of absence. Time, they say, could be entirely absent, from beginning to end, so there is no contradiction in time being absent before and after its existence.

But this reply does not fit their own principles. Even if time could be entirely absent, it would still follow that the time that lies between earlier and later absence must exist necessarily. Then it would not need a cause in order to continue existing. Yet, on their own account, something whose existence depends on another needs a cause both to begin and to continue existing.672

They try another reply. The opposite of an earlier or later absence, they say, is simply the denial of that absence. But that denial may be true whether time exists continuously or is completely absent from beginning to end. So they claim that the answer does not prove time must exist.

With God’s help, we can avoid these strained replies. In our account, what is necessary in itself is existence without limit. What is impossible in itself is what cannot have existence in any way. A general nature can exist through any one of its examples, and it is absent only if all its examples are absent. But existence is not general in the same way as an abstract idea. It has an openness and reach that the deeply learned understand.

The necessity of the complete reality of existence means that all its levels and forms must exist. Its impossibility would mean that every one of its levels and forms is impossible. Time, with its continuous flow, is one expression of the First Cause and a weak level in the unfolding of existence. It is among the weakest things that depend on another for their existence, and among the lowest in rank of the things we know.673

There is another answer to the last objection. Time and motion exist by changing from moment to moment. They do not last as fixed things. Their whole existence is a process of coming to be, moment by moment. This is true whether the movement has an end, like the straight movement of the elements, or continues without end, like the circular movements of the heavens. So it makes no sense to ask whether time needs a cause to keep existing: it has no separate state of continued existence apart from its coming to be.

There is also another way to answer. Time and motion are unlike ordinary features that belong to a thing. Motion is the process of seeking a perfection, whether through a natural tendency or a deliberate choice. It is not a separate thing in its own right. What exists is what is sought, or what can be sought. Time is the measure of that seeking.

As long as we mean time and motion in this way, we cannot ask directly whether either one exists necessarily or possibly, lasts or ends. Such descriptions apply to them only because of something else. If we stop considering them in this way, they are no longer time or motion; they have become something else with different rules.674

Chapter — What depends on something impossible in itself need not itself be impossible

If something depends on what is impossible in itself, that does not mean the dependent thing is impossible in itself. It is impossible because of something else: the thing it depends on is impossible in itself.675 Someone might say the case is different when what is depended on is the subject—the thing that is impossible in itself—and what depends on it is a property, such as its being impossible in itself. Then the subject's impossibility in itself would entail that the property is impossible in itself too. They say this follows from the special relation between a subject and the property that describes it.

I think that view comes from confusing two kinds of description. Saying that something exists, or does not exist, is not like saying that a thing can receive a quality, or that it lacks that quality. Nor is it like describing an absent thing as lacking a quality it could have received. In those cases, the quality must follow the thing it describes, whether that thing exists or not.

For example, a body must exist before we can describe it as white or not white. The body has its own existence, and the whiteness or lack of whiteness is another fact that follows from it. Only after the body itself exists can we describe it by that quality. The same distinction applies when we speak of a body's absence and the absence of whiteness: one does not simply amount to the other.

Existence works differently. To say that existence belongs to a thing and to say that the thing exists are one and the same: the thing's existence is its own existence. There is no separate quality attached to it. The distinction between the thing and existence is made only in thought, as we explained earlier. The same is true of nonexistence. For a thing not to exist means that it is absent in itself; it does not mean that some other thing is absent from it.

So when we say that existence is necessary, this is the same as saying that the thing that exists is necessary. In reality, neither depends on the other; they differ only in how we consider them. The same is true when we say that a thing's nonexistence is impossible: that is simply to say that the thing that does not exist is impossible.

The same pattern continues when we describe that necessity as necessary again, or say that the impossibility itself must hold. We can keep doing this only as long as we keep extending the analysis in thought. In each case, describing the subject by one of these properties is the same as describing the property itself, or something that follows from it. There is no real dependence between them, and neither comes before the other.

Our conclusion is this: anything that depends on what is impossible in itself is always impossible because of something else, not impossible in itself. It is impossible because it depends on that thing, not because it is that thing. In the same way, anything that is necessary because of something else is possible in itself; it is neither necessary nor impossible in itself, as we have already shown.

Later, we will see that the familiar claim that one impossible thing entails another is not always true.676 It is true only when there is a rational link between them, as there is between what is impossible in itself and what is impossible because of something else—that is, something that depends on what is impossible in itself. Two things that are each impossible in themselves do not entail one another, just as two things that are each necessary in themselves do not. Nor does a thing entail its opposite.

Why? For one thing to entail another, one must depend on the other. Either one causes the other, or both are caused by something else. So at least one of them must be caused by something else. But anything caused by another is possible in itself, because a thing needs something else only if it is possible in itself. So what is impossible because of something else is possible in itself. Two things that are impossible in themselves do not entail one another, and neither does a thing entail what opposes it.

A seeming problem, and its answer

Someone might object: if the idea of something possible or impossible does not entail its opposite, how do proofs by assuming the opposite work? They establish something by assuming that it is false, then showing that the assumption leads to a contradiction. For example, to show that time has no beginning or end, they say that if it were absent before it existed, that earlier absence and its later existence could not be together. They make the same argument about its absence after it exists. And to show that spatial magnitudes are finite, they say that an unlimited magnitude would have to be limited.

If you mean that these proofs show that, if the supposedly impossible thing were real, its opposite would also be real—or that if time really were absent before or after it existed, it would not be absent at that time—then the proofs would be false. If those assumptions were real, they would have the consequences and effects that belong to them. They would not contradict themselves or produce effects that oppose them.

But if you mean that these proofs show what follows when we assume one of these things while leaving all the other actual and possible conditions in place, then that is what they do.677 The assumption, combined with those other conditions, leads to a contradiction: it makes the thing and its opposite both true, or makes the thing both absent and present. That does not mean the thing itself entails its opposite. It means that assuming it, while keeping the other conditions in place, leads to the opposite of what those conditions require. On closer inspection, the assumption amounts to placing two incompatible things together.

In short, a proof of this kind treats something as a supposition, not as something that has actually happened. It assumes the thing and then shows that, together with what follows from it, the assumption leads to its opposite. If we treated it as real, we would also have to accept all that follows from it and everything it depends on. We would have to set aside whatever contradicts it, its consequences, or the things it depends on. Only then would we be treating it as a real state of affairs.

But that is not what the proof does. It says: if we assume this thing and think through what follows, we find its opposite. It does not say: if this thing were really the case, its absence would also be real. The supposed impossible thing, considered as an idea in the mind, leads to the idea of a contradiction. But two conflicting ideas can be considered together in the mind. As we have noted, they are possible as ideas.

The proof then shows that the conclusion it draws does not stand for anything that exists in the world of possible things.678 So it argues from the absence of that conclusion to the falsehood of the original assumption. The conditional claim and the denial of its conclusion together show that the assumption is impossible; the assumption alone does not.

Take note: we established earlier that what is necessary in itself cannot be necessary because of something else. Apply the same reasoning to what is impossible in itself. It cannot also be impossible because of something else. Otherwise, its own impossibility would disappear if that other thing disappeared.

Also, one thing cannot have two nonexistences or two impossibilities. Nor can one nonexistence and one impossibility belong to two different things. By contrast, one thing can have two existences or two necessities, and two different things can share an existence or a necessity. This shows that existence and nonexistence, and the necessity of existing or not existing, multiply only when their subjects do.

It is therefore impossible for the same thing to be impossible in itself and impossible because of something else, either at once or at different times. What is impossible in itself is impossible through its own nature alone.

We have now seen that anything made necessary or impossible by something else is possible in itself. We have also seen that possibility in itself must be understood so that it can become either necessary or impossible because of something else, as something incomplete can be brought to completion. That is why a possible thing can take on either description.

Remember that the human mind cannot bear the radiance of the First Reality, God, or grasp the full reality of His glory and majesty. His light, perfection, and actuality are too great. In the same way, the mind cannot grasp what is impossible in itself, because it falls so far short of existence that it is not even a thing. A thing cannot be separated from existence; what does not exist is not a thing.

The human mind can understand what things are, but it cannot fully grasp pure existence itself, which is not one thing among others, as in God—exalted is His name—or pure nonexistence, which is not a thing in any way. It cannot grasp the first because it is complete and fully real; it cannot grasp the second because it is entirely lacking and unreal.

Anything closer to God shares this condition in some way, such as the First Intellect and the intelligences that follow it. Anything closer to what is impossible likewise shares its condition, such as basic matter, motion, and things like them.

In short, some things we know have the strongest existence: God, followed by the intelligences that do not depend on bodies and other spiritual beings. Others have such weak existence that they are close to nonexistence because they are mixed with it. These include basic matter, time, and motion. Between these two extremes are things such as material bodies, in the philosophers' view, and the bodies we form in imagination, in our view. We will explain later, when discussing the senses and what they perceive, that we can understand a body only by grasping its form apart from its matter in some way.

As long as human minds are occupied with guiding these earthly bodies, they cannot grasp the first kind, just as bats cannot see sunlight because it overwhelms their eyes. They also cannot grasp the second kind, because these things have such weak and incomplete existence, just as sight cannot detect objects that are very far away or very small. The third kind, however, is within our power to know and understand: things such as distances, shapes, tastes, and colors.

This is because most human souls in this world work mainly through imagination and the senses. What perceives must be of the same kind as what it perceives, just as food must be suited to the one who eats it. That is why these things are easy for us to know.

Chapter — Can human beings know what things truly are?

Some books say679 that we can know composite things because we can define them by their constituent parts, but we cannot know simple things because their true natures cannot be understood. At most, we can describe them through their properties and effects. For example, the soul is said to be something that moves the body.680 What we know about it, then, is that it moves the body; its true nature remains unknown. The argument is that people disagree about what things are because each person notices a different property and judges the thing by it. If we knew the true natures of things, we would also know their properties, near and remote, because knowing a cause leads to knowing its effects. If that were so, no claim about the properties of a thing would need to be proved. That is the argument.

Perhaps this writer has confused knowing an aspect of a thing with knowing the thing through one of its aspects.681 The first belongs in a statement about a concept itself. What is said there does not carry over to the things that fall under that concept, let alone to their properties or consequences. The second belongs in an ordinary statement about actual things. What is said of them applies directly to their real instances, but only indirectly to their accidental features and what follows from them. If a claim applies to one thing directly and to another only indirectly, that does not make it apply to a third thing, much less to anything further removed.

We should also note that necessary connections between things arise from their actual existence, not from their abstract natures—except for features that belong to a nature simply because of what it is. What the mind takes from things in the world is their natures and concepts, not their actual existence as individuals. The intellect knows what a thing is; its actual existence is what brings about its actual consequences. So understanding a thing in thought does not mean that we also understand its consequences, whether near or remote. This resolves the difficulty.

Al-Razi says in al-Mabāḥith al-Mashriqiyya (Eastern Investigations) that simple natures can be understood. His proof is this: composite things must be made up of simple things, since every plurality contains unity. If simple things could not be understood, composite things could not be understood by definition. Nor could they be understood by description, since a description defines a thing through its properties. If those properties are simple, they could not be understood; if they are composite but their own simple parts cannot be understood, they too would remain unknown. In short, the same problem applies to the things those properties imply. So the claim that simple things cannot be understood would mean that we understand nothing at all, neither by definition nor by description. But that conclusion is plainly false, so the claim that leads to it must be false too. That is the end of his argument.

There is a weakness here. Even if we can understand things made of parts, it does not follow that we must first understand each of their simplest parts. We need not accept that a definition of a composite thing requires knowledge of every part, down to the simplest ones; it may be enough to know its nearest parts, perhaps through a description. Nor must we know composite things by knowing their parts, near or remote. We may know them another way: not through their full nature or a definition,682 but through direct experience683 or a description based on their properties and effects. If asked how we know those properties and descriptions, we can say that we know them in some way, but not in their full nature. So the claim that simple things cannot be understood means that we cannot know their full nature, not that we cannot know anything about them—not even through general ideas such as “thing” and “possible.”

The right course here is to ask what “simple” means. Does it mean a simple concept, or a simple thing in the world? If it means that the intellect cannot know an individual real existence through a mental image that matches it, there is some truth in that, as we showed earlier in our discussion of existence.684 But if it means that the intellect cannot understand any simple concept, that is plainly false. The intellect understands existence, thinghood, and concepts such as “which” and “what,” among others. Whatever the intellect understands about a thing is either a simple concept or a composite one. If it is simple, it is either the full nature of a simple thing or one aspect of it. In the first case, the intellect has understood that thing’s full nature. In the second, it has understood that aspect, even if it does not know the full nature of the thing it belongs to.

Otherwise, if every aspect had to be understood through another aspect, we would either go back forever or move in a circle, and so understand nothing at all. But that is clearly false. If what the intellect understands is a composite concept, it must contain at least one simple concept: a concept cannot be made from an endless series of concepts nested within one another. And even if the series were endless, there would still have to be a simple concept within it, since every multiplicity includes unity.

Avicenna says in The Notes:685

Human beings cannot grasp the true natures of things. We know their characteristics, the features that necessarily follow from their nature, and other features they may have. We do not know the defining features that make each thing what it is. We know that things have properties and accidents, but not their true natures. We do not know the true nature of the First, the intellect, the soul, the heavenly sphere, fire, air, water, or earth. Nor do we know the true natures of accidents. For example, we do not know what a substance truly is. We know686 that it is something that exists in its own right, rather than as a quality belonging to another thing. But that is not its true nature. We do not know what a body truly is; we know something with length, breadth, and depth. We do not know what an animal truly is; we know something that can perceive and act. Being able to perceive and act is not the true nature of an animal, but one of its properties and necessary features. We cannot grasp its real defining feature. That is why people disagree about what things are: each person notices something different and judges the thing by it.

We identify a particular thing through one or more properties that distinguish it. Then, through what we first learn, we discover other properties of that thing, one by one, until we establish that it exists. This is how we reason about the soul, place, and other things whose existence we do not establish through their own natures, but through their relations to things we already know, or through an accident or a necessary feature. For example, we see a body moving and infer that something moves it. We see a kind of movement unlike the movements of other bodies, and infer that it has a particular mover or a special feature unlike the other movers. Then we follow its properties and necessary features, one by one, until we establish that it exists. That is the end of his argument.

I say that we should understand Avicenna’s words as we have already suggested and shown in our discussion of existence. We can establish individual instances of existence only through indirect reasoning, in a way that resembles reasoning from cause to effect. We have explained that the true nature of any existing thing can be known in its particularity only through direct awareness. For us, the defining features of things are their actual forms in the world. We know them through concepts and descriptions that truly apply to them. These concepts may be part of a definition, which is made up of what are called a broader kind and a distinguishing feature. But they are not the same as the thing’s actual form of existence—the reality that makes it what it is.

In some parts of The Healing, Avicenna says that the defining feature of an animal is not the concept “able to sense,” but the very soul that completes the animal’s nature, identity, and reality. The same is true of the defining features of other kinds of things. The first is the defining feature as we express it in words; the second is the feature as it exists in the thing itself. The feature itself is not what we say of the kind as a whole. What we can say is the idea drawn from that feature, which follows from the thing’s nature.

This shows that existence has real instances outside the mind. It is not merely an abstract idea in the mind, defined by its relation to whatever it is applied to and multiplied as those things multiply, as later thinkers have claimed. Avicenna’s words here are almost direct evidence for what we have argued.687

Chapter — Different kinds of possibility

Possibility divides into what can exist in itself and what can exist in something else.688 Anything that can exist in something else can also exist in itself, but the reverse is not always true. Something may be possible in itself without its existence being merely possible for another thing. It may have to exist for something else, as forms do for matter and underlying subjects do for their qualities. Or it may be unable to exist in something else at all, like substances that exist on their own.

Now, something that can exist in itself may or may not be able to exist through its own possibility alone. To explain this, we need to begin with a point we have already proved: every possible thing depends on a cause that is necessary in itself and necessary in every respect. Since this cause is necessary in every way, it cannot give existence to some things but not others, or to some things ready to receive existence but not others. Its relation to everything must be equal, and its giving must be universal and complete.689

Yet reason shows that some possible things exist before others in the chain of causes. We also see some events happen before others in a sequence over time. This difference in how things receive existence does not come from the Necessary Existent. It comes from differences in the natures of possible things and in the readiness of the things that receive existence.690

All possible things share this: each is possible in itself and in its nature. If that possibility alone is enough for them to receive existence from the Necessary Being, they must exist through direct creation, without being brought into existence at one particular time rather than another. Even so, their possibilities may differ in priority, how early they are, and in strength.691 The possibility of the Second Intellect is not like that of the First Intellect, since its existence is impossible from the standpoint of the Second Intellect. In truth, the Second Intellect’s possibility of existence is its possibility of existing after the First Intellect, just as the First Intellect is possible in relation to what comes after the Necessary Existent. The same applies to the other things brought into being. We will return to this question later.

But if a thing’s own possibility is not enough for it to receive existence, then further conditions beyond its basic nature must be met before it is ready to exist. Such a thing has two kinds of possibility. One belongs to its nature: considered in itself, assuming that it exists or does not exist involves no contradiction. The other is its readiness to receive a particular kind of existence. This readiness comes only when the conditions are in place and the obstacles are removed. It is not quite right to say that this is a wholly different meaning of possibility,692 though the two kinds differ in what they apply to, as we will explain later when we discuss potential and actual existence.693

These conditions must come before the thing exists; otherwise, it would not be something that comes into being. For this readiness to form, there must be earlier events, with no first event at the beginning of the chain. There must also be something that keeps changing in its very being and identity, so that coming into being and passing away belong to its nature.694 And there must be a place for these events to occur. Through them, the thing becomes fully ready to receive what comes next. That place is matter.

PreviousStage One — Existence and its first divisionsNextStage Three — What it means to bring things into existence

Stage Three — What it means to bring things into existence

Chapter — Where the debate lies about making things, and the different views

There are two ways of bringing something about. In the first, a thing itself is brought into existence. This act concerns that thing alone, without joining it to anything else.695 Compound making is making one thing be something, or making it have a quality. Its result is a statement such as “the human being is wise,” which requires two terms: what is made and what it is made to be. Anyone who thinks compound making ultimately reduces to simple making—that only one thing is made, such as the relation of having a quality, becoming something, or being described—has missed the point.

A relation such as becoming or being described is understood between its two terms. It helps us consider the terms together, or consider one through the other; we do not attend to the relation itself as a separate thing. So in compound making, the relation is included only as a subordinate part, not as an independent object.696 If we focus on that relation by itself and treat it as a thing in its own right, whether in the mind or outside it, we must ask a further question: does it need a maker in itself, or can it exist without a maker in itself but still need one to connect it to something outside its nature? Only clear proof can decide.

The same distinction appears in mental knowledge.697 Forming an idea is one kind of knowing; it concerns what a thing is, whatever the thing may be. Judging a statement is another kind; it always requires two terms, a subject and what is said of it, with the relation between them included only as a subordinate part. Forming an idea brings the thing itself into the mind; judging makes the thing be something. Compound making applies only to qualities that come to a thing after it exists, when the thing does not have them by nature. It cannot apply to a thing and itself, or to a thing and its essential features, as in “a human being is a human being” or “a human being is an animal.” A thing’s being itself, or having one of its essential features, is necessary and does not need a maker.

I do not mean that bringing the thing itself into existence,698 or bringing its essential parts into existence, does not need a cause. This is exactly where the followers of Aristotle and the Stoics disagree, though they agree that a thing’s essential parts cannot be separated from existence itself.699 Some theologians have argued otherwise; I have already mentioned some of their confused claims. Most of Aristotle’s followers hold that the first thing a cause brings about is its effect’s existence. Later thinkers explain this as the effect’s being existent: its nature is described as existing, in the sense we have already explained. They do not mean that the first effect is the relation itself, the caused thing’s nature, or existence itself. In their view, a thing’s nature as understood in thought does not need a maker.

Another group of philosophers, known as the Illuminationists, says that the maker’s first and direct effect is the thing’s very nature. Once that nature is brought about, it is also existent; the maker does not separately give it existence or attach the relation “exists” to it. Those are ideas in the mind, and what they refer to is the nature itself that comes from the cause. The reality of a thing’s being itself is simply the thing; nothing else is needed. For example, once a cause brings about a human being’s nature, no second act is needed to make that nature what it is.

Do not assume that because a nature’s being itself follows from the nature, and the nature is made, this relation also needs a maker. Nor, on this view, does the thing’s being existent need a separate act that first makes the nature itself. There is a difference between need that belongs to a thing in itself and need that arises only indirectly or by coincidence. A thing’s essential features and the qualities that necessarily follow from its nature do not need a maker’s separate action. They follow from the making of the nature, whether it exists or does not exist. If the nature is made, its essential features and necessary qualities are made by that same act. If it is not made, they too are unmade along with it. Just as eternal necessity removes the need for a cause, so does necessity that belongs to a thing’s own nature. The difference is that the first carries no dependence, even indirectly, while the second carries an indirect dependence. The maker brings about the nature of a human being, for example, and it is then human, animal, and able to learn by its own nature—not through a separate act of compound making.

Nor is this because those features are made by the very same simple act, as al-Dawwani and his students thought the Illuminationists meant.700 When they say that a thing’s essential features are made along with its nature, they do not mean that a maker must separately make a human being human or an animal, or make those descriptions apply to it. They mean that bringing about the nature itself is one simple act. The act first brings about the essential parts; the nature follows, and its necessary qualities follow from it. The maker does not act on those qualities directly. The same applies to the view of Aristotle’s followers that existence is what is made: the nature becomes itself, and has its own essential features, without a separate act directed at each one.

The fact that a nonexistent thing can be denied of itself701 means only that, on one view, its nature must be made, or, on the other, its existence must be made. It does not mean that the maker must act directly on it merely for us to point out a contradiction in arguments against existence being the effect. The early philosophers left no proof that settles either view. Each side seems to have treated its claim as self-evident. In their writings, we find only hints and brief indications.

Some thinkers have argued that existence itself cannot be caused. Their arguments assume that existence is only an idea in the mind, something we add when we think about a thing. On this view, it is a thing's nature that begins, ends, comes to be, or disappears. We say that a human being exists or comes into being, not that existence itself does so. They therefore ask how existence alone could be what a cause brings about. With God's help, we have answered these objections in our discussion of existence.

A later thinker offers another argument.702 If a cause produces only existence, he says, then every cause would be the cause of every effect. This is clearly false. His reasoning is that existence is one reality. If a cause can produce one instance of existence, why could it not produce any other?

Take water that becomes hot after being cold. The heat has a particular nature. Does its coming from the sources that give things existence require some new condition, or not? If it requires no new condition, the heat should always be there: the thing can receive it, and the source is always able to give it. But if a condition is required, does that condition belong to the existence of the heat, or to its particular nature?

Suppose it belongs to existence alone. If contact with water is a condition for coldness to exist, it would also have to be a condition for heat to exist, since both have existence and like cases must be treated alike. Whenever that contact occurred, heat would have to occur too: there would be something able to receive it, a source ready to give it, and the required condition. On the same reasoning, every event would follow from every condition. Particular events would no longer have their own particular causes and conditions. Experience plainly shows that this is false.

The thinker concludes that the condition must therefore belong to the nature of heat, not to existence as such. And since whatever depends on something else needs a cause, causes must produce the natures of things, or both their natures and their existence—not existence alone. That is the end of his argument.

This argument is weak in several ways. First, although existence is one reality, its levels differ in priority and lateness, in need and independence. We explained this near the beginning of the book. If existence were a general nature with many identical instances, the argument would have force. But we have shown that existence is not a general kind shared by many matching examples, nor a kind within a wider group or an extra feature added to things. The mind does draw from existence a general idea, like the word “being,” which it applies to things when it considers them. But that idea is not the reality of existence itself. The existence of each nature makes it distinct through that nature alone, without any extra feature. And yet the meaning of existence differs from the meaning of a thing’s nature, even though existence is one reality and the source of their differences.703 Seeing this distinction takes careful thought. Existence, simply as existence, can be a cause or an effect, a condition or something conditioned. The existence of a cause differs from the existence of its effect, and the existence of a condition differs from that of what depends on it. These are all different through existence itself, without any added feature.

Second, the same argument would rule out the Necessary Being’s existence as the cause of the first caused thing, since the argument applies just as well here. Following that reasoning, if the Necessary Being’s existence causes the first caused thing, it must do so either because of its existence or because of its nature. The first option is impossible. Existence is one reality in the Necessary Being and in contingent beings alike. If the first caused thing could come from the Necessary Being’s existence, then it could also come from the existence of any contingent thing, such as an accident or a motion. But that conclusion is plainly false, so the premise must be false as well.

The second option is also false, because the Necessary Being has no nature apart from its complete existence, beyond which nothing can be more complete. It does not help to say that existence is an attribute of the Necessary Being’s essence rather than identical with it. Decisive proofs show that existence cannot be an attribute of a thing in the technical sense. As we have already seen, existence itself is necessary in the Necessary Being and possible in contingent things: in the first it is independent and prior; in the others it is dependent and later. Being independent or dependent, and coming before or after, belong to existence itself. They are not features added to it from outside.

Third,704 the claim that the nature of heat must exist forever if it depends on no condition or cause is neither sound nor well grounded. Those who say that a maker’s effect is a thing’s existence, not its nature, do not claim that the nature stands on its own without existence, and then serves as something that receives existence. In their view, only existence is real outside the mind. What we call a thing’s nature is united with that existence. The mind can consider each existence and draw from it a meaning that it then describes as the thing’s nature. Existence is what is described; nature is the description. Nature comes from existence as a shadow comes from the person who casts it, and a shadow has no separate existence. We have explained this more than once.

Chapter — Refuting the arguments that a cause makes a nature existent

Some later thinkers argued for the view held by Aristotle’s followers as follows. What makes something need a cause is its possibility, and possibility is only the way existence and the like relate to a nature. So what first needs a maker, and what the maker first brings about, is this relation.

They also argued that, since existence has been shown to be something added to contingent natures, those natures themselves cannot be what the word “existent” truly applies to.705 How could they be? This would be like treating a nature’s essential features as separate from the nature itself.

They argued, too, that the priority of a nature to existence is not among the five familiar kinds of priority. It would have to follow if the nature itself were made. Finally, they argued that, although a thing’s denial of itself is always impossible, in contingent natures this is impossible only when we consider them as existent. We can say that a nonexistent thing is not itself, and a negative statement can be true even when its subject is absent. A contingent thing, considered in itself, does not resist nonexistence; in itself, it is not itself.706 The divine names include “O He, O who is He, O who is no he but He.”707 Until a thing exists, it cannot truly be said of itself. So what first and directly makes it need a cause is its being existent, not its nature.

The first argument was answered by saying that possibility is not what most people take it to be: its meaning is more precise, as we have already explained.708 As for the second argument, it is indeed a thing’s nature that we describe as existent, but not in either of the usual ways. It is not like an essential feature, which applies when we consider the nature alone; nor is it like an accidental feature, which requires some further aspect to be added to the thing. Rather, the nature is described as existent because it has been brought about and established by its maker. This aspect lies outside what is being described, and is considered as a condition for the judgment, not as a limit on the thing itself.

In short, before a nature has been brought about by its maker, none of its essential or accidental features can be truly predicated of it. Once it has been brought about, its essential features apply—not because it was made, but simply while it is in that state. Existence, by contrast, is predicated of it because it was brought about: through its maker and at the time it was made.709

The third argument is answered by saying that a nature’s priority to existence is another kind of priority, established by the proof. This is priority in what something is, rather than priority in time. A thing’s defining features also come before the thing in this sense and, in another sense, by the order of nature.

The fourth argument is answered by saying that the fact that we can deny a nonexistent thing of itself does not mean that we can deny a contingent thing of itself without qualification. Not considering a thing’s existence does not mean that we are considering its nonexistence. And the fact that a thing is itself when it exists does not mean that it is itself only on the condition that it exists.

The essential features of a thing are predicated of it while it is made and exists. Existence is predicated of the Necessary Being through its own eternal reality, without any condition of time or other qualification. In this sense, only God is the absolute “He”: He is only He. Predicating existence resembles predicating a thing’s essential features in one respect, and differs from it in another.

In al-Mutarahat, Suhrawardi argues that natures are made by simple making. Since, on his view, existence is only a mental concept, a cause can be prior to its effect only by nature: the nature of the effect is a shadow of the nature of its cause, and the cause’s own nature comes first. A similar argument appears in another writer: we know directly that a maker’s first effect is the caused existent; but the caused existent must be a nature, since being described as existent, like other such relations, is only a mental consideration.

An even stronger version was given by our revered teacher, may God preserve his honor and standing. Since a nature itself is what makes it true to say that something exists, consider what would follow if the nature, in its own constitution, did not depend on a maker.710 Then it would be existent in its own right and would no longer be contingent. That is impossible. So it must depend on a maker both in its basic constitution and in its being described as existent. In itself, in both respects, it is pure nonbeing, sheer negation, and pure potentiality. Its maker brings it into an established state by simple making; its existence then follows necessarily, without a separate act of making. These are our teacher’s words. We include them here as a mark of honor, in discussion with those who hold the opposing view.

Notice that all their arguments rest on treating existence as a mental concept, like “thingness” or “possibility.” We have shown that particular existences are real—indeed, they are the truest realities—and that only general existence is an abstract concept of the mind, like the general idea of animality. We have already hinted at the difference, and it will become clearer. Once their starting point is shown to be false, the rest of their argument falls with it.

Even if we grant that existence is only a mental concept, we still cannot grant that a nature itself is what “existent” applies to after the maker has brought it about.711 If that were so, the nature would no longer depend on its maker in order to exist. This would turn a contingent nature into something necessary in itself.712 For those thinkers, what makes something necessary in itself is that its own reality is the source of the judgment “existent.” What makes something contingent is that its own reality is not such a source. If, after its nature had been brought about, a contingent thing could itself be the source of the judgment “existent,” without our considering anything else or any other relation, then existence would belong to it by its own nature.

It does not help to say that a thing has its defining features without any reference to a cause or condition, whereas calling it “existent” requires us to consider that its maker brought it about.
