  55. Someone may object that lacking a definition means lacking a cause that makes a thing what it is, but does not mean lacking a cause of its existence. And the absence of a proof depends on the absence of all four kinds of cause. The answer is that the author has already said that everything except God has a composite structure of matter and form. Lacking a cause that makes it what it is—even if that cause is matter and form in the mind—therefore means lacking a cause of its existence too. When he says in The Beginning and the Return, “Since it has no definition and no cause, it has no proof,” he is reinforcing this answer to the objection. It is also enough simply to deny that existence has a definition; there is no contradiction.

    A second objection appeals to the real existence of a possible thing: existence itself has no definition, yet the existence of a possible thing can be proved because it is caused in its very nature. The answer is that if we mean existence simply as existence, it has neither definition nor proof. If we mean existence with a qualification, then it can have both.

    A third objection asks: If what has no definition cannot be proved, how can one thing be proved by another when neither causes the other? For example: every human can laugh, and everyone who can laugh can write. Laughter and writing are not causes of one another; both result from a third cause. The answer is that philosophers who study the divine use “proof” in a strict sense for proof from cause to effect. Avicenna says in the Metaphysics of The Healing: “It has no definition and no proof; rather, it is the proof of everything, though clear signs point to it.” That is why they say things with causes can be known only through their causes. If a logician also uses “proof” for reasoning from an effect, that is a broader use of the word. And in the case where two effects share a third cause, we really reason from one effect to that cause, then from the cause to the other effect we want to establish. In the example, we move from laughter to the rational soul, then from the rational soul to the human capacity to write. The proof thus ultimately proceeds through a cause. — س ره

The same distinction applies to “universal.” Strictly speaking, the real existent is existence itself; in common usage, “existent” means the essence to which existence belongs. — ه ره

  59. That is, the feature belongs to existence without needing any additional qualifying condition. This is also what it means for existence to be suited, in itself, to receive that feature. Nothing can come between the subject and its feature, not even something equal to the subject, and the feature must apply to the whole subject. If it applied only to a narrower kind, the subject would need an added qualification before it could receive that feature. If it applied more broadly, the qualification would serve no purpose. This also shows why the division must cover every case: otherwise, one of its branches would be narrower than the subject and would not be an essential feature of it. — ط

  60. As explained above, if a feature belongs essentially to a subject, the division must cover every case. The reverse is true only in some cases: a complete division does not always mean that its members are essential features. — ط

  61. As explained above, shared features must be defined as features that apply to existence as a whole, either by themselves or together with their opposite in a complete division. Here, “opposite” means the alternatives that result when something is divided. This resolves the objections the author has raised. — ط

  62. Limiting each science to the study of the essential features of its subject is not just a matter of convention. It is required by proof in sciences that rely on proof, as explained in the logical study of demonstration.

    A proof aims to give certainty, so its premises must be certain. Certainty means knowing that something is so and that it cannot be otherwise. A certain premise must therefore be necessary in truth, even if it is possible in the modal sense; otherwise its opposite would remain possible and there would be no certainty. It must be true at every time; otherwise it might be false at some time, leaving the opposite possible. It must be universal across circumstances; otherwise it might be false in some cases, again leaving the opposite possible. Its predicate must also belong to its subject itself: when the subject is affirmed, the predicate is affirmed with it, and when the subject is denied, the predicate is denied, setting everything else aside. This is why an essential predicate must be equal in scope to its subject. If it were narrower—for example, being prone to wonder in relation to animal—simply being an animal would not be enough for that feature to apply. If it were broader, as walking is in relation to human, the qualification “human” would add nothing to the feature’s application.

    Because an essential predicate belongs to its subject necessarily, the subject helps explain why the predicate exists. It must therefore appear in the full definition of that predicate. This is the rule for recognizing an essential feature. If a predicate has another predicate, and that predicate has one more, the original subject must appear in the definition of each, all the way down the chain. Each feature is essential to the original subject as well as to the subject of its own proposition. For example, a human being is capable of wonder, can laugh, and shows the teeth when laughing. The same rule applies in the other direction: if a subject has a subject, that first subject must be included in the definitions all the way back. For example, blackness is a visible quality; visible quality is a sensible quality; sensible quality is a quality; quality belongs to essence; and essence is something that exists.

    If a predicate is narrower than its subject, that predicate and its opposite in a complete division together form one essential predicate of the broader subject. Each side is essential to the corresponding part of that subject. For example, what exists is divided into what must exist and what may exist. In the definition of either part, the broader subject is included; in the definition of the combined division, the broader subject itself is included. A science, then, is a set of propositions whose subjects share one subject, which appears in the definitions of the subjects and predicates of its questions. This chain begins with a proposition about the science’s broad subject and ends with a proposition whose predicate no longer includes that subject in its definition. The highest branch of philosophy studies body as something that exists; the study of nature begins with body as a natural kind, not merely as something that exists. Likewise, philosophy studies the circle as something that exists, while mathematics studies it as a geometric shape.

    These points establish eight things. First, a science is a collection of propositions about one subject, which appears in the definitions of the subjects and predicates of its questions. Second, every science must have a subject shared by its propositions. Third, that subject is what the science examines through its essential features. Fourth, an essential feature belongs to a thing in itself and can be recognized because the thing appears in its definition. Sometimes the subject and predicate are reversed, so the rule is that either the subject appears in the predicate’s definition or the predicate appears in the subject’s definition. For example, what exists is divided into one and many; and what must exist exists. Fifth, an essential predicate does not apply through an intermediary feature—whether that intermediary is broader, narrower, or equal in scope. An intermediary here means something included in the predicate’s definition without the subject itself being included. For example, blackness belongs to a crow through its feathers. Sixth, the predicate must match the subject in scope: it cannot be broader or narrower. Seventh, the predicate in any question must be essential both to the subject of that question and to the subject of the science as a whole. Eighth, sciences differ according to their subjects.

    These rules apply to sciences that prove their claims. There is no reason to suppose they apply in the same way to conventional disciplines whose subjects are constructed ideas rather than things that exist in reality. — ط

    ↩

  63. This note explains the statement that a science studies the essential features of its subject. An essential feature truly belongs to a thing, without metaphor or error. In Arabic grammar, it is a description of the thing itself, not a description of something merely related to it. Put another way, it has no intermediary in how it belongs to the thing. There are different kinds of intermediary, however. A ship’s motion, for example, is an intermediary for the motion of someone sitting on it; not every kind of intermediary works this way. The author discusses these distinctions later, in connection with the primacy of existence.

    The features of a distinguishing feature are also features of its general kind because, when the general kind is considered without restriction, it is united with that distinguishing feature. Their features are therefore the same in reality. The features of the intellects, for example, truly belong to existence as existence when existence is considered without qualification. This differs from the features of a body considered as changing: matter and motion are what make it a subject for the study of nature. A body considered simply as something that exists, or as composed of matter and form, is instead a subject for the highest branch of philosophy.

    Many later scholars found this difficult. Al-Khwansari, for example, wrote in his notes on The Healing that discussing something narrower than a science’s subject is done only for convenience, because the narrower thing is one kind or class of it. Remember, though, that the older definition of an essential feature—as an external predicate that belongs to something in itself or through something equal to it—can be understood correctly. “In itself” does not mean that the thing causes the feature or necessitates it; that reading would make it hard to explain features of narrower kinds. It means that no intermediary stands between the thing and the feature, and that the feature belongs to the thing itself rather than to something merely related to it.

    An equal thing here means a concept equal to the subject in the respect under discussion, even if the two concepts differ. Unity and existence, for example, are different concepts but apply to the same reality. If indivisibility belongs to existence because of unity, it is still an essential feature. Likewise, if existence cannot be truly applied to many things because of individuality, that too is an essential feature. But two things may be equal in what exists while belonging to different qualifying aspects. If one feature belongs to a subject only through another aspect attached to it, it is incidental, just as a feature that belongs through something narrower would be. That is why earlier thinkers spoke broadly of a property beyond a thing’s definition, including properties considered with an added qualification. Otherwise, unity, being a thing, possibility, and other features grasped by reason would be left out. — س ره

  64. Here are examples from the study of nature. An essential feature of its main subject is that every body has a natural shape. An essential feature of one kind is that one element changes into another. A general feature of a kind is that an element is in motion. An essential feature of a kind of essential feature is that the lights of the heavens stimulate plant life. A general feature of that kind is that the lights of the heavens, especially the sun, warm the world of the elements. In the last two examples, the feature stays within the scope of the subject of the science. — س ره

The statement made from a general kind and its distinguishing feature is a particular claim: “Some animals are rational.” This shows that the distinguishing feature belongs to the relevant share of the general kind, not to the general kind as such. The claim that a kind’s essential or incidental features belong to its general kind is rejected, for the reasons already given. — ط مد

  66. A careful reader should see that a feature attached to something narrower—such as a particular subject in a science narrower than the highest branch of philosophy—can in one respect be essential to the broader subject and in another respect incidental. The reason is that a general kind has its own reality at the level of the concept and its reality in the world, and these are far apart. When the broader subject and narrower subject are one in the world but not at the level of the concept, a feature of the narrower subject is incidental to the broader concept but essential to the broader thing in reality. This resolves the difficulty. What matters for a feature to be essential is that no intermediary lies between it and its subject. But we may consider the subject as it is at the level of a concept or as it is in reality, and the judgment changes accordingly. This creates no contradiction for a clear-minded reader. — ن ره

  67. The argument shows that existing things differ in degree. It does not show that the parts we imagine within the concept of existence differ in degree. Strictly speaking, it is real existence that has degrees; its concept does so only indirectly. This is what is meant when the author says that existence is a general concept applied to things by degrees. — ط

  68. Be aware—may God guide us both—that Aristotle's followers, philosophers of illumination, and other careful thinkers do not seriously disagree that the natural universal exists. Philosophers call it “essence”; mystical writers call it the “fixed reality”; different schools use other names for it. By “natural universal,” I do not mean an essence considered without restriction, whose existence is only in the mind and is a mental construct. I mean the underlying essence that can be considered as absolute, combined with conditions, or separate from matter. This underlying essence is even harder to grasp than “absolute essence,” one of its divisions. How could it fail to exist if the combined essence is one of its divisions? That alone is enough to establish the point.

    There is no need to use the older argument that the natural universal exists because it is a part of a composite essence. An essence considered without restriction is not literally a part of an essence considered together with a condition; only an essence considered specifically apart from other conditions is a part. If Avicenna meant by “without restriction” the essence as it exists within what is considered apart from other conditions, his part-and-whole argument would work: it would establish the general essence from matter itself. But the argument I have given from the combined essence is already enough. There is also no need for Lahiji's explanation that the “part” in this argument is merely a part in thought.

    The real dispute is whether, once a cause brings an essence about, the essence exists in its own right and existence is what lets us affirm it, or whether the essence is called existent only because existence is a feature that belongs to it. There are three kinds of such attribution. First, something may be described as moving only because something connected to it moves, as when we say a passenger moves because the ship moves; in truth, the passenger is not the source of that motion. Second, a subject may truly have a feature, as when a body is black because of its blackness. Both the body and blackness exist, and the body is genuinely black, though it can exist without being black. Third, a general kind and its distinguishing feature may form one reality: the general kind cannot exist without the distinguishing feature.

    The view that existence is fundamental is not like the first case, since the natural universal truly exists; its existence is not merely figurative. Nor is it exactly like the second, since a body can exist without blackness, while an essence has no actual existence apart from existence. It is closer to the third case, though with a difference: the existence of a species is attributed to its general kind, its distinguishing feature, and the complete species made from both; the relation between essence and existence is more like that between a shadow and what casts it.

    Both sides agree that when we say an essence exists, we must explain what makes it real and in what respect we are calling it existent. An essence by itself is open to both existence and nonexistence. If the only qualifying factor were the mental idea of existence, or a merely conceptual relation to the cause—as those who have not seen this clearly claim—then the essence would still not be real. Adding one mental concept to another does not create an existing thing. The concept of existence is itself just an idea; it is “existence” by its definition, not because it exists as a separate thing in the world. The same applies to the idea of “necessary existence.” By contrast, the illuminating relation is itself the light of existence, just as real bringing-into-existence is actual existence. In that light, the different expressions point to one reality. This shows why accusing the author of assuming what he is trying to prove is mistaken.

    There is another reason the accusation fails. The author's point is that reality is an essence taken together with existence. Without existence, an essence is not yet real. So how could existence itself fail to be real when it is what makes an essence real? — س ره

  72. If we included the kind of thing described in the distinguishing feature itself, the species would become part of its own distinguishing feature. This is an even stronger objection than the one given afterward. Someone could challenge that later objection by saying that it is not really a case of a thing being affirmed of itself. But this would not affect the claim that a merely possible statement would become necessary: its logical status would still be necessity.

    Here is the point. In the statement, the predicate may be the whole qualified expression, “human,” with the qualification outside it but included in the way the predicate is restricted. Then “human” is what is directly being said of the subject, and the statement is necessary. Or the predicate may be “human” with the qualification included in it. In that case the qualification is considered only indirectly; the main point is still that the subject is human. Compare “Zayd is in the house,” where his location is the point, with “Zayd is standing in the house,” where the location is secondary. The statement “a human is a human who can laugh” contains two claims: “a human is a human,” which is necessary, and “a human can laugh,” which is possible. This is like the way philosophers analyze the subject phrase in a statement: Avicenna treats it as unrestricted, while al-Farabi treats it as possible. It is also established that before we know a description, it functions as a report; once we know it, a report can function as a description.

    Another argument that the thing itself is not built into a derived adjective is that describing a cloth as white does not repeat the subject, either generally or in a narrower sense. If the word “white” included the thing it describes, the subject would be repeated. — س ره

  79. By “its own reality,” the author means existence without limiting it to one particular degree. He does not mean only the highest degree. Existence has levels. Imagine them rising from weak to strong, then from strong to stronger still. Each lower level is limited because it lacks some of what the next higher level possesses. The higher level, in turn, contains the completeness of the lower. Yet each higher level is itself limited in relation to one above it. This continues until we reach a level with no limit at all—its only limit is that it has none. This is pure reality taken with the condition that it be considered apart from other levels, making it one level among them. Taken without that condition, it would include all the levels and would not be one level opposed to the rest. — ط

  80. The author chooses “particularization” here instead of “individuality,” as he also does in The Divine Witnesses, to point to a subtle idea: existence is one reality that unfolds through different forms and states. In a hierarchy of levels, existences are distinct through their own priority or posteriority. Being prior is part of what an existence is, though not in the way a part belongs to a whole. The concept “priority,” by contrast, is a relation and does not make up the existence itself. In a series of things at the same level, that concept necessarily follows and does not arise later than existence. A thing may also be distinguished by material features when it exists in matter.

    To see how features can make a thing distinct, consider the difference between an adjective and the underlying feature named by it. When “black” is considered as a description of a subject, it is an adjective that applies to the subject. When “blackness” is considered on its own, it is a feature that the subject bears. The difference depends on how we consider them. A similar distinction applies when we consider a body without qualification or as something set apart from what belongs to it. Features distinguish a thing in the first sense because they share one existence with their subject; a thing becomes distinct through its particular way of existing. In the second sense, the feature is not predicated of the subject in the same way and does not share its existence. The feature exists for the subject, rather than being the subject’s own existence, so it comes after the subject exists. How could it make the subject distinct before that? We may still call such features signs of distinctness. In the first sense they are necessary consequences of the thing; in the second, their being necessary while separate from the subject is harder to explain. That is why philosophers treated certain quantities, qualities, and positions as necessary features.

  83. Someone may ask: How can essences distinguish existences if essences are not established before existence? On the view that existence is fundamental, existences themselves have no prior independent reality either. The first answer is that essences need not come before existence or be fundamental in their own right. It is enough for different essences to arise together with existence. An essence is real only in a secondary sense, because existence is real; it is made only in a secondary sense, because existence is what is made. Think of colored light appearing at the same time as colored glass is formed. Second, essences may be prior in what they are. Third, they may have earlier forms of existence, so their differences in an earlier realm can distinguish existences in a later one. Ultimately, the explanation reaches the fixed realities linked to God's names and attributes at the level of divine oneness. These are not made, and neither are their differences; this is where the question of what caused the differences comes to an end. — س ره

  85. The question is whether the reality of existence is made from a general kind and a distinguishing feature, as the argument supposes. The author does not discuss the possibility that it is made from something still broader and the third element of a three-part division, since that would obviously lead to an endless chain. Nor can the general kind be broader than both the first and third elements: in the third case, the general kind would not become one of the parts that make up the whole. By “something else,” the author means a species.

    In the first case, a distinguishing feature, considered on its own, brings the general kind into actuality. The two then stand as matter and form, with form acting alongside matter to make the whole. Some commentators say that a distinguishing feature causes only certain qualities of a general kind, such as its ability to exist in a particular form or to be definite. But since the general kind also causes some qualities of the distinguishing feature, the argument instead makes the feature a cause of the very essence of the general kind. That would contradict the assumption that existence's reality is their composite whole.

    In the second case, what makes broader kind and species the same in reality would also have to be what makes them different. General kind, distinguishing feature, and species are different ideas but one reality, as predication requires. Here, however, the idea of the distinguishing feature and the idea of the species are both identical with the reality of existence. So none of them could really be a broader kind, a feature that distinguishes it, or a species. Existence could not be composed of them. This reasoning establishes both that existences are simple realities and that existence itself is not a general kind. — س ره

A distinguishing feature is only part of a nature, though the species becomes what it is through that feature. What the mind pictures as a complete, definite thing is actually matter considered apart from its form, not a general kind.   99. The point is that considering an essence stripped of every kind of existence and every other feature does not, by itself, give it existence. It removes all existence and all features from it. Only when we add a second thought—that this very stripping is itself a kind of mental existence—does the question of existence arise. Even then, there is no problem or endless chain: the sequence ends when the mind stops considering it. We can also say that stripping essence is itself a kind of “mixing” with the idea of stripping, not with actual existence, so no further act of stripping is needed. This is like saying that prime matter is the potential for form and other things in a body. If we then ask whether this potential itself has actual existence, we might imagine an endless series of potentials and actualities. The answer is that the actuality of the potential is the potential itself, not something added to it—just as parts of time do not need another time in order to be earlier or later. In short, essence is stripped of existence when considered in its primary sense; it is mixed with existence only in the common, expanded sense.   125. People who speak of God's oneness take four positions. (1) They may accept that both existences and existent things are many, while professing God's oneness aloud and holding to it in a general way. Most people are at this level; this is ordinary monotheism. (2) They may say that both existence and what exists are one. This is the view of some Sufis; it is the most special form of monotheism. (3) They may say that existence is one but existent things are many. This is the position attributed to the spiritual insight of the divine philosophers; it is special monotheism. (4) They may say that existence and what exists are one within their very multiplicity. This is the author's view and the view of the highest mystics; it is the highest form of monotheism. Another classification divides monotheism into oneness of effects, acts, attributes, and essence.

    The difference between the author's way and the view attributed to the divine philosophers is this. The author accepts many existences and many existent things, while also affirming unity within that multiplicity. Think of one person standing before many mirrors. The person appears many times, and each reflection has the form of a human being. There are many images, and yet, because each image is only a reflection and has no independent reality, they are one in the very midst of their multiplicity. If you attend to the person who is reflected, the images become ways of seeing that person. If you treat the images as independent things, you lose sight of what they are. The same relation can hold through a hierarchy of levels or across levels that are far apart, as when the same face appears tiny in ice, dimly in muddy water, or clearly in a mirror.

    The presence of the one who is reflected is like a thread that strings together the many different images, connects them, gathers what is scattered, and joins opposites. In the same way, when we see existences as dependent manifestations of God—as flashes of His light—they are never wholly separate from His own appearing. But if we take them as independent things, we misunderstand their reality, because dependence belongs to them by their very nature. For the author, existence is one reality with levels that differ in strength and weakness. The very feature that makes the levels different is also what they share, and this confirms their unity: the more fully reality is affirmed and found, the wider its scope and the less it is marked by absence and loss. This is why he calls the multiplicity of existences luminous, while the multiplicity of essences is dark.

    Particular contingent existences are real, but they are rays of the sun of reality and pure relations of dependence; they are not separate things that happen to have a relation to God. The author will soon criticize the claim, made in a treatise called al-Zawrāʾ, that the existence of things is a relation to God rather than a relation that itself exists.

    By contrast, the other group's view is that real existence is one individual, with no multiplicity in any way, while the many existent things are essences. They exist by being related to real existence, not through distinct contingent existences understood as need and dependence. They allow the derived word “existent” to apply more broadly than something in which the source meaning of the word inheres: it can also apply to what is merely related to that source, and even to the source itself. They say that the realities of things cannot be established by ordinary language, so there is no problem in saying that an essence is “existent” simply because it is related to existence. Arabic usage allows similar words, such as names for someone who sells milk, dates, or iron. They also hold that essences are real; if essences were only ideas drawn from something else, they would have to be drawn from God's existence, since they recognize no other existence.

    The author rejects this view for three reasons. First, how can one and the same real existence belong to itself and to other things—making it both a substance and an accident, and both prior and later—when things with the same essence, such as human beings, do not differ in their essence or admit degrees? Second, if the relation to God is a real, illuminating connection, it would itself have to be another existence beyond God's one existence, which this view denies. The relation must therefore be an ordinary relation that depends on both things already existing. But essence is not simply identical with dependence: the essence whose existence we question is not the same as its relation to God. This objection does not apply in the same way to the author's view, because existence cannot be grasped as a concept apart from the realities we encounter; still, such a relation of identity does not fit the other group's view. They treat essences as fully real in themselves, whereas identity through relation can hold only between what is not yet fully determined and what makes it definite—not between two already complete realities, as will be explained later.

    Third, if existence is simply what makes things existent, then those relations must themselves be many existences. How, then, can this view count as special monotheism or as belief in one existence? It becomes ordinary monotheism, like the view that both existence and existent things are many. By treating essences as primary realities distinct in their very nature from existence, they end up affirming a second reality alongside existence. So they do not escape a subtle form of associating others with God. May God make us among His sincere servants—indeed, among those made wholly sincere for Him. The author, by contrast, treats what is related to God as existence too. There is nothing in the house but existence.

    The first and third objections may seem inconsistent. The first assumes that God's necessary existence is the existence of things; the third assumes that their existences are many mental relations. We can answer that the proponents of this view express it in different ways: sometimes they say that what makes things existent is their relation to God; at other times, they say that Zayd's existence serves as a means of presenting Zayd. One objection addresses the first version and the other the second. Consider this carefully. — س ره

  126. If “thing” means something whose existence is in question—that is, an essence, as in the author's earlier distinction between the familiar names for kinds of thing and the unfamiliar names for kinds of existence—then saying that thinghood and existence go together means that they are realized together. Wherever an essence is realized, its particular existence is realized too, and the two move together. Otherwise, the claim means that they are one in reality. To explain this: as we have seen, existence has a reality of its own. It is one reality that differs in strength and weakness, necessity and possibility, and other ways. Its highest level, complete in every respect and without any deficiency, is the Necessary Existence, which has no essence apart from its existence. Every level below it has a limit and a deficiency. The definition of a human being as a rational animal, for example, tells us about the limits of that person's existence; the definition of an animal as a body that grows and moves by sensation and will tells us about the limits of an animal's existence. A deficiency depends on the existence it limits; it cannot be real without it. This also clarifies a further dispute: does existence become real before essence is established, or does essence become established first? Some people argue that a nonexistent thing must still be a thing because it is necessary for something to be itself, and impossible for it not to be itself. We reply that a thing is itself by its very nature, not because it has existed from eternity. It can fail to be itself when it does not exist, because then there is no thing at all—only nonexistence. This view is extremely weak, unless its supporters mean to defend God's eternal knowledge. But in eternity a nonexistent thing is sheer nothing: it has no disclosure or distinction by which it is known, and it has neither external nor mental existence. Otherwise there would be multiplicity in God's essence and things would be eternal alongside Him. Still, we do not need to say that things have a fixed reality detached from every kind of existence. Their reality follows from God's own existence, as the Sufis hold. — س ره

As Naṣīr al-Dīn al-Tusi says, they explained differences among nonexistent essences by means of states. For them, a state is a feature of a thing that is neither existent nor nonexistent. But under the familiar definition—a feature of something existent that is itself neither existent nor nonexistent—a state would be like the abstract features of existing things. Existence itself would then be a state belonging to something that already exists, not a feature of an essence while it is nonexistent.   132. The three modalities—necessity, possibility, and impossibility—are features of this kind of existence. To sum up: there is linking existence and existence stated as a predicate. Linking existence means that one thing is affirmed of another. It is what we mean in “whiteness is present in the body” or “the body is white”; even if we omit the linking word, the connection is still there. This link is not an idea that stands on its own. It is like a grammatical particle: we cannot make it a separate subject of a statement without changing it into existence stated as a predicate. It links parts of affirmative statements; a negative statement denies the link. It is also different from the judgment that subject and predicate are one, which occurs in every statement. This kind of linking existence occurs in affirmative statements with a subject and predicate, but not in simple statements such as “X exists.” The author calls it linking existence, following his teacher in The Clear Horizon, to avoid confusing it with dependent existence. Al-Lahiji, in one of his books, called the existence of accidents in their subjects “linking existence” and confused the two. Existence stated as a predicate, by contrast, means that something exists in itself, as in a complete statement such as “X exists.” A thing may exist in itself and for itself, as an intellect or body does; or it may exist in itself but not for itself, as an accident does when it depends on a subject. The first is existence in itself; it is either through itself, as God's existence is, or through another, as the existence of substances that do not inhere in a subject. — س ره

Al-Khafrī argues that if we suppose the Necessary One does not exist, the nature of an existing thing depends on the nature of a maker, and the maker's nature depends on that existing thing. The author replies that a circle between two natures is not itself a problem; it is like the old puzzle about which came first, the egg or the chicken. Even if an impossibility followed, it would not be clearer than the assumption that God does not exist. That is different from the impossibility of God's nonexistence itself, which needs no further result to make it impossible. Just as every existence must ultimately depend on what is necessary in itself, every impossibility must ultimately depend on what is impossible in itself: God's nonexistence. — س ره

  150. We will see that the possibility of dependent existences means their essential need: they are relations and connections in their very nature, not things that first exist on their own and then acquire a relation. Necessity is existence made firm; impossibility is nonexistence made firm. Possibility is the absence of both kinds of firmness: it is neither necessary existence nor necessary nonexistence, but lies between them. In this sense, possibility can be stronger or weaker depending on how near it is to either side. — ن ره

    ↩

  151. This division raises three problems. First, it seems to divide everything that exists into what exists through itself and what exists through something else, leaving no room to divide what is necessary into what is necessary in itself, through another, or in relation to another. Second, “existent” must be broad enough to include both what exists through itself and essences that exist through existence. And “drawing existence from something” must mean judging that it is independently existent, either through itself or through another. If it simply means finding something existent, the division applies equally to every case, including necessary and contingent existence. A clearer form would be: anything the mind judges to exist independently either exists through itself or through another. This also leaves out purely relational existence, which is not independent even when considered together with the things it relates. Including the relation and its two ends in the same division creates another problem. The division can be rescued by asking instead: is anything the mind describes as existent in any way dependent on something else, or not? The first is possible; the second is necessary. Third, as stated, the division really separates independent existence from relational existence. It does not explain how necessity and possibility function in statements, as the three modalities do. — ط

    ↩

  152. The phrase “we do not judge them” refers to essences considered only in themselves. — ه ره

    ↩

  153. That is, universal composite essences such as human being and horse. Even though we can understand what they are in themselves, once we set aside their defining concepts, we can no longer point to them as things. — س ره

  154. The “causes” here are the causes included in a definition. As Avicenna says, the middle term is what we place after the word “because,” and it is the same in kind and reality as the final element in a definition: the thing's own nature. A defining feature is a thing's form, and a thing is what it is through its form. Avicenna says that a thing's form is its essence, the basis on which it is what it is. These three ways of speaking are close in meaning.

    The account suited to philosophers who seek divine wisdom is this. Aristotle's claim that the answers to “What is it?” and “Why is it?” are often the same points to a subtle truth. The cause of a limited, particular existence, such as Zayd's, is the sacred outpouring of existence. The appearance of the limited thing is contained within the appearance of its source, as the lights of the stars are, in a certain respect, contained within the sun's light. Its reality is also that source, because the source brings it to completion; a thing is what it is through its completeness, not through its deficiency.

    In The Beginning and the Return, the author says that, for careful thinkers in Aristotle’s school, the agent's causal role is included in what makes a thing existent. Elsewhere, he asks: if prime matter is nothing but pure potentiality, possibility, and vagueness, what distinguishes one prime matter from another? Some philosophers say that the heavenly spheres have their own prime matter, different from the matter of the elements. He replies that the different kinds of matter are distinguished by their causes. Their actual form comes from the nearest causes, the active intellects, which contribute to the material things along with the forms that enter them. He adds that one might say, by analysis, that a thing becomes definite through its proximate agent and so is determined by something outside it. But we must remember that an agent is like the thing's own reality—indeed, closer to it than it is to itself. So a thing's determination by its agent is not a determination by something outside its reality.

    The point is that the actualization of forms is also the actualization of matter, and the differences among forms are the differences that make matter definite. If we ask what matter is in reality, we can answer: fire, air, and the other forms it takes on. Matter joined to what is continuous is continuous; joined to what is separate, it is separate; joined to water, it is water; joined to air, it is air. The form and its cause work together to make matter definite. In many things, the same is true of particular existences and the sacred outpouring: the source's manifestation is contained within theirs. Some mystics even use “matter” for this outpoured existence, reversing the usual philosophical account of matter and form. The author may also mean separate immaterial lights, which have no cause other than existence itself. For them, the answer to “What is it?” and “Why is it?” is the same, whether the cause is understood as what brings them about or as what they are directed toward. — س ره

The author distinguishes three things: eternal necessity in itself; necessity that holds while a thing exists, without being caused by its existence; and necessity that depends on a description or condition. The objector confused the second with the third, treating necessary features of an essence as conditional on its being created. The existence in “four is even while four exists” marks when the statement holds; it is not the reason evenness belongs to four. Nor should necessity while a thing exists be confused with God's eternal necessity. A feature can be necessary to its essence even if that essence is not necessary in itself; the statement itself is necessary in the essential sense. — س ره

  167. Both claims are self-evident; the author's discussion draws attention to them. Each part would remain a separate simple being, contrary to what we have established. Another consequence is that there can be no endless chain of necessary beings. This will appear in the Illuminationist philosopher's proof that the Necessary One has no essence beyond His existence: if He had an essence, there would be infinitely many instances of it that were each necessary in themselves. We could not then reject them by saying that they form an endless chain, since none would be more basic than another. — س ره

  168. When a statement is qualified by “insofar as” or “considered as,” the qualification can serve three purposes. For example, “An essence considered just as an essence has this rule” means that we consider it without reference to anything else. In one later discussion, the author divides this unrestricted case into two. Second, the qualification can give the reason why the statement applies, as in “A human being laughs insofar as he is amazed.” Third, it can tell us to consider the subject and the qualification together, as in “A body, insofar as it is a surface, is white.” — س ره

More precisely, the list should mention explanatory and limiting conditions before features that are attached or abstracted, and should distinguish negative from positive and relational from nonrelational conditions. — س ره

  174. Sometimes a definition must repeat an idea in order to explain a relation. To know either of two related things, we have to know the other; they are equally familiar or unfamiliar. Yet a definition is supposed to start from what is already known. So we must mention the cause that makes them related, so that both can be understood at once, while directing the definition to whichever one we mean to define. Consider Avicenna's definition of a father: “An animal who brings forth another of his kind from his seed, insofar as he is such.” “Animal” and “another of his kind” name the father and son without yet mentioning their relation. “Brings forth from his seed” gives the cause of their relation. “Insofar as he is such” repeats part of what has already been said, but the repetition is necessary: it makes the relation belong to the animal specifically as a father. Otherwise the definition could apply to an animal who is a father in some other respect, even though the aim is to define what makes him a father. — س ره

  176. This discussion is needed even if we divide existents into what the mind recognizes as existing through itself and what it recognizes as existing through something else. The Necessary One exists through Himself, without an external intermediary of either kind. Still, the proofs for God's existence establish that nothing stands between Him and the fact that He exists; this discussion is needed to show that nothing stands between Him and the judgment that He exists, and so to complete the division. — ط

  177. By “the thing exists before its existence,” we mean that its essence would be prior through its own existence. This makes the contradiction immediate; the author is not relying on the proof in The Discussions that the claim leads to an endless series. If a thing could be prior to itself, it would also be prior to what is prior to it—again, itself—and the sequence would continue. Saying that it would “exist twice” is only a brief way of making the point. The sentence about whether the prior existence is the essence or something else is not needed to show that a thing cannot exist before itself; this contradiction is far clearer than an endless series. How could the less obvious problem prove the more obvious one? The series could instead be used as an additional argument against self-priority, which would make that sentence relevant. “Essence” here can mean any essence, not only God's. — س ره

  178. You might ask: how can existence be necessary in itself if it is made necessary by the essence? If existence were necessary through itself, it would not depend on the essence. For someone who holds that the Necessary Being has an essence, being necessary in itself means that the essence itself requires its own existence, with no help from anything else. This thinker also holds that existence is not found at the level of the essence considered in itself. To argue against that view by assuming the opposite is to assume what needs to be proved. — س ره

  179. It would be better to call this priority a priority in what a thing is. When we consider an essence in itself, we set aside both existence and nonexistence. Even if essences were established separately from every kind of existence—as the Muʿtazilites held—this priority would remain. Both what comes first and the respect in which it comes first belong to what the thing is. — س ره

Someone might object that the author himself often recognizes other kinds of priority, including priority by essence and by what is more entitled to something, and that these would support the objection.   187. The argument rules out real, external existence as a necessary feature of essence. The general idea “existent,” by contrast, can be applied to an essence at any level we consider it. — ط

  188. The sound answer, I think, is that existence does not have existence as an added feature that needs a cause. Saying instead that existence causes its own being-existent without a second existence does not remove the difficulty. For what does “being existent” mean? If it means actual existence, to put existence before its being-existent is to put a thing before itself. If it means the concept of being existent, such priority is not impossible—but neither is it impossible for something other than existence to come before that concept.

    One might escape the difficulty by taking “existence” to mean the level of divine oneness, the hidden treasure, and “being existent” to mean the level of manifestation, being known, and the outpouring of existence. We will later discuss a further kind of priority, priority in truth. But that does not fit the approach of the thinker who presents this argument, the author of The Adjudications.

    Again, perhaps in saying that the same objection applies to existence, he means the concept of existence. But that concept is itself among the essences and needs real existence. He cannot then say that the essence of existence precedes its being-existent through itself: the concept counts as “existence” only in the primary sense in which a meaning is predicated of itself, not as an independently existing reality. — س ره

  189. The contradiction follows only if “A human being is a human being” means “A human being is a human being on the condition that he exists.” It does not. The statement is considered while the subject exists; existence is simply the setting in which it is true, not a condition that causes its truth. These are the difficulties to which the author points when he says that the argument “requires examination.” — س ره

  190. The proof can be completed on the view of those who hold the truth, not on the Shaykh's view, since he considers existence to be conceptual. — س ره

  191. In fact, the opposite is clear: the two supposedly necessary beings would be possible in relation to one another, not necessary in relation to one another or through another. — س ره

  192. You may ask: how is this different from the earlier objection, which asked why the mind could not separate an existing thing into existence and something that receives it? I answer: the earlier point concerned what is logically conceivable; this one concerns what follows from their own principles. Also, here they allow particularity to belong to an essence without its being part of the essence's defining level. The earlier objection allowed it at that level. — س ره

  193. Aristotle’s followers treat substance as a broader kind: an essence that, when it exists, is complete in itself. Suhrawardi, however, says in The Philosophy of Illumination that substancehood is not something added in the world to corporeality. Making something a body is itself making it a substance. For us, substance is the completeness of a thing's essence, which lets it stand without depending on a subject. Aristotle’s followers define it as “what exists in no subject.” “Does not exist in a subject” is a negative description, while “exists” is an added feature, as he goes on to explain. — س ره

    ↩

  194. This objection does not work. Someone who holds that the Necessary Being has an essence need not agree that all essences are either substances or accidents. The usual account distinguishes an accident, which exists in a subject, from a substance, which has an essence but exists in no subject. The Necessary Being, however, may be described without qualification as existing in no subject. Similarly, a defender of divine essence can say that God has a simple, necessary essence that requires its own existence, just as four entails evenness; substances and accidents, by contrast, have possible essences that do not require existence. Although it is false that an essence can entail existence, that is the earlier argument, so this is not a separate proof.

    Still, the conclusion can be established by another argument from composition. If the Necessary Being had an essence other than existence—even a simple, specific essence—He would be a composite of essence and existence. The premise that essence is “what is set against existence” means that essence considered in itself is simply itself; it cannot, by itself, be the complete reality of God without existence. Nor can the reality of God be only an essence that causes existence, with existence remaining outside that reality. It must be the whole made up of essence and existence. This cannot be avoided by saying that one is the cause and the other its effect, just as a possible being remains composite whether existence is treated as an accident inhering in its essence, or essence as an accident inhering in existence, or their connection as real or merely analytical. What rules this out is composition itself.

    For a possible being, the aspects of having existence and lacking it are distinct, just as the argument that “the simple reality is all things” assumes. Likewise, there is the aspect of an essence that does not rule out existence or nonexistence, and the aspect that rules out nonexistence. These aspects are distinct even if the mind reaches them by analysis. It judges that one occurs in the other and depends on it. That judgment of dependence is impossible in God, even at the level of analysis.

    There is another proof of this central claim, which is as clear to us as the midday sun. Even the leading skeptic says in one of his books that knowing God's essence is a knot no one can undo: is existence identical with God's essence or added to it? If God had an essence, it would be possible for human beings to understand it. That is false, both rationally and by common agreement. The connection follows because an essence, wherever it exists, can in principle be understood and grasped; this is what people mean when they say that an essence is defined through itself. We are discussing the technical sense of essence: what is other than existence and, in itself, does not rule out either existence or nonexistence. Even if no one actually understands an essence, it must at least be possible to understand it, just as a common person may not actually understand the essence of a human being even though it can be understood.

    If a possible being had no essence, it could not be understood either, because its external existence cannot enter the mind; otherwise it would change from external to mental existence, as explained earlier. This is why philosophers say that an individual, particular thing cannot be used to explain or understand something else. An individual thing outside the mind, distinct in itself, can be known only through direct awareness of it. Even then, the reality of existence is reached only when the mystic loses all awareness of the self. Such awareness still takes place behind a veil, or several veils—even for the First Intellect. The Necessary Being is pure existence, whose reality cannot be fully grasped.

    One more proof: if God had an essence, He would not encompass every particular determination, because the specific character of any essence is incompatible with the specific characters of other essences. He must therefore be existence itself, which is compatible with every determination and extends throughout all essences. — س ره

Since their necessary features differ, the underlying realities must differ too; the premise that their existence is the same is therefore false. This gives another reply: on the view held by Aristotle’s followers, God's existence differs from all others in reality; on the ancient Persian view, it differs in fullness and independence. — س ره

  221. This refers to the discussion of the intellect and what it knows. In brief, some philosophers explain the “form” by which we know a thing as its essence—what makes it what it is. But essence alone cannot account for knowledge, whose nature is light and awareness. Others take it to be the essence of a material thing, with the matter mentally removed. Yet material existence belongs to matter and, because it is extended and measured, is hidden even from itself; it cannot be what knows or is directly known in itself. Once these accounts are ruled out, the accomplished philosophers mean by “form” another mode of existence, one more free of matter in eight respects, as they explain elsewhere. Since it is a mode of existence, and existence is itself a relation to God, it is what knows in every act of knowing. — س ره

  222. In The Origin and Return, the author says that, for the most discerning philosophers in Aristotle’s school, the agent's role as a cause seems to be included in what makes it true to say that a possible thing exists. — س ره

  223. This may be difficult for those who have not studied the deeper sciences, but it becomes clear when their principles are kept in mind. Knowledge is a great aid and guide. For example: existence, at whatever level, is good; existence is light, life, knowledge, will, and power, though these become hidden as existence descends and more visible as it rises, as in the soul and what lies above it; in what is pure and simple there are no separate features; and the unity of the Real is not numerical unity. Once such principles become settled in a seeker of truth, doubts fall away. — س ره

  224. The Qur'an says: “Wherever you turn, there is the Face of God.” A poet puts it this way: “Whatever I look at, You have been there before me; though Your face is unseen, You are present in all things.” — ه ره

  225. This is a subtle and profound indication: this natural witnessing and direct presence are intellectual, even though the things that reveal God and the senses through which they do so are physical. God makes Himself known to every thing; He appears to every thing and within every thing, but His appearance is free from limits and change, and His presence is not confined. The reason is that the aspect through which any thing faces its Lord and is connected to Him is itself unlimited. A limited thing cannot be without the unlimited: it depends on the unlimited and exists together with it. This does not mean that the unlimited is a part of the limited, as some ordinary people imagine. If it were truly a part, it would be limited, because a part is bounded by the other parts. The unlimited Truth is within limited things, but not as one thing enters another; and outside them, but not as one thing stands apart from another. Glory be to the One whose mercy embraces all and whose power includes all, and who is established above the Throne. — ن ره

  226. Here is why the explanation follows from what was said. Ordinary speech is called speech because certain sounds are arranged so that, when we hear them, particular things come to mind. We might instead imagine other movements or qualities, not sounds, assigned to particular things, with the same familiar link between the sign and what it signifies. If one appeared in the mind whenever the other did, these too would truly be words, not merely words by comparison. Sounds would be no more essentially speech than those movements or qualities. That speech is sound is accidental; it is not essential to speech that it be sound. People chose separate sounds made by the mouth because they are easy to produce and quickly understood.

    Every thing in the world is an existing reality with qualities that can be sensed, just as other things can. What makes something speech is not that it is sound, but that it is assigned a meaning and that the meaning repeatedly comes to mind when the sign does. Once this is understood, we can say that every existence has an inherent meaning: by a divine assignment, it points to a particular beauty or majesty in the source of all beauty and majesty. Whoever recognises that sign and its meaning recognises the thing's praise of God. Because this sign and its assignment belong to the thing itself, they remain; they exist alongside the conventional signs and meanings people give things. The first relation is vertical, leading from a thing to its divine source. The second is horizontal, linking one created thing with another. These latter, conventional links are incidental and can pass away, unlike the signs that belong to a thing's very being. God's messengers came to explain the divine signs and establish the passing away of merely conventional meanings.

    I can hear acts of remembrance themselves remembering God, and acts of praise themselves praising Him. I may see someone utter God's name with a distracted mind and no attentive heart, while the very act of remembrance remembers God without the speaker noticing it. When we understand that things really are words, then, considered in relation to God, they are His speech; considered in relation to the created things and their essences, they are those things' praise and glorification. The verse points to both sides: every thing glorifies God by His own act of glorifying Himself, and also by its own act of praise. If the verse is read “but they do not understand” rather than “but you do not understand,” it means that people do not grasp this praise through reflective knowledge.

    Someone may ask: suppose you have shown that existences are words. How can all beings—even bodies and physical things—be aware? We answer that this awareness has several grounds. One is that existence is awareness, will, power, and the like, especially when these become more evident at higher levels of existence. Another is the presence of the spiritual source of each kind within its members. A third is the presence of the Lord of all sources. How can the soul's presence in a body make that body aware, while the more complete presence of the Spirit of spirits could not? — س ره

  227. The author mentions application by degrees to cover every possibility. If particular existences were wholly separate realities, there would be no room for degrees in the shared concept of existence, since degrees are possible only within one reality. — س ره

  228. If particular existences are separate realities, then their necessary features differ. The words “as though he had not distinguished” do not mean that agreement is only in the concept and not at all in reality. That would allow one concept to be drawn from realities that differ in every respect, which would make Ibn Kammūna's objection succeed and leave no single reality of existence. It would also contradict the Razi's own words. Rather, the different levels of existence differ in one respect, which explains why their necessary features differ, and agree in another, which explains their shared meaning and underlying kinship.

    Or the Razi may mean that, in general, agreement in necessary features belongs to things that agree in essence and concept. In the case of existence, however, the agreement lies in reality itself. Unlike essences, existence has no fixed nature preserved across every level, carrying the same necessary feature wherever it appears. The Razi has failed to distinguish agreement in necessary features that belongs to essences from agreement that belongs to existences. Or he may mean that sharing a concept directly establishes only that the concept is one; agreement in reality is true for other reasons, including that one concept cannot be drawn from realities that are wholly different in every respect. — س ره

  235. The proof consists of two linked conditional arguments. First: if God's reality were not enough for His attributes, one of them would come from something else. If that is so, then His reality, considered without any condition, would not make His existence necessary. Second: if God's existence is not necessary without a condition, He is not necessary in Himself. Together these show that if His reality were not enough for His attributes, He would not be necessary in Himself. That is impossible. — س ره

  236. The objection asks how the absence of a cause can be inferred from merely not considering it. The point of the answer is that it does not follow that the cause is absent, and so the attribute's absence cannot be inferred from that. Nor does it follow that God's existence would fail to be necessary from eternity. In reality, His existence cannot be without either the attribute and its cause, or the absence of both. Otherwise, opposites would both be absent from reality. But God's existence is reality itself, with no essence behind existence and no potentiality behind actuality. If His reality were empty of both cases, it would be empty of existence altogether. That is what the proof's denial of the link is meant to prevent. — س ره

  237. This is especially clear if an effect is nothing but its relation to its cause: turning away from the cause is then turning away from the effect itself. The author says “first” because the same reasoning could also be used against the philosophers' argument. — س ره

  238. The argument compares existence with essences, but they differ in a crucial way. An essence can be considered at a level apart from reality, without considering other things, even if those things accompany it in reality. Existence is reality itself and has no separate level where it could be considered without regard to what exists or does not exist. — ه ره

  239. How can things be necessary in relation to God when their own light-filled aspect is dominated by necessity and their possibility is almost hidden? Their necessity is their very relation to God, while their possibility means that they are poor and dependent. So how could God Himself be possible in relation to an effect?

    The Shaykh may have meant only the abstract idea of a relation of agency, and its imagined instances. God has a true, real agency in His own reality, through which He brings forth the Sacred Effusion and the all-pervading existence; and He has a dependent, reflected agency at the level of the outpouring, in relation to what receives it. Both are necessary. The first is necessary through His own reality; the second is necessary through His reality, since it belongs to His domain and has no independent standing apart from Him. He also has a purely relational kind of agency: a mental concept that names the first two. That concept is added to His reality. The same applies to the other relational concepts people call attributes. They are no less attributes than negative descriptions are. Fatherhood, ownership, universality, and particularity are all attributes of a human being, yet their being added does not mean that something new has to happen in the external world. As with the concepts of thinghood, unity, and individuality, what is added is the concept, not an externally existing feature. This also explains why philosophers call mental concepts “attributes,” and why they sometimes speak of them as the “realities” of things.

    The careful view is that mental, verbal, and written forms, considered as signs, are neither identical to the things they signify nor wholly separate from them. They are aspects in which those things appear, and are connected to them as features rather than as separate realities. Because they are ways the things appear, some judgments about the signs also apply to what they signify, and some judgments about what they signify apply to the signs. This is why religious teaching calls for respect toward the written and spoken forms of the names of God, the Prophet, and the Imams. Theologians have disagreed over whether a name is the same as what it names. The truth is that it is neither simply the same nor simply different. — س ره

  240. This is the definition of being necessary in relation to something else.   241. God's being the Creator and cause of Zayd is an illuminating relation through which He brings Zayd into being. True creation is real existence, not simply the act of saying or describing. The relation works in both directions: when existence is related to created things, it is their coming to be; when related to God, it is His bringing them into being. His bringing Zayd into being comes before Zayd, though Zayd's own existence does not.

    Although Zayd's existence is possible in itself, God's bringing him into existence is necessary. Everything needed for Zayd's existence and for God's true act of bringing him into being is present in God's real causal reality, because the simple reality contains all things in a higher way. The same is true of God's reflected causal activity: just as multiplicity exists within unity, unity is present within multiplicity. God is the cause when there is no effect, and the Creator when nothing has yet been created, as the reports from the Imams say. How, then, could God's being the cause of Zayd be merely possible, as the author of the objection suggests? — س ره

  242. The Shaykh's point is not the view his respected teacher later quotes: that changes in temporal things are changes only in relation to themselves, not in relation to God. God's disclosure and the One disclosed are eternally one and unchanging. The mirrors through which that disclosure appears in some levels—the world of time and matter—do change and move. The world of the heavens and the world of souls both truly change, though in different ways; change in the first follows change in the second. We will return to the full explanation later, God willing. — ن ره

  243. Because this claim is broader, the commentator connects it to the earlier discussion. Particularity can belong to an essence as a necessary feature, as when the kind is confined to one individual; or it can be identical with a thing, as with real existence. But the claim that particularity is the very reality of a thing is only the broad conclusion in the conditional argument, not its specific starting point. — س ره

  244. This is like the different modes of existence: there are several, and each is particular through itself, since particularity is identical with existence. — س ره

  245. The proof lists only the simplest cases. In general, two things may differ through the whole of one, through part of one, through something outside one, or through a combination in which the difference is the whole or a part of one thing but outside the other. The cases where both sides are of the same kind are easy to picture. Here are examples of mixed cases. The broader kind “animal” differs from human beings and horses through its own nature, while they differ from it through their specific features. A broader kind also differs, by itself, from its shares in particular species, while those shares differ from it through features outside the broader kind, since the species-defining features are not part of the broader kind. Or think of whiteness: it differs by itself from a black person, while the person differs from whiteness through blackness. One actual difference does not rule out another difference through the thing's own nature. Likewise, the animal nature found in a horse differs from a human being through neighing, while the human being differs from both through reason.

    Since the author's aim is to list the non-overlapping cases, he gives the simplest ones and also hints at the mixed cases. In fully real, independent beings, the possible differences reduce to the three same-kind cases he names, so the options in his proof do not overlap. — س ره

  247. This resembles explaining away the attributes by saying that one thing stands in for another: impressive in wording, but weak in substance. — س ره

The cause must therefore be something other than the essence receiving existence. The word “other” could, however, include something joined to the essence, such as existence added to it. — س ره

  250. The objection avoids saying that necessity comes from an outside cause, which would make the Necessary Being dependent, or from a part of the essence, which would make it composite. In substance, Ibn Kammūna chooses the first of the options in the earlier proof of unity: each reality is wholly different from the other, while the shared concept of necessity is drawn from each as a feature.

    There is no contradiction between calling each Necessary Being necessary in itself and saying that necessity is predicated of it as a feature. The objection rests on the primacy of essence: “pure existence” means an essence from which existence is drawn as a feature. This will be discussed later. Some also interpret the claim that God's necessity of existence is identical with Him to mean that the effect of necessity appears from Him. That, too, assumes this view.

    There is also a difference between what is called “essential” in the Posterior Analytics and what is called “essential” in the Isagoge. The commentator seems to be answering an objection: if necessity is a feature, it must belong to God after His essence, rather than at the level of His essence. But a feature need not be something added to a thing in the external world. It can be a feature only in how we think and speak about it. Here “accident” means any predicate that is not part of the subject's definition, whether or not it is an added quality. “Thing” is predicated of both the Necessary Being and possible things; “accident” is predicated of the categories of quality and quantity; and “possible” applies to possible essences. None of these predicates has to be an added thing in the world.

    Someone might answer the original objection with the rule that every incidental feature must ultimately rest on something essential, and a shared incidental feature on a shared essential kind, while any essential common ground must be paired with an essential difference. That would make the Necessary Being composite. But the rule fails for “thing,” which applies to both the Necessary and the possible, and for “accident,” which applies to the highest categories, even though they share no defining essence. The rule works only for features added to subjects in the world. These are instead features abstracted by the mind. The author's replies are the sound way to answer the objection; on the view that existence is fundamental, this objection carries little force. — س ره

  251. The author considered both senses of “feature”: something added to the subject in the world, and a predicate that applies to it without being part of its definition. A possible essence may be considered at a level apart from existence, and possibility is not identical with or a part of that essence. The Necessary Being, however, cannot have a level beyond existence and necessity. So the argument establishes composition from an essential common element and an essential difference. — س ره

  252. The author means: if we regard existence as one concept that names a single, simple, luminous reality, setting aside all particular features, we see that this pure reality includes everything of its own kind and nothing foreign to it. What is foreign to existence belongs to nonexistence and illusion. Existence is the broadest of all realities, and so cannot be two separate pure existences. The Necessary Being must be pure, intensified existence itself—not some other kind of essence from which existence and necessity are then drawn. — س ره

  253. The argument combines a supposition of two with the claim that two are impossible. The “two” exist only in the supposition; in reality, there can be no two. The commentator distinguishes between supposing something impossible and making a supposition that is itself impossible. Sometimes we can imagine a thing from an angle that leaves open its opposite; that is an impossible thing we can suppose. But sometimes the very way we suppose it requires us to affirm what it is and deny what would contradict it. In that case the supposition itself is impossible. This is what happens here. The author makes this point in The Secrets of the Verses: whatever is pure existence, beyond which nothing is fuller, cannot even be supposed to be two, much less actually become two. — س ره

  254. This is the proof based on the principle that simple reality contains all things. — س ره

  255. This applies whether the two aspects are directly in God's reality or arise through further aspects that depend on His reality. — س ره

  256. The conclusion is that a truly simple, necessary reality cannot contain “this and that”: necessity and possibility, having and lacking, light and darkness, actuality and potential, good and evil. The same applies to its attributes: knowledge and ignorance, power and helplessness, and so on. Of each pair, God has the nobler side.

    Someone may object that combining existence and nonexistence, possession and deprivation, necessity and possibility—or any similar pair—is not real composition, since nonexistence is not a thing alongside existence. But the worst kind of composition is precisely a mixture of existence and nonexistence, when the nonexistence is a lack of good or perfection rather than a lack of something bad. A lack of what is bad is itself a kind of good; a lack of good is not. Nonexistence is a distinct opposite of existence. The same is true of a supposed composition of existence and essence: it amounts to existence together with nonexistence. By contrast, two aspects of existence, considered simply as existence, do not make a real composition, because what distinguishes one existence is the very thing it shares with existence as such. — س ره

  279. The answer is first by counterexample: we can truthfully say of every part of a single continuous body that it is a substance and can be divided, even when no actual division has taken place. The subject of the external judgment may be the parts without an actual division; an imagined division is enough, especially since the parts in thought reflect the parts in the thing.
