The author objects that writing is a condition in the world and such a condition needs a subject that exists there. If he means actual writing, I grant that it is a condition in the world. But we are not saying Zayd is actually writing. We are saying only that he could write, which remains true even if he never comes to exist. If he means that the possibility of writing is an external condition, ordinary possibility is a denial, not an existing quality. Readiness to write is different: that is a feature we can attribute to a subject, not a qualification of a statement, which is our subject here.

    His own admission that possibility, considered simply as the link in a statement, does not demand an existing subject supports the philosopher he is criticizing. It is possible that the author means to rely on an argument he will give later in the second stage, in the chapter following the discussion of restoring what has ceased to exist. There he maintains that negative as well as affirmative statements require a subject, even though denial considered simply as denial does not. The familiar rule that negations apply more broadly concerns how we consider them. Likewise, possibility considered on its own does not require an existing subject, whereas a statement that something is possible may do so. Keep this distinction in mind. — س ره

  306. A possible thing can be considered in two ways. First, we can consider its essence as an existing thing whose existence is separate from other things.   312. There are three relevant kinds of statement. In a simple negative statement, such as “Zayd is not a writer,” we consider the subject and predicate, then deny that they are connected. In an affirmative statement with a negative predicate, such as “Zayd is a non-writer,” we affirm that a negative feature belongs to the subject. A statement with a negative subject and a negative predicate has both kinds of negation. The first statement has four parts in the mind: the subject, the predicate, their possible connection, and the denial of that connection. The affirmative statement with a negative predicate adds a fifth: assigning the negative feature to the subject. In a statement with a negative subject and predicate, both terms are themselves treated as statements. This is why “Zayd is not a writer” differs from “Zayd is a non-writer”: in the first, the denial comes before the connecting verb; in the second, the connection is affirmed and the predicate is negative. The second kind of statement still requires the subject to exist, because it assigns something to that subject. Some logicians deny this and say that “vacuum is nonexistent” does not require a vacuum to exist as its subject. But the proper way to say that no vacuum exists is “No vacuum is existent,” which does not assume a vacuum as a subject. Then the broader claim “Nothing existent is perceptible” would be false. The same issue appears in an argument that says, “A substance is not an accident; whatever is not an accident does not need a subject.” The first statement is affirmative with a negative predicate, not a simple denial. — س ره

  313. Three objections are raised. First, if possibility is only a denial, and denial removes the connection between subject and predicate, possibility could not be a way of qualifying a statement alongside necessity and impossibility. Second, if possibility is two denials taken together, it would not be one simple meaning like necessity and impossibility. Third, this would contradict the earlier claim that possibility is the positive statement that both necessities are absent. The answer is to distinguish the essence considered just as it is from the mind’s judgment about it. Of an essence in itself, we make two simple denials: its existence is not necessary, and its nonexistence is not necessary. These denials contain no further judgment. The mind can then restate them as one affirmative claim: the essence is such that neither existence nor nonexistence is necessary. That is how possibility is affirmed of the essence. Since this affirmative claim is true of the essence, it requires a basis; and because nothing else is under consideration, its basis is the essence itself. This avoids all three objections. It also resolves the apparent conflict between an essence’s own lack of necessity and the necessity or impossibility it receives through another. The first claim concerns the essence by itself, where there is no demand either way. The second concerns the essence together with its cause. The statements differ in meaning and refer to different circumstances, so they do not conflict. — ط

  345. One possibility cannot differ from another simply by being possible: possibility has one meaning. Nor can matter make them different, since matter, considered in itself, has no distinctions. And the future things to which they refer cannot distinguish them either, since those things do not yet exist. If each possibility is said to differ only because it is a different possibility, the argument goes in a circle.

    This argument also seems to apply to readiness in matter, even though that readiness exists in the world; so the proof would wrongly make it only mental. It also applies to any number of possibilities, not only an unlimited number. The answer to the second objection is that the author means that a multiplicity of possibilities in themselves cannot be conceived. The first objection is answered by distinguishing readiness from possibility as such. Readiness, considered merely as possibility, has no reality for the author. Those who say it exists mean that it exists as a readiness or feature of matter, which is the subject prepared to receive something. The author later distinguishes two kinds of possibility: possibility in itself, where an essence can be considered without contradiction as existing or not existing; and readiness for a particular way of existing, which arises only when the conditions are in place and obstacles removed. These differ in their subjects, as will be explained in the discussion of potentiality and actuality.

    The author says elsewhere that readiness means removing an obstacle or its opposite, either fully (near potentiality) or partly (remote potentiality). Even if we grant that readiness has real existence because it is the very state of the prepared thing, it exists in relation to what it is prepared for, and as a weak existence of that thing. Prime matter itself exists only as a deep potential. The author’s descriptions of readiness as nothing, as a quality, or as a relation can be reconciled: it is “nothing” when viewed as potentiality in itself; a quality when viewed as a weak form of existence; and a relation when viewed as something that necessarily points to what the thing is ready to receive.

    A further objection to the claim that possibility exists in the world is that it would make nonexistent essences real. Possibility in itself belongs to an essence considered just as it is. If it were a real feature, it would have to exist before the essence exists, even though it is not a substance. Also, if possibility were real, an endless chain would follow, since possibility itself would be possible. One cannot say that possibility is possible through itself: if it were a real possibility, it would be an essence under one of the ten categories, with existence added to it, and their relation would itself have to be qualified by possibility. Saying that possibility is possible through itself merely repeats the word; the question is how existence relates to it. — س ره

  411. The difficulty is this: if existence alone is real in its own right, then every true statement that matches neither the outside world nor our minds considered as mental states would be impossible. One example is “the effect’s absence is caused by the cause’s absence.” This statement is true, even if nobody happens to think it. But it does not match anything in the outside world, since absence is nothing and has no external reality.

    The usual answer is that such truths correspond to “reality as such” (nafs al-amr), rather than to the outside world or the mind. Philosophers say that “reality as such” includes everything in the outside world, and overlaps with what is in the mind while also reaching beyond it. Some explain it to mean the thing itself: saying that a thing is such-and-such “in itself” means that the thing itself is such-and-such; the wording puts “the thing” in place of “it.”

    But this explanation does not solve the problem. If “the thing itself” means its real existence, the original difficulty returns. If it means the thing’s essence, distinct from its existence, that cannot be right either, because nothing besides existence is real. Others explain “reality as such” as the World of Command: a universal, immaterial intellect containing the forms of all true statements. But if those forms are direct knowledge—things present to that intellect—then they are just the external realities themselves, and would not match a statement such as “the effect’s absence is caused by the cause’s absence.” The problem remains. If they are ideas in that intellect, there is no reason to posit them, since similar ideas already exist in our minds; and again the problem remains.

    The better answer is this: what is real in its own right is actual existence, and it is what truly exists. Every true fact belongs to it. Essences are ways existence appears to our rational minds. So the mind is forced to extend the idea of “existence” to essences as well, then make whatever true judgments it must about them. In this way, the concept of “existence” or “being” comes to apply more broadly, both to real existence and to essences.

    Then the mind is forced to take a further step: it applies the bare idea of being real to every abstract concept it has had to form, such as nonexistence, unity, action, and potentiality. It also accepts the judgments about these concepts that reason requires. The place the mind imagines for reality in this broadest sense is what we call “reality as such.” The author will return to this later, God willing, in the discussions of mental existence and other topics. — ط

  427. You may ask: if existence already has the advantage, how can the two outcomes still be equally open? I answer: even a cause that will eventually make one outcome necessary leaves both outcomes open until it has done all that is needed. A cause that merely favors existence has not ruled out every way the effect could fail to exist. The preference, considered without the final purpose or condition that settles the outcome, has left both possibilities open. To claim that the preference already belongs to existence is to confuse what the mind considers with what has actually happened. The thing does not yet exist. As we have seen, possibility is not a separate state alongside the thing's existence or nonexistence; nor is a mere preference.

    Consider the argument another way. If a preference truly fixed one outcome, that outcome would be necessary—contrary to the assumption. The preference is itself something that may occur or not occur and therefore also needs an explanation. Al-Sayyid al-Sharif objects: why should the greater weight supplied by an outside cause not suffice for the favored outcome? What is obviously impossible, he says, is for two equally balanced outcomes to occur without a reason, or for the less favored one to occur. I reply that if the favored outcome actually happens, the supposed mere preference has given way to what makes its occurrence necessary. Beforehand, necessity is something we understand; when the possible thing exists, it exists through the necessity supplied by its cause. Its actual existence reveals that the cause made it necessary.

    You may reply that, for us, existence reveals necessity, but for those who accept mere preference it reveals only preference. We mean by necessity nothing more than what makes the thing truly exist. If you choose to call that 'preference,' our disagreement is only about a name; you might as well call it 'possibility.' But how could actual existence, which excludes nonexistence, show only a preference that still allows nonexistence?

    To say that a possible thing comes into existence through a preference that has not reached necessity is like saying that a person reaches a rooftop merely by thinking about it, deciding to climb, setting up a ladder, and stepping on every rung except the last one. The final part of the complete cause is still missing. However many incomplete conditions have been met, they do not settle whether the person reaches the roof. Even endlessly many such preferences would not explain why the cause brings about existence rather than leaving the thing nonexistent. That would still be choosing one outcome without what decides it. I have explained this at length because the distinction is easy to miss. Do not let it escape you. — س ره

    Saying that the sides cannot be equal because the preference points towards existence confuses what the mind considers with what exists outside the mind. Existence has not yet occurred in the outside world, so the possible thing’s existence is no more actual than its nonexistence. As explained earlier, possibility applies only when we consider the thing in itself, not to its actual absence or to its actual existence—whether outside the mind, in the mind, now, or in the future. Preference, too, has meaning only at that level. It is not yet an actual state.

    Another way to put the argument is this: if the preference is not equal and truly belongs to one side, then that side has become necessary through its cause. But the claim under discussion assumes that no necessity has been reached. Also, preference itself is one of the things the mind can consider; it too may occur or fail to occur. Its own occurrence would therefore need a preference.

    A later commentator raises this objection: Why can’t the favored side occur simply because an outside cause has made it more likely? This does not seem obviously impossible; what is obviously impossible is that one of two equally likely sides, or the less likely side, should occur. The answer is that when the favored side actually occurs, this goes beyond mere preference. How is it different from saying that the cause made it necessary? In the mind, necessity is distinct from existence and is considered before it. Outside the mind, necessity is the existence itself. So when we know that a possible thing exists, we know that its cause made it necessary.

    Someone might reply: “That is your view. Those who accept mere preference without necessity say that existence shows only that the cause favored it.” We answer that by “necessity” we mean whatever grounds the judgment that the thing exists. If you call this “preference,” then we disagree only about the name. Call it “possibility” if you wish. But how could actual existence, which cannot be absent, show a preference that can fail to occur, even if its absence is less likely? Existence and necessity cannot fail to be; mere preference can.

    To say that a possible thing can exist through a preference that falls short of necessity is like saying that someone can reach a roof by imagining the result, deciding to do it, wanting it, setting up a ladder, and climbing every rung except the last. The result would occur even though the final part of the complete cause was missing. Having many conditions and incomplete causes in place does not remove the equal chance of reaching the roof or not reaching it, when the outcome is considered in relation to the person who acts. Those conditions are only being considered in the mind. Even infinitely many weak preferences would not settle what the person brings about. For the person to produce existence rather than nonexistence would still be a choice without a reason. The author expands the discussion because it is easy to misunderstand. — س ره

  428. Calling the concept “existent” an essential feature of a real instance of existence is slightly imprecise. That is why the author adds that it must be true as long as the reality exists. As explained earlier, existence is not a species, a general kind, a dividing feature, a universal, or a particular. The real point is that the concept of existence is an abstract idea the mind draws from descriptions; as a concept, it has no reality outside the mind. If it did, existence, whose very nature is to be outside the mind, would itself exist in the mind in the same way it exists outside. It would then have one nature in the mind and another outside it, and would become an essence equally open to being and not being. That is impossible. — ط

    ↩

  429. The argument is that if nonexistence were possible while the thing exists, opposite claims would be true at once. That is impossible in itself. Whatever entails something impossible in itself is also impossible in itself. So existence would be necessary in itself. — س ره

  430. For this speaker, the condition is the essence’s relation to its maker. — س ره

  431. This answer works if the condition is part of what we call the subject. The claim that a cause must exist for its effect works differently: there the cause explains why the effect exists. The reply to the earlier scholar changes the objection rather than answering it directly. The author says 'even if the argument were complete' because it is not. Possibility and impossibility concern existence and nonexistence in general, not some special kind of either. Motion, for example, can exist, but not as something fixed and unchanging. A thing impossible in itself must be nonexistent, not merely absent in one particular way. Yet the other scholar speaks of 'nonexistence while the thing exists,' which is a special case. Moreover, he treats 'while it exists' as a condition on the denial of existence. It really qualifies the subject, for the subject is already 'the existing essence.' Adding the condition to the denial repeats what the subject already says. An essence considered as existing cannot, while it exists, be nonexistent. Its opposite—existence—is therefore necessary. — س ره

    There is another problem. The phrase “nonexistent while it exists” makes “while it exists” sound like a condition on the claim that the thing is absent. But it is really a condition on the subject: it means the essence is being considered as existing at that time. So adding the condition to nonexistence repeats the same idea. An essence that exists at a given time cannot be absent at that time; its opposite, existence, must hold. — س ره

  432. This can be so when the opposite side is nonexistence; when the opposite side is existence, it may be impossible. — س ره

  433. The essence considered by itself can receive existence, and existence belongs to it in that respect. The opposite claim, nonexistence, concerns the essence under the condition that it exists. This reading fits the view of the Imam and is also suggested by the author’s later words. — س ره

  434. In the second way, the difference comes from applying a condition. Here, the difference comes from the condition itself. A difference made by adding a condition is weaker than one made by the condition itself, though both involve a condition. — ن ره

  435. This is a proof, not just an argument meant to trap the other side. So it does not show that the author rejects the view that existence is real in itself. — س ره

  436. This rule is very useful. If a possible thing exists at one time, it cannot be absent at that time, since it must exist while it exists. It cannot be removed from another time when it was never there. Nor can it be absent from reality altogether: for reality as a whole to lack it, it would have to be absent at every level, which is not the case. This is why things are said to remain fixed in relation to the higher sources, and even more so in relation to the First Source. Each thing is present to Him at its own level, with no fading or loss. One of God's beautiful names addresses Him as 'You from whose treasures nothing is diminished.' God's knowledge does not change. This concerns an essence insofar as it has become real. As for a particular real existence, nonexistence cannot belong to it: a thing cannot receive its own opposite, and existence has no separate underlying subject on which its contrary could arrive and replace it. Understand this. — س ره

  437. This is an important principle with further consequences. For example, every material being implies the existence of a corresponding being that does not depend on matter, is of the same order, and oversees it. Why? If the material being has a place in reality as a whole, it cannot be lost from that whole; and in that respect it cannot undergo any change. Every change involves some loss of what was there. Yet every material thing, precisely because it is material, can change in some way. So at every level of material beings there must be a corresponding being free from matter, loss, and change.

    Some Western students of nature, noticing something of this principle, supposed that a thing might eventually cease to need a cause. They reached that conclusion because they considered only causes made of matter. They overlooked two points. First, a material being's relation to reality as a whole does not do away with the relations among material beings themselves. Second, not every cause is a material cause. There is also the cause that acts and produces an effect, which anything that depends on another for its existence still needs. We shall establish this later. — ط

    This idea led some Western scientists to wonder whether the need for a cause might end if “cause” meant only a material cause. But they missed two points. First, the relation between a material thing and reality as a whole does not cancel the relations between material things themselves. Second, causes are not only material; there is also the cause that brings a possible thing into being, and no possible thing can do without it. This will be proved later. — ط

    ↩

  438. Here, “reality altogether” means reality in general, without limiting it to one level or a particular set of levels. — ن ره

    ↩

  439. On the view that each kind has a higher, guiding reality, every essence has one kind of possibility in the realm of intellect, but may have two in the material world. According to this view, the higher realities of kinds are each represented by a single individual, while in the material world a kind may have many members. The difference comes from matter and the further conditions it needs. — س ره

  440. This is a hidden point that few understand. The movement at issue is a thing’s passage from potential to actual. This passage must ultimately rest on a simple reality that changes from within itself, not because another thing changes it. Otherwise, the chain of changing things would go on without end. This simple, ever-flowing present is the timeless order that connects what changes with what does not. Time measures ordinary motion: the gradual change of something that receives new actuality from an active source. Time is the very reality of this changing thing as it passes step by step from potential to actual. A sequence of events in time leads, in one direction, to the timeless order, which joins the eternity beyond time. The active source remains; what receives its action begins and ends. So we speak of the source’s continuous giving, not of the world as a product that has continued forever. — ن ره

    ↩

  441. Some things brought into being through direct creation are joined to time and place without themselves changing gradually. The heavenly spheres, for example, are living beings whose matter is formed by souls that have no parts of measurable size. A sphere's nature and its soul are one in existence, though we can consider them separately. Its measurable parts belong to its body insofar as its body is matter, not insofar as it belongs to a general kind. Such a being is alive by its nature and does not die through the usual process in which one bodily form replaces another. It may cease to appear, but that is not the same as dying. Disappearance is broader than decay, just as existence is broader than coming into being. A link with time and place that does not involve gradual change can end without one thing being destroyed by another. Existence itself cannot be destroyed, for that would require a change in God's knowledge—far be it from Him. On the day when the heavens are rolled up like a scroll, their disappearance is the drawing back of what was spread out; what seemed mixed is no longer mixed, and what comes into view does so in a new form. Consider this carefully. — ن ره

  454. The word “some” matters because not every concept fails to apply to itself as a real thing. The concepts “thing,” “universal,” and “essence,” for example, can also apply to themselves in that sense. All concepts apply to themselves in the first, basic sense—as ideas. — س ره

  455. This expands the brief point made earlier. The author could have left it out there. — س ره

  456. Here is how a circular dependence leads to an endless chain. Suppose A depends on B and B depends on A. Then A depends on itself. But what something depends on must be distinct from the dependent thing. So, on this supposition, A and “A itself” must be different. Yet A itself is nothing other than A. We can repeat the argument, replacing A with “A itself,” then with “the self of A itself,” and so on. This produces an endless chain on both sides of the original circle. Al-Sayyid al-Sharif presents the argument this way in his notes on al-Mataliʿ; the details can be found there.

    I can give a shorter and firmer explanation. On the assumption of circular dependence, A depends on B, B on A, then A on B again, then B on A, without end. None of these steps establishes that A or B actually exists. They are like a chain of conditions: “If B exists, A exists; if A exists, B exists; if B exists, A exists...” We never reach the point where we can say, “But B exists, therefore A exists,” or the reverse. Nothing establishes the first condition, so the chain cannot stop. — س ره

  457. An accidental conditional can connect true claims: “If a human being speaks, a donkey brays.” Both may happen, but one does not require the other. The cases at issue here are false claims, such as “If a human brays, a horse speaks,” “If two identical things cannot be together, neither can a vacuum,” or “If Zayd does not exist, the phoenix does not exist.” We cannot treat such pairings as true just because both claims are false; at most, they can be supposed together. — س ره

    ↩

  458. A universal “if … then” statement covers every possible way the first claim may be assumed. So “whenever two is a number, this follows” includes the case where two is assumed to be odd, as in the example. — س ره

On this reading, “by reflection from higher realities” concerns nearness and distance from God; “the light of existence appearing within us” concerns how ready or unready we are to receive it.   467. This knowledge does not come merely by drawing an idea from things, as people commonly suppose. A Persian verse says: “Free yourself from matter to see what is free of matter.     Following their example fills the heart with light and purifies one's inner life until the person reaches the intended goal: knowing things as they truly are through direct experience. While this work prepares the seeker, it is called the path; when it achieves its aim, it is called the reality, and people reach it to differing degrees. I have explained as much as space allows of the subtle meaning suggested here, but few fully attain it. Do not suppose that this contradicts the earlier statement that existence is added to the essences of possible things. — ن ره

  472. The soul is existence without an essence beyond it because every description we imagine for it—such as “the first perfection of a body,” “the ruler of the body,” or “a substance separate in itself but not in its actions”—is different from the soul itself. The note also says the soul has no fixed limit to its growth; it can always go beyond what it has reached. Scripture says that human beings were created weak and are deeply unjust and ignorant. Existence with no limit has no essence beyond itself. Concepts such as God’s knowledge, will, and power do not describe a limited existence, so they are not essences. An essence is an idea that describes existence with a limit. The same applies to the intellects. — س ره

  475. The Shaykh calls existence one and simple because he believes that a shared idea can be part of what a thing is, while still applying by degrees. They therefore think that the same idea in the mind does not prove that the realities themselves are one.   500. Mental existence is defined by contrast with external existence: an external thing has its characteristic effects, while a mental thing does not. In these respects, they are real in the mind. Every mental thing is measured against something outside the mind; whatever has no counterpart outside the mind has no mental form either.   505. “Outside the place of imagination” means outside the knower’s own imagination. This distinguishes true creation from magic or sleight of hand, which may show images outside the magician’s imagination but only by influencing the imaginations of the audience. — ه ره

  506. The five realms are the divine realm, the realm of power, the realm of spirits, the visible human world, and the all-encompassing human realm. The human realm itself can contain and preserve the ordered, unseen realms above the world of meanings and fixed realities. — س ره

    ↩

  507. The word “and” begins a new sentence here. It does not describe a state or join this point to the previous one, which would make the passage contradict itself. — س ره

    ↩

  508. The passage through “the forms preserve one another” describes the knower’s awareness of all the realms. The following passage describes the fact that a knower must always be present to at least one realm. Every thing that exists outside the mind passes through all the levels of knowledge before appearing. One form can preserve the others because a form in a higher realm is the cause, spirit, and meaning of the forms below it. A lower form reveals its higher cause, since an effect points back to its cause and an image represents its meaning. — س ره

    ↩

  509. This means that no one is entirely inattentive—not ordinary people and not the special few. Ordinary people also witness a display of reality, though they may not know what is appearing through it. — س ره

    ↩

  510. A person creates and preserves things through resolve, but even when the person creates an act, God is the true Creator. “There is no power or strength except through God, the Most High and Mighty.” — س ره

    ↩

  511. The note says the reply as given is not quite right. If the mental form is simply the reality of the known thing, with no difference between the two, then there is no distinction between a thing and its mental counterpart; this seems to deny mental existence. The philosophers mean that an essence remains the same while its existence differs, which would allow a counterpart and bring back the original problem. The reply’s phrase “shadow-like appearance” may mean only that the mind is related to the reality known. But if it means a separate existence for the form, then the same question arises about the essence shared by different kinds of existence. The better answer is that each thing has a counterpart suited to its own nature. For a nonexistent thing, the counterpart is precisely the lack of any external reality. Its mental form is also an idea of absence, not a different object. The mistake is to assume that a counterpart must always be something that exists.

    ↩

  512. Knowledge of nonexistent things was explained earlier by distinguishing a thing’s basic meaning from the fact that it is absent. Absolute nonexistence is absent in its very nature. — س ره

    ↩

  513. The supposition itself is real as a thought, but “flies” is stated as an actual feature. So the subject must have some actual existence. — س ره

    ↩

  514. A universal statement concerns whatever falls under a general title in reality, whether its examples exist outside the mind, are only possible, or do not exist at all. If the statement is to apply to those real or possible examples, it cannot be limited to actual external things. Since the subject understood in this way is not present outside the mind, it must be present within it. — س ره

    ↩

  515. The shared idea exists in the mind, but we do not have to consider it as existing there. Its commonness comes from the mind’s way of considering it. In many places, the author holds that commonness comes from existence itself—specifically, a dependent mental existence—rather than from essence by itself. This may be what he means when he says that the point will be explained later. — س ره

    ↩

  516. “Applies to them” does not mean that the mental universal is literally predicated of external individuals as one and the same thing. The proof concerns an idea in the mind. Here, “same” means that the idea shares the individuals’ basic nature. The universal term that can truly be applied to each person is the nature “human being,” considered without a condition. — س ره

    ↩

  517. The word 'natural' is unnecessary here and would be better omitted, as the author’s later words make clear. A thing’s nature, considered by itself—not even as the subject of a general idea—exists outside the mind. The error is to confuse that nature with the general idea of it in our minds. — س ره

    ↩

  518. This is true: the idea that applies to many is the natural kind, which is indistinct from its individual examples in its basic meaning. The argument still works, as the author says. — س ره

    ↩

  519. This argument assumes that anything that exists for something else must exist in the same place where that relation applies. Some philosophers instead say that a relation’s being true of a thing requires only that the thing it describes exist, not that the relation itself exist in that same place. The author may mean that ideas drawn from things, though they do not exist outside the mind, still have a real standing. For example, being Zayd’s father or owning a horse is not an external object; these are relations we understand in the mind. The note says this point, despite its qualifications, belongs to the first method. — س ره

  520. Ali is reported to have said, “I tore down the gate of Khaybar through God’s power, not through bodily strength.” A Persian poem makes the same point: “The power and action of God rose through him; he uprooted Khaybar’s gate by a force beyond his own. And what is Khaybar? Even the fortress of heaven would have been weak before that hand.” — س ره

    ↩

  521. Knowledge, like life, will, and other perfections, accompanies existence wherever it is found. Indeed, these perfections are one with existence itself. Natural beings have existence, though it is incomplete and mixed with potential and lack. They also have a weak kind of knowledge and life. The Qur'an says, “There is nothing that does not praise Him, though you do not understand their praise.” This awareness is basic knowledge, not the power to feel through touch. Otherwise, plants would be animals, since an animal can sense and move by choice. A thing in nature does not reach sensation until its powers of movement have developed, as the stages of life require. There is also another answer: natural things act under the direction of higher powers that know the ends toward which they are directed. A shot arrow moves toward a goal, but the archer knows the goal, not the arrow. In the same way, natural things may be directed toward ends that are known by the powers directing them. — س ره

  522. This meaning differs from the previous one. The previous one was “what exists as existing,” meaning existence itself. This one is an essence that actually exists. It differs from the last meaning because it includes actual existence and the condition “not in a subject,” while the last meaning includes neither. — س ره

    ↩

  523. The concept of something existing in a subject—which is what an accident is—cannot be a broad category for the nine kinds of accidents. That would conflict with the philosophers’ view that these nine are the highest categories. al-Muhaqqiq al-Damad does say that substance and accident are two broad categories. But the better view is that “accident” describes how these things exist in relation to something else. An essential feature belongs to a thing without reference to anything outside it. In truth, an accident has a dependent kind of existence: its existence in itself is the same as its existence in the subject it depends on. Even if most philosophers leave relation out of their definitions, they agree that it belongs to the way these things exist. Since being an accident means having a relational existence, and existence is not part of a thing’s basic nature, being an accident is not essential to it. — س ره

    ↩

  524. This means considering something with a condition, or without one. By “taking the universal where the particular belongs,” the author means treating the general idea as if it were the particular magnet. — س ره

    ↩

  525. Earlier in this commentary, the natural universal was explained as a nature that can be considered in several ways: by itself, joined to other conditions, or separated from them. It is even more open-ended than an unrestricted nature, since it can take on many conditions that cannot coexist. This is what the author means when he says it can be joined to incompatible conditions. Other writers use “natural universal” for a nature considered without any condition; the author calls this an intellectual universal. al-Taftazani writes in The Refinement of Logic that its subject is natural. Some copies read, “as the essence described as universal is called an intellectual universal.” On that reading, the meaning is clear. — س ره

    ↩

  526. Many things do not fall under the ten categories, such as particular possible existences, which are not necessary existents, and simple distinguishing features. These are either particular existences, as the author holds, or simple natures that do not belong to any category, as other philosophers hold. Even some qualities, such as a point or unity, do not belong to the nine categories in their view. — س ره

    ↩

  527. The first problem was answered earlier. The second and third are these: a general idea is universal as an idea, yet it exists in a particular mind, and its subject is one of the things that makes it particular. How, then, can it be both general and particular? Also, in their view, knowledge and the thing known are one. Yet knowledge of blackness belongs to the knower, not to blackness itself. God’s knowledge of things is identical with His being, but the things He knows are not. The commentator then explains the view with a mirror example. Imagine a person standing before a mirror, with his body reflected in it. There are two images: the person’s natural image, which is not in the mirror, and the reflection on the mirror’s surface, which depends on the mirror. The view says that the mind works like a mirror. For each thing we perceive, it posits three forms: the external thing, known indirectly; a mental form, which is present to the mind but does not depend on it; and a form that depends on the mind, which this view calls the external thing. Each form has its own subject. — س ره

    ↩

  528. This view combines two positions. It says that the form in the mind is like the external thing in its nature and features, while the form that depends on the mind is its shadow because it is a quality. The actual external thing, meanwhile, belongs to another category. Or else it invents a third position by claiming there are two forms: those who say the mental form is a likeness, and those who say it is a shadow, each speak of only one form. No one spoke of two. — س ره

    ↩

  529. The point is to show the flaw in saying that what exists in the mind, apart from the mind, is general and immaterial. Generality and being free of matter depend on its existence for the mind. This also supports the author’s claim that there must be a causal link: the mind must be one of the causes of what exists in it. — س ره

    ↩

  530. Just because a thing exists for another in the same way it exists in itself, it does not follow that it must exist inside that other thing. The claim cannot simply be turned around. But here the point is that a mental form cannot exist for the mind in the way that something produced exists for its maker. The mind, especially when it is only potentially able to understand, receives forms passively. So this particular kind of existence for the mind must mean that the form depends on the mind. — س ره

    ↩

  531. That is, the mental form is not in matter and is not covered by material features. The author says that, if this form did not depend on the mind, it would have to be particular and perceptible, not general and intelligible. The author is showing that the other view leads to a contradiction, as his words “we assumed it was intelligible” make clear. According to that view, the mind frees forms from matter by removing their material features. But that process depends on the forms existing for the mind. If the forms do not depend on the mind, they remain material, whatever names one gives them. — س ره

    ↩

  532. This is the position he takes on mental forms to answer several objections.

    ↩

  533. This objection will arise in two forms later, in the section of this book on the intellect and what it knows. — س ره

    ↩

  534. Someone might say that the reverse must also follow. The answer is that there is no quality in the mind, as we will explain when discussing God’s knowledge and the beings that govern the kinds of things. All these forms exist through the soul’s existence. Their concepts, of course, can be applied to themselves in the basic, definitional sense. — س ره

    ↩

  535. The phrase “their relation to bodily kinds” can be read as referring either to the intellectual forms themselves or to the forms together with the ideas drawn from them. On the author’s view, and on Plato’s, the objects of intellect are the intellectual realities seen from afar in the creative world.

    The author distinguishes the soul’s perception of sensed and imagined forms from its perception of intellectual forms. It brings the first about through its own activity, but reaches the second through an illuminating connection. Why? Individual forms are marked by size, shape, change, and limits. So the author often says that the soul perceives them by making them. He sometimes describes this as union, since these forms are the soul’s own lights and appearances, not separate things. As a saying about the appearance of the First Reality puts it: “All are expressions; You are the meaning, the magnet of hearts.”

    General forms, by contrast, are marked chiefly by unity, freedom from matter, and their reach across the subtle details of imagined and natural things. They rise above both worlds and both regions. So the author says that the soul knows them by becoming one with them. This is what he means by an illuminating connection and by direct, present knowledge. Such knowledge can occur through union or through causation. Causation does not fit here, though some writers sometimes say that the simple intellect or soul creates detailed intellects and forms of knowledge. The author has reasons for rejecting this, including his reply to al-Qushji. So union is what remains.

    If you ask what he says about general ideas that have no separate intellectual beings as their source, he says they too represent the sources of existing things, but they are labels that do not accurately fit them. Even an inaccurate definition points toward the thing it is meant to define. To see how this can happen, consider how the light of existence reaches even its opposite, nonexistence, including absolute nonexistence, and an essence considered apart from existence. We can understand universal existence—the most obvious and wide-reaching thing—by seeing from afar the light of existence itself, which is brighter and wider than any light or shadow. In the higher world, a quality and the thing it belongs to are one, just as the scent of musk and the musk itself are one; otherwise, potentiality would follow.

    Many minds find the idea that knowing a general form means seeing the source of a kind unsettling. The author discusses the reasons elsewhere. Most come down to two. First, people treat a concept as if it were the whole reality and overlook existence itself: its unity includes all its levels and details, so it can both know and be known. Second, they treat the general idea only as a mirror for looking at particular things, instead of turning it around and seeing what the idea itself reveals. — س ره

    ↩

  536. This does not mean a limited kind of existence, such as the existence of water, fire, or other natural things. It means another, form-like and luminous existence for these natures, unlike their dark material existence, which cannot support knowledge. The author means that the existence of natures in the mind—in the signs within the soul—is like their existence in external things—in the signs of the world. Just as external existence is God’s sacred outpouring and illuminating act, not a substance or quality in itself, so knowledge is an existence that flows from the soul and is lit by it; in itself, it is neither a substance nor a quality. The natures themselves are substances, quantities, and qualities in the basic, definitional sense, not in the ordinary sense. This distinction between the two ways of applying a term matters to the argument that follows. The reply rests on two points: things in the mind are themselves in the basic sense, not in the ordinary sense; and the forms are truly qualities, not merely called qualities as a figure of speech. The reply accepts the familiar philosophical principles; the author has already offered other answers that do not depend on them. — س ره

    ↩

  537. The author says “in our view,” even though everyone agrees that a nature considered by itself is neither existent nor nonexistent. The reason is that those who treat a nature as a real thing are, in effect, saying that it exists in itself, though they may say it exists only through its relation to its maker, as the author says of existence. They accept the point in words, while the results of their view imply it. As Imam al-Razi says, the claim that a nature is not made follows from the question of what a nature is in itself. — س ره

    ↩

  538. At first, this seems to conflict with the author’s earlier claim that universality comes from intellectual existence itself. But intellectual existence is so wide that it extends evenly across all its details. In the section on the soul, he says that the generality and individuality of an intellectual form are not two separate things. How, then, can its nature be general? Perhaps he means that generality comes from the nature’s lack of individual features and its great openness, as he suggests here. Its ability to apply to many comes from being seen from afar, with its inner reality not fully grasped. “They forgot God, so He made them forget themselves.” Or perhaps he means that the nature does not resist being general, as something able to receive that feature, though it does not require generality by itself. The discussion of the soul makes this point clearer. — س ره

    ↩

  539. This is the standard definition of a human being, though it can be challenged. A definition may tell us what truly makes a thing what it is, or it may merely help us tell that thing apart from others. Here we need the first kind. So the definition should include each level it passes through: its material and mineral form, its ability to have dimensions, growth, the senses, the powers that prompt and carry out movement, voluntary movement, and reason both as a capacity and in use. A thing cannot reach a higher kind until it has all the conditions of a lower kind. If “mineral form” is included under “able to have dimensions,” then growth and sensation should be included too. Otherwise the definition does not show all the essential parts. It is not enough simply to distinguish humans; the words “rational” or even “laughing” would do that. A full definition would be: a human being is a substance that can have dimensions, has an elemental and mineral form, grows, senses, moves by choice, and reasons. — س ره

    ↩

  540. This follows the common view. The author will discuss later whether it is a quality only incidentally. — س ره

    ↩

  541. Ordinary predication concerns the shared existence of subject and predicate, and existence is incidental to an essence. The second kind of predication is different. — س ره

    ↩

  542. Predication requires a difference in one way and identity in another. When a definition is said of the thing it defines, the difference is between the general and the detailed meaning. For example, “human being” is “animal that reasons.” The two are the same in nature, but one is the full definition and the other is the thing defined. The phrase “human being is human being” can also have meaning if someone has first suggested that a human being can be separated from itself. The reply says that the human being whose existence you question is exactly the human being whose existence cannot be denied. Similarly, when philosophers say that a human being, considered just as a human being, is only itself, they mean that it is neither existent, nonexistent, nor anything else beyond its own nature. This is not empty repetition: it says that the two meanings are identical, not merely that they share an existence. — س ره

    ↩

  543. “Essence” here means the actual thing or example. If two concepts are identical, they share an existence; but the reverse does not always follow. Primary predication is about identity of meaning. The existence in question may be actual, mental, or merely assumed. Claims such as “nothing is nothing” or “contradictions are contradictions” use this kind of predication, even though they have no actual existence. — س ره

    ↩

  544. For example, “a laughing person is a writer” and “a laughing person is not a writer” can both be true in different senses: one may be a writer in actual existence without being one by nature. The concept “laughing person,” which is shared by all people who laugh, is “laughing” by primary predication but not by ordinary predication. — س ره

    ↩

  545. The author means natures considered without any condition—the natural universals discussed before the two kinds of predication. He does not mean “intellectual universals” in the usual technical sense. This is clear from his argument, especially since he treats intellectual universals as the real sources of kinds, seen from a distance. On that view, they are substances just as an individual is an example of a nature. Here, “universal” means the nature’s indeterminacy; “intelligible” means the concept as it exists in thought. — س ره

    ↩

  546. The author’s view is that particular mental images are produced by the soul, while general forms are reached when the soul sees separate intellects from a distance. In the first case, the soul brings the forms about. In the second, it is a place where higher realities appear. If these forms exist in the soul as qualities, that is because they are features of the soul; their intelligible, general nature is not itself one of the categories. By themselves, the general forms are separate substances. As features of the soul they are qualities; as ideas they are meanings of the categories, not the categories themselves. — ط

    ↩

  547. Existence makes the hidden features of essences appear. But existence itself is neither a substance nor an accident, so how could it be a quality? Another way to put it is that existence makes an essence actually show a quality, as the sun makes water hot or darkens a face. It is not like a passenger’s movement being attributed to a ship that moves. — س ره

    ↩

  548. The soul is a place where general intellectual forms appear, but it produces particular sensory and imagined forms. — س ره

    ↩

  549. The argument rests on the view that mental concepts are not examples of categories in the ordinary sense. Natures as general ideas are only ways of considering things; an actual example comes from existence. A concept of substance or quantity, considered apart from its particular existence, is true of itself only in the primary sense. So it would have been enough to say that the mental idea of substance does not produce the effects of substance. The author adds that even an intellectual universal does not become an example of itself by being universal. Since a concept exists through the soul, it is not an individual example of the category it names. — س ره

    ↩

  550. The author makes the effects of a category the test for whether something is an actual example of it. On this test, even an image in the imagination would not be an example unless the effects of the category were present. — س ره

    ↩

  551. The author says this because he is still completing and strengthening the argument, not because he thinks the proof has failed. — س ره

    ↩

  552. This also shows that the author denies that natures, by themselves, are examples of categories—not only that intellectual universals are. The same reasoning works whether one follows the usual view of universals or the author’s view that the soul sees separate intellectual forms from a distance. Some might say that a particular image in the imagination, such as a human being, is a human and a substance in the ordinary sense. The author’s reply is that even an external human being is an individual because of its particular existence, not because of its nature alone. The imagined human image exists through the soul’s existence, especially if knowing is the soul’s union with what it knows. One simple existence can give rise to both general and particular ideas without dividing. Every imagined form is a light or appearance of the soul. Another way to say this is that mental forms are above the categories, like the soul, not below them. The author discusses this in the section on intellect and what it knows. — س ره
