  553. The author has established that mental ideas are not categories in the ordinary sense, though they are categories in the primary sense. He now adds that they are qualities only incidentally, not by nature. The source of the difficulty is that he does not explain fully how this incidental quality works. Existence itself is not a quality, and the nature of a thing is already the category of the thing known. If the connection to the soul is an illuminating relation, then it is existence, not quality. If it is ordinary relation, the forms would be related to the soul, not qualities of it. The commentator’s answer is that the author follows the common view that mental forms exist in the mind as qualities. The forms are present in the mind, and this presence is what we call knowledge; the forms themselves are qualities only because they exist in the mind. — س ره

    ↩

  554. “Quality” and “power” may refer to one thing. “Power” can mean an accidental faculty, as discussed later. Or “quality” may reflect the view that imagination is an accident, while “power” reflects the view that it is a substance, like a substantial form. — س ره

    ↩

  555. Physical forms exist outside the senses and have physical effects on the sensory powers when the senses meet them. At that stage there is no awareness. The soul’s awareness accompanies them and makes the forms appear as particulars or as general ideas. These two kinds of forms appear to the soul in two worlds free from matter: the greater or smaller imaginal world—the philosophers disagree on which—and the world of universal intellects. The three worlds of matter, imagination, and intellect correspond to one another. — ط

    ↩

  556. This prepares for the claim that the image in a mirror is not in the eye, and leads to the claim that it must exist in the imaginal world. Suhrawardi treats these images as mirrors that let us see particular material things, not as objects we look at for their own sake. He explains their attractiveness and beauty by the body’s needs, but may confuse the body’s role with the image itself. Without the liver’s heat, for example, cold water would not be so desirable. — س ره

    ↩

  557. The author does not also say that the image is not in the mirror itself because the same argument applies there. He has shortened Suhrawardi’s reasoning. Suhrawardi first rejects the ideas that vision happens through a ray from the eye or through an image stamped into the eye. He then argues that the image is not in the mirror, since it looks different from different viewing positions. The author combines these arguments: the first prepares for the second, which supports the existence of the imaginal world. Suhrawardi gives a Persian riddle: “I found a mountain inside a cottonseed; can you guess what it is? I found an ocean inside a kohl pot; can you guess what it is?” The eye and brain are not containers for a huge image; they are surfaces through which it appears. — س ره

    ↩

  558. That is, the imaginal world, also called the world of meanings. — س ره

    ↩

  559. The soul cannot know anything until it exists for the soul. So whatever it knows, whether particular or general, must exist within the soul’s own being. This would mean that each soul has its own image, distinct from the general imaginal world, since the soul’s particular nature changes what it perceives. The same happens when the senses distort what they see, or when mirrors change an image by their shape. The same argument should apply to intellectual forms: what the soul knows must exist within its own being. — ط

    ↩

  560. In my view, the author should say about imagination what he says about understanding: the soul sees the sources of kinds from a distance. Ugly images may be distortions caused by the surface through which they appear, and the same kind of distortion may happen in intellectual ideas. I agree with the author about imagined forms, but about understanding I hold that the luminous soul sees reflections of divine Forms that differ from those Forms in level. The soul’s imagined world is its smaller imaginal world, and its intellectual forms are its smaller world of intellect—not the greater intellect itself, unless the soul is absorbed into the Active Intellect. — س ره

    ↩

  561. The images do not exist as real beings in the higher spiritual world. They have only a shadow-like existence: they are reflections that depend on the things they copy. A reflection or shadow is not the thing itself. It is like a mirage beside the realities of the natural world: we see it, but it shows us the appearance of a thing, not its true nature. This is a strong argument that an image corresponds to what it represents. Many spiritual writers use reflections, shadows, and echoes to explain this relation. One mystic writes: “Everything but Him that appears to you is a second image seen by a squinting eye.” The point is that things seem to exist separately in their own right, though they depend on existence itself. — س ره

    ↩

  562. The Persian verse in the main text says that the Beloved plays music behind the veil and begins a new note at every moment. Here the melody means the outpouring of existence, also called the Breath of the Merciful or God’s word “Be.” The echo means the natures of things, which reflect the different modes of existence. Jami uses the same image: “One sound reaches your ear in two ways: sometimes you call it a call, sometimes an echo.” Elsewhere he writes: “An echo of your call entered the sanctuary, and the people of Arafat answered with a hundred cries of ‘Here I am.’” The second line of the verse quoted by the author also suggests that God’s words never run out: God is never silent but continually makes truth known. The author connects the image of existence and essence without the earlier verse, which speaks of love. Read together, the verses show that God’s true love flows through every kind of love, just as His beauty appears in every reality. His love is the call; all other loves are its echo. In perfect love, the echo returns to its source. — س ره

    ↩

  563. The main problem is not simply that one thing would be both an individual and a general idea. The real problem is that every bodily kind would need an immaterial individual of its own. One kind would then have a material individual, an immaterial one, a quality, and a substance. Being free of matter is a higher state than being a substance or quality. The claim that one thing is both particular and general is a secondary difficulty, not a separate objection; the author already answered it while addressing the first objection. — س ره

    ↩

  564. This explains why the objection says that every bodily kind must have an immaterial individual of its own. — س ره

    ↩

  565. If the idea retained those material features, it could not apply to things that lack them. It would no longer be general or truly apply to many things. — س ره

    ↩

  566. These are the two claims made by the objector. The author rejects both, as he will explain when he speaks of those who accept the higher spiritual world. — س ره

    ↩

  567. If we remove the features that make something particular, whether in the outside world or in the mind, what remains is its nature, which is neither general nor particular. This is another philosopher’s answer. The author’s own view is that generality comes from the wide reach of intellectual existence, as explained earlier. — س ره

    ↩

  568. Mental forms count as qualities only when we consider them as features of the soul and as forms of knowledge it has. Compared with things in the outside world, they are concepts, neither substances nor qualities. — ط

    ↩

  569. Existence applies to all things in one meaning. In the Necessary Being, existence is not joined to an essence; in other things, it is joined to one. If you ask what belongs in the definition of a human being, the answer is that “body” must include both natural bodies and imaginal bodies, even if the latter are shadow-like. “Rational” must include both actual reason, such as the active intellect, and reason as a capacity, such as the possible and passive intellect. “Sensing” and “moving” must include both the source or power for these acts and their actual performance. “Knowing” includes direct, present knowledge. “Growing” includes both the power to grow and actual growth. “Feeding” includes feeding in the imaginal world. The life of the plant soul is also present in the human soul in a higher and simpler way. — س ره

    ↩

  570. The author’s first reply followed his own view: the soul makes the images it imagines. They arise through its activity rather than entering it and changing it. Here, however, he adopts Suhrawardi’s approach. He focuses on imagined images, though the objection also applies to intellectual forms. On the author’s account, the soul does not contain intellectual forms as separate features; it knows them by joining with them and rising toward the higher world. In that world, forms and the things they belong to exist as one. No thing there can be a subject without its qualities, or a quality without its subject, because that would require matter and potentiality, which do not exist in that realm. The sweetness of sugar and sugar itself, for example, exist there as one. The answer is that the forms do not exist in the soul as separate qualities. This applies to intellectual forms as well, so the author did not need to discuss them separately here. The first answer applies more directly to imagined forms, the second to intellectual forms, and the third to both. — س ره

    ↩

  571. Someone may ask: if the mental forms were not in the soul at first and then came to be there, is that not a change in the soul? And is change not a kind of being affected? The terms “passive knowledge” and “active knowledge” also seem to support this. The reply is that the author denies the soul is affected by the real material things themselves—the actual forms that exist in the physical world—not that the soul changes in any sense when it knows. The higher causes contain knowledge of all worldly things but are not changed by their bodily features. They contain these forms as their causes, not as things they receive. The forms in the soul are prepared either to flow from a higher source, as the philosophers held, or to be formed by the soul itself, as the author held. If we grant that mental forms exist in the soul as qualities, their presence there still need not mean that the soul is passively affected by them. The measure of being affected is that a form comes from something else and is received through matter, not simply that it appears in a subject. — س ره

    ↩

  572. This point is explained later. The real existence of evenness is the state of a thing that can be divided into two equal parts. This applies to an even number, such as four, whether it exists outside the mind or in it. It does not apply to the soul simply because the soul has an idea of evenness. The philosophers who say that abstract ideas exist through the things from which we draw them accept this much. — س ره

    ↩

  573. The author could also agree that mental things exist in the outside world in one sense: the mind itself is an outside thing, and the mental form exists as a state of the mind. It is “mental” only in relation to the thing outside the mind that it represents. A spoken name or written mark is also an outside thing in its own right, while representing a person named Zayd. — س ره

    ↩

  574. The sciences build proofs around real subjects and the features that truly belong to them. They do not need to discuss every general or accidental meaning. So a word can have one shared meaning in everyday speech but several separate meanings in a technical discussion. The words “in the mind” and “the mind in the outside world” sound alike, but “in” means something different in each. In technical language the word works like two different words, not one word with one shared meaning. — ط

    ↩

  575. There is another important objection, the seventh after the six in the main text. If mental ideas are only reflections of things, each idea must have a real thing outside the mind that it reflects. Then the soul could not imagine what is impossible, what does not exist, or any simple idea with no matching thing outside. An answer based on supposition and statements that do not assert actual existence seems to assume what it is trying to prove: the very act of supposing gives a mental existence to something with no external example, which is the problem raised by the objection. A full answer depends on the later account of how ideas arise from their examples, and on the difference between concepts that state what a thing is and other ideas that simply serve as mental names or labels. — ط

    ↩

  576. This note applies to statements about both impossible things and the Necessary Being. The author’s phrase “when no nature has been formed at all” refers to impossible things; “or in the mind” refers to God. It is strange to place statements about the Necessary Being among non-assertive statements, since a claim is plainly true when its subject exists in reality, and non-assertive when the subject exists only as an assumption. The Necessary Being is the deepest reality; everything else depends on it. One possible reply is that an ordinary, unconditional statement says: anything that is an example of this nature is such-and-such. That requires both an actual example outside the mind and a concept in the mind that lets us consider it. Impossible things have no actual examples, while God has no nature that can be formed in the mind, even though God truly exists.

    Someone might object that if the mind cannot grasp God’s full reality, then statements about any outside thing would also be non-assertive, because its actual existence cannot enter the mind without changing into something else. The answer is that a possible thing has a nature that can be fully understood and is shared by its mental and external forms. God has no such nature. The concepts “Necessary Being,” “pure being,” and “pure existence” are only ways of pointing toward God. They act like a mirror: they direct thought toward God without making God an object pictured in the mind. A concept can be true of itself by essential predication, while the reality it points to remains beyond the mind. This is how we can make true statements about the Necessary Being without grasping God’s full reality. — س ره

    ↩

  577. Some people attribute the copy-and-shadow view to the ancient philosophers as well. — س ره

    ↩

  578. Many thinkers have said that the name and what it names are one. The clearest examples are the philosophers’ view that God’s attributes are identical with His essence and the mystics’ view that a true name is absolute existence considered together with one of the highest attributes. The same idea applies here in a broad sense: a spoken or written name, as the way a thing appears and is considered, is not wholly separate from it. That is why a judgment about the thing can also be made about its name or written form. In this respect, neither is entirely separate from the thing. — س ره

    ↩

  579. The commentator asks how the scholar can say that existence comes before a thing’s nature while also saying that existence is only an idea, has no example outside or inside the mind, and does not even exist as a feature of the nature. The answer is that “the existing thing” that comes first means the thing as produced by its maker. “Nature” means the thing considered simply as what it is; that nature is an idea, a point on which the philosophers agree. The scholar says that everything outside the mind after it is made, and everything in the mind, is some nature. What we point to as a nature is itself the thing made and existing. The idea of “existent” does not name an extra feature joined to it, because existence is the thing’s being real, not something added to it.

    This is close to Mulla Sadra’s view that two things do not exist here except in thought: the human being, for example, is real by being one with a mode of true existence. No separate thing corresponds to the idea of “existent” to make that unity impossible. The scholar likewise says that the idea of “existent” corresponds to the nature itself. A possible thing has a nature that can be described as either existent or nonexistent; the Necessary Being can only be described as existent, never as nonexistent. The scholar interprets the philosophers’ claim that God is “pure existence” to mean that God is “purely existent,” since God cannot be neutral between existing and not existing. The commentator rejects this account of God, but says that it is not the issue being discussed here. If being produced is real, it must be real existence; if it is not, it cannot rule out nonexistence. Mulla Sadra considers the account close to the truth because it agrees with some principles discussed earlier. — س ره

    ↩

  580. The objector has taken “becomes” to mean that one thing changes into a different thing. The right reading is a simple change: something comes to exist. It does not mean that one already existing thing turns into another. The scholar’s second answer amounts to this. — ن ره

    ↩

  581. The priority is at the level of existence in general, not at the level of a definite nature such as human being or horse. The “existent” in the second answer is not a specific thing that first appeared. — س ره

    ↩

  582. This kind of identity is true of real existence. But for the scholar discussed here, there is only a concept and the nature that gives rise to differences of kind and broader kind. What, then, is this “one thing” that is supposed to remain through the change? It seems to be no more than the general idea of nature or thinghood, a second-order idea. — س ره

    ↩

  583. If no real feature is shared by two natures, we should not insist that one can turn into the other. Why say that the sky has become the earth? In this scholar’s view, distinct essences are what make things different, while existence is only an idea. There is no real principle that joins one essence to another. A vague idea of “something” does not supply one. It is a second-order idea, not an essential part shared by the two things. The proposed common ground is only something the mind imagines. But two genuinely different things do not become one because we choose to think of them together. In ordinary change, some real basis remains through the change; without it, there is no one thing in the first state and the second. — س ره

    ↩

  584. Some copies of the text add: “How can this be, when some things known by the mind have no subject or container at all?” — س ره

    ↩

  585. This is the point the objector intends. It does not apply to the copy-and-shadow view, because its supporters do not say that the external thing changes into its image. They say that its image is not the thing itself, and they avoid claiming that the two are identical. — س ره

    ↩

  586. This explanation does not work unless there is something real that remains through the change from A to B. Without that, the word “change” itself cannot connect the two. This objection does not apply to the copy-and-shadow view, for the reason given in the previous note. — س ره

    ↩

  587. The comparison with prime matter is misleading. Prime matter is undetermined only with respect to the forms it can take; its own nature and basic kind are still fixed. The general natures proposed here are different. Every possible nature, whether a kind or a broader kind, can be understood by the mind. So what is the one reality called “water” that is supposed to remain the same in a physical body and in a mental quality? If it is a real part of both, then simple things such as qualities and intellects become compounds made of parts and must fall under one of the basic kinds. If the shared part is only mental, then it is a broader kind, not something simple; the highest categories would no longer be simple. If it is merely a feature added to each, then the two are not the same nature but only share an added feature. And if it is only a general idea, it cannot make two different things one.

    Mulla Sadra can speak of one existence appearing at different levels—as divine, intellectual, spiritual, bodily, or even spoken and written—because real existence is what unites these levels. The natures and concepts mark their differences. But the scholar discussed here accepts only natures and denies real existence as a distinct reality. What, then, could unite the different forms of water for him? The commentator says they are as far apart as flint and a fragrant flower, or a lamp and the sun at noon. — س ره

    ↩

  588. This passage concerns pure existence itself, not the vague general nature discussed here. Pure, simple, luminous existence cannot be pointed to as one definite thing, though it is the basis of identity. Our question concerns the general nature considered together with existence. Particular natures are already ideas; a wholly vague general nature is even more plainly a second-order idea. There is a difference between something that cannot be pointed to because it has no reality and something that cannot be pointed to because it is too full and real to be limited. So the claim that the nature is wholly undefined has no real subject. — س ره

    ↩

  589. This is a second meaning of “the essential features remain.” Earlier it meant that a nature stays the same when we consider it with existence in general. Here it means that the external nature’s essential features also apply to its mental image when we use that image to think about the outside thing. For example, the mental idea of water is a quality of the mind, but we can consider it as water outside the mind and apply to it the features of external water. — س ره

    ↩

  590. This means the wide, all-embracing intellectual existence of water, of which particular waters are partial reflections. The general idea of water is its nature, since every possible thing includes both a nature and existence. This wide existence includes particular waters in a higher and simpler way; they are its appearances, while it represents them more fully. This account fits Mulla Sadra’s view, but not the view of the other scholar. — س ره

    ↩

  591. The passage up to “Here is the right way to understand it” uses direct experience to show that knowledge is a real quality and to set out the problem. — س ره

    ↩

  592. To resolve the problem, there would have to be something in addition to each mental image’s nature and its existence in the mind: another nature, with its own existence, joined to the nature of the thing known. Only then would a real quality be present. But where is this added thing? The account itself says that when we look within, we find only the image. Simply calling knowledge a quality at one point and the thing it describes at another does not solve the problem; nothing has been added to the image.

    The comparison with Zayd or a body is not exact. We call Zayd “white” or “laughing” because a feature has been added to him. The subject and that feature do not exist in the same way, so their combination is only a union in thought. Here, by contrast, there is nothing beyond the image itself, which belongs to the same basic kind as the thing known.

    When people say that a quality and the adjective that describes it are one, they mean that the quality, considered simply as belonging to something, can be said of that thing. In that statement, the quality and the thing described share one reality: the quality is not separate from the thing but belongs to its existence. This does not mean that exactly the same mode of existence belongs to both. If it did, the basic kinds of qualities would disappear, because one existing thing cannot be both a substance and a quality. — س ره

    ↩

  593. In the example of Zayd, his existence and the existence of his features are distinct. In the case discussed here, the thing known and knowledge share one existence, as the main text explains. — س ره

    ↩

  594. This seems to assume what it needs to prove. Without a separate feature added to the image, there is no basis for calling it a quality; qualities are usually features added to a subject. The same objection applies to two similar claims made later, unless the argument adopts the philosophers’ view that qualities exist in a subject. — س ره

    ↩

  595. Since a quality is a feature that exists in a subject, the earlier example of Zayd and whiteness fits better. The author also holds that relations have their own kind of existence. If the case discussed here worked in the same way, knowledge would belong to the basic kind called relation. — س ره

    ↩

  596. The author has already explained how a quality and the thing described by it can be one without making the basic kinds of qualities disappear. That is what he means here. The Sayyid takes a different view. The author’s account works: it preserves both quality and substance without adding a separate feature, as explained earlier. The Sayyid’s account of their unity does not work on its own. — س ره

    ↩

  597. The opening of this chapter draws on an earlier distinction between existence in itself and existence in another thing. Some beings have no independent existence at all, such as links between things. If a link had any independence of its own, it would become one end of the link, connected to another end; that contradicts the assumption that it is only a link. Since everything that exists outside the mind has at least some independence, a pure link can exist only together with an existence that supports it. It is not separate from that existence but belongs within it. A link between two things therefore joins them, and both are present in some way within that relation.

    This also means that linking existence and existence in itself differ in kind; there is no shared idea that covers both. A pure link cannot itself be named or used as a subject or predicate, or called general or particular, because it has no independent existence. All this concerns the first part of the argument.

    At the end of the chapter, the author says that all possible beings are links in relation to God’s existence, and that God supports them and watches over every soul. This means that an essence considered by itself has no status, either independent or dependent. What matters is the existence that supports it and accompanies it. The same essence can be viewed as a complete, noun-like meaning, or from another angle as an incomplete, relation-like meaning. This is a useful idea for understanding degrees of existence, God’s knowledge, and other questions. — ط

    ↩

  598. A compound statement does not mean that the subject and predicate point to the same thing, as some theologians mistakenly think. It means that one thing is affirmed of another. — س ره

    ↩

  599. The author will later say that a predicate, simply as a predicate, has no existence in itself. So here “predicate” means the link between the terms, not an ordinary thing that is said of a subject. The objection that one thing cannot be said of another unless it first exists does not apply to this link. Nor does the existence of the first predicate in a compound statement create the alleged endless series. The series arises only if we mistake the link for a separate thing that exists for another and then needs a further link. The link is not an independently existing object; it is the fact that something is established of another, not a separate thing that is established. This is the difference between linking and dependent existence. — س ره

    ↩

  600. Here “subject” means the subject-term in logic, not the thing in which a quality exists or the whole subject-predicate pair. In this sense, the questions of a science are predicates linked to their subjects. This link is what the author calls linking existence. — س ره

    ↩

  601. The earlier thinkers either treated essence as real in its own right, dividing reality into two kinds—existence and essence—or held that each existence is distinct from every other, as the philosophers in Aristotle’s school appear to have done. Either way, a possible being has an existence of its own; it is not a pure link. Mulla Sadra, by contrast, says that existence alone is real and that essences are ideas. What is related and the relation itself are both existence, at different levels: limited existence, absolute existence, and true existence. The possible being is pure connection, complete need, and dependence. — س ره

    ↩

  602. Saying that a quality has existence in itself, like a substance, does not conflict with saying that it is one level of the substance’s existence. The author says this elsewhere. As explained in an earlier note, a quality’s existence in itself means that the mind can understand what the quality is without also thinking about its subject. Yet its actual existence in itself is the same as its existence for that subject. This differs from a pure link, which cannot be understood without both things it connects. — ط

    ↩

  603. The point is confirmed by the fact that the simple, luminous reality of existence cannot itself be an idea, whether of the first kind or the second. It is the reality to which an idea refers. At first it may seem strange, if existence is real in its own right, to call the abstract idea “existing” a second-order concept. Concepts such as human being, horse, water, fire, white, and black are first-order concepts because they refer to things outside the mind. The concept of existence also refers to real things: God’s existence and the existences of possible beings. These are its main referents, since essences exist only indirectly.

    There is a difference, however, between the actual individuals of a natural kind and the different modes of existence. A human nature has individuals both in the mind and outside it; the same nature is found in both places. But the various modes of existence outside the mind are not individual examples of one shared nature called “existence.” There is no common essence shared by general existence and its particular modes. As we explained earlier, general existence is a mental idea, not a part that makes up its individual instances.

    It is possible to distinguish the abstract idea “existence” from the idea “being existent,” just as Persian distinguishes hastī from hast būdan, and “whiteness” from “being white.” That distinction has some basis, but it does not help to make it a separate philosophical issue, since the author does not keep the two senses apart in many places.

    The word “thingness” is also an abstract noun. It means what can exist—the nature that answers the question “What is it?” It is a second-order concept because the special natures of human beings, horses, cows, whiteness, and blackness have no shared feature called “thingness” over and above their own differences. If they had a shared essential feature, the highest kinds would not be highest. If it were an added, nonessential feature, particular things would count as things only after that feature was added, as a body would be white only after whiteness was added. That is plainly wrong. Possibility and necessity, which describe how one thing relates to another, have been explained earlier. — س ره

    ↩

  604. It is better to say that mental existence is “not part of” a second-order concept, rather than saying that it is “not a condition” for one. There is no problem in saying that mental existence is a condition for a logical second-order concept to apply, as when universality applies to the idea of human being. Some philosophers define a second-order concept in this way. Perhaps the author means that the logical concept applies to the nature itself, while its existence in the mind is only the setting in which the concept applies. On that view, the statement is about what holds whenever the nature is in the mind, not a conditional statement. — س ره

    ↩

  605. This conflicts with the accepted rule that each science studies the features of its own subject, while a higher science establishes the subject and its basic principles. For example, the study of matter and form belongs to the highest science; physics treats them only as principles. Perhaps the author means that a lower science defines a thing’s nature before proving that the thing exists. But defining a thing as it actually exists belongs to the higher science, because a thing’s nature depends on its existence. This is why definitions before a statement that something exists are only verbal definitions; after its existence is established, they become real definitions. — س ره

    ↩

  606. Existence is applied to a natural kind through its individual examples, as we attribute a ship’s movement to the person sitting in it. To say that a natural kind exists is to say that one of its individuals exists. Those who deny that natural kinds exist and those who say that essence is what truly exists take opposite extremes. The truth lies between them: a natural kind exists as a reflection or shadow of existence. It has no separate thing corresponding to it, yet it has some share in real existence through the individuals that embody it. As we said earlier, a natural kind is real in the mind’s ordinary judgment, but is only figuratively real from the viewpoint of direct insight and philosophical proof. The different ways that existence can be attributed are relevant here. — س ره

    ↩

  607. “Particularity” here means the logical feature that applies to a particular instance of a natural kind: a specific nature together with the features that make it an individual. Sometimes “particularity” means individual existence or being distinct. In that sense, it is a kind of existence, not a mental feature or second-order concept. — س ره

    ↩

  608. The point is that Zayd is particular in the mind’s view of him. Logical particularity means that a concept cannot be thought of as applying to many things. This mental feature applies to the Zayd in the mind—that is, to the idea of Zayd—not to the person outside the mind. Particularity does not simply mean being unable to be shared. At most, it is a philosophical second-order concept, not a logical one. So why should logic study it? — س ره

    ↩

  609. There are four objections to the scholar’s account. First, it reverses the author’s argument, as he explains later. Second, it assumes the point at issue: the scholar defines being described one way, but his opponents mean that the subject and the feature both exist in the setting where the feature is attributed. Third, if a subject can be described without the feature existing, there would be no difference between true and false statements. “Zayd is a father” is true, though fatherhood does not exist as a separate thing in Zayd; but then the same claim could be made of a wall. Fourth, this account would erase the difference between essential features and added features. The commentator has discussed these points earlier. — س ره

    ↩

  610. I do not think this account is right, because it would overturn many accepted philosophical principles. The author himself does not follow it consistently. For example, a feature being true of something depends on the subject’s existence, not on the feature’s existing as a separate thing. This is clear from negative descriptions such as “Zayd is blind.”

    It would also make relations into real things. If a relation existed as an independent substance, that would plainly be impossible. If it existed as a feature like whiteness, it would have to exist in a subject. But existing in a subject is itself a relation. If each relation were a separate real thing, it would need another relation to connect it to its subject, and so on without end. The chain stops if relations exist through the things from which the mind draws them, rather than as independent things.

    The same problem arises with a lack, such as blindness. If a lack existed outside the mind without the thing it was a lack of, it would stand against the positive feature as one contrary stands against another. Yet these thinkers say that lacks exist. For them, “exists” must therefore mean two things: either that something has a real thing corresponding to it, or that it has a basis from which the mind can draw it.

    The author is right that being described is a relation, but a relation can depend on existence on one side and on a nature on the other. As we explained earlier, natures are features of existences, and possibility is a feature of existence. Another scholar’s explanation of this point is weak, even though the conclusion is right.

    The sound argument is this: being described means predication, and predication means that subject and feature are one in existence. This unity is possible when one existence—the subject—supports the statement. The subject side is considered as the thing itself; the predicate side is considered as a concept. The predicate therefore does not need to exist in its own right. If it exists, it does so for some other reason. To be said of a subject, it must also be considered without restriction. So when something is described, what matters on the predicate side is only the concept; existence is required on the subject side, not the predicate side. We can see this in ordinary statements too: “Zayd is blind,” “Zayd is ignorant,” and “Zayd is possible” are all meaningful even though their predicates do not exist as separate things. — س ره

    ↩

  611. This is plainly right. A linking relation exists only together with its two terms, and both terms must exist in the setting where the link holds. A statement cannot have one side only in the mind and the other outside it, or one side real and the other merely figurative. — ط

    ↩

  612. Relations exist as links, not as independent things or as containers. Other features, such as powers and capacities, exist potentially. Potentiality has existence too, though it is weaker than actual existence and depends on it as a shadow depends on what casts it. Perhaps this explains how the two views can be brought together. — س ره

    ↩

  613. Even without the author’s main principle, these philosophers can answer the objection. Relations are drawn by the mind, but they are not imaginary fictions: they have a real basis. A relation exists through the thing from which the mind draws it, so studying relations is still studying real things. Second-order concepts are also features of real things. Universality, for example, applies to the mental idea of human being, whose nature is the same as that of human beings outside the mind.

    Things in the mind are real in their own right; they are “mental” because of their relation to the mind. Relations guide the mind and help it reach what it does not yet know, producing real effects. This answer works for those who regard logic as part of philosophy. For those who do not, there is no problem. — س ره

    ↩

  614. This is a key and very useful question, especially for understanding God’s oneness. Some thinkers regard it as self-evident; others have proved it. It is discussed in the commentary on The Wisdom of Illumination and in the metaphysics section of this book. So the claim that the philosophers never proved it is false. As we have seen, it is self-evident. — س ره

    ↩

  615. The proof begins by asking what “good” means. A thing is good when it is preferred to other things; that preference gives rise to desire and choice. Some things are wanted for their own sake, others for something connected to them. The things wanted for another reason ultimately lead to something wanted for its own sake. There must be a good that everything seeks and every goal leads back to. That good can only be existence: nonexistence has no reality of its own, and essence is not an independent reality. So existence is good, and since goodness belongs to existence itself, existence is good in its own right. Evil is nonexistence.

    This proves two of the chapter’s three claims: that existence is good and nonexistence evil, and that good has degrees matching the degrees of existence. The third claim—that existence can be evil in relation to something else—is explained in the next chapter. Evil in this relative sense occurs only in the material world, not in the higher world. The question of how this kind of evil enters the divine plan is taken up later. — ط

    ↩

  616. Someone may object: later, in the discussion of causes and effects, the author will say that essences have some reality. How can evil and deficiency belong to essences if evil is only nonexistence? The answer is that assigning evil to an essence does not conflict with assigning it to nonexistence. Without an essence, nonexistence could not be attributed to a possible thing. Existence cannot accept nonexistence at the same time, just as whiteness cannot accept blackness, or connection cannot accept separation. There must be something that can take either side. For colors and other changing features, that is matter; for existence and nonexistence, it is essence. — س ره

    ↩

  617. One might ask: if prime matter has no completed form of its own, and is only the capacity to receive one, how can it be what catches the heavenly souls? If the text means “by means of it,” the answer is that matter makes change possible and brings new pleasures. Without it, the elements could not become bodies ready to receive souls. Forms that belong to the world of images do not undergo that change from a lower state to a higher one, because they are free of matter. If the text means “within it,” the image is clear: the rational souls are heavenly birds held in the cages of the elements. — س ره

    ↩

  618. How can the reality of existence have a counterpart? One of its deepest consequences is that it cannot be absent. As the previous note explained, one opposite cannot be present where the other is. When one opposite enters a thing, it removes the other: blackness removes whiteness, cold removes heat, and separation removes connection. — س ره

    ↩

  619. If the opposites truly existed in relation to existence, the first problem would follow; if they could exist there only potentially, the second would follow. — س ره

    ↩

  620. They can come together in thought when we consider them apart from their opposition. This point appears again shortly. — س ره

    ↩

  621. Later, in the discussion of opposites, the author will explain that the standard definition is two positive features that take turns appearing in the same thing and differ as much as possible. If two features take turns appearing in the same thing, one cannot exist within the other. The standard account also says that opposites must belong to the same nearest kind. This rules out opposition between a substance and one of its features, since they do not belong to the same closest broad kind.

    People do sometimes say that one feature belongs to another. They mean either cases where the features do not share a nearest kind—for example, when properties specific to quantities are applied to them, or when relations are applied to other features—or cases where their nearest kind includes more than two subtypes, as when a geometrical body, a surface, and a line are described in relation to one another. The standard account also says that there can be only two opposites. The author disagrees with the standard view on most of these points. He will discuss them fully later, if God wills. — ط

    ↩

  622. Do not take the author’s claim that the mind can imagine every idea to mean that ideas such as nonexistence and absolute nonexistence have a reality of their own, which the mind discovers just as it discovers other things. That would be wrong. If they had a reality of their own, they would be essences outside the mind. As explained in earlier notes, saying that a concept is real in itself does not fit the view that existence is what is real. Saying that it is present in the Active Intellect—the higher intellect in this account—does not solve the problem of what real thing the concept refers to.

    These ideas have no reality outside the mind. The mind forms them, but does not make them into independent things; if it did, they would be things, not ideas. Rather, it forms them as ideas that point beyond themselves, as ideas of essences do. They can therefore be applied to the outside world and to what is treated as outside it. We say, for example, that Zayd exists outside the mind, or that Amr does not exist outside the mind. Since these ideas are not truly present outside the mind, the mind places them there only as assumptions. This is what the author means when he says a few lines later that such a statement is made as an unconfirmed claim, with the force of a conditional whose two sides are both false.

    Earlier, in the discussion of things existing in the mind, we showed that what produces effects by its very nature—the real existence of things—or what is by its nature devoid of effects—nonexistence—cannot enter the mind. In the first case, its effects would have to appear; in the second, there would be no effects at all. The ideas of existence and nonexistence, and the other ideas the mind forms, are therefore not drawn directly from anything established outside it. The mind forms them by making assumptions.

    To explain: the mind can give one thing the idea or feature of another. It may suppose a horse to be a rational animal, which would make it a human being. Or it may suppose a horse to be a human being, and then say it can laugh and wonder. By using this habit of attributing one thing to another, the mind can suppose one relation to be like another and form a new idea that is not taken directly from anything real outside the mind. For example, the mind can imagine something related to outside natures as light is related to something in darkness: it brings it to light, lets a searcher find it, and makes its effects appear. The mind calls this “existence.”

    The mind can also imagine something related to a nature or to existence as the removal of a thing from the place where it was, the removal of clothing from someone wearing it, or the absence of something from view. This gives it the idea of “nonexistence.” The same applies to other ideas the mind forms in this way.

    The mental act that gives rise to these ideas has two kinds of cause. The first is stable and constant: it always leads the mind to form the idea. This is the cause behind ideas such as existence, nonexistence, unity, and multiplicity, which can be established by proof. The second is temporary and depends on circumstances. It gives rise to social ideas such as leadership and being led, mastery and service, as well as metaphors and poetic images. There is much more to say; some of it will appear later, in the discussions of essence and other subjects, if God wills. — ط

    ↩

  623. From what we said in the note to the previous chapter, it may seem that the idea of nonexistence and other ideas formed by the mind are made up of parts, rather than being simple. The same is true of what the ideas “sentence,” “speech,” “ten,” and “many” refer to. — ط

  624. Everyone agrees that what does not exist is not a thing, and that we cannot make claims about it or point to it as a thing. That is why the author uses it as the comparison. Also, “nonexistent” has a broader meaning: it can mean nonexistence itself, or an essence that does not exist. — س ره

  625. Do not think the author means that a person first understands the idea of absolute nonexistence, then forms each particular absence by attaching that general idea to a positive thing. If they later want to think of particular absences, they can form them by adding the relevant relation. This is like how we first see Zayd, Amr, and Bakr, then form the general idea of being human, and later distinguish tall people from short people.

    The real process is this: we notice many distinct existing people, such as Zayd and Amr, and compare them. When we focus on Amr, Zayd is no longer present in our thought. The mind mistakes not finding Zayd for finding his absence. From Amr’s presence, it forms the idea of Zayd’s absence; from Bakr’s presence, the idea of Amr’s absence. These particular absences are like separate examples. The mind then forms the general idea of nonexistence from them, as it forms a general kind from its examples. — ط

What these ideas refer to is not an existing thing but the absence of the thing they suppose. Call it the nature, name, or example of the impossible: it exists only as impossible. Every real example must fit the nature of what it is. If it did not, the thing itself would disappear, and the claim would contradict itself. For example, if a real example of motion were fixed and unchanging, it would not be motion. The same applies here. — س ره

The later absences, considered toward the future, are endless and not ordered among themselves. The earlier absences, considered toward the past, are without a beginning and not ordered among themselves. Since these absences are described as eternal, this seems to conflict with the rule that whatever has existed from eternity cannot cease to exist. In the same way, the mind assumes the idea of existence and gives it features of essences, such as being general, applying to many things, or being said of something. — ط

  632. To say that God never reveals Himself in the same form twice is to say that each appearance is new: each day He is at work anew. This concerns the forms through which He appears. Nothing is lost and then renewed.

    Think of existence itself. Apart from the natures that receive it, existence is not a substance or feature, quality or quantity. It has no size, and so no time, no decay or coming-to-be, and no measurable parts. It does not change. Time and change belong to the material forms and natures that receive existence. This is the inner meaning of the issue; it is not limited to this world or the next. — س ره

  633. Since there is no individual thing before or after itself, and we have explained that absences become many only when the things they are related to are many, nonexistence itself is not multiple. — س ره

  634. By “imagination” here, the author means that the mind takes the general nature of a thing in place of its individual identity. The mind expects the individual to last, then mistakes its absence for something that arrives and replaces it. It does not see that each temporal thing exists only in its own time; each has its appointed term.

The later and earlier absences come from the times when the thing does not exist. Each existence is a sign of the One who has no equal. Existence itself does not set or pass away; only forms and natures have a past and a future. If someone looks only at existence and ignores the forms and natures that receive it, there is no morning or evening, no coming or going.   636. The objection is: why can’t the difference be that one time is earlier and the other later, without leading to an endless chain? Even if time’s nature has degrees, being earlier is essential to one point in time and cannot be separated from it. If that point returned, it would still be a beginning, even while being assumed to be restored; it could not be restored as that very point. The only remaining difference is that one point is earlier and one later, which leads to an endless chain.

    The author’s objection is not answered by saying that restored time has lost its status as a beginning and is only a restoration. If restoration means that it exists in a second time, then that time needs another time, and the chain continues without end. If it means that it is later by its very nature, then it is not the same time that began in its own nature. It has not been restored as itself. — س ره

  642. Then the person would have to repeat the evil acts and sins in the next world, which is meant for reward, not action. The theologians allowed God to restore what lies within His own power.   643. What his words seem to mean is that the early philosophers divided statements into different parts according to the kind of statement. A simple affirmative statement has three: subject, predicate, and judgment. It has no separate linking relation, because it says that the subject exists, not that some added feature belongs to it. A simple negative statement has only the subject and predicate; it has no affirmative judgment. It denies the judgment and removes the subject’s existence. Nothing outside the mind corresponds to that removal as a separate thing.

    A compound affirmative statement has four parts: subject, predicate, the link between them, and the judgment that affirms the link. A compound negative statement has the subject, predicate, and link, but no affirmative judgment. That is the structure of the statement itself. If we also consider its status—necessary, possible, or impossible—the early philosophers treat the status as a quality of the affirmative link. The judgment affirms that qualified link in positive statements; in negative statements, negation removes it. A necessary negative statement therefore denies that the predicate necessarily belongs to the subject; it does not affirm that the predicate necessarily does not belong to it. Otherwise, statements would not contradict one another in the right way. Contradiction is between affirming a judgment and removing that judgment, not between affirming a judgment and affirming its removal.

    Most later philosophers say that every statement, whether simple or compound, affirmative or negative, has four parts: subject, predicate, link, and judgment. They claim that negative statements have a negative link just as positive statements have an affirmative one, and that negative statements also contain a judgment. They base this on what seems to be the ordinary meaning of statements. For example, they take “A human is an animal, necessarily” and “No human is an animal, necessarily” to affirm opposite relations, rather than to deny the necessary affirmative relation.

    The early philosophers’ view is correct, but one point needs care. Judgment—what we call assent—is not a feature in a category of things, nor is it a picture in the mind. It is an act of the soul: the mind makes the subject and predicate one in its judgment. This act does not require the mind to picture a linking relation. In simple statements, it can judge by considering only the subject and predicate. Assent itself does not change between simple and compound statements; it does not sometimes require a link and sometimes not. The link is something the mind pictures alongside the statement, not a part that makes the judgment what it is.

    We can see that the mind uses the idea of a link in simple statements and negative statements too, just as it does in compound affirmative statements. But it generalizes this idea by mistake. In compound statements, the predicate exists in the subject in a dependent way, so the mind has to picture how they are connected. It then wrongly extends this to every statement. In short, an affirmative statement joins subject and predicate in its judgment; a negative statement does not. — ط مده

  684. The indefinite wording “one aspect” points to further questions. Saying that real existence cannot be known could mislead readers: real existence is the subject of the highest science, so how could it be unknowable? There are three kinds of knowledge of real existence. First is acquired knowledge of existing natures as they exist; through the mental forms by which we consider them, we learn about the different kinds of real existence. This is why definitions correspond to levels of existence. Second, also acquired, is knowledge of existence in general through universal descriptions that truly apply to it: that it is what the general idea of existence refers to, true unity, identity, light, life, will, love, knowledge, awareness, and the like. Third is direct awareness of existence, which has two forms. One is the soul’s direct awareness of itself, which does not fully encompass it; since the soul is a real existence, this gives a general awareness of existence. The other is the direct awareness of the reality of existence by souls turned toward God: the awareness of one who is absorbed in what is known. What the Shaykh says, even if read as a statement about existence, needs more explanation. This is turning into a long sermon; there will be time for it. — س ره

  686. Once we distinguish knowing a thing in one respect from knowing it through one of its aspects, the examples become clear.   699. The author rejects this reading because he recognizes one act as primary; the other acts are only indirect. The author’s point is to deny that essential features are made by compound making: a human being is human and an animal by its own nature, not through compound making and not because a maker separately makes its nature.   701. This answers a possible objection: someone might say that we can deny a thing of itself when it does not exist, because a negative statement can be true even when its subject is absent. Since truth and possibility require two terms, if one term is possible, then the other—the thing’s being itself—must also be possible. And if it is possible, and possibility is what makes something need a cause, then it must be made. This would differ from eternal necessity, to which no denial can apply.

    The reply is that even if the possible denial of a thing of itself entails that it is itself, and this possibility requires making the thing’s nature according to the Illuminationists or its existence according to Aristotle’s followers, that does not mean the maker acts on it directly. The dependence may be indirect. The possibility of denying a thing of itself removes eternal necessity, not the necessity that belongs to its own nature; that necessity also removes the need for a cause. So when the author says “no need,” he means no direct need.

    There is a clearer answer. The possible denial applies only when the thing does not exist, and that is a contradiction: a positive statement requires its subject to exist. The argument also proves less than it claims. And the claim “if a thing can be denied of itself when absent, then it can be affirmed of itself in every case” is not a valid inference. It is also wrong to allow this denial in the argument that a thing’s being described needs a maker. “The nonexistent human being is not human” amounts to “what is nonexistent is not human.” The truth is that a thing cannot be denied of itself in any case. Just as existence is distinct from a thing’s nature, so is nonexistence. Once we take the subject to be a human being through its nature, even without its existing in the world, how could we deny its nature of itself? And if we have not conceived any thing at all, how could we identify it as human? Avicenna says, in his discussion of whether the Necessary Existent’s nature is its existence, that whatever nature we suppose is that nature, whether we suppose it to exist or not. — س ره

If it does depend on a condition, and what depends on that condition is his nature, then Amr could also come into existence when Zayd does, since the condition is present and like cases should be treated alike. This is a sound point, but it does not prove that the relation of being existent is what is made: that relation is also only a mental consideration. It follows that existence is what is made, and is primary both in making and in reality. Apart from the first argument, these arguments are incomplete. The speaker wants to prove that the relation of being existent is made, but that does not follow simply from disproving that the nature is made. The other two views must also be ruled out, and he has not ruled out the view that existence is made, which is in fact the strongest one. It is telling that the opponent never even argues against it: “They seek to extinguish God’s light with their mouths, but God will bring His light to completion.” — س ره

  708. The first argument would make sense if “possibility” meant that neither existence nor nonexistence is necessary, or that the two are equal, and if this possibility were only a step in proving the need for a cause. It would not, however, establish the conclusion the speaker wants. The argument also works if “possibility” means what the author calls the particular contingent existences, and “causation” means that these existences do not cause themselves: they are intrinsically dependent on God, and what is essential is not caused.

    But if “possibility” means either of the first two things, and “causation” means the real source of need, the argument does not work. Possibility in that sense exists only in the mind, so it would make a possible thing dependent only in the mind. The basis of need would also need a cause, since a cause stands to its effect as the complete stands to the incomplete; this would make the basis itself possible through another, which is false. One could avoid this only by saying that possibility is neither a mental step nor the real source of need, but something like the sun’s relation to the heat of water. The thing that truly needs a cause must also be what the cause is needed for. From this, a discerning reader can see that existence is what is made: it is what needs a cause, indeed it is need and relation itself.

    The saying that “possibility is what makes a thing need a cause” also shows that a nature is not made directly. What is made directly must be intrinsically dependent; if a nature were intrinsically dependent, it would not need a separate cause of its need, since what belongs to a thing essentially is not caused. The thing that needs a cause must be the thing that needs it in reality. If you need someone to build a house, it is you—or the house—that needs the builder, not your nature as such. Everyone agrees that a nature needs an agent in order to exist. So existence is what needs the agent and is made directly; possibility is how the mind sees that need, and nature is how it sees what has been made. In reality, when existence is what is made, the thing that needs a cause, the basis of need, and what needs the cause are one. — س ره

  734. One might object: if each nature is an independent cause, two independent causes would converge on one effect; if the group of them is the cause, then the differences would not belong to the natures themselves. The author points to two ways of explaining the differences. On the first, because natures are ideas, their differences in reality follow from differences among existences, and the differences among existences belong to them in themselves. In that case, “substance is substance by itself” refers to existent substance, and “accident is accident by itself” to existent accident. On the second account, the differences among existences as known by the mind follow from differences among natures, and those differences belong to the natures themselves. Here, “substance is substance by itself” refers to the nature of substance, and “accident is accident by itself” to the nature of accident.   755. This question was first raised in logic, in discussions of universals and particulars. A universal may be univocal, applying in the same way to all its instances, or gradable, applying with differences of degree. Since universality is treated as a feature of essence, the discussion of gradation began with essences: philosophers had observed that things in the world differ in intensity and degree. Later, relying on Avicenna’s argument, they said that essential concepts do not vary by degree, only accidental ones. Their reasoning was that an accident has no real counterpart by itself: what exists is the subject and its accident. A derived term such as “black,” formed from blackness as it exists in a body, does not have a separate counterpart in reality, so it can vary. The difference between an accident and a derived accidental term is difficult to grasp, even though neither concept changes in meaning. On this basis, they said that two distinct essences differ either in their whole nature, in part of it, or through something outside it. The author broadens the account to include differences in existence or in thought, so it can also include degrees of existence. — ط

A fixed concept cannot support this. — ط

    ↩

  764. As the later discussions of knowledge, power, will, good, and purpose will show, there is another kind of difference between two things. It does not fit the rule for gradation given here, nor any of the three kinds of difference listed at the start of the chapter: difference in the whole essence, in part of it, or through something outside it. Knowledge and power, for example, differ, yet each is identified with existence itself. The same is true of other realities called “existential attributes.” Their difference is not a matter of one having more than the other: knowledge is not greater than power. Nor do they differ as two essences, since they are not separate kinds of essence. But the truth is that the broader idea of difference within one reality—where what distinguishes its instances is also what they share—covers more than the rule stated here. Not every difference within a thing’s own reality, without anything added to it, is a difference that can be expressed as “more” or “less.” The philosophers should have discussed this kind of gradation separately, as they did mental and external existence, possibility and necessity, and potentiality and actuality.

    The familiar kind of gradation, by degrees of excellence, requires two simple instances of one reality: the stronger includes all the perfection of the weaker and something more, while the weaker does not include all the stronger has. The weaker is intrinsically related to the stronger, though this is not a relation in the technical category of relation. The mind also sees the weaker as lacking the perfection found in the stronger, even though existence itself excludes nonexistence. This comparison is between two levels at a time. With three levels—weak, intermediate, and strong—there are two comparisons: weak to intermediate, and intermediate to strong. The intermediate is strong relative to the weak and weak relative to the strong. Treating all three as one comparison would require one relation to hold among more than two levels, and would make the middle level contain the shared reality with no increase or decrease. That would conflict with the assumed difference between what the levels share and what distinguishes them. So calling the levels “weak,” “intermediate,” and “strong” is not entirely precise. — ط

    ↩

  765. There are two cases to consider. One is a thing changing through stronger or weaker states as it moves from one kind to another—for example, from white to yellow, or from yellow to green. This is different from a weaker green becoming a stronger green. The other case is when stronger and weaker levels exist at the same time in separate things. This second case is clearer, because the levels differ both in how we understand them and in how they exist. — س ره

    ↩

  766. Some who follow Aristotle’s school allow existence to have stronger and weaker degrees, but do not allow existence itself to grow stronger or weaker through change. — س ره

    ↩

  767. This means that the levels are made individual by their own simple identities, while sharing one reality; what distinguishes them is also what they share. This can reconcile the two views. Those who say essential features can vary by degree mean “essential” as existence, the basis of a thing’s reality. Those who deny gradation in essence but allow it in what is accidental to essence mean “essence” as what a thing is, and treat existence as something added to it. — س ره

    ↩

  768. The objector is Sayyid Dāmād, in al-Taqdīsāt. — س ره

    ↩

  769. The same explanation would not work for imagined quantities that differ in length, since they have no matter whose readiness could account for the difference—unless one denies that the imaginal world exists. — س ره

    ↩

  770. Some call this mutual opposition. In fact, each intermediate shade is a simple quality and a thing in its own right. The opposition between them is the ordinary, familiar kind; it does not require the greatest possible difference. — س ره

    ↩

  771. Here “blackness” is used in more than one way. When Aristotle’s followers say that blackness is what varies, they mean each individual blackness. When they say that blackness is not what varies, they mean the shared, general nature of blackness. Their statements about the two blacknesses, the bodies that bear stronger or weaker blackness, and the idea of “black” all point to the same view: the feature that accounts for the difference is something other than the shared nature. This fits their claim that the adjective “black” applies to bodies by degrees, while blackness itself does not. — س ره

    ↩

  772. One objection is that a single motion is continuous and has one identity. If the thing it moves through is continuous too, its parts should match the whole in kind and name. How, then, could its stages be different species? The commentator replies that the quality undergoing change is not itself continuous or divisible; continuity belongs to the motion. The usual argument against Democritus concerns parts of continuous bodies, so it does not by itself prove that the levels of a quality are one species. Another reply is that a single motion must occur in one individual thing during that motion. This does not mean the mover stays the same throughout every process: a body can move through places under a series of pulls, and water can change in quality under successive fires. The point is that what one motion occurs in must be one individual thing for that motion, not a series of different species. — س ره

    ↩

  773. The difference in kind here is not between the levels of red themselves: they are all levels through which the motion passes. Red differs from black or white because it is where the process begins or ends. This is a difference in what the quality is, not in the one connected motion. — س ره

    ↩

  774. Some copies read “its arrival” here.

    ↩

  775. The original meaning of “strong” as the power to resist can apply to substances as well as to qualities: one thing can be more able to resist than another. This does not conflict with the technical point in the argument. It conflicts only with the wider meaning of “stronger” in everyday speech. — س ره

    ↩

  776. This refers to length itself, a kind of quantity, and to size, a feature of quantity. The author uses this to show that people do say one line is longer than another. He is not saying that measured quantity is strong in exactly the same sense as a quality; “longer” and “bigger” can simply mean “greater in amount.” — س ره

    ↩

  777. Some copies read “length is the line itself.” — ط

    ↩

  778. The distinction assumes what it is trying to prove. Strength and increase have the same basic meaning: strength that stops at a limit is increase with a limit, while increase without a limit is strength. So this does not separate them. — س ره

    ↩

  779. Both strength and increase can be divided again into forms that have a limit and forms that do not. This is a second division, made after the first division into stronger and weaker. — س ره

    ↩

  780. The examples are being compared in different ways. Five differs in kind from a smaller number such as four, and so differs in its existence as well. But one five differs in existence, not in kind, from another five. Adding five and four gives nine; adding two equal fives gives ten. With length, by contrast, a longer and a shorter measure share the same nature even though their individual extents differ. Another reading is possible: the “equal” part means the amount that matches after the extra part has been added. — س ره

    ↩

  781. That is, the shared broader kind exists in the world as a real thing; “and its existence” explains what is meant by this. — ن ره

    ↩

  782. This disproves the claim that anything that allows degrees of priority or strength must have an opposite. Existence has no opposite, yet it can be deficient, complete, or even beyond complete. — س ره

    ↩

  783. This also answers the claim that anything that admits priority or strength must undergo a process of growing stronger. Existence is a counterexample: its essence does not move or change in this way, as explained earlier. — س ره

    ↩

  784. For Aristotle’s followers, sensation is something that happens to the animal; for the author, it is an action. Movement is an action for both sides. In either case, these are features that happen to a thing; a substance is not made up of them. — س ره

    ↩

  785. Unless we rule out the possibility that effects vary because of different organs, tools, obstacles, or conditions, the objector will not agree that those effects come from the powers themselves. We must show that they do. If the tools include powers that themselves differ in completeness, then a stronger or weaker power in the substance is established. A horse’s power to perceive, for example, is more complete than a mosquito’s, especially if the soul itself has levels of development. If the difference came only from a missing condition or an obstacle, the difference between a horse’s soul and a mosquito’s would have to be permanent. That would mean the power is blocked forever, like saying that an ant can understand general ideas but never does so because a condition is always missing or an obstacle is always present. — س ره

    ↩

  786. The terms “what differs in” and “what makes the difference” are used here in the reverse way from the earlier discussion of degrees. There, the feature that causes the difference was called “what makes the difference,” and the thing that varies was “what differs in.” In discussions of priority, the feature that varies is called “what differs in.” The author is following that usage here. — س ره

    ↩

  787. The word bi-ḥayth (“such that”) appears to be a copyist’s error. The correct reading is bi-ḥasab mā (“according to what …”).

    ↩

  788. Aristotle’s followers can reply that differences in time belong to existence, not to time’s essence. This does not conflict with their claim that time itself is always passing, since “essence” here can mean either existence or the idea of time, which includes passing and is only a concept in the mind. They can also say that existences differ as separate realities, not by degrees, just as the most general kinds differ. But there is a problem: the author understands their claim about different existences as a difference attached to natures, because they are careful thinkers. If they instead mean that the existences themselves are entirely separate realities, then a single idea would have to be drawn from realities that share nothing. That would revive Ibn Kammunah’s objection and remove the shared ground between cause and effect, among other problems. — س ره

    ↩

  789. The note first states the general rule for things that overlap, then applies it to matter and form. Taken as broader kind and defining feature, they overlap as parts of one essence. Taken as matter and form, they differ, but their priority and posteriority belong to existence. — س ره

    ↩

الحكمة المتعالية في الأسفار العقلية الأربعة

الأمور العامة: الوجود والماهية

صدر الدين محمد الشيرازي

الجزء الأول — السفر الأول

المحتويات

  • مقدمه المؤلف

  • السفر الأول — وهو الذي من الخلق إلى الحق في النظر إلى طبيعة الوجود وعوارضه الذاتية وفيه مسالك

    • المسلك الأول — في المعارف التي يحتاج إليها الانسان في جميع العلوم وفيه مقدمه وستة مراحل

          • فصل — في أن واجب الوجود أنيته ماهيته

          • فصل — في أن واجب الوجود واحد لا بمعنى ان نوعه منحصر في شخصه على ما توهم

        • فصل — في الشدة والضعف

بسم الله الرحمن الرحيم

التاليمقدمه المؤلف

مقدمه المؤلف

الحمد لله فاعل كل محسوس ومعقول وغاية كل مطلوب ومسؤول والصلاة على صفوه عباده وهداه الخلق إلى مبدئه ومعاده سيما سيد المصطفين محمد المبعوث إلى كافه الثقلين اللهم فصل عليه وعلى الأرواح الطاهرة من أهل بيته وأولاده والأشباح1 الزاهرة من أوليائه وأحفاده. وبعد فيقول الفقير إلى رحمه ربه الغنى محمد المشتهر بصدر الدين الشيرازي ان السعادة ربما يظن بها انها الفوز بالدرجات الحسية والوصول إلى الرياسات الخيالية وما أبين لمن تحقق الأمور وتفطن بالمعارف ان السعادات العاجلية واللذات الحسية الفورية ليس شئ منها سعادة حقيقية ولا ينالها بهجة عقلية لما يرى كلا من متعاطيها منهمكا فيما انقطعت السكينات الإلهية عن حواليه وامتنعت المعارف الربوبية عن الحلول فيه وتعذر عليه اخلاص النية الإلهية الصادرة عن حاق الجوهر النطقي من غير معاوقة همه دنياوية أو مصادمة طلبه عاجلية التي يرجى بها نيل السعادة الحقيقية وتعاطيها والاتصال بالفيض العلوي الذي يزال به الكمه2 عن حدقه نفسه الموجود فيها بسبب انحصارها في عالم الغربة ووجودها في دار الجسد واحتباسها عن ملاحظة جمال الأبد ومعاينة الجلال السرمد

ولا شك ان أقصى غاية يتأتى لاحد الموجودات الوصول إليها هو الكمال المختص به والملائم المنسوب اليه وكلما انحط عنه فهو نقصان بالحقيقة فيه وإن كان كمالا بالإضافة إلى ما في رتبه الوجود تاليه وما من دابة فما دونها الا ومن شانها البلوغ إلى أقصى ما لها في ذاتها ما لم يعقها عائق ولنوع الانسان كمال خاص لجوهر ذاته وحاق حقيقته لا يفوقها فيه فائق ولا يسبق به عليها سابق وهو الاتصال بالمعقولات ومجاورة الباري والتجرد عن الماديات وان كانت له مشاركه بحسب كل قوه توجد فيه لما يساويه من تلك الجهة أو يليه فلسائر الأجسام في حصوله في الحيز والفضاء وللنبات في الاغتذاء والنماء وللعجم من الحيوان في حياته بأنفاسه وحركته بإرادته واحساسه وتلك الخاصية انما تحصل بالعلوم والمعارف مع انقطاع عن التعلق بالزخارف.

ثم لما كانت العلوم متشعبه وفنون الادراكات متكثرة والإحاطة بجملتها متعذرة أو متعسرة ولذلك تشعبت فيه الهمم كما تفننت في الصنائع قدم أهل العالم فافترقت العلماء زمرا وتقطعوا امرهم بينهم زبرا بين معقول ومنقول وفروع وأصول فهمه نحو نحو وصرف واحكام3 وهمه نحو فقه ورجال وكلام. فالواجب على العاقل ان يتوجه بشراشره إلى الاشتغال بالأهم والحزم له ان يكب طول عمره على ما الاختصاص لتكميل ذاته فيه أتم بعد ما حصل له من سائر العلوم والمعارف بقدر الحاجة إليها في المعاش والمعاد والخلاص عما يعوقه عن الوصول إلى منزل الرشاد ويوم الميعاد وذلك هو ما يختص من العلوم بتكميل احدى قوتيه اللتين هما جهة ذاته ووجهه إلى الحق وجهه اضافته ووجهه إلى الخلق وتلك هي النظرية التي بحسب حاق جوهر ذاته من دون شركه الإضافة إلى الجسم وانفعالاته وما من علم غير الحكمة الإلهية والمعارف الربانية الا والاحتياج اليه بمدخلية الجسم وقواه ومزاولة البدن وهواه وليس من العلوم ما يتكفل بتكميل جوهر الذات الانسية وإزالة مثالبها ومساويها حين انقطاعها عن الدنيا وما فيها والرجوع إلى حاق حقيقتها والاقبال بالكلية إلى باريها ومنشئها وموجدها ومعطيها الا العلوم العقلية المحضة وهي العلم بالله وصفاته وملائكته وكتبه ورسله
